title: The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: The Service You Imagine, and the Service Jesus Spoke Of
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion we are going to reflect together on a subject that looks utterly familiar and yet is one of the easiest to misunderstand — what is service?

First, let me ask you to be still for three seconds and answer one question in your heart: when you hear the word “service”, what is the first picture that comes to mind?

I suspect most of us would answer in much the same way. Some picture someone on the platform leading worship, playing the piano or preaching. Some picture Saturday afternoons wiping down chairs, sweeping the floor and washing cups. Some think of driving people to and fro, welcoming, keeping the accounts, running the AV desk, teaching Sunday school. And some think of “having a post, a role, a name printed on the serving roster”.

All of these are service, of course. But if service is only these things, we run into three very real problems.

The first problem is that “the scope is too narrow”. There are one hundred and sixty-eight hours in a week. Take away sleep and work, and serving at church may take up three to five of them. If only those few hours count as service, then ninety-seven per cent of our lives becomes a blank that has nothing to do with God. Our faith is cut in two: one half spiritual, the other half secular; one half for God, the other half for ourselves. And so we live divided lives.

The second problem is that “the bar is too high”. Older brothers and sisters say, “I can’t sing, I can’t preach, and my health isn’t good — I probably can’t serve any more.” New believers say, “I don’t know the Bible well yet; I’ll wait until I’m better equipped.” Busy parents say, “When the children are a bit older, when work settles down a bit.” And so service becomes the preserve of a small group of people “with gifts, with time and with a position”, while everyone else sits in the pews as long-term spectators.

The third problem is that “the motives get too mixed”. When someone has served for a long time, the greatest danger is not physical tiredness but an invisible line in the heart that slowly shifts. What was once done for the Lord comes to be done for people’s praise; what was once done gladly and willingly becomes “I have to”, “it’s my turn”, “no one else will do it, so I suppose I must”. The work still gets done, the smile is still on the face, but inside, everything has already dried up.

There is one picture I often come back to. A sister had been preparing the fellowship meals in the church kitchen for twenty years, faithful day after day. One year, at the thanksgiving testimony meeting, the chair invited her up to share, and the first thing she said was, “I don’t have anything to say. I just wash vegetables in the kitchen — I don’t serve.” In that moment the whole room went quiet. She thought service was what happens on the platform, and she had no idea that her hands, soaked in cold water for twenty years, had long been carrying the love of Christ to every table.

Brothers and sisters, the problem is not that we aren’t diligent enough. The problem is that our definition of service is far too small.

Jesus’ definition of service goes far beyond what we imagine. He shows us that service is not only about “what we do”; it is even more about “whom we do it for, and why we do it”. What we do determines the shape of the task; whom we do it for determines its worth; why we do it determines whether we can go the distance.

When we truly understand service, our lives are no longer cut into “spiritual” and “secular” halves; our whole life becomes service. Washing a bowl, revising a spreadsheet, sitting with a child over homework, saying one extra gentle word to a stranger — any of these can be true service.

Today we’ll look at service from three angles: the essence of service, the heart of service, and the scope of service. May God, through his word, renew our mindset about service. For on the 321 road we often say: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This morning’s devotion begins with the mindset.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Road Behind a Single Sentence
sections.html:
Our theme text is just one short verse, but it stands within a profoundly important setting.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally held to have been written by the apostle Matthew, and most evangelical scholars date it between AD 50 and 70. Its first readers were believers from a Jewish background. That is why Matthew lays special stress on Jesus as the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King who brings the kingdom of heaven.

The context of Matthew 20:28 is a turning point in the whole book. From chapter 16 onwards, Jesus three times foretells that he will suffer, be killed and be raised on the third day. In 20:17–19 he says it plainly for the third time: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and will hand him over to the Gentiles to mock, to scourge, and to crucify; and the third day he will be raised up.” (Matthew 20:18–19)

The Lord has already set the cross squarely before them. And yet what happens next is heartbreaking to read.

The mother of the sons of Zebedee comes straight up to ask for seats for her two sons, James and John: “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand, and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom.” (Matthew 20:21) When the other ten disciples hear it, they are indignant with the two brothers. The Lord is speaking about laying down his life; the disciples are squabbling over seats. The Lord’s eyes are fixed on the cross; the disciples’ eyes are glued to the league table.

So the Lord calls them over and speaks words that overturn the values of the human race: “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:25–28)

Brothers and sisters, notice the Lord’s short phrase: “It shall not be so.” The system of the nations is about climbing upwards, wielding power and keeping others under control; whoever holds the higher seat is the one who gets served. The Lord says: among you, it shall not be so. The system of the kingdom of heaven is turned upside down — not climbing up but going down; not getting people to serve me, but going out to serve them.

This is exactly the difference between the two systems that 321 speaks of. The Babylonian system is a self-centred system, whose core is grasping for power and expanding the self; God’s system is a selfless system, whose core is denying of self and letting Jesus be King. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When the disciples squabbled over seats, they were leaving their originally intended position; when the Lord walked towards the cross, he was returning to his.

Let’s look at two key words.

“Serve” in the original is the Greek διακονέω (diakoneō), whose most basic picture is “the one who waits at table” — the person who brings the dishes, pours the water and bends down. The later word “deacon” (διάκονος, diakonos) comes from it. In other words, the service the Lord speaks of is not sitting at the head of the table giving orders; it is tying on an apron, going to the table and giving yourself away.

“Ransom” in the original is λύτρον (lytron), a technical term of the marketplace in those days, meaning the price paid to buy back a slave or a prisoner of war. Once that sum was paid, the person was released from slavery. The Lord says his life is that ransom. He did not pay some token amount; he poured out his whole life to buy us back from slavery to sin.

So Matthew 20:28 is not an inspirational motto; it is a road marked with blood. The Lord walked this road first, then turned back to us and said: you should do likewise.

With that background in mind, we can enter today’s three key points.

sections.heading: 1. The Essence of Service: Living Out the Life of Jesus
sections.html:
“Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28)

1. His Life Was Service

Brothers and sisters, notice how the Lord describes his own life. He didn’t say, “The Son of Man came to build an organisation,” nor, “The Son of Man came to gather disciples and plant branch churches.” He said: the Son of Man came to serve, and to give his life.

That is a summary statement. From the manger to the cross, from the shores of Galilee to the night of Gethsemane, the Lord’s whole life can be summed up in one verb — serve.

When he broke bread for the five thousand, that was service. When he touched the leper, that was service. When he prayed for Jairus’ daughter, that was service. When he talked with Nicodemus in the middle of the night, that was service. When he waited by the well for a Samaritan woman, that was service. When, at the Last Supper, he took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet one by one, that was service. John’s Gospel records that after washing their feet he said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:14–15)

Paul distilled that whole life into a passage of rare beauty: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

“Emptied himself” in the original is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), meaning “to pour oneself out”. The Lord did not set aside his divinity; he set aside the glory, the rights and the honour that were his due, and took the form of a servant. 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. The Lord Jesus is the one who was utterly selfless and yet utterly displayed the glory of God.

So the essence of service is not a job; it is the overflow of a life. A job can be outsourced; you can take leave from it or resign from it. A life cannot. An apple tree doesn’t have to strive to “carry out a fruit-bearing ministry”; it only has to be an apple tree, and in season it bears apples. The Lord put it even more directly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

2. First Be with the Lord, Then Be Sent Out

“He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” (Mark 3:14)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the Lord’s blueprint for raising disciples, and the order is vitally important.

The Lord appointed twelve, and the first purpose was “that they might be with him”; only the second was “that he might send them out to preach”. The structure of the original is clear: being with him comes first, being sent comes after. The disciples were not sent out because they had been trained; they were sent out because they had been with the Lord and their lives had been changed.

Sadly, we often reverse the order. When we recruit helpers, we ask first: can you do it? Do you have time? Are you willing? We rarely ask first: how is your relationship with the Lord? Have you met with him this morning? The result is that the ministry grows bigger and bigger while life grows thinner and thinner; the meetings get more and more crowded and prayer gets less and less.

The story of Martha and Mary is a mirror. Martha was busy with much serving and troubled in heart; Mary sat at the Lord’s feet listening to his word. The Lord said, “But one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:42) The Lord was not dismissing serving; what he was dismissing was serving that had lost its order.

Psychology confirms this truth from another angle. The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, the longest-running study of its kind. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has summed it up many times: the strongest predictor of whether a person is healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, nor fame, nor achievement, but the quality of their relationships. A lifetime’s sense of fulfilment comes from relationships, not from performance.

If that is true of our relationships with one another, how much more of our relationship with God. And that is exactly the order of 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

3. A 321 Insight: Life, Relationships, Ministry

Without life there is no true service; without a relationship with the Lord there is no power to serve.

We can picture it as a tree. Life is the root, relationships are the trunk, ministry is the fruit. When the roots go deep, the trunk grows strong; when the trunk grows strong, the fruit comes in abundance. Turn it the other way round — demand the fruit first, patch up the trunk next, and only think about the roots at the very end — and that tree will wither in the first dry summer.

Suzanne Simard, a forest ecologist at the University of British Columbia in Canada, published research with her colleagues in the journal Nature in 1997 showing that the trees of a forest are linked to one another through underground mycorrhizal networks, through which they can pass carbon and nutrients to each other. When we look up, we see one separate tree after another; underground, there is a single living system in which each supplies the others.

Brothers and sisters, the church is the same. On the platform we see one area of service after another, but what really supplies it all is the unseen part underground — each person’s time with the Lord in the early morning, every prayer nobody knows about, every tear nobody sees.

So today, don’t start by asking: what can I do to serve? Ask first: have I been with the Lord today? When we receive the life of Jesus, stop putting ourselves at the centre, and begin to live for God and for others — that is where service begins.

sections.heading: 2. The Heart of Service: Done for the Lord, Not for Ourselves
sections.html:
“Whoever receives one such little child in my name, receives me, and whoever receives me, doesn’t receive me, but him who sent me.” (Mark 9:37)

1. What Matters Is Not the Size of the Task but Whom It Is For

The scene in Mark 9 is strikingly like Matthew 20. The Lord foretells for the second time that he will be delivered into human hands, be killed and rise on the third day; yet on the road the disciples argue among themselves about who is the greatest. The Lord sits down, calls the twelve and says, “If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all.” (Mark 9:35) Then he does something you can almost see — he takes a little child, sets him among the disciples, takes him in his arms and says to them the verse we are looking at today.

In the first-century Mediterranean world, a small child had no social standing, no productive value and no voice — “someone not worth your time”. And it was just such a child that the Lord took in his arms, saying: whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.

“Receive” in the original is δέχομαι (dechomai), meaning “to welcome, take in, show hospitality” — it carries the warmth of inviting someone into your home and setting food before them. The Lord did not mean “pat them on the head and say hello”; he meant genuinely taking an insignificant person to heart.

Notice the crucial qualifying phrase — “in my name”. Those three words are the centre of gravity of the whole saying.

A seemingly tiny act — welcoming a child, giving someone a cup of cold water, caring for a person — if it is done in the Lord’s name, is service to the Lord. The Lord himself said, “Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.” (Matthew 10:42) Under the Middle Eastern sun a cup of cold water might be worth only a few pennies, but as long as it is given “in the name of a disciple”, heaven records it.

So service has never been measured by the size of the task but by the direction of the motive. First Samuel tells us, “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7b) And Zechariah asks a question that shakes us to the core: “Who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10a)

2. Done to the Least, It Is Done to the Lord

“Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40b)

This verse comes from the Lord’s parable of the final judgement. He tells how on that day all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. The reason for his commendation is surprising. It isn’t “You built such a large church”, but: I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you looked after me; I was in prison, and you came to me.

The righteous themselves are taken aback. They say: Lord, when did we see you like this? And the Lord’s answer is this very verse.

Brothers and sisters, this turns our mindset completely upside down. The Lord, it turns out, hides himself in the least of people. That elderly brother in the hospital bed whose speech is slurred, that child in the corner of the church whom nobody notices, that sister who arrives late and leaves early every time — the Lord says that what you do to them, you do to him.

So: service is not only the pulpit; service is daily living. Service is not a time slot; service is a way of seeing.

The Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, in I and Thou (Ich und Du), published in 1923, drew a famous distinction: a person may relate to another as “I–It”, treating the other as an object to be used, or as “I–Thou”, meeting the other as a whole person. This philosophical insight has a far deeper root in the Lord’s words — because in each of the least of these, we meet not only a “Thou”; we meet the Lord himself.

The sixteenth-century Reformer Martin Luther argued in his 1520 To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation that all believers are priests: the shoemaker, the smith and the farmer are each, in their own calling, equally consecrated priests. Later he went further and said that a mother washing her baby’s nappies, if she does it in faith, is more pleasing in God’s sight than a monk’s austerities. That is exactly what the Lord teaches in Mark 9 and Matthew 25: no task is great or small; the only question is whom it is for.

3. Whom You Do It For Decides How Far You Can Go

Here is a very practical question: why does “whom we do it for” matter so much?

Psychology offers good supporting evidence. In 1973, Mark Lepper and David Greene of Stanford University, together with Richard Nisbett of the University of Michigan, carried out a famous experiment. They took a group of nursery-school children who already loved drawing and divided them into three groups. The first group was told in advance, “When you finish, you’ll get a certificate.” The second group was told nothing but unexpectedly received a certificate after drawing. The third group got no certificate. Two weeks later the researchers quietly observed them during free play. The result was startling: the children who had “drawn for the certificate” afterwards spent noticeably less time drawing of their own accord. Psychologists call this the “overjustification effect”.

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, through the Self-Determination Theory (1985) they developed at the University of Rochester, explain it further: when the motive for doing something shifts from within to without — from “I love this” to “for a reward, for people’s approval” — inner motivation is eroded.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that the story of so many who serve? At first they did it because they loved the Lord; somewhere along the way it became about applause, about not being talked about, about keeping up an image. When the motive changes, joy leaves; when joy leaves, all that remains is grim endurance.

The Lord warned us long ago: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1)

And Paul gives the positive answer: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.” (Colossians 3:23–24)

4. A 321 Insight: For Jesus, for Others, Not for Yourself

This is the selfless life that 321 speaks of: for Jesus (J), for Others (O), and not for Yourself (Y) — JOY.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. When people put themselves at the centre, service becomes an extension of the self — my team, my results, my reputation. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When the disciples argued over who was greatest, ten were indignant with two and two were on guard against ten — a miniature of how both sides lose.

Paul’s testimony is the best commentary: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When we stop living for ourselves, we begin truly to enter into service.

Here, too, we can step into 321’s “920 practice”: everyone we are connected with is our “2”; as we live out the selfless “0” before them, the Holy Spirit bears his fruit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a) The “little child” you are to receive today may well be your own child, your colleague, or that neighbour beside you who isn’t easy to get along with.

sections.heading: 3. The Scope of Service: All of Life Is Service
sections.html:
“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

1. There Is No Corner God Does Not Govern

Brothers and sisters, look at how wide Paul draws the circle: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do.

What is eating and drinking? It is the most everyday, least “spiritual” thing there is, the thing nobody would ever put in a ministry report. And that is precisely where Paul starts. In 1 Corinthians 8–10 Paul is dealing with the dispute over “whether food sacrificed to idols may be eaten”. The standard he finally gives is not a rule but a direction: do all to the glory of God.

“Glory” in the original is the noun δόξα (doxa); the Hebrew word behind it in the Old Testament, kabod, literally means “weight”, and so carries the sense of “showing something’s weight, showing its true worth”. To do all to the glory of God is to let God be shown great, shown true and shown beautiful in that very thing.

So service is no longer a rota; it is a set of coordinates. The same task can be done for ourselves or for God; it can be an ordinary chore or a holy work. The difference lies not in the task itself but in whom it faces.

Hebrew gives us the same light. In the Old Testament, “to serve” and “to work” come from the same root, עָבַד (avad). Genesis says, “Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.” (Genesis 2:15) “Cultivate” here is avad. When Moses said to Pharaoh, “Let my people go, that they may serve me” (Exodus 8:1b), the word is avad as well. In God’s original intention, tilling the ground and worship were never two separate things — work was service, and service was found in work. It was humanity’s fall that tore daily living and worship in two; Christ’s redemption is meant to stitch them back together.

So: at home, loving your family, bearing with them and giving of yourself is service; at work, working conscientiously with honesty and integrity is service; at school, studying hard and influencing your classmates is service.

Whatever is done in the Lord’s name, for the good of others and for the glory of God, is service.

A saying commonly attributed to Mother Teresa puts it beautifully: not all of us can do great things, but we can do small things with great love. What God measures has never been the size of the deed but the depth of the love.

2. From Action to Life Touching Life

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

The Lord’s last charge before his ascension was not “You must go and try hard” but “You will receive power”.

“Witness” in the original is μάρτυς (martys), the word that later gave English “martyr”. Bearing witness isn’t reciting a prepared script; it is standing there with your whole life and saying: the One I have met is real.

Notice the map the Lord gives: Jerusalem, all Judea, Samaria, to the uttermost parts of the earth. These are concentric circles — starting from the nearest place and moving outwards ring by ring: from the individual, to the family, to the church, to the world. No one can skip Jerusalem and go straight to the ends of the earth; and no one can stay in Jerusalem and never see the ends of the earth.

True service is not just action; it is life touching life.

I mentioned earlier Simard’s forest research in Nature. That underground mycorrhizal network is the best picture of “life touching life”: a great tree can send carbon to the little saplings in its shade and carry them through their hardest years. What you see is a forest; what is actually at work is a system in which each supplies the others.

321 says: establish God’s system. A system is not an organisational chart; a system is a network of lives. A selfless person becomes another person’s spiritual companion (2); two companions give rise to spiritual parents and spiritual children (3); the spiritual family grows into a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades (5). This is the 235 relationship.

3. A 321 Insight: Selflessness, Being Filled with the Spirit, the Road to Revival

Only with selflessness can the Holy Spirit fill us; only when we are filled with the Spirit can life touch life. This is the road to revival.

Why is selflessness the key? Because if a vessel is full of “self”, there is no room for anything else. Zechariah says, “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6b)

The Path of Serving is revealed here too: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). First let the Holy Spirit guide, then let the Bible shine its light, then live out the likeness of Jesus — only then can we speak of serving, and in the end all the glory goes to him.

Peter sets out the whole principle with great completeness: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms. If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” (1 Peter 4:10–11a)

Look at that phrase, “as of the strength which God supplies”. Not by our own strength, but by the strength God supplies. And the purpose? “That in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” This is precisely the Two Core Values of 321 — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Putting Service Back in Its Proper Coordinates
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we have seen today and set it in order within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations answer the question, “Whose pattern do I serve by?” Jesus is my role model — he came not to be served but to serve, and we follow his likeness down that downward road. The Bible is my standard — the direction, boundaries and motives of our service are decided not by our feelings but by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the power to serve is not natural enthusiasm but the Holy Spirit of whom it is said, “you will receive power”.

The Two Core Values answer the question, “Where does my service end up?” Let Jesus be King: on my schedule, in my home, at my desk, he is King. Let Jesus receive all the glory: not giving him a share of the glory, but giving all the glory to him.

The Goal answers the question, “Where is service meant to take us?” Establish God’s system — not building a more efficient organisation, but establishing a spiritual family of selfless people who are joined to one another, life touching life.

From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The disciples squabbling over seats — that is the self-centred life; the Lord walking to the cross — that is selflessness. When self-centred people serve, the more they serve the wearier they become, because they are carrying the heaviest load of all, the “I”. When selfless people serve, the more they serve the sweeter it grows, because they have given themselves away and are instead filled by God.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When, in our serving, we are willing to say, “I don’t need to be seen in this,” Satan loses his foothold in that very place.

The Fivefold Change

Change has an order: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

This morning’s devotion is precisely the first step — a change of mindset. When we no longer think of service as a few hours at church but see that the whole of life is service, our life begins to change; when life changes, every detail of daily living is renewed; when daily living is renewed, relationships are healed; and when relationships are healed, ministry can at last be healthy.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. So many of the wounds of service come from putting that last item first.

A Shift of Perspective

The greatest renewal in service is a renewal of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

From man’s perspective, twenty years of washing up in the kitchen is “not serving”; from God’s perspective, it is twenty years of a fragrant offering. From an earthly perspective, a cup of cold water is worth a few pennies; from heaven’s perspective, “he will in no way lose his reward” (Matthew 10:42b). From a temporary perspective, being overlooked is a loss; from an eternal perspective, “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58b).

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are connected with is our “2”. Everyone you will see today — family, colleagues, shop assistants, neighbours — is someone God has arranged for you to serve. As you live the “0” (selfless) life before them, the Holy Spirit bears in you the “9”-fold fruit.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with a selfless person, supporting each other and praying for each other; in spiritual nurture, build the “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally grow into the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Service is not one person’s heroics; service is a family walking together.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart, rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down with worry. For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices, and we’ll take them deeper using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Practise the Mindset of “Doing Everything for the Lord”

Every day, before you do anything, ask yourself two questions: whom am I doing this for? Can I do it for the Lord?

Turn daily living into service, so that everything becomes an act that glorifies God.

Information: first commit today’s verse to memory — “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you see that your desk, your kitchen and your classroom are the altar God has given you.

Conviction: say to God in your heart, “Lord, I believe this is true: my whole life can be service.”

Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, at the beginning of each task, be still for three seconds and say, “Lord, this one I do for you.” Say it before you drive, before a meeting, before you cook, before you reply to a message.

Evaluation: before bed, look back: how many things today did I truly do for the Lord? Which one did I do to be seen?

Correction: take the thing you did for yourself and do it again tomorrow with a heart set on the Lord.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row, until the action becomes a habit and the habit becomes your nature.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister, teach them this practice, and remind each other.

Practice 2: Practise Serving, Starting with Small Things

Don’t wait for “the big opportunity”; start in the smallest places: a word of care, a helping hand, a smile.

Be faithful in small things, and God will enlarge your influence. The Lord himself said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10) And again: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Matthew 25:21b)

Paul says, “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2) God isn’t looking for capable people; God is looking for faithful people.

Information: copy Luke 16:10 onto your phone’s lock screen.

Revelation: ask God to point out the small thing around you that “you’ve always felt wasn’t worth doing”.

Conviction: admit that in God’s eyes there are no small things — only small faith.

Implementation: do three small things today — send a message of greeting, carry something for someone, and sincerely thank someone who serves you.

Evaluation: which of those three small things brought you real joy inside?

Correction: if you did it grudgingly, first go back to the Lord to draw on his love, then go and do it.

Repetition: three a day, twenty-one a week, ninety a month.

Multiplication: share your list of small things in your small group and invite others to join you.

Psychology backs this path too. Elizabeth Dunn and Lara Aknin of the University of British Columbia in Canada, together with Michael Norton of Harvard University, published research in the journal Science in 2008 showing that people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent the same amount on themselves — and that the amount mattered far less than the direction itself, “for others”. The outward direction of giving brings joy in itself. This fits the Lord’s words perfectly.

Practice 3: Practise a Selfless Life of Service

As you serve, keep examining yourself: am I doing this for myself or for the Lord? Am I trying to perform, or seeking to glorify God?

Learn to lay yourself down and let Jesus live in you and reign as King in you.

Information: get to know Galatians 2:20 well — read it three times a day.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on the self-centred life in your service — is it a desire to be affirmed? A fear of being replaced? A need to prove yourself?

Conviction: accept the fact: I have been crucified with Christ.

Implementation: this week, deliberately do one act of service that “nobody knows about”, and when it’s done, tell no one.

Evaluation: when no one praises you, are you at peace inside, or disappointed? The place of disappointment is the place where “self” is still alive.

Correction: put that place into the Lord’s hands and pray, “Lord, I give up this seat to you.”

Repetition: every time you are overlooked, misunderstood or replaced, that is another chance to practise.

Multiplication: when you are truly free, your freedom will become a way out for others.

A Gentle Reminder: Why Serving Wears Us Out

Brothers and sisters, many people grow weary after serving for a long time. Often the reason is not that there is too much to do, but that we are serving by ourselves and serving for ourselves.

Serving by ourselves is a problem of power; serving for ourselves is a problem of motive. Put the two together and you get burnout.

In her research at the University of California, Berkeley, the psychologist Christina Maslach defined occupational burnout in three dimensions: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (cold detachment from people), and a diminished sense of personal accomplishment. Her scale (the Maslach Burnout Inventory, 1981) remains the most widely used tool in the field. Notice the second dimension — when someone is exhausted to a certain point, people stop being people and become nothing more than items to be processed. That is the most dangerous warning sign in service.

But true service flows out of life and walks by the Holy Spirit.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is weariness.

The Lord’s invitation still stands: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

And the prophet promises us: “But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31)

A saying commonly attributed to Hudson Taylor goes: God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply. If we do God’s work in our own way, we will surely lack supply, and we will surely grow weary.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: what is service?

Today God’s word has given us the answer: service is not how much you do, but whom you do it for.

When you live for the Lord, everything you do becomes service. When you live out Christ, your life is full of influence.

This is true service.

So this morning I want to issue three calls to you.

First, hand the throne back to the Lord. Ask the Lord to forgive us for treating service as a stage for self-fulfilment and the church as a place to build up a reputation. Today, let Jesus truly reign as King in your life.

Second, open up the scope. From today on, stop saying, “I don’t serve.” Your family, your workplace, your school, your sickbed, your frying pan and your keyboard — all of them are altars. “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (Romans 12:1)

Third, give the glory to him. Don’t seek to be seen by people; seek only his pleasure. The Lord says, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) The light shines out, and the glory returns to the Father — that is the complete circle of service.

It is commonly said that in 1732, when two young men of the Moravian Brethren set out as missionaries to the West Indies, they called out from the quayside to the friends and family seeing them off: “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.” Brothers and sisters, this is the ultimate goal of service — not what we gain, but that the Lamb who was slain receives what he is worthy of.

Let us look up together: “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Hebrews 12:2)

May our whole lives become one act of service offered to him.

keyVerses: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I declare: my life is lived to serve you.
I no longer live for myself; I will live for you and for others.
Whatever I do, I will do it in your name.
Help me to live a selfless life, and let my whole life become service that glorifies you.
practices: Practise the mindset of “doing everything for the Lord”
Practise serving, starting with small things
Practise a selfless life of service
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You came into the world not to be served but to serve, and to give your life as a ransom for many. Lord, you loved us first; you served us first.
Forgive us, for we so often see service as a job, grace as a duty, and your house as a stage to perform on. Forgive our comparing, our competing and our weariness in service.
Lord, renew our mindset: help us see that the essence of service is living out your life, the heart of service is doing it for you, and the scope of service is the whole of life.
Help us first to be with you, and then to be sent by you; first to have life, then relationships, and only then ministry.
Fill us with the Holy Spirit, so that we no longer serve by ourselves or for ourselves; make us faithful in the smallest things and joyful in places no one sees.
Lord, I lay my family, my work, my time and my body on your altar. Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord lift up his face towards you and give you peace.
discussion: Mark 3:14 says, “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” Please share: in your life at the moment, which is there more of — “being with the Lord” or “doing things for the Lord”? If you were to put them back in order, what specific thing would you start with?

Matthew 25:40 says, “Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” Think about it: which “least of these” has God placed beside you? What small thing will you do for them this week, purely for the Lord’s name?
l157.title: What Is Service?
l157.subtitle: A Life Lived Wholly for the Lord
l157.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: A Sigh from the Depths of the Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me start by describing a scene that is very common in churches.

There was a sister who had served in her church for twelve years. She had led children’s Sunday school, she had been in charge of welcoming, and later she took on pastoral care in her small group. Every week she was always the first to arrive and the last to leave. One day after the meeting had ended, she sat in the empty sanctuary and said to her pastor, “Pastor, it isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just… so tired.”

She paused, and the tears began to fall. Then she said, “I often feel as if everything gets pushed onto me. When people have a need, I go and do it; when the church has a gap, I go and fill it. But somewhere along the way, I lost track of what I’m even doing.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever heard a sigh like that? Or has a sigh like that ever risen from the depths of your own heart?

If so, please don’t blame yourself, and don’t assume it means you aren’t spiritual. That kind of weariness is actually pointing to something very important — our mindset about service needs to be renewed by God.

Many of us began serving for two reasons.

The first reason: other people have needs. Someone is ill, someone is weak, someone has fallen; I see it, so I go and help.

The second reason: the church has needs. Sunday school is short of teachers, the worship team is short of members, the fellowship meal is short of helpers; the pastor makes an appeal from the platform, my heart softens, and up goes my hand.

Neither of these reasons is bad; you could even say they are good. God often calls us through other people’s needs. But brothers and sisters, please hear this clearly: if the drive behind our service stops “only” at the needs outside us, then sooner or later that drive will run out.

Why? Because the needs out there are endless, and our strength is limited. You fill this gap, and a hole opens over there; you help one person up, turn round, and three more have fallen. If it is “need” that drives us, we will be crushed by need. In the end, service becomes a burden, the burden becomes complaint, complaint becomes withdrawal, withdrawal becomes hurt, and hurt leads people to leave.

This cycle repeats itself over and over in churches. Not because those people don’t love the Lord, but because the drive did not come from within.

Today God wants to show us a crucial truth, one that will turn our mindset about service completely upside down.

The first statement: service is not only about other people’s needs.

The second statement: service is a need of our own life.

Please meditate on those two statements once more. Do other people need my service? Yes. But at a deeper level — do I need to serve? I need it very much.

It’s like exercise. When you go to the gym and lift weights, do the weight plates need you? No, they don’t. It is you who need to lift them. As you lift, you sweat, you ache, you gasp for breath — but a few months later, what has changed is not the dumbbell. It is your muscles, your heart and lungs, your whole physique.

Service is the same. When we go out to serve someone, the person most deeply changed is often not them, but ourselves.

That is why the vision of Kingdom 321 says: the fivefold change begins with mindset — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This morning we ask God first to change our mindset about service. For once the mindset changes, our service will move from “reluctance” to “joy”, from “just getting by” to “delight”, from “being drained” to “being built up”.

Brothers and sisters, may God speak to us this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Sent from Prison
sections.html:
Our theme text today comes from Ephesians 2:10. To truly understand this verse, we first need to get to know the letter it belongs to.

First, who was the author?

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. The letter opens with these words: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus:” (Ephesians 1:1)

Second, when was it written, and in what circumstances?

When Paul wrote this letter, he was in prison. He says so himself: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,” (Ephesians 4:1) It is generally held that this was during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome, around AD 60–62. Philippians, Colossians and Philemon come from the same period, and together they are called the “Prison Epistles”.

Notice the contrast: a man with chains on his wrists, his movements restricted, wrote the loftiest, broadest and most glorious teaching on the church in the whole Bible. Paul couldn’t go out to serve, so he served with his pen; he couldn’t go and stand before people, so he knelt before God and prayed for them. That in itself is a fine sermon — the heart of service lies not in how big a stage our circumstances give us, but in whether we have within us a heart that lives for the Lord.

Third, to whom was it written?

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, a thriving harbour and a great commercial city. It was home to the temple of Artemis, famous throughout the ancient world and counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Acts records that Paul lived in Ephesus for about three years (Acts 20:31), and also tells how Demetrius the silversmith, because Paul’s preaching had hurt the trade in idols, stirred up a great riot throughout the city (Acts 19:23–41).

In other words, the believers in Ephesus had been rescued out of a system that worshipped idols, money, lust and power. They had once lived in a city that asked only, “What can I get?” Paul wants to tell them: you have not only been saved “out of” something; you have been saved “into” something — into God’s eternal plan.

Fourth, the context.

Ephesians 2:10 is not an isolated verse. It is a summit, with nine whole verses of build-up before it.

Paul begins with our original condition: “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins,” (Ephesians 2:1) “Dead” means utterly powerless. The dead cannot save themselves, the dead cannot do good, the dead cannot even stretch out a hand to cry for help.

Then Paul speaks of what God has done: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved.” (Ephesians 2:4–5)

Next Paul nails down the foundation of salvation: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)

See it clearly: salvation is absolutely not by works, not by service, not by merit. Anyone who tries to earn salvation through service has turned the gospel upside down.

Then Paul writes verse 10: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.”

In the Greek, the second word of this verse is the connective γάρ (“for”), which carries the thought straight on: “For we are…” Paul’s meaning is this: precisely because salvation is entirely grace, our good works and our service are not in any way meant to earn something; they are the fruit that grace inevitably bears.

Brothers and sisters, fix this order firmly in your mind:

We are not “saved because we serve”; we “serve because we are saved”.

The first order is religion; only the second is the gospel.

And today’s lesson takes us a step further: this “serving because we are saved” is not a burden God lays on us; it is a need God has placed within us.

Key Point 1: Service Is the Purpose of Our Salvation

sections.heading: 1. We Are God’s “Masterpiece”
sections.html:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

This verse is only a few words long, yet it makes clear the place of a Christian’s whole life. Let’s go through it phrase by phrase.

“For we are his workmanship.” The word “workmanship” in Greek is ποίημα (poiēma). It appears only twice in the New Testament; the other occurrence is Romans 1:20, where it refers to the things God has made. The word does not mean “an odd item”; it means “a work” — a finished piece the craftsman has made with his own hands and takes delight in. The English word “poem” comes from it.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? In God’s eyes you are not a part on an assembly line; you are a poem he has written in his own hand.

“Created in Christ Jesus.” “Created” in Greek is κτίζω (ktizō), a word the Septuagint and the New Testament use specifically for God’s work of creation. By using this word, Paul is saying that when a person is born again and saved, it carries the same weight as a fresh act of creation. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

“For good works.” The “for” here introduces a purpose clause. God re-created us with a purpose. And what is the purpose? “Good works.” And these “good works” are not worldly moral charity, but “which God prepared”.

“Which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” “Prepared before” in Greek is προετοιμάζω (proetoimazō); the prefix προ means “beforehand”. It means that God had already arranged these good works in advance, before we were even born.

Brothers and sisters, think how wonderful this is.

God has not only prepared salvation for us to receive; God has also prepared work for us to complete.

sections.heading: 2. Your Life Is a Picture God Sketched Long Ago
sections.html:
Before a painter lifts the brush, the composition is already in his mind. He knows a tree goes here, and a shaft of light must be left there. We see one brushstroke of paint after another; he sees the finished painting as a whole.

So it is with God and our lives.

“Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” (Psalm 139:16)

So, before you were even born, God had already prepared:

which good works you would do;

which people you would influence;

and what kind of testimony you would live out.

All of this is contained in the one word “service”.

Brothers and sisters, this is why we say — service is the purpose of our salvation.

We are not saved merely so that we can go to heaven one day. If God only wanted us in heaven, he could have taken us home the moment we made our decision for Christ. Why leave us for decades in a world so full of tears?

He leaves us here because he still has work for us to do. He leaves us here because there are people who will come to know Jesus only through you.

We are saved to live out God’s will. And God’s will, worked out concretely on earth, is service.

sections.heading: 3. The Parable of the Talents: What the Non-Serving Lose
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. A master about to travel to another country entrusted his property to his servants, each according to his ability: to one five thousand, to one two thousand, to one a thousand. The ones who received five thousand and two thousand went and traded and doubled what they had been given. When the master returned he commended them: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Matthew 25:21)

But the one who received a thousand buried the money in the ground. His reason even sounded devout: he said he was afraid; he said his master was a hard man. Yet the master answered, “You wicked and slothful servant…” (Matthew 25:26), and finally said:

“Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” (Matthew 25:30)

Brothers and sisters, notice: that servant didn’t steal the money, didn’t squander it, didn’t do anything wicked. What was his sin? His sin was — doing nothing at all.

This parable reminds us of two things.

First, not serving is not just a loss to ourselves. What is lost is the people who could have been blessed through you.

Second, not serving means losing the meaning of life. The master calls him an “unprofitable servant”. “Unprofitable” in Greek is ἀχρεῖος (achreios), meaning “useless, of no use”. A life that doesn’t serve is a life left in a corner, never put to use.

A fine violin locked away for ever in its case — is it still a fine violin? In terms of its materials, yes; but in terms of its purpose, it has lost what it means to be a violin.

sections.heading: 4. The Deep Human Longing for “Meaning”
sections.html:
On this point, psychology bears witness alongside Scripture.

The Jewish psychiatrist Viktor Frankl (1905–1997) was imprisoned in the Nazi concentration camps. In Man’s Search for Meaning, published in 1946, he observed that in extreme suffering, what best sustained a person’s will to live was not physical strength, nor luck, but a “sense of meaning” — a task still unfinished, someone still waiting for them. From this Frankl developed “logotherapy”, which holds that humanity’s most fundamental drive is the search for meaning in life.

Martin Seligman, the founder of positive psychology, served as president of the American Psychological Association (APA) in 1998. In Flourish, published in 2011, he set out five elements of well-being, known as PERMA. The M stands for Meaning, which he defined as “belonging to and serving something bigger than the self”.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Even psychology has reached this conclusion: unless a person serves something greater than themselves, they cannot find meaning.

And more than sixteen hundred years ago, the Church Father Augustine (354–430), at the very start of Book One of his Confessions, wrote the prayer that has echoed down the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

Frankl tells us that people need meaning; Seligman tells us that meaning comes from serving something greater than ourselves; Augustine tells us who that “something greater” is — God himself.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight
sections.html:
The vision of Kingdom 321 gives us two statements here:

We were created for God.

We were saved to serve.

When a person does not live a life of service, their life slowly collapses inwards. Their attention shifts from “Whom can I give to?” to “Who can give to me?”; from “Whom did I serve today?” to “Did anyone notice me today?” That is how being self-centred begins. And once life is centred on the self, it loses its direction and loses its worth.

321 says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This first key point is meant precisely to change our mindset — service is not an “add-on” to my life; service is my life’s “factory setting”.

Do you remember the Three Foundations? Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When we accept that service is the purpose of our salvation, we are letting the Bible be our standard rather than letting our own feelings be the standard. Feelings say, “I don’t feel like serving today,” but the Bible says, “For we are his workmanship… for good works.”

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please take this to heart: my being alive is no accident; my salvation is not the finishing line. Before I was born, God had already prepared a path of service for me.

Key Point 2: Service Is the Way We Train to Reign with the Lord

sections.heading: 1. Two Completely Opposite Value Systems
sections.html:
“Whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Mark 10:43)

In what setting were these words spoken? We have to look at the context.

James and John, the two sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus and said, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand, and one at your left hand, in your glory.” (Mark 10:37) When the other ten disciples heard it, they were indignant with them. So Jesus called the disciples together and said:

“You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.” (Mark 10:42–44)

Brothers and sisters, two completely opposite systems are set out here.

In the world’s system, the great are the ones who are served; the high are the ones who hold power. One person stands at the tip of the pyramid, and everyone beneath lives for him.

In God’s kingdom, the great are the ones who serve others; the high are the humble. The pyramid is turned upside down, and the One at the top holds everyone else up.

“Servant” in Greek is διάκονος (diakonos), originally “the one who carries dishes to the table at a meal”, later the title for a “deacon” in the church. “Bondservant” in Greek is δοῦλος (doulos), a heavier word still — a “slave”, someone with no sovereignty of their own.

The Lord Jesus doesn’t say, “You must not seek to be great.” He says, “You must be great in a completely different way.” God’s kingdom doesn’t forbid us to aspire upwards; it simply turns the ladder round a hundred and eighty degrees — in God’s kingdom, the way down is the way up.

sections.heading: 2. Jesus Himself Is That Role Model
sections.html:
“But I am among you as one who serves.” (Luke 22:27)

The setting of these words is even more astonishing. This is the Last Supper; the Lord Jesus is about to be betrayed and crucified. And on that very night, Scripture records: “A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.” (Luke 22:24)

Brothers and sisters, can you imagine it? The Lord is preparing to go to the cross, and the disciples are arguing about whose seat is the grandest.

The Lord doesn’t lose his temper. He says, “For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.” (Luke 22:27)

On the same night, John’s Gospel records that eternal picture: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:3–5)

Pay special attention to the word “knowing”. He knew that the Father had given all things into his hands — and then he went and washed feet.

In other words, he didn’t wash feet out of a sense of inferiority; it was because he had absolute authority and absolute security that he could stoop down and wash feet.

The less sure people are of their identity, the more they need others to serve them to prove their worth; the more secure people are in their identity, the more freely they can serve others.

He had all authority, yet he chose to become a servant. That turns our values completely upside down.

The Reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546), in his 1520 The Freedom of a Christian, summed up the Christian life in two seemingly contradictory sentences: “A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.”

Because we are perfectly free in Christ, we can gladly become the servant of all. That is the logic of the gospel.

sections.heading: 3. Serve First, Then Reign
sections.html:
“That you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Luke 22:30)

Notice the verse just before it: “I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me,” (Luke 22:29)

Having rebuked the disciples for arguing over who was greatest, the Lord then turns round and promises that they will sit on thrones. This is no contradiction; it reveals a profound spiritual law:

Serve first, and then you can reign.

Be humble first, and then you can receive glory.

Paul says too, “If we endure, we will also reign with him.” (2 Timothy 2:12) And Revelation says of God’s people that he “made us kings and priests to our God, and we will reign on the earth.” (Revelation 5:10)

Brothers and sisters, what does this mean? It means that every little act of service we do today is not wasted.

That stack of dishes you wash in the kitchen today is preparing your future crown.

That tear you shed today for a struggling brother is preparing your future place.

That row of chairs you set out today in a corner where no one saw — God saw it all.

Service is really God preparing our future:

preparing our life — a character that has not been shaped through service cannot bear the weight of glory;

preparing our identity — only those who start as servants can one day reign without becoming tyrants;

preparing our place in the kingdom — the one who is faithful in small things, the Lord will set over many things.

sections.heading: 4. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
sections.html:
Israel has two seas, and both are fed by the same river, the Jordan.

The Sea of Galilee, in the north, has both an inflow and an outflow. The Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again to the south. So it teems with fish, its shores are shaded with green trees, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place in that region.

The Dead Sea, in the south, only takes in and never gives out. Once the Jordan flows in, it never flows out again; the water can only evaporate. Day after day, year after year, the salt grows ever more concentrated. The salinity of the Dead Sea is about 34 per cent, close to ten times that of ordinary seawater, so fish cannot live there and water plants cannot grow — which is why it’s called the “Dead Sea”.

Brothers and sisters, the same source of water — so why is one teeming with life and the other lifeless?

The difference comes down to a single word: outflow.

A life that only receives and never gives — grace flows in but never flows out — in time grows “salty”, “bitter” and “hard”. A life with both inflow and outflow, through which grace flows on, becomes a Galilee full of fish and trees.

Service is that outlet. God doesn’t lack our service; it is our lives that lack that outlet.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight
sections.html:
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The 321 vision says it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

When James and John asked for the seats on the right and the left, that was “leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights”; when the Lord Jesus wrapped a towel around himself and washed feet, that was “laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position”.

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Look at the ten disciples: the moment they heard James and John asking for seats, they were indignant — that is pride provoking pride. But as soon as the Lord washed their feet, the atmosphere that night grew quiet — that is humility drawing out humility.

What are the Two Core Values? Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, when we practise serving here on earth today, we are practising “letting Jesus be King”; when we learn today not to grab the credit, we are practising “letting Jesus receive all the glory”. Only people like this will one day reign with the Lord. For someone who is willing today to let Jesus be King will, when one day seated on a throne, still take off their crown and lay it before the Lamb.

Key Point 3: Without Service, We Easily Slip into the Self-Centred Life

sections.heading: 1. The Son of Man Came to Serve
sections.html:
“For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)

Many commentators call this verse the key verse of Mark’s Gospel. The whole of Mark is an unfolding of this one sentence.

“Serve” in Greek is διακονέω (diakoneō), from the same root as “servant” above. “Ransom” in Greek is λύτρον (lutron); in the society of the day, it was the money paid to buy a slave’s freedom. By using this word, the Lord Jesus is saying that his service was no mere show, no simple carrying of plates; his service went all the way — all the way to the cross, all the way to laying down his life.

Brothers and sisters, notice the structure of the verse: “not to be served, but to serve.”

There are two roads, and only these two. Every human life is walking either the road of “being served” or the road of “serving others”; there is no middle ground.

sections.heading: 2. Where Do Those Who Won’t Serve End Up?
sections.html:
If someone is unwilling to serve, they won’t stay where they are; they will naturally slide onto the other road.

They will want to be served. When the meeting ends, they’ll be watching to see whether anyone comes over to care for them.

They will want to be affirmed. When they’ve done a little something, they’ll mind whether anyone says “thank you”.

They will want to be exalted. When they see someone else on the platform, they feel a twinge of envy; when they see someone else praised, their heart goes cold.

Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 calls the self-centred life.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. In the Garden of Eden, Satan said to the woman, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) At the heart of those words is “self” — I want to be my own god; I want to sit in the seat at the centre.

The self-centred life does not always show itself as wickedness; far more often it shows itself as touchiness, comparison, feeling hard done by, withdrawal. The more self-centred a person is, the more easily they are hurt; the more easily they are hurt, the more they wrap themselves up; and the more they wrap themselves up, the bigger that “self” becomes.

Paul tells of the opposite road: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: 3. Service Is God’s Training Ground for Us
sections.html:
Service is precisely the training ground God gives us for dealing with “self”. Through service, God trains us in three things.

First, training in denying of self. The Lord says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) Denying of self is not an abstract idea; it is concrete. It is when you meant to rest but went visiting instead; when you meant to speak but kept quiet and heard the other person out; when you should have been praised but passed the credit on to someone else.

Second, training in humility. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” — that is selflessness. Nothing exposes the pride in us like service — when the person I serve doesn’t appreciate it, when I’ve done a great deal and nobody mentions it, what I am really like inside comes to the surface.

Third, training in loving people. Love is not an emotion; love is a verb. We often say, “I don’t have enough love, so I can’t serve,” but in fact the order is often the reverse: it is because we serve that love grows. Pray for someone for a month, and you will begin to love them.

When a person keeps on serving:

the self is dealt with, because service will always bring you up against people and situations you would rather avoid;

life is renewed, because every denying of self is a small resurrection;

love is enlarged, because your world no longer contains only you.

sections.heading: 4. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology
sections.html:
Even science has seen this.

Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science in 2003. They followed four hundred and twenty-three older married couples for five years and found that, after controlling for health, finances and other variables, those who regularly “gave” practical help to others had a significantly lower risk of death than those who did not, while “receiving” help from others did not bring the same benefit. The title of the study was blunt: providing support may be more beneficial than receiving it.

Then there is the Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history; its current director is Robert Waldinger. Spanning more than eighty years, its core conclusion is this: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives is not wealth, nor fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes the order of 321 exactly: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Let’s take another picture from the body. Your heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, pumping blood to your whole body without a moment’s rest. How much of that blood does the heart keep for itself? It keeps only a tiny portion to supply itself and sends all the rest out. A heart that only wanted to hold on to blood wouldn’t be called healthy; that’s called heart failure.

Everywhere in the bodies God has made, the same thing is being said: to live is to let things flow.

sections.heading: 5. There Can Be No Revival Without Service
sections.html:
That is why we say: for there to be revival, there must be service.

Because life is shaped in service.

Because in service, life touches life.

321’s “920 practice” becomes very practical here. Everyone we are connected with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless (0) life towards them, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that not one of these nine graces can be produced in isolation? Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. When God places people beside you, he is placing the soil for your fruit tree beneath your feet.

Without service, there is no one to grow towards; with no one to grow towards, no fruit can grow; and with no fruit, life stays exactly where it is.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s bring today’s message together with the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. He had all authority, yet he wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet. The highest standard of service is not a method; it is a person — it is Jesus.

The Bible is my standard. Whether or not I serve is not decided by feelings or by mood but by God’s word. And God’s word says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” (Ephesians 2:10)

The Holy Spirit is my guide. The thing to avoid above all in service is “making our own plans and then asking God to bless them”. The right order is to ask the Holy Spirit first: Lord, whom do you want me to serve today?

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. The essence of service is giving up the throne. On my schedule, who is King? Over my wallet, who is King? Over my emotions, who is King?

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The greatest temptation in service is quietly keeping a little of the glory for ourselves. When we learn to pass every word of praise straight on as an offering to him, our service becomes worship.

Establish God’s system. We are not doing scattered good deeds; we are building. A family, a small group, a church, a workplace — each can become a brick in God’s system.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson begins precisely with the first link: exchanging the mindset that “service is other people’s need” for the mindset that “service is my life’s need”. Once the mindset changes, life changes; once life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry flows out naturally.

Brothers and sisters, remember that the order cannot be reversed. Many people are worn out because they skipped over life and relationships and charged straight into ministry. Ministry built on life is living water; ministry built on the flesh will sooner or later run dry.

Four Shifts of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective — not asking, “Is this person worth my serving?” but asking, “How does God see this person?”

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective — not asking, “Will this produce results people can see?” but asking, “Will this last in heaven?”

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective — the bowls washed today will get dirty again, the chairs set out today will be stacked away, but the heart offered to the Lord lasts for ever.

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective — the world says “climb up”, God says “go down”; the world says “get more”, God says “give more”.

The 235 Relationships

Service is not a solo battle. 321’s “235 relationships” tell us: become a “2” with a selfless person — that is a spiritual companion; build a “3” — that is spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

For that sister who had served for twelve years and was worn out, the problem was often not that she did too much, but that she had always been doing it alone. God never meant for us to carry a church on our own. The Lord Jesus himself chose twelve disciples, and sent out seventy two by two (Luke 10:1).

Brothers and sisters, find your “2” today. When someone walks with you, service is no longer a heavy burden.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
