The lesson gives us three practices. We will take these three practices deeper by placing them within 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Treat Service as “the Purpose of Life”

Every morning remind yourself of two sentences: today I am not living for myself; I am living for God and for others.

In every setting, ask one question: whom can I serve today?

At home, whom can I serve? At work, whom can I serve? At church, whom can I serve? Online, whom can I serve?

Let service be the direction of your daily living, not an item in your diary.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — first memorise Ephesians 2:10 and let the truth enter your mind.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to bring this verse down from your head into your heart, so that you truly see: I am God’s masterpiece; my whole life was prepared by God long ago.

Conviction — make a decision: from today, I will no longer ask, “Shall I serve today?” I will only ask, “Whom shall I serve today?”

Implementation — do one thing today, even if it’s just sending a message to greet someone.

Evaluation — in the evening spend three minutes looking back: whom did I serve today? What was my motive?

Correction — if you find your motive was to be seen, confess it to the Lord at once and ask him to cleanse you.

Repetition — forty days in a row without a break. A change of mindset takes time; it doesn’t come from one moment of being moved.

Multiplication — teach this practice to someone else, and take them along with you as you do it.

Practice 2: Learn Humility through Service

When you serve, don’t seek to be seen, don’t seek to be praised.

Instead, learn three things: serve in secret, serve gladly and willingly, serve without counting the cost.

The Lord Jesus says, “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

Peter also urges the elders: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly;” (1 Peter 5:2)

Let service become a way of dealing with pride.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — read Matthew 6:1–4 and see clearly the Lord’s warning against “doing it to be seen”.

Revelation — ask the Lord to shine his light: the last time I was upset, was it because my service went unnoticed?

Conviction — admit that pride is the deepest problem in my life, and that humility is the only way out.

Implementation — this week, do one act of service that nobody at all knows about.

Evaluation — when it’s done, is your heart at peace, or a little disappointed? Disappointment is the proof that “self” is still there.

Correction — turn that disappointment into a matter for prayer, and ask the Lord to take back the throne.

Repetition — do at least one unseen act of service every month.

Multiplication — when you see others serving quietly, go and thank them and pray for them, and pass on this unseen faithfulness.

Practice 3: Serve Faithfully in Small Things

Don’t wait for a big platform; start from the smallest places.

Help one person. Care for one person. Bless one person.

What God values is not size but faithfulness.

The Lord Jesus says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10)

And the prophet says, “Who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10)

Before David became king, he was a boy keeping sheep in the wilderness (1 Samuel 16:11); before Moses led the Israelites, he spent forty years tending sheep in the wilderness of Midian. God’s training ground has always been in the “small”.

And the Lord himself put it most movingly: “Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)

Brothers and sisters, that cup of water you hand out — the Lord has taken it into his own hands.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — list three people in your circle who have had a need recently.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to point out the one “the Lord wants you to go to first”.

Conviction — believe that small things are not small in God’s eyes.

Implementation — this week, do one specific small thing for that person.

Evaluation — write it down: what did I do? How did they respond? What changed in my heart?

Correction — if you did it and saw no result, don’t give up; adjust your approach and try again.

Repetition — turn this small thing into a long-term habit.

Multiplication — invite a brother or sister to become your “2”, to remind each other and go and do it together.

An Important Reminder: Why Serving Wears Us Out

Brothers and sisters, if you find serving exhausting, please don’t immediately blame yourself. First be still and ask three questions.

Am I doing it “for people”? If I’m doing it for people, the moment they don’t appreciate it, I collapse.

Am I doing it “for the task”? If I’m doing it for the task, the moment things don’t go smoothly, I collapse.

Am I doing it “for myself”? If I’m doing it for myself, the moment someone else is praised, I collapse.

True service comes down to three phrases:

Do it for the Lord. “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Do it by the Lord. “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Work together with the Lord. We are not working for God in his place; we are working together with God. The heavy burden is on him, not on us.

321 has a saying that puts it superbly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is exhaustion.

Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart; rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down with worry.

For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The Lord also says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord’s yoke is a “yoke for two”. When you feel the whole weight pressing on your shoulders, it may well be that you have asked the Lord to step out from the other side of the yoke and are pulling it all by yourself.

A Declaration of Faith

Let us declare together:

Lord Jesus, I declare: service is not a burden; it is my calling.

I was saved to serve you and to live out your life.

I will learn humility through service, and practise denying of self through service.

Lead me, so that my whole life is lived in service, preparing myself to reign with you one day.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this morning we have seen three things together.

First, service is the purpose of our salvation. We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.

Second, service is the way we train to reign with the Lord. Serve first, then reign; be humble first, then receive glory.

Third, without service, we easily slip into the self-centred life. Service is the training ground God gives us for dealing with the old self and living out Christ.

So let’s say the lesson’s final sentence once more:

We serve not because others need you, but because — you need to serve.

Because service lets you live out your true self — the self created in the image of God and re-created in Christ.

Because service brings you into God’s plan — the plan prepared before you were born.

Because service prepares you for eternal glory — the crown that one day will be taken off and laid before the throne of the Lamb.

When you understand this, you will move from “serving because you have to” into “serving with joy”.

This is the life of an overcomer.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord is asking us a question: are you willing?

He isn’t asking whether you have the gifts; he isn’t asking whether you have the time; he isn’t asking whether you’re qualified. He asks only one thing: are you willing?

If you are, then say to the Lord in your heart, “I am willing.”

Then walk out of this morning devotion and go and find that one person. It needn’t be anything big — handing someone a cup of water is enough; you needn’t wait for a platform — one phone call is enough.

Let Jesus reign as King in your service.

Let Jesus receive all the glory through your service.

“Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 15:58)

keyVerses: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

Lord Jesus, I declare: service is not a burden; it is my calling.
I was saved to serve you and to live out your life.
I will learn humility through service, and practise denying of self through service.
Lead me, so that my whole life is lived in service, preparing myself to reign with you one day.
practices: Treat service as “the purpose of life”
Learn humility through service
Serve faithfully in small things
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you, for our salvation is entirely by grace, through faith; it is not of ourselves, and not of works. Plant this gratitude deep in our hearts first of all.

Lord, renew our mindset about service. We confess that at times we serve for people, for the task, for ourselves — and so we grow weary, resentful and ready to give up. Today, turn our service from “other people’s need” into “our life’s need”.

Lord, deal with the “self” within us. The heart that wants to be served, the heart that wants to be affirmed, the heart that wants to be exalted — deal with them by the cross. Make us like you: though you had all authority, you gladly wrapped a towel around your waist and stooped to wash feet.
Lord, give us eyes that see people, a heart willing to give, and hands ready to do small things. Make us faithful in small things, glad and willing in secret, and never losing our joy in hard labour.
Help us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Let us share the yoke with you every day and find rest in you.
Lead us to live our whole lives in service; prepare our life, our identity and our place in the kingdom, that one day we may reign together with you.
Reign as King in our service, and receive all the glory through our service.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ephesians 2:10: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” Looking back over your experience since you came to faith, which “good work” do you think God prepared for you before you were born — one that others could not easily do in your place? Are you walking that path now?

Mark 10:45: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” Please share honestly: the last time you felt weary or hard done by in your service, were you doing it “for people”, “for the task” or “for yourself”? If you changed that to “doing it for the Lord, by the Lord, and together with the Lord”, how would you adjust? Please pray for one another.
l158.title: Whose Need Is Service?
l158.subtitle: Service Is Not Others’ Need but the Need of Our Own Life
l158.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: One River Jordan, Two Kinds of Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by taking you on a trip to Israel.

Running from north to south is a river called the Jordan. It rises from the snowmelt of Mount Hermon and flows all the way south. This river first flows into one lake and then flows out again; then it carries on south and finally empties into another lake — and from there it never flows out again.

The first lake is called the Sea of Galilee. Water comes in, and water goes out. Its water is living, the grass grows lush along its shores, fishing boats come and go, and fish gather in shoals. It was there that the Lord Jesus called Peter, Andrew, James and John; there that he stilled the wind and the waves; there that he fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. Almost all the warmest stories in the Gospels happened beside those waters.

The second lake is called the Dead Sea. Water comes in, but nothing goes out. Once the Jordan’s water flows in, it cannot get out; it can only evaporate under the blazing sun. Day after day, year after year, the minerals keep building up, until the salinity is above about 33 per cent — nearly ten times that of ordinary seawater. You can float on it and read a newspaper, yet not a single fish can survive in it. Not a blade of grass grows on its shores. That is why people named it the “Dead Sea”.

The same river water, the same sunshine, the same land. The greatest difference between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea is not how much each one receives, but this — one is willing to give out, and the other is not.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what today’s lesson wants to say to us.

In the last lesson we came to understand one thing: serving is actually our own need. When we truly grasp that “serving is my need”, our lives turn from passive to active. We no longer serve only when there’s a need, or only when we’ve been rostered on; instead, whenever we see an opportunity we serve, and we make serving part of our lives. For serving is not only giving; it is a tremendous blessing and opportunity that God gives us.

Today we’re going to see three things more deeply: serving brings growth in our lives; serving is the way to invest in eternity; serving makes us useful people.

First, I’d like you to ask yourself a question in your heart — a question we’ll keep coming back to all this morning:

Right now, is my life more like the Sea of Galilee, or more like the Dead Sea?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Focus
sections.html: Before we come to the key points, let’s get clear on the background of today’s two theme passages. When a passage has its background, the interpretation won’t go astray.

sections.heading: 1. 2 Corinthians: An Apostle Who Gave His Life Away
sections.html:
The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written around AD 55–56, possibly in Macedonia, and its recipients were the church in Corinth.

Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia, a commercially prosperous port city full of competing ideas. Its people prized eloquence, valued appearances and chased after success. In the church there was a group who questioned Paul: his body was weak, his speech was unpolished, and he was always being beaten, imprisoned and driven out — how could a man like that possibly be an apostle of God?

Paul did not argue for any outward splendour of his own. Instead, he laid his brokenness open for them to see. He said, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Clay vessels were the cheapest, most easily broken containers of the day. Paul was saying: I am a clay vessel, yet inside me there is a treasure.

Then he said, “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.” (2 Corinthians 4:16) “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory.” (2 Corinthians 4:17)

And only then comes our theme verse for today: “While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. Paul did not write these words in a quiet study on a calm day. He wrote them while he was being misunderstood and attacked, pouring out his life for the church day after day. The word “look at” in Greek is skopeō; it means “to fix your gaze on, to make something your target”, the way an archer keeps his eye locked on the bullseye. What Paul meant was: I have moved the sights of my life from what can be seen to what cannot be seen.

This is the secret of serving. Someone who looks only at what can be seen will keep calculating how much they’ve given, how much they’ve got back, and whether it was worth it. Only someone who looks at what cannot be seen can give out in serving, gladly and willingly.

sections.heading: 2. Mark: A Young Man Who Could Not Give It Away
sections.html:
The Gospel of Mark is generally held to have been written by Mark, around the AD 60s, most likely in Rome, for Gentile believers who were facing persecution at the time. The key verse of the whole book is Mark 10:45: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

Our second theme passage today is in the same chapter. The Lord Jesus was on the road to Jerusalem, walking step by step towards the cross. On the way a man ran up, knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” Matthew’s Gospel tells us he was a young man; Luke’s tells us he was a ruler; Mark’s tells us he had great possessions. He was young, he had status, he had money, and he was devout and kept the commandments. From every angle he was the kind of success everyone envies.

Scripture records a deeply moving sentence: “Jesus looking at him loved him.” The Lord Jesus was not trying to make things hard for him; it was because the Lord loved him that he said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Mark 10:21)

Brothers and sisters, see the Lord’s logic clearly: first give it away, and then you will have treasure in heaven; first let go of what is on earth, and then you can follow the Lord of heaven. When this young man heard these words, his face fell, and he went away sorrowful. It wasn’t that he didn’t believe. It was that he couldn’t give it away.

On one side, Paul, who gave himself away; on the other, the young man who couldn’t. One is the living water of the Sea of Galilee; the other is the dead water of the Dead Sea. Today’s message stands between these two pictures.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Serving Is the Path to Growth in Life
sections.html: The principle of life comes down to a few simple words: what comes in must go out.

sections.heading: 1. Everything God Made Follows the Law of “In and Out”
sections.html:
Look at your breathing: you breathe in, and then you breathe out. If you only breathed in and never out, you couldn’t last a minute. An adult at rest breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute — around twenty thousand times a day. Every single breath goes in and comes out.

Look at your body: what goes in must also come out. Doctors say a person can go several days without eating, but cannot go several days without eliminating. Once the gut is blocked, even the best food turns to poison inside.

Look at your blood: as the heart contracts, it sends the blood out; as it relaxes, it draws the blood back in. A heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, sending blood all round the body. The reason it can keep beating is that it keeps on giving out.

Brothers and sisters, the law God wrote into the natural world he has also written into our spiritual life.

sections.heading: 2. Only In and Never Out: Spiritual Life Stagnates
sections.html:
Only hearing the word and never doing it — our spiritual life will stagnate. James puts it very bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice the phrase “deluding your own selves”. When someone hears a great deal of preaching but never once puts it into practice, over time an illusion sets in: they think they’re very spiritual. In fact, only their knowledge has grown; their life hasn’t grown up.

Only receiving and never sharing — our spiritual life will grow weak. Information is so convenient today; one phone can hold hundreds of sermons. But brothers and sisters, collecting is not absorbing, absorbing is not digesting, and digesting is not growing. If someone just keeps listening and keeps saving, yet never gives anything out, their life will become like the Dead Sea — it has everything, except life.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38) Notice: the Lord did not say a reservoir will be stored up inside you; he said rivers will “flow” from within you. The mark of living water is that it moves.

sections.heading: 3. Serving Is the Key That Keeps Life Flowing
sections.html:
For “serving”, the New Testament uses the Greek verb diakoneō, with the noun diakonia. Its original meaning is very homely: “to wait at table, to bring out the food”. Later it became the root of the church’s word for “deacon” (diakonos). It is not a lofty word; it is a word that bends down.

When we serve, two things happen: we are no longer only receiving, and we begin to learn to give out. And in the very moment we give out, our life begins to grow.

That is why Paul says, “While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, serving takes us from “the needs we can see” into “the growth of life we cannot see”. What you can see is a fellowship meal, a lift to church, a phone call, a chair set out; what you cannot see is the extra love, patience, endurance and gentleness that grow in you through it all. The thing you can see is over once it’s done; the life you cannot see remains.

sections.heading: 4. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology
sections.html:
The University of Michigan psychologist Stephanie Brown and her colleagues published their findings in the journal Psychological Science in 2003. They followed 423 older married couples for five years and found that those who regularly gave others practical help and gave their spouse emotional support had a markedly lower risk of dying within those five years, while simply receiving help from others showed no such benefit. The researchers concluded that giving support may be more beneficial than receiving it.

Brothers and sisters, this is not the Bible leaning on psychology; it is psychology confirming what the Bible said long ago. At Miletus Paul said to the elders of Ephesus, “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” (Acts 20:35)

Solomon had seen it long before: “There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.” (Proverbs 11:24–25) “He who waters shall be watered also himself” — this is a law of spiritual physics that God has set in the universe. You water others, and God waters you.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Life Grows by Giving Out; Selflessness Is Shaped in Serving
sections.html:
The 321 vision says that the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Many people walk this order backwards: they take on ministry first and only talk about life afterwards. As a result, serving becomes a heavy burden; the more they do, the more tired and the more bitter they become. 321 reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

But brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand — “life first, then relationships, then ministry” does not mean “I’ll serve once my life is mature”. This order is about importance, not about what comes first in time. Life is the root, relationships are the trunk, ministry is the fruit. The root grows deep as it is watered, and giving out is precisely how a life gets watered.

The old self, the self-centred life, is always calculating “What do I get?”; the new self, living in selflessness, begins to ask “What can I give?” Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

When you begin to serve, you’ll discover something wonderful: you become more loving, you become more patient, you become more like Jesus.

That love isn’t something you squeeze out of yourself; that patience isn’t something you grit your teeth for. It’s because the water has started to flow, and the spring wells up.

By Jacob’s well the Lord Jesus said to the Samaritan woman, “But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.” (John 4:14) A spring is different from a pond: a pond depends on someone pouring water in, while a spring wells up from below. Someone who only knows how to receive is forever looking for the next person to pour water into them; only someone who starts giving out discovers that there was a spring inside them all along.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had this experience? One day you’re feeling low and don’t really want to go to the meeting, but you’ve promised to pick up an elderly sister, so you drag yourself out. Then on the way you chat with her for a while and pray for her once, and by the time you get home you find that the one who has been comforted is you.

That is no coincidence. That is a law of life God designed: when you give out, God passes through you first.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Serving Is the Way to Invest in Eternity
sections.html: “Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, ‘One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.’” (Mark 10:21)

sections.heading: 1. The Lord Jesus Reminds Us of the Difference Between Two Worlds
sections.html:
What the Lord Jesus said to that young man was not a harsh command, but a piece of better investment advice. What the Lord meant was: what you’re clutching in your hand right now is temporary; if you’re willing to loosen your grip and give it away, you’ll exchange it for what is eternal.

Everything on earth is temporary. In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus put it very plainly: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:19–21)

The Lord names three enemies of earthly treasure: moth, rust and thieves. Moths eat clothing, rust corrodes metal, thieves steal money. In other words, there is not one thing in this world you can keep for ever.

The word “treasure” in Greek is thēsauros — “a treasury, a place where treasure is stored”. The Lord Jesus says that where your treasury is, there your heart is. Brothers and sisters, the reverse is also true: do you want to know where your heart is? Look at your diary and your bank statements, and you’ll know.

sections.heading: 2. What Can Be Stored Up in Heaven?
sections.html:
So what, in the end, can be stored up in heaven?

Not how much you own, but how much you give away.

The Lord Jesus made this as clear as it could be in the Olivet Discourse. Matthew 25 records three parables: the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and the goats. In the last of them the Lord says, “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’” (Matthew 25:40)

Notice what “it” refers to. The verses before spell it out: I was hungry and you gave me food; thirsty, and you gave me drink; a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; in prison, and you came to me. Every one of them is the most ordinary, unremarkable little thing.

Yet the Lord Jesus says that when these things are done to the least of these, they are done to him. Brothers and sisters, this sentence turns the value of serving completely upside down. So the bowl of soup you carried was carried to the Lord; the person you kept company with — you were keeping company with the Lord; the phone call you made — the Lord himself picked up.

The Lord also said, “Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.” (Matthew 10:42) A cup of cold water costs nothing, yet it leaves a record in heaven.

So when you help someone, when you care for someone, when you give your time and your love, you are really investing in heaven.

sections.heading: 3. A Missionary’s Arithmetic
sections.html:
On 28 October 1949, a 22-year-old American wrote a sentence in his journal that became one of the most famous lines in the history of missions: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” A man who gives away what he cannot keep, in order to gain what he cannot lose, is no fool at all.

His name was Jim Elliot. In January 1956, he and four co-workers, seeking to bring the gospel to the Auca people of Ecuador, were speared to death on a river beach. He was 28 that year.

By earthly arithmetic it was a colossal loss: five young men, five families, five bright futures. But what about by heaven’s arithmetic? The very people who killed them later came to Christ in large numbers; Elliot’s wife, Elisabeth, later went to live and serve among that tribe. And their story has, for more than sixty years, inspired countless people all over the world to take up the path of mission.

Brothers and sisters, this is an eternal investment. Earth’s books will be closed out; heaven’s books are never closed.

sections.heading: 4. Relationships: The Asset That Holds Its Value Best
sections.html:
Harvard University has a study that has run from 1938 to this day, the Harvard Study of Adult Development, one of the longest-running studies of happiness in human history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has condensed more than eighty years of findings into one sentence: what truly keeps people healthy and happy through life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

This conclusion fits exactly with what the 321 vision says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

And brothers and sisters, serving is the most genuine way to build relationships. When you’ve set out tables together, stacked chairs together, stayed up late together praying for someone, that relationship is different from having just shared a meal. Ministry will pass; relationships remain. Things decay; people last for ever.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Only What We Give Away Is Eternal; Everything We Hold On To Will Pass
sections.html:
The 321 vision speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Serving is turning earthly resources — money, time, energy, love — into heavenly treasure. It’s an exchange at the best rate there is. Money on earth is eaten away by inflation; treasure in heaven never loses its value.

Paul said to Timothy, “That they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share; laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.” (1 Timothy 6:18–19) “Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come” — this is exactly what an eternal investment is.

Heaven keeps an account too: “For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them.” (Hebrews 6:10) God will not forget. What you do where no one sees is all recorded in heaven.

In Revelation John heard a voice saying, “that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow with them.” (Revelation 14:13) Brothers and sisters, when the day comes for us to leave this world, we can take nothing with us. Only one thing will go with us — our works.

sections.heading: 6. The Worth of Two Small Coins
sections.html:
Do you remember that poor widow? In the temple the Lord Jesus watched many rich people putting large sums into the treasury, and he also saw a poor widow put in two small coins. The Lord said, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury, for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.” (Mark 12:43–44)

By earthly accounting, two small coins couldn’t even buy a meal; on the balance sheet they were mere small change. Yet in heaven’s ledger they were worth more than all the rich people’s offerings put together.

Brothers and sisters, heaven counts differently from earth. Earth counts “how much you gave”; heaven counts “how much you kept back”. Earth looks at the figures; heaven looks at the heart.

So don’t belittle what you are able to give. That bit of time, that bit of money, that one prayer you think is insignificant — put into heaven’s treasury, the Lord himself enters it in the books for you.

So every act of service is an eternal investment.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Serving Makes Us Useful People
sections.html: “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’” (Matthew 25:21)

sections.heading: 1. What God Gives Each Person Was Never Meant to Be the Same
sections.html:
The parable of the talents begins like this: “To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one; to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.” (Matthew 25:15)

Where the Chinese Union Version speaks of “a thousand” pieces of silver, the Greek has “one talent” (talanton). One talent was roughly six thousand denarii, and one denarius was a labourer’s wage for a day’s work at the time. In other words, even the servant who “only got one” was holding nearly twenty years’ wages in his hand. God has never given anyone “just a little”. In God’s eyes, even the smallest entrustment is a fortune.

Some have five, some two, some one. Gifts differ, resources differ, opportunities differ. That is simply a fact, and there’s no need to compare. Peter says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” (1 Peter 4:10) “In its various forms” means many and varied, of every kind. God’s gifts are like a rainbow, not a single colour.

sections.heading: 2. The Point Is Not How Much, but Whether It Is Used
sections.html:
Notice how the parable ends: the one who received five talents gained five more, and the one who received two gained two more, and the praise the two of them received was exactly the same, word for word: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things.” (Matthew 25:21, 23)

To the one with five, the master didn’t say he was more impressive; to the one with two, the master didn’t say he was second-rate. For the master was looking not at quantity, but at faithfulness. “Good” in Greek is agathos, and “faithful” is pistos, a word from the same root as “faith”; it means reliable, trustworthy. Paul says, “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2)

So what happened to the servant who received one talent? He said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.” (Matthew 25:25) He didn’t gamble it, he didn’t spend it — he simply didn’t use it.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: it wasn’t that he did something wrong; it was that he did nothing at all. And the master’s verdict on him was: “You wicked and slothful servant.” (Matthew 25:26) In the ledger of the kingdom of heaven, “not using” is itself a sin.

Used, it has value; unused, it becomes useless.

sections.heading: 3. God’s Principle: The More You Use, the More You Have; Unused, Even What You Have Is Lost
sections.html:
“For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.” (Matthew 25:29)

At first hearing this sounds unfair, but in fact it describes a law of life.

Just look at your muscles and you’ll understand. In the weightlessness of space, unless people deliberately exercise, they lose muscle and bone mass rapidly, which is why NASA requires astronauts on the International Space Station to exercise for about two hours every day. Muscles aren’t ruined by use; muscles are ruined by sitting idle.

The brain is the same. Neuroscience has shown that the brain has “neuroplasticity”: neural circuits used again and again are strengthened, while connections left unused for a long time are pruned away. A language you’ve learned but never speak will be forgotten; a piece you can play but never practise will grow rusty. This is not punishment; it is design.

Spiritual gifts work by the same law. The more you use them, the more you have; unused, even what you have is lost. The more you open your mouth to pray for people, the better you pray; the more you go and care for people, the softer your heart becomes; the more you share the gospel, the better you share it.

sections.heading: 4. Stop Saying “I’m Not Enough”
sections.html:
Many people don’t serve because three sentences are running in their hearts: I’m not good enough, I don’t have enough, I’m not capable enough.

But God says: it isn’t about how much; it’s about whether you’re willing to use it.

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy”. He found that the main source of people’s confidence in their own abilities is not other people’s encouragement, nor self-talk, but “the first-hand experience of success”. In plain words: you don’t first have confidence and then do it; you do it, and then you have confidence.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the Gentle Reminder in today’s lesson is getting at: many people think, “I’ll serve once I’m better”, but God’s principle is “use it first, and then you’ll get better”.

Scripture is full of examples. Moses said, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) God still sent him. Jeremiah said, “Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” (Jeremiah 1:6) God still sent him. That boy had only five loaves and two fish — nothing at all in the face of five thousand people — but he handed them over, and the Lord broke them and fed the crowd.

The Lord never waits until you are enough before he uses you; the Lord adds to you after you have handed yourself over.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Unused Becomes Useless; Used Is Enlarged
sections.html:
When you begin to use what you have, God will add to it, God will enlarge it, God will use you. You’ll become someone with influence, someone of value, someone God uses.

The 920 practice of the 321 vision lands right here: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Before them we practise living a life of selflessness (0), bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice that not one of the nine graces can be borne behind closed doors on your own. Love needs someone to love; patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness, gentleness and faithfulness all need someone to be shown to. God has put people around you precisely so that you have somewhere to “use” it.

Paul says, “If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work.” (2 Timothy 2:21) “Suitable for the master’s use” — the honour of a vessel lies not in how big or how beautiful it is, but in whether the master uses it.

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that you’re not enough; it’s just that you haven’t started using what you have.

sections.heading: 6. Useful People Are People the Lord Uses
sections.html:
Our generation loves to talk about “worth”. The world tells you that your worth equals your income, your job title, your number of likes. But these things have one thing in common: they all pass away. The day you retire, the job title is gone; the day the server shuts down, the likes are gone.

The values the Bible gives us are completely different: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

Notice the three layers in this sentence. First, we are God’s workmanship — your worth comes from the one who made you, not from other people’s opinions. Second, we were created for good works — you were made with a purpose; you weren’t just dumped here. Third, these good works are ones “which God prepared before that we would walk in them” — God has already prepared the very thing you are to do today, and it’s waiting for you along your path.

So “becoming a useful person” doesn’t mean climbing the world’s rankings; it means being used by him in God’s work. Paul says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (Romans 12:1) A living sacrifice means offering your whole self, ready to be sent wherever the Lord wills.

Brothers and sisters, if you asked me what makes a successful life, I would say: a life the Lord has used is a successful life.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Serving to Selfless Serving
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, let’s put today’s three key points back into the big picture of 321, and you’ll see them more clearly.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model. The Lord said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45) When the Lord of the universe himself bent down to serve, can we still stand on our own status?

The Bible is my standard. Whether or not I serve isn’t decided by my feelings, but by God’s word. God’s word says, “It is more blessed to give than to receive”, so I do as it says.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Serving isn’t gritting our teeth in our own strength; it’s relying on the Holy Spirit. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

Let Jesus be King. The greatest temptation in serving is to make ourselves king — my way, my schedule, my face. Letting Jesus reign as King means handing over the sovereignty.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. When things succeed, the glory goes to the Lord; when they don’t, we keep trusting. If people’s praise after we serve sends us floating up into the clouds, that shows we’ve been serving for ourselves.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Every bit of service we offer today lays one more brick in this great building project.

sections.heading: 2. The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless
sections.html:
The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

How does the self-centred life show itself in serving? Keeping score of who does more and who does less; caring whether anyone notices, whether anyone says thank you; feeling this role is too small, beneath me; or the opposite — feeling I’m not good enough, not worthy to serve. Have you noticed that these two voices are really the same disease? In both, the focus is on ourselves.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. If everyone on a team is guarding their own face, serving becomes a battlefield; if everyone is willing to bend down first, serving becomes a blessing. Paul says, “Doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4)

Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When the “I” steps aside, God’s riches flow through.

sections.heading: 3. Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Many people serve until they’re dried up because the order has been turned upside down: they build a relationship with tasks first and think of God last. So they do a great deal, yet feel empty inside.

321 reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Look at yourself, and you’ll feel either inferior or superior; look at others, and you’ll compare or resent; look at your circumstances, and you’ll lose heart or complain. Only by looking at Jesus can you keep on walking.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The same act of service, done with the heart, leaves you full inside when it’s finished; done with the brain, it leaves you empty.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. The family member, the colleague, the neighbour, the brother or sister in your group chat whom you’ll meet today — all of them are God’s training ground for you. Before them, live out selflessness (0), and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

235 relationships: becoming a “2” with someone selfless — that is a spiritual companion; establishing a “3” — that is spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” — that is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, serving has never been a one-man show. What you give out today may well be paving the way for spiritual children to come.

sections.heading: 5. The Path of Serving
sections.html:
Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory.

These five steps are not five separate stages; they are one road. As we walk on along this road, we are establishing God’s system, fulfilling the Lord’s Prayer, moving towards the end time revival, and walking alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
Practice 1: Practise letting your life have both “in and out”

Each day, don’t only receive; give out as well. When you’ve heard a message, share it with someone; when you’ve received a grace, become a blessing to someone else. Keep your life flowing.

How, concretely? After this morning’s devotion, pick out the one sentence that touched you most, and pass it on to someone in your own words. Don’t forward the whole thing; say it in your own words. Because forwarding is just “passing water through”; saying it in your own words is “digesting”.

Practice 2: Practise investing in eternity through serving

Ask yourself two questions every day: Who can I give myself for today? How can I invest in heaven today?

Turn your time, your resources and your love into eternal value. I suggest you choose one person today and do one small thing: a phone call to say hello, a prayer, a bit of practical help, some time spent together. It needn’t be big, but it must be real. Remember what the Lord said: even a cup of cold water will not lose its reward.

Practice 3: Practise using everything God has given you

Don’t belittle yourself. A word, an act of care, a little time — all of them can be used by God.

Take out a pen and paper and list three things God has given you — a skill, a free slot in your week, some money, a connection, a hurt you’ve been healed from. Then after each one, write a name: who can I use this for?

Start using them, and you’ll discover that God keeps adding to you.

A Gentle Reminder: Use it first, and you’ll get better

Many people think: I’ll serve once I’m better. But God’s principle is: use it first, and then you’ll get better.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll grow; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll stagnate.

Taking the practice deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset

The 321 vision tells us there are eight stages in changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s put today’s practice into these eight stages.

Stage one, Information. Today you’ve heard three statements: serving makes your life grow; serving is an investment in eternity; serving makes you a useful person. That is information, and anyone can hear information.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn one of these statements into a word spoken specifically to you. Quiet yourself and ask: Lord, of these three statements today, which one are you saying to me? Information goes into the brain; revelation goes into the heart.

Stage three, Conviction. Not “that sounds very reasonable”, but “I believe this is true, and I’m willing to obey”. Conviction is the surrender of the will, not a stirring of the emotions.

Stage four, Implementation. Do it today; don’t wait. Start with the smallest thing. The opposite of implementation isn’t failure; the opposite of implementation is procrastination.

Stage five, Evaluation. Tonight, take three minutes to look back: Did I give anything out today? Was it with the heart, or with the brain? Was it for the Lord, or to save my own face?

Stage six, Correction. When you find you’ve drifted, adjust. If you’re doing too much and your heart is growing bitter, correct it; if you’re doing too little and your heart is growing cold, correct that too.

Stage seven, Repetition. Doing it once is not change; doing it again and again is life. When psychology talks about forming habits, the key has never been a one-off resolution, but the number of repetitions. Spiritual growth is the same: it comes from repetition, day after day.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once you’ve tasted the joy of serving, go and bring someone to serve alongside you. Bringing one person into serving is better than doing ten more things yourself. This is the “3” in 235 — spiritual parents raising spiritual children.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the River Jordan we visited at the start this morning.

The same water flows into the Sea of Galilee and becomes living water; it flows into the Dead Sea and becomes dead water. There is only one difference: whether it is willing to give out.

Serving is not merely giving; it is the beginning of growth, of investment and of worth.

In serving, you will grow; in serving, you will store up eternity; in serving, you will be used by God.

Once you understand this, you will no longer ask, “Why should I serve?” You’ll begin to say, “Lord, give me more opportunities to serve!”

That young man went away sorrowful, because he couldn’t bear to let go. Paul joyfully finished the whole race, because he had long since given himself away. This morning the Lord is looking at you too, and loving you, and saying the same thing to you: come, follow me.

Let Jesus be King, and don’t make yourself king; let Jesus receive all the glory, and keep not one bit of glory for yourself.

Paul says, “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 15:58)

Brothers and sisters, every minute, every word, every bit of love you give out today is not in vain in the Lord.

keyVerses: “While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)
“Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, ‘One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.’” (Mark 10:21)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I declare: serving is my opportunity, not my burden.
I will let my life flow — no longer only receiving, but willing to give out too.
I will serve with everything you have given me, investing it in eternity.
I believe that when I am willing to use what I have, you will add to it and make me a useful person.
practices: Practise letting your life have both “in and out”
Practise investing in eternity through serving
Practise using everything God has given you
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you for speaking to me this morning. You have let me see that serving is not an extra burden, but a blessing and an opportunity you have given me.

Lord, forgive me. So often I only want to receive and not give out; so often I wait to be rostered on, and won’t take the initiative to see the needs; so often I say I’m not good enough, I don’t have enough, I’m not capable enough — when really I can’t bear to let go, and I’m afraid.
Lord, please turn the Dead Sea in me into a Sea of Galilee. Please open up the outlet of my life, so that the grace you give me can flow out and become a blessing to others.
Please help me turn my time, money, energy and love into treasure in heaven; help me no longer to look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.
Please teach me to use what I have first, and grow better by using it. Whether you give me five talents, two or one, I am willing to bring it out and use it.
Lord, I place myself in your hands. Be King in my life, and receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Looking back over the past three months, has your life been more like the Sea of Galilee or more like the Dead Sea? What have you kept receiving but not yet given out? (“While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” 2 Corinthians 4:18)

What is the “one talent” God has given you? What has made you bury it in the ground? This week, how will you dig it up and use it? (“For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.” Matthew 25:29)
l159.title: Service Is My Own Need
l159.subtitle: Growing and Investing in Eternity Through Service
l159.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: The Moment of Raising Your Hand
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together before God to listen quietly to a question that is very short, yet one that will follow us all our lives.

Let me first describe a scene that has played out in many churches. The Sunday service ends, and the pastor stands at the front and says, “Next month we’re starting a new area of service, and we need a few brothers and sisters. If you’re willing, please raise your hand.”

What happens next?

A silence. A very curious silence. Suddenly everyone’s eyes are very busy — some look down at the bulletin, some sort out their bags, some study their own shoes intently. It isn’t that they don’t love the Lord, nor that they’re unwilling; it’s that in those few short seconds, a voice is speaking in each person’s heart.

That voice says, “I’m not good enough yet.”

That voice says, “I don’t have the gift.”

That voice says, “I don’t have the time.”

Brothers and sisters, do these three sentences sound familiar? I believe there’s no one here to whom they are completely foreign. These three sentences are practically the common language of Christians the world over. They sound humble, honest, perfectly reasonable. Yet today we are going to see together that none of these three sentences is really “a statement of fact”; each is “a stronghold of mindset”.

In the last lesson we saw together that serving is our need. It isn’t that God needs us to serve, but that we need to serve; a life that doesn’t serve will dry up, become self-centred, and gradually lose the glory that God’s children ought to have. Once we understand that “serving is our need”, a very practical question follows —

Who can serve?

Who is qualified to stand in God’s work? Who is good enough to be used by God? Those who have studied theology? Those who speak well? Those with plenty of time? Those whose gifts are obvious, who shine the moment they step onto the platform?

Scripture’s answer is so simple it’s startling — and so simple there’s nowhere to hide from it —

The willing can all serve.

Notice that God has never asked, “Are you able?” What God asks is, “Are you willing?” The words Isaiah heard in the temple were not “Who is able to go for me?” but “Who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8). “Will go” — that is willingness. God’s call-up has never been a checklist of abilities, but an invitation to the heart.

Brothers and sisters, this is a turning point in our mindset. Most of the stagnation in our lives comes not from a lack of ability, but from a wrong mindset. The light of 321 says it clearly: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Today’s lesson is about removing four wrong mindsets from our hearts, one by one, and putting God’s perspective in their place.

Today we’ll look at four things: first, we don’t serve once we’re equipped; we are equipped in serving. Second, we don’t serve because we have the gift; we experience God’s provision in serving. Third, it isn’t that we have no time; it’s that we haven’t put God first. Fourth, serving is grace, not a burden.

Four key points, all pointing to the same conclusion: whether you are able to serve has never been the question; whether you are willing is the only question.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An “Unworthy” Man Writes “I Am What I Am”
sections.html:
Our theme verse today comes from 1 Corinthians 15:10. To really taste this verse, we need to know who wrote it and under what circumstances.

The author of 1 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written around AD 55, when he was in Ephesus during his third missionary journey (1 Corinthians 16:8 says, “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost”). Its recipients were the church he himself had planted in Corinth.

What kind of place was Corinth? Corinth lay on the isthmus in southern Greece. It was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, and its two ports, east and west, made it one of the busiest commercial cities in the Mediterranean. The city was wealthy, mixed in population, confused in religion and corrupt in morals. A church in a city like that naturally had plenty of problems: factions and quarrels, sexual immorality, believers suing one another, disorder at the Lord’s Supper, and comparing and boasting over spiritual gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12 to 14, Paul spends three whole chapters on gifts — because that church’s greatest sickness was using gifts to rank one another.

Then Paul comes to chapter 15, on the resurrection. He first lists the witnesses of the resurrection: Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred brothers, James, all the apostles. Finally he says, “And last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also. For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.” (1 Corinthians 15:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to Paul’s self-assessment: the least, unworthy, one who had persecuted the church. Judged by qualifications, Paul was the least qualified of all to serve. With his own hands he had thrown believers into prison; when Stephen was stoned to death, he stood by, minding the clothes. If “serving” required an impressive CV, Paul would be the first one out.

Yet next he writes the most moving sentence in the whole letter: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

“But” — this word is the turning point of the gospel. Human qualifications end here; God’s grace begins here.

“The grace of God” — the word for grace here is the Greek charis, meaning a free, undeserved gift. Interestingly, the New Testament word for “gift” (charisma) comes straight from charis — a gift is grace made concrete. That is to say: whatever ability you have in your hands, you didn’t earn it; it is the fruit that grace has borne.

In the same verse Paul says three more things, and with them he lays out the whole logic of serving. First, “His grace which was given to me was not futile” — when grace comes, it must bear fruit. Second, “I worked more than all of them” — those who receive grace don’t lie back; they’re the ones most willing to work. Third, “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” — when the work is done, the credit doesn’t go to ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this one verse answers both extremes at once. To the one who says, “I’m not good enough”, Paul says: I wasn’t worthy either, but God’s grace has made me what I am today. To the one who says, “I’m very capable”, Paul says: Yet not I, but the grace of God. The first is lifted up, the second is brought down. This is how the gospel works: it lifts up the lowly and humbles the proud.

This is exactly what 321 says: the old self, the self-centred life, is always weighing whether it’s good enough, whether it’s better than others; the new self, living in selflessness, sees only grace and lets Jesus alone be King. Paul’s “not I, but the grace of God” is the finest declaration of selflessness there is.

Now, carrying this verse with us, let’s walk step by step into today’s four key points.

sections.heading: 1. We Don’t Serve Once We’re Equipped; We Are Equipped in Serving
sections.html:
That voice in our hearts: “I’m not ready yet”

Many people are afraid to serve, and their reasons sound entirely reasonable: “I’m not ready yet”, “I’m not mature enough yet”, “Once I’ve read the Bible for a few more years, heard a few more sermons, become a bit more stable, then I’ll come and serve.”

Brothers and sisters, I have to be very honest: this “waiting” often lasts ten years, twenty years, even a lifetime. Because “ready” never has a clear line. Today you finish reading one book of the Bible, and tomorrow you find there are sixty-five more; today you overcome one weakness, and tomorrow the light shows up another gap. If we wait until we’re perfect, we’ll never begin.

And there’s a deep myth hidden here: we think spiritual growth means “first you know how, then you do it”. The truth is just the opposite — the spiritual principle is “first you do it, then you know how”.

Not knowing first and then doing; doing first and then knowing.

God’s order: first he sends, then he equips

Let’s look at a few people in the Bible.

Moses. God called him from the flames at Horeb, and Moses’ first reaction was to make excuses: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) He was telling the truth — he really wasn’t a good speaker. But God didn’t first send him on a public-speaking course. God said, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12) Notice the order: first “go”, then the gift.

Even more interesting is the passage just before. God asked Moses, “What is that in your hand?” Moses said, “A rod.” (Exodus 4:2) It was nothing but a shepherd’s stick, the most ordinary thing of his forty years in the wilderness. Yet when Moses obediently threw it on the ground and picked it up again at God’s word, from then on Scripture calls that rod “God’s rod”. Brothers and sisters, God doesn’t first give you a new rod; God wants to use the one you already have in your hand.

Gideon. When the angel appeared to him, he was threshing wheat in the winepress, hiding from the Midianites. God said, “Go in this your might, and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Haven’t I sent you?” (Judges 6:14) Gideon immediately replied, “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.” (Judges 6:15) The poorest family, the least person — his self-assessment wasn’t wrong at all. But God’s answer was: “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.” (Judges 6:16)

Jeremiah. When God called him, he said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” (Jeremiah 1:6) God said, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you.” (Jeremiah 1:7)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed what they have in common? The first thing every one of those called said was, “I can’t.” And God’s answer was never “Yes, you can”, but “I will be with you.” God never denies our inadequacy; he simply adds himself to it.

Now look at how the Lord Jesus led his disciples. In Matthew 10, Jesus sent out the twelve disciples to preach, to heal and to cast out demons. Were the disciples mature at that point? Not in the least. Later they were still arguing over who was the greatest, still so frightened in the boat that they woke Jesus up, and Peter was still going to deny the Lord three times. Yet the Lord sent them anyway. The Lord didn’t wait until they were perfect before using them; he shaped them as he used them.

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

Brothers and sisters, notice “from above”. Since every good gift comes from above, “Am I enough?” isn’t the key; the key is “Will he give from above?” And God has already told us: in his giving there is no variation, no turning shadow — he won’t be willing to give to you today and change his mind tomorrow. You needn’t worry that the supply will run out.

Learning to ride a bicycle

My favourite picture for this is learning to ride a bicycle.

You could buy ten books and read the world’s most authoritative “Mechanics and Balance of the Bicycle”, memorising every formula for the gyroscopic effect, shifting your centre of gravity and the self-correcting front wheel. Then I ask you: can you ride now? No.

On the other hand, a six-year-old who understands none of the principles is lifted onto the bike by his dad, pushed a few metres, falls twice and skins his knee. Twenty minutes later he can ride. And he’ll never forget it as long as he lives.

Why? Because you don’t learn to ride a bicycle by “understanding”; you learn by “getting on”.

Brain science confirms this too. Skills like cycling, swimming and playing the piano belong to “procedural memory”, handled mainly by the cerebellum and the basal ganglia; this is a different memory system from the one we use to memorise facts, and it can only be built through actual, repeated practice. In other words, when God made us, he wrote “learning by doing” into our very bodies.

Serving is the same. A hundred classes on “How to Care for People” are worth less than actually going on one visit; ten books on prayer are worth less than actually kneeling down once to pray for someone.

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy”. He pointed out that the most powerful source of people’s confidence that “I can do this” is not other people’s encouragement, nor giving yourself a pep talk, but “mastery experience” — actually getting something done yourself. Brothers and sisters, this explains exactly why so many people become more afraid to serve the longer they don’t serve: they’ve never had a first time. Confidence isn’t something you wait for; confidence is something you get by doing.

Hudson Taylor, the founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” Notice the order of that sentence — first “done”, then “supply”.

A 321 insight: take the first step with your heart, and the Holy Spirit begins to work

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad.

Whose voice is “I’m not ready yet”? That is the voice of the “brain”. The brain calculates: Will I make a fool of myself? Am I qualified? What will people think of me? It calculates this way and that, and the conclusion is always “Wait a bit longer.”

Whose voice is “I’m willing”? That is the voice of the “heart”, the voice of the Holy Spirit’s prompting. The heart doesn’t calculate; the heart simply responds: Lord, here I am; send me.

And this “willingness” is exactly what 321 calls “selflessness”. The self-centred keep looking at themselves — my level, my face, my sense of security; the selfless look only at the Lord — you send, and I go. The old self is self-centred, so it is never enough; the new self is selfless, so it is ready to be used at any time.

So please remember these two sentences:

Take the first step with your heart, and the Holy Spirit begins to work.

When you’re willing to begin, you’ll fall, but you’ll learn; you’ll be imperfect, but you’ll grow. Serving itself is the best equipping there is.

sections.heading: 2. We Don’t Serve Because We Have the Gift; We Experience God’s Provision in Serving
sections.html:
Our God makes something from nothing and much from little

The second common reason is: “That isn’t my gift”, “I don’t have that gift; I can’t do it.”

To pull down this stronghold, we first need to know what kind of God we believe in.

“For he spoke, and it was done. He commanded, and it stood firm.” (Psalm 33:9)

Brothers and sisters, what a great verse this is. In Genesis 1, the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was on the surface of the deep. God didn’t first go and look for materials; God spoke just one sentence: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) Between nothing and something there was only a single word.

Our God is the God who creates. And what is creating? Creating is making something out of nothing, making much out of little.

So when you say, “I don’t have the gift”, you are really saying to a God who “spoke, and it was done”: this is something you can’t do.

Paul says, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God.” (2 Corinthians 3:5) Notice that Paul admits he is “not sufficient” — this isn’t low self-esteem; it’s a fact. But he doesn’t stop there; he goes on to say, “our sufficiency is from God”. Seeing clearly our own limits while looking up to God’s limitlessness — that is true humility.

Five loaves and two fish: hand them over, and it’s enough

The Lord Jesus gave us a picture we can never forget.

As evening fell, there were five thousand men out in the wilderness, besides women and children. The disciples said, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17)

Listen to that word “only”. “Only” is the word we use most. I only have a little time. I only have a little money. I only have a tiny gift. I only finished junior high. I can only cook. I can only drive. I can’t do anything — I can only pray.

John’s Gospel gives us more detail: these five loaves and two fish were a boy’s lunch, and they were barley loaves — barley was the food of the poor at the time (John 6:9). The disciples’ assessment was: “But what are these among so many?” By human reckoning, this was a sum that could only end in failure.

But Jesus said something very short: “Bring them here to me.” (Matthew 14:18)

And then? “He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes. They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.” (Matthew 14:19–20)

Not enough became more than enough; the limited became limitless. And there were still twelve baskets left over — twelve disciples, a basket each. God’s provision always has “some left over”.

Brothers and sisters, notice where the decisive action of the whole miracle lies. Not in the loaves, not in the fish, not in the disciples’ ability, but in “Bring them here to me” — in that act of handing over. Bread left in the boy’s hands is one meal; bread placed in Jesus’ hands is a banquet for five thousand.

We often get this wrong, thinking it has to become more before we hand it over. No. First we hand it over, and then it becomes more. The bread multiplied only after it was “broken”; if it had never been broken, it would have stayed five loaves for ever.

The picture of a single cell

God’s power to make much from little is actually written on our own bodies every day.

Every human life begins as a fertilised egg — a single cell almost invisible to the naked eye. And an adult body, according to an estimate published in 2013 in the Annals of Human Biology by Bianchi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy, is made up of about 37 trillion cells. From one cell to 37 trillion.

Brothers and sisters, could the God who turned one cell into you not turn that little gift in your hands into a blessing?

A gift is not a qualification but an entrustment

We often have a misunderstanding about “gifts”: we think a gift is a certificate of qualification, and only with one can we step onto the field.

But Scripture says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” (1 Peter 4:10) The emphasis here is on “serving one another” and “good managers”. A manager is not the owner; a manager is the one entrusted. Gifts are not for proving who you are; they are for the benefit of others — “But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all.” (1 Corinthians 12:7)

What’s more, gifts are often discovered only in the “using”. Many brothers and sisters were first roped into leading a small group once, and only then discovered they had a shepherd’s heart; were first asked to drive an elderly member home once, and only then discovered the great joy they had in serving people. Gifts are like muscles: unused, they waste away; used, they grow.

God says, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Notice — not in our strength, but in our weakness. You think weakness keeps you from serving; God says weakness is exactly where his power shows itself.

This doesn’t mean we should do everything or say yes to everything. We still need wisdom; we still need to discern before God. What we want to pull down here is that self-imposed limit, the sentence “I can’t do it, so God can’t either.” Don’t limit what God can do.

A 321 insight: placed in the Lord’s hands, the limited becomes limitless

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness.

Five loaves in the boy’s hands were “something” — but a very small something. Once the five loaves were in Jesus’ hands, the boy had “nothing” — and yet that day five thousand people were fed because of him. This is selflessness: letting go of the small “something” in your hand and entering into God’s great limitlessness.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) No longer I — that is selflessness; but Christ lives in me — that is limitlessness.

So please remember:

Placed in the Lord’s hands, the limited becomes limitless.

You be willing first, and God will provide. When there is a need, God will give you strength, and God will enlarge your gifts.

sections.heading: 3. It Isn’t That We Have No Time; It’s That We Haven’t Put God First
sections.html:
The truth about “I don’t have time”

The third reason is the one used most often, and with the clearest conscience: “I’d really love to serve, but I genuinely don’t have the time.”

Brothers and sisters, I completely understand. Modern busyness is real busyness: work, overtime, ferrying children about, caring for elderly parents, the mortgage, health, relationships. None of these are excuses; they are real, heavy burdens.

But please allow us to face one thing honestly together.

Time is the fairest thing in the world. Rich or poor, high or low, everyone has twenty-four hours in a day and 168 hours in a week. The president and the cleaner, the billionaire and the student — exactly the same, not a minute’s difference.

So when we say, “I don’t have time”, strictly speaking, that isn’t accurate. The accurate version is: “This hasn’t yet made it to the front of my priorities.”

The time-management writer Laura Vanderkam has long studied people’s time logs, and she has said something that cuts to the quick: rather than saying “I don’t have time”, say honestly, “It’s not a priority.” She suggests we try replacing “I don’t have time to exercise” with “Exercise is not a priority”, and you’ll immediately hear the weight of that sentence.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t to condemn us, but to move our focus from “time” to “priority”. For we cannot add a single second to our time, but our priorities are something we can adjust today.

We always make time for what matters

Just think about it.

However busy someone is, if their child has a 40-degree fever, will they take time off work? Yes. However busy someone is, if their parent is in hospital for surgery, will they rush to the hospital? Yes. However busy someone is, if someone they love dearly asks to see them, will they squeeze out two hours? Without fail.

We never make time for things because we’re “free”; we make time for things because they’re “important”.
