Even the busiest people make time for the people who matter.

So the question isn’t “Do I have time to serve God?” but “Is God the one who matters in my heart?”

The Lord Jesus said it directly: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) The word “first” is all about priority. The Lord didn’t say you needn’t look after your daily life; he said: put the order right, and he’ll take care of the rest.

Luke 10 records how Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). Notice that Martha wasn’t a bad person; she was the one who welcomed the Lord in — she was serving. But the Lord said to her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42)

Brothers and sisters, Martha’s problem wasn’t doing too much; it was getting the order wrong. She did the work first and drew near to the Lord afterwards; Mary sat at the Lord’s feet first and then went to do the work. The same day, the same guest, the same kitchen — change the order, and life tastes completely different.

Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” (Psalm 90:12) We count our days not to make ourselves anxious, but to gain a heart of wisdom, so that we spend our limited days on things that are eternal.

The Reformer Martin Luther is generally credited with saying, “I have so much to do today that I shall have to spend an extra hour in prayer.” By human reckoning that’s a waste; by God’s reckoning, it’s handing the whole day to the Lord who rules over time.

Serving isn’t adding one more thing; it’s doing everything with a different heart

At this point we need to pull down the biggest misunderstanding of all.

Many people think “serving” means “taking on one more role at church”, squeezing one more slot into a schedule that’s already full to bursting. If that were so, serving would of course become a burden — the last straw that breaks the camel’s back.

But the definition Scripture gives us is far broader:

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Eating and drinking — the two most ordinary, least “spiritual” things in daily life. If even eating and drinking can be done to the glory of God, what can’t be?

Paul also says, “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Brothers and sisters, did you catch that? What makes something serving isn’t what the thing is, but who it’s done for. The same washing-up done for yourself is housework; done for the Lord, it’s worship. The same meeting held for sales targets is work; held for the glory of God, it’s ministry.

So:

Work can be serving. Family can be serving. Daily living can be serving.

Serving isn’t doing one more thing; it’s doing everything with God’s heart.

When you see it this way, you’ll suddenly realise: it isn’t that you have no time to serve; you can serve twenty-four hours a day.

A 321 insight: where your focus is, there your time will be

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Most of the weariness of our generation comes from having the order upside down: things first, then people, and last of all, barely squeezing out a little time for God. So the tasks multiply, the heart grows drier, and people grow ever more tired.

Put the order back the right way, and you’ll find you seem to have more time. Because when you align yourself with God first, you no longer need tasks to prove yourself; and when you don’t need to prove yourself, you don’t have to do so many things that never needed doing.

321’s 920 practice puts it very practically: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Your spouse, your children, your parents, your colleagues, the person you meet every day — all of them are the “2” God has set before you. Live out a life of selflessness (0) towards them, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, this is serving that needs no extra time set aside. You were going to eat with your family anyway, going to work with your colleagues anyway — just lay down the “self” and invite Jesus onto the throne, and all that time becomes time for serving.

So please remember:

Where your focus is, there your time will be.

Your diary is your heart’s confession.

sections.heading: 4. Serving Is Grace, Not a Burden
sections.html:
How Paul saw himself

The last key point is also the foundation of the whole lesson.

“But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Everything Paul achieved in his life — three missionary journeys, thirteen letters, countless churches — he summed up in one sentence: by the grace of God.

He also said to Timothy, “I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service.” (1 Timothy 1:12) Notice the words “I thank him”. Paul doesn’t say, “Lord, look how much I’ve done for you”; he says, “Thank you for appointing me to serve.”

In Paul’s dictionary, serving was not something he gave to God; it was something God gave to him.

David was the same. When the Israelites gave willingly for the building of the temple, David prayed before God: “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” (1 Chronicles 29:14)

Brothers and sisters, what a way of seeing things. What we offer, what we lay down, what we serve with — it all came from God in the first place. We are simply giving God’s things back to God, and yet God still praises us and rewards us.

Even the ability to serve is God’s gift. So — there’s nothing to boast of, only thanks to give.

Understand that it’s grace, and three poisons lose their power

When we truly understand that serving is grace, three things are taken out of us.

First, we stop comparing. Comparison is the greatest killer of serving. That’s exactly what the Corinthian church was like: those who spoke in tongues looked down on those who didn’t; those who prophesied felt a cut above those who served at tables. Paul wanted them to know that the gifts are all worked by one and the same Spirit, and that no member of the body is superfluous. Since it is all grace, comparing is utterly meaningless — you wouldn’t take a present someone gave you, measure it against someone else’s, and then feel you were something special.

Second, we stop complaining. The root of complaining is “I’ve given so much — why does nobody notice?” The assumption behind that sentence is: serving is something I give out, so I ought to receive something back. But if serving is itself grace, an opportunity God has given me, then I’ve already received first — so what is there to complain about?

Third, we stop being lazy. In Matthew 25 the servant who received one talent said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” (Matthew 25:25) And how did the master answer? “You wicked and slothful servant” (Matthew 25:26). Brothers and sisters, notice that his problem wasn’t small ability, but burying what God had entrusted to him. The root of laziness is often fear; and the root of that fear is seeing the Lord as a harsh master, not as a Father full of grace.

In their place come three beautiful things: gratitude, treasuring, and seizing the opportunity.

Because being able to serve is itself a blessing.

Those who serve are blessed first

This is not just a spiritual way of speaking; it is also an observable fact.

In a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that participants who kept a regular record of things they were grateful for did markedly better in well-being, optimism and physical comfort than control groups who recorded only their troubles or ordinary events. Gratitude isn’t self-consolation; gratitude really does change a person.

On the serving side, Rodlescia Sneed and Sheldon Cohen of Carnegie Mellon University in the United States reported, in a study published in 2013 in the journal Psychology and Aging, that adults over fifty who had volunteered at least two hundred hours in the past year had a significantly lower risk of later developing high blood pressure.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t saying we serve for the sake of our health. It simply confirms once again what Scripture said long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35) When God made us, he wrote “giving out brings greater joy” into our design.

Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying, “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.” This is exactly the attitude of grace — not because I am great, but because the Lord’s love is great.

A 321 insight: not that I can, but that the Lord can

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

“Not that I can, but that the Lord can” — these few words say everything about both core values.

“Not that I can” — this is letting Jesus be King. Only one can sit on the throne. When I say, “I can”, I climb onto a seat that doesn’t belong to me; that is exactly what 321 calls pride: leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Humility, on the other hand, is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

“But that the Lord can” — this is letting Jesus receive all the glory. If our serving makes people see my competence, my eloquence, my sacrifice, then we’ve stolen the glory; if our serving makes people see the Lord’s grace, the Lord’s faithfulness, the Lord’s power, that is the very purpose of serving.

The secret of Paul’s whole life lies in that one sentence: “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

So please remember:

Not that I can, but that the Lord can.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From “I Can’t” to “I’m Willing”
sections.html:
Let’s put everything we’ve seen today back into the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45) The Lord is the ruler of the universe, yet he took a towel, wrapped it round his waist, crouched down and washed his disciples’ feet, and said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” (John 13:14) Who can serve? First look at the Lord who serves us.

The Bible is my standard. It isn’t my feelings that say whether I’m qualified, nor other people’s opinions that say whether I’m up to it, but what God’s word says. And God’s word says: the willing can all serve.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. We don’t grit our teeth in our own strength; we rely on the power of the Holy Spirit. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll have strength; rely on the brain and yourself, and all you’ll have left is anxiety.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King — King over my schedule, King over my sense of competence, King over my weakness.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when the serving is done, the applause goes to him; when it fails, we still trust him.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. One person’s serving is a point; a group serving together is a system. God has never set out to make a few stars; God is building his body.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

“I’m not good enough”, “I don’t have the gift”, “I don’t have the time” — brothers and sisters, all three sentences have the same subject: “I”.

The self-centred always have their eyes fixed on themselves: my level, my face, my schedule, my gains and losses. So the more they look, the less they dare to move.

The selfless have their eyes fixed on the Lord: the Lord sends, and I go; the Lord provides, and I have; the Lord values it, and I offer it.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Interestingly, “I’m not good enough” sounds very humble, but at its core it is still pride — because it is still calculating about the self, still insisting on being good enough before daring to step out. True humility isn’t thinking less of yourself; it’s not thinking about yourself. It isn’t feeling that you can’t; it’s knowing that the Lord can.

The Fivefold Change and the Shift in Perspective

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that ministry comes last. So we don’t start by pushing people into serving roles; we first let the mindset change — when someone truly believes that “the willing can all serve”, their life begins to loosen, their daily living begins to adjust, their relationships begin to be filled with God’s love, and ministry naturally grows out of it.

The shift in perspective happens here too: from man’s perspective to God’s — man says, “I’m not worthy”; God says, “My grace is sufficient for you”; from earthly to heavenly — earth calculates gains and losses, heaven counts faithfulness; from temporary to eternal — a cup of cold water offered today will never lose its reward; from worldly to godly — the world looks at the size of the gift, God looks at whether the heart is willing.

920 and 235

The 920 practice: start with the one “2” beside you. You needn’t wait for the church to advertise a vacancy; your family, your colleagues, your neighbours are the ones you serve. Living a selfless life towards them and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — that is the most solid serving there is.

235 relationships: become a “2” with a brother or sister who is likewise selfless, supporting each other and starting out together; establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that the experienced lead those just starting out; and finally become a “5” — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11) — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together.

Brothers and sisters, no one serves alone. If you’re afraid to take the first step, find a “2” and take it together.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: Practise taking the first step

Don’t wait until you’re ready to begin. Begin today: do one small act of service, help one person. Let action bring growth.

Information: first let the truth into your mind. Commit this sentence to memory — not knowing first and then doing; doing first and then knowing. God’s order is first sending, then equipping (Exodus 4:12).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your brain to your heart, so that you “see” it for yourself. You might pray like this: Lord, open my eyes, and let me see that you have never once despised my inadequacy; you are only waiting for my willingness.

Conviction: make a decision. Not “I’ll give it a try”, but “I believe God can use me right now.” Conviction is standing on God’s word before you’ve seen the outcome.

Implementation: this week, do one act of service so small it couldn’t be smaller. Pour a glass of water, wipe down a chair, send a message to say hello, pray for someone for five minutes, see an elderly member home. “Indeed, who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10) The Lord says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10)

Evaluation: when you’ve done it, be still for three minutes and ask yourself: What was I thinking about while I did it? Was I thinking about being seen, or about that person? Did I get upset because I didn’t do it well? Getting upset usually means I’m still looking at myself.

Correction: hand what you’ve discovered over to the Lord, adjust your motives, adjust your approach — but don’t give up. A child who falls off doesn’t stop learning to ride; he picks up the bike and rides again.

Repetition: don’t do it just once. Set a rhythm — at least one thing every week. Only repetition turns an “event” into “life”.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister who is just as afraid to step out, and invite them to do it with you. You’ll go from being someone who is equipped to someone who equips others. That is the “3” of 235.

Practice 2: Practise handing your limits to God

Place what you have — your time, your abilities, your resources — in God’s hands, and let God use it and enlarge it.

Information: God is the God who makes something from nothing and much from little (Psalm 33:9). Five loaves were handed over, and five thousand were fed (Matthew 14:19–21).

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you truly see what the “five loaves” in your own hands are. Don’t belittle them. A skill of yours, a free slot in your week, a car, a kitchen, a pair of ears willing to listen — they are all loaves.

Conviction: believe that “what is handed over doesn’t become less; it only becomes more.” This is the exact opposite of the world’s arithmetic, so it takes faith.

Implementation: this week, hand over one specific thing. It could be a fixed fifteen minutes each day to intercede for others; it could be a monthly offering; it could be opening up your skill for the church or your neighbours to use. As you hand it over, learn to say what the disciples said: Lord, take it — it’s yours.

Evaluation: check whether you’re handing it over with one hand and taking it back with the other. After handing it over, do you keep watching to see whether it’s being used properly?

Correction: if you find you’re still calculating gains and losses, come back to the cross and say to the Lord again: Yet not I, but your grace (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Repetition: keep on handing it over. Faith is like a muscle: hand it over once and it’s a moment of being moved; hand it over a hundred times and it’s life.

Multiplication: tell the story of your own “five loaves and two fish” — give your testimony. Your testimony will become someone else’s courage to step out.

Practice 3: Practise adjusting your priorities

Examine your life: is God in first place? Deliberately set aside time to draw near to God and to serve others. Let your life return to the right order.

Information: the Lord says, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) Get the order right, and God takes care of the rest.

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see your real priorities. The method is very simple — lay out how you spent the past seven days. Where your time has gone, there your heart is.

Conviction: decide to believe that “giving my best time to God won’t cost me anything; I can only gain.”

Implementation: do two things this week. First, set a fixed time every day for morning devotion and prayer, write it in your diary, and treat it like an important meeting. Second, reserve a fixed slot in your diary for “serving others”. Whatever isn’t scheduled never happens.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back and ask yourself: Where did I rank God this week? Is there something I keep saying matters, yet never seem to have time for?

Correction: don’t change too much at once. First protect the smallest, most sustainable unit — even if it’s just ten minutes a day. A small habit you can keep up beats a grand plan that collapses after three days.

Repetition: let it become the rhythm of your life, like eating and sleeping.

Multiplication: agree with a family member or your spiritual companion to remind each other and report back to each other. One person easily slackens; two people go a long way.

A Gentle Reminder: What is holding you back?

The lesson reminds us that what holds you back from serving is not ability, but three things: fear, limits and self-centredness.

Fear. Fear of not doing it well, fear of being judged, fear that once you commit you’ll never get out of it. Scripture says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” (1 John 4:18) It isn’t that you stop being afraid first and then love; it’s that in love, fear is cast out.

Limits. These are the lines we draw for ourselves: “That isn’t my gift”, “Someone with my personality isn’t suited to it”, “I’m too old”, “I’m too young”. These lines weren’t drawn by God; we drew them. God says, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child.’” (Jeremiah 1:7)

Self-centredness. This is the deepest layer. At the core of fear is being afraid that “I” will lose face; at the core of limits is protecting “my” comfort. So 321 is right: the self-centred life is the root of every problem.

Rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll shrink back; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll step out.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please hand these three things over to the Lord one by one, by name. Don’t just say vaguely, “Lord, please help me”; say specifically: Lord, this is what I’m afraid of; Lord, this is the line I’ve drawn for myself; Lord, this is the part of me I want to protect. What we name and hand over, God can take away from us, one thing at a time.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Willing
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we started with.

Who can serve?

Not the most capable. If it were, Moses would be out, because he was slow of speech and of a slow tongue.

Not those with the most time. If it were, Paul would be out, because he’d been in prison, was always on the road, and still had to make tents.

Not the most gifted. If it were, the boy who offered the five loaves would be out, because all he had was a lunch of barley bread.

Then who?

The willing.

“Your people offer themselves willingly in the day of your power, in holy array.” (Psalm 110:3) What God wants has always been a willing heart.

When you are willing, God goes to work. When you step out, God adds to you.

For “it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Even that “willingness” is something God put in your heart first. So if this morning there’s even a little stirring in your heart, even a little desire — that isn’t just your emotions; that is God’s call.

“I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)

When Isaiah said this, he had only just seen that he was “a man of unclean lips”, and his mouth had only just been touched by a live coal from the altar. He didn’t go after becoming worthy; he went after being touched by grace.

Brothers and sisters, today, let Jesus reign as King in your life; today, pass the five loaves in your hands over to him; today, put him back in first place in your diary. And then you’ll see with your own eyes: not enough becomes more than enough, the limited becomes limitless, the ordinary becomes glorious.

This is — a life of serving in grace.

All glory to our Lord Jesus Christ.

keyVerses: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
“I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)
practices: Practise taking the first step
Practise handing your limits to God
Practise adjusting your priorities
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I am willing to be used by you.
I will no longer look at my own inadequacy; I will trust in your provision. You speak, and it is done; you command, and it stands firm. You can make something out of nothing, and much out of little.

Lord, I confess that there is fear in me, there are lines I have drawn for myself, and there is a hidden self-centredness. Today I place each of these in your hands. Please take away my fear, tear down the limits I have set myself, and remove my self-centred life.
I am willing to take the first step of faith and place all that I have — my time, my abilities, my resources — in your hands. Like that boy, I pass my five loaves to you.
Thank you for the grace of serving you. Yet not I, but your grace which is with me.
Please help me serve you faithfully all my life, let you be King in my life, let you receive all the glory, and live out your glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “I’m not good enough yet, I don’t have the gift, I don’t have the time” — which of these three sentences comes up most often in your heart? Set it beside 2 Corinthians 12:9: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” If this verse is true, what is the one small step you are willing to take today?

Look at Matthew 14:18: “He said, ‘Bring them here to me.’” Which of the “five loaves” is in your hands — time, ability, resources, a skill, a relationship? This week, how will you concretely place it in the Lord’s hands, and invite a spiritual companion to do it with you?
l160.title: Who Can Serve?
l160.subtitle: A Life of Service Within Grace
l160.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: If Serving Has Worn You Out, Perhaps It Isn’t Too Much Work — Perhaps It’s the Wrong Source
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion we are going to walk a road together — the Path of Serving.

Before we begin, I’d like you to be still for ten seconds and answer one question honestly: over this past year, has your serving grown more and more full of life, or more and more like a burden?

I once heard a brother who had served for many years put it like this: “It isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just tired. I go to the prayer meeting, I go on the visits, on Sundays I’m the first to arrive and the last to leave. But one morning I was sitting in the car and suddenly I didn’t want to get out. I realised it had been a long time since I’d felt any joy in working for the Lord. I was just getting through the things I ‘ought to do’.”

Brothers and sisters, does that kind of weariness sound familiar?

Many people think serving means doing things, finishing tasks, giving our time and our abilities. And so the way we measure our serving comes down to three numbers: how much I did, how long I did it, and how many people saw. When the job is done, we say we served today; when it isn’t, we feel we’ve let God down.

But the Bible shows us a deeper truth.

Serving is not about “what we do”.

Serving is about “where it comes from, whom we rely on, and for whom we live”.

At the close of Romans 11, Paul wrote the loftiest line of praise in the whole letter: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36) It is one short sentence, yet it traces the whole arc of a life: everything comes out of God, everything moves through God, everything returns to God.

True serving is walking along that arc — beginning from God, moving by God, living for God, and in the end giving everything back to God.

This road can be summed up in five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”; Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that these five words are exactly the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values of 321? Spirit, Understanding and Life are the Three Foundations — the root of our life; Service and God are the Two Core Values — the fruit of our life. And all of this together accomplishes the one Goal — to establish God’s system.

So the Path of Serving is not a set of ministry techniques, not a duty roster, and certainly not a job description. It is a cycle of life, the road we walk before God all our days.

This morning, let’s walk this road step by step: first the starting point of serving — beginning with “Spirit”; then the process of serving — from “Understanding” to “Life”; and finally the goal of serving — from “Service” to “God”.

May the Lord, through his word, renew our mindset about serving. For on the 321 road we often say: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This morning’s devotion begins with a renewed mindset.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: How a Single Line of Praise Becomes a Lifetime of Service
sections.html:
Our theme scripture is a single verse, yet it is the summit of an entire book. To really understand it, we first need to know where it stands.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally thought to have been written between AD 56 and 57 in Corinth, Greece, as Paul’s third missionary journey was drawing to a close and he was preparing to take the gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia up to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26).

The church in Rome, which received the letter, was not one Paul had founded himself. It was a church he had never set foot in, yet had long carried on his heart, made up of believers from Jewish backgrounds and believers from Gentile backgrounds. Between the two groups there was tension, comparison, and mutual contempt. The Jewish believers saw themselves as the original root; the Gentile believers saw themselves as the vigorous new branches.

So in Romans 1 to 8 Paul sets out the heart of the gospel — all have sinned, and we are justified by faith alone; and in chapters 9 to 11 he deals specifically with the question of Israel and the Gentiles. He uses the picture of an olive tree: the Gentiles are only wild olive shoots grafted in — “it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you” (Romans 11:18b).

By the end, Paul finds that human reasoning has reached its limit. God’s plan is too deep, too wide, too wonderful for anyone to fathom fully. So he stops analysing and begins to worship:

“Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!” (Romans 11:33)

“For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34)

“Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?” (Romans 11:35)

“For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

Brothers and sisters, notice the pointed question in verse 35: “Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?” That one sentence cuts clean through every bargaining instinct within us. No one can give God anything first so that God ends up in our debt. Everything we have, we first received.

That being so, serving is never “I’ve done this much for God, so God owes me that much”; serving is “I have received everything from God, so I give everything back to him”.

Now let’s look at the original language of this verse. Paul uses three very simple Greek prepositions, and with them he says everything there is to say about the order of the universe:

“Of him” is ἐξ αὐτοῦ (ex autou), meaning “out of him” — it speaks of the source. All things come out of him.

“Through him” is δι᾽ αὐτοῦ (di autou), meaning “by means of him” — it speaks of the process and the means. All things exist through him and move through him.

“To him” is εἰς αὐτόν (eis auton), meaning “towards him” — it speaks of the destination and the purpose. All things ultimately point to him.

Source, process, destination — brothers and sisters, this is the very skeleton of today’s lesson. The source of serving is “Spirit”; the process of serving is “Understanding” and “Life”; the destination of serving is “Service” and “God”. This one verse of Paul’s is the firmest biblical foundation for “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God”.

There’s one more key point that many people overlook when they read Romans: the verse right after 11:36 is 12:1.

“Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (Romans 12:1)

Do you see it? Paul’s praise and worship did not stop at feeling; it led straight into a life offered up in service. That word “Therefore” is the hinge of the whole letter to the Romans. Because all things are of him, through him and to him, therefore — I offer myself.

The word for “service” here is λατρεία (latreia), which originally referred to the priests’ work of worship in the temple; and “spiritual” translates λογικήν (logikēn), which means “reasonable, rational, fitting”. Paul is saying: once you understand that God is the source, the means and the destination, offering your whole self is the only conclusion that makes sense.

Brothers and sisters, this is the starting point of the Path of Serving. Not that someone put you on the roster, not that someone asked you to help out, but that you have seen the riches of God, and so you gladly lay yourself on the altar.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Starting Point of Serving — Beginning with “Spirit”
1. The Starting Point of Serving Is Not Ability, but the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if someone asked you, “What do you need most to begin serving?”, most people would answer: gifts, time, experience, eloquence, stamina.

But the answer the Bible gives us is: the source.

“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

“Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, ‘This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies.’” (Zechariah 4:6)

These two passages — one about daily living, one about ministry — are saying the very same thing: don’t do God’s work out of your own reserves.

“Trust” in Hebrew is בָּטַח (batach), and the picture in this word is vivid: “to lean your whole weight on something”, like an exhausted man slumping his whole body against a wall — not steadying himself lightly with a hand, but entrusting himself completely. “Understanding” is בִּינָה (binah), the capacity to discern, to judge, to see into things. Solomon isn’t saying understanding is bad; he’s saying that however sharp your powers of analysis, they can never take the place of your reliance on God.

sections.heading: 2. A Lampstand Cannot Make Its Own Oil
sections.html:
The background to Zechariah 4:6 is even more stirring.

In 538 BC, King Cyrus of Persia issued a decree allowing the exiles of Judah to return. Zerubbabel led the first group of people back to Jerusalem and began rebuilding the temple. But the work had barely begun when it stopped, and it stood still for some sixteen years. Enemies opposed it from outside; the people lost heart within. Then God raised up the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, around 520 BC.

God gave Zechariah a vision: a lampstand of pure gold with a bowl on top, seven lamps on the lampstand, and two olive trees beside it, one on the right of the bowl and one on the left (Zechariah 4:2–3).

Brothers and sisters, what is the crucial point of this vision? It is this — a lampstand cannot make its own oil.

However precious, however finely made, however bright the golden lampstand may be, it cannot produce a single drop of oil by itself. The oil flows from the olive trees beside it, supplied unceasingly through the pipes. The only thing the lampstand has to do is stay connected to the source of the oil, and then shine well.

And then God spoke those words: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”

Zerubbabel had no army, no treasury, no royal authority. God said: never mind, you don’t need any of those. What you need is my Spirit.

It’s the same for us as we serve today. You may feel you’re not eloquent enough, not learned enough, short of time, short of influence. God says: never mind. You are not the maker of the oil; you are the lampstand. Your only responsibility is to stay connected to the Holy Spirit who supplies the oil.

The Lord Jesus himself put it very plainly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) The branch doesn’t manufacture life; the branch simply stays connected. Get the connection right, and the fruit will come of itself.

sections.heading: 3. Why Serving Runs Dry: Burnout through the Lens of Psychology
sections.html:
Many people grow tired, dry and unmotivated in their serving, not because there’s too much to do, but because the source is wrong.

Modern research offers us some indirect confirmation of this.

In 2019 the World Health Organization (WHO), in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), formally listed “burnout” as an “occupational phenomenon”, defining it as “a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”, and naming three characteristics: first, exhaustion of energy; second, mental distance from one’s job and negative feelings towards it; and third, reduced professional efficacy.

Earlier still, in 1981, the American social psychologist Christina Maslach, together with Susan Jackson, published the Maslach Burnout Inventory, which identified three dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed something? The first sign of burnout is not “I can’t get it all done”, but “I’m empty inside”. People aren’t crushed by the workload; they’re crushed when what goes out is greater than what comes in.

A phone that’s only used and never charged will run down to zero in half a day, however new the battery. A well that’s only drawn from and never refilled will run dry, however deep it is. Serving is just the same.

So the question has never been “Should I do a bit less?” The question is “Am I connected to the source?”

sections.heading: 4. Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set these two roads side by side.

Rely on the brain and on yourself, and the result is pressure, anxiety and exhaustion. Because your head has to do all the calculating, all the controlling, and predict every outcome. When things don’t turn out as expected, you blame yourself; when others don’t cooperate, you get angry; when things do succeed, you quietly grow proud.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and the result is peace, strength and joy. Because you know it isn’t you who makes things happen. You simply hand over your hands and let the God who is truly at work do the work.

In 321 we often say: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. This isn’t looking down on reason; it’s putting reason back in its proper place. The Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The wellspring of life doesn’t flow out of your diary; it flows out of your heart.

Paul puts it even more directly: “not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Brothers and sisters, relying on the Holy Spirit is not a feeling; it is a choice. Feelings rise and fall; a choice can be made afresh every day.

Every morning you can make a choice: today I will not rely on my own cleverness; I will rely on your Spirit. That choice is the first step on the Path of Serving.

In the opening of Book One of his Confessions, the church father Augustine wrote a prayer that has been handed down for sixteen hundred years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Brothers and sisters, if our serving does not rest in God, it too will never find rest.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves
sections.html:
Among the Three Foundations of 321, the very first is: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

It isn’t the least important of the three; it’s the one that comes first. Because if you don’t first let the Holy Spirit guide you, your Bible reading is just reading for knowledge, and your following of Jesus is just imitating the outside.

That is exactly why the first word on the Path of Serving is “Spirit”: the first question isn’t “What am I going to do?”, but “Whom am I relying on?”

This is also a shift of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from the worldly perspective to the godly perspective. Man’s perspective says: however many resources I have, that’s how much I can do. God’s perspective says: however great God’s power is, that’s how much he can accomplish through me.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s plug our serving back into its power source, the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Process of Serving — From “Understanding” to “Life”
1. The Work of the Holy Spirit Is to Lead Us into the Truth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the work of the Holy Spirit is not only to give us power, but even more to lead us into understanding God’s word.

“But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.” (John 14:26)

“However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.” (John 16:13)

These two verses are promises the Lord Jesus gave his disciples with his own lips at the Last Supper, before he went to the cross.

“Counselor” in Greek is παράκλητος (paraklētos), which literally means “the one called alongside” — a helper, an advocate, the one who is always at your side. He doesn’t watch you from a distance; he comes and walks beside you.

“Guide” in the original is ὁδηγήσει (hodēgēsei), a word made up of “way” (ὁδός) and “lead” (ἡγέομαι), meaning “to lead the way, to take you along this road”. The Chinese Union Version even adds a small note here: “the original reads ‘into’”.

Brothers and sisters, this word is so precious. The Holy Spirit doesn’t hand you a map and say, “Off you go on your own.” The Holy Spirit takes you by the hand and leads you, step by step, into the truth.

So “Understanding” isn’t something we crack with our own cleverness; “Understanding” is where the Holy Spirit leads us in. That’s why the order of the Three Foundations is: first the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and only then does the Bible become our standard. Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just an ancient book; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible is a living word.

sections.heading: 2. The Crucial Turn: Don’t Stop at “Understanding”
sections.html:
But brothers and sisters, there’s a great danger here.

The danger isn’t that we don’t understand; the danger is that we understand and then stop at understanding.

The Lord Jesus spoke about this very solemnly. At the close of the Sermon on the Mount, he said:

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)

In the next verse he said: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” (Matthew 7:26)

Notice that these two kinds of people have one thing in common: they both “heard”. The same sermon, the same Lord, the same words. The only difference lies in two little phrases: “does them” and “doesn’t do them”.

The Lord didn’t say “everyone who understands these words of mine”; he said “everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them”. In the kingdom of heaven, the foundation is not built on comprehension; the foundation is built on obedience.

James is even more blunt: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Brothers and sisters, hearing the word without doing it isn’t merely a pity; the Bible calls it “deluding your own selves” — with the words “I know”, we fool ourselves into believing we’ve already changed.

This is the turn from “Understanding” to “Life”: understanding has to go on to living it out.

sections.heading: 3. The Parable of the Seed: From Drifting in the Air to Taking Root and Bearing Fruit
sections.html:
The lesson uses a beautiful picture, so let’s open it up.

A prompting of the Holy Spirit on its own is like a seed drifting in the air. It is real, it is precious, but it cannot come to land. You’re touched in a meeting, you weep, your heart burns within you — and three days after you get home, it has faded. That is the seed drifting in the air.

Add the word of God, and the seed begins to land. When a prompting is caught by the truth, it is no longer just emotion; it becomes direction. You don’t just “feel you ought to be a little kinder to someone”; you say, “Because the Lord said to forgive seventy times seven, I’m going to make that phone call today.”

When we actually go and do it, the seed begins to take root. Action carries truth out of the head into our life, and out of our life into our daily living.

In the parable of the sower the Lord Jesus said: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.” (Luke 8:15) Look at those three actions: having heard the word, holding it tightly, producing fruit with perseverance. Hearing is the beginning, holding on is the process, bearing fruit is the result. Leave out the holding on in the middle, and you will wait for fruit for ever.

Speaking of seeds, I’m reminded of something that really happened. In 2005, Israeli scientists planted a Judean date palm seed recovered from the ruins of Masada. Radiocarbon dating placed the seed between roughly the first century BC and the first century AD — in other words, it was almost exactly contemporary with the Lord Jesus. Astonishingly, it sprouted, and grew into a healthy date palm, which the scientists named “Methuselah”. The research was led by Sarah Sallon and colleagues, and the results were published in the journal Science in 2008.

Brothers and sisters, a seed can lie dormant in the ground for two thousand years and still be alive. The word of God placed in your heart is the same. There are truths you heard ten years ago that you thought were dead; in fact they have only been waiting for a chance to be “done”. When you are willing to take that step, two-thousand-year-old life will sprout in you.

sections.heading: 4. From “Knowing” to “Doing”: Confirmation from Psychology
sections.html:
Why is it that we understand, and yet we cannot do it?

Psychologists call this the “intention-behaviour gap”. In a review published in 2016 in Social and Personality Psychology Compass, the British psychologists Paschal Sheeran and Thomas Webb pointed out that while people’s intentions do predict their behaviour, they explain only a fairly limited part of the change in behaviour. In other words, between “I want to” and “I actually did” there runs a very wide river.

So where is the bridge?

In research published in 1999 in the journal American Psychologist, the German psychologist Peter Gollwitzer put forward the concept of “implementation intentions”: when someone doesn’t just say “I’m going to pray”, but says specifically, “Tomorrow morning at seven, as soon as I sit down at my desk, I’ll first pray aloud for five minutes”, the rate at which the action is carried out rises markedly. A meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran in 2006, drawing together ninety-four studies, also supported this effect.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a very practical reminder: making the truth concrete is the best bridge from “Understanding” to “Life”.

Don’t say, “I want to love people more.” Say, “At lunchtime today, I’ll take the initiative and phone the relative I’ve been avoiding.”

Don’t say, “I want to read the Bible more.” Say, “Tomorrow morning at half past six, I’ll read John 13 and write down one sentence God says to me.”

Once a truth has a time, a place and a person attached, it has come down from the air to land.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Change the Mindset and You Change the Life; Change the Life and You Change Daily Living
sections.html:
The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice that ministry comes last. Not because ministry doesn’t matter, but because ministry is the fruit, not the root. If the root isn’t deep enough, the fruit won’t last.

“Understanding” is a change of mindset; “Life” is a change of life and of daily living. If you skip mindset and life and rush straight into ministry, your serving is a house built on the sand — in peaceful days you can’t tell, but when the storm comes, it falls.

This is also what 321 means by: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, this stretch of the road also corresponds exactly to the second and third of the Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard (Understanding), and Jesus is my role model (Life). The Holy Spirit leads us into the Bible, the Bible brings us before Jesus, and Jesus becomes the pattern we live out all our lives.

From Spirit, to Understanding, to Life — this is a road that drives its roots downward. The deeper the roots go, the longer the fruit keeps coming.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Goal of Serving — From “Service” to “God”
1. When Life Grows, Serving Flows Out Naturally
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when life truly grows, serving doesn’t need anyone to push it; it flows out naturally.

It’s like an apple tree. Nobody has to tell it, “You must try hard to produce apples.” As long as its roots are deep, it has water enough and sunlight enough, in due season it bears fruit. Bearing fruit isn’t the tree’s job; bearing fruit is the tree’s nature.

The Lord Jesus left us that everlasting pattern:

“For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)

When did he say this? Right after he had washed his disciples’ feet.

Let’s look at what comes before it, for it is one of the most moving turns in the whole Bible:

“Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:3–5)

Brothers and sisters, notice the cause and effect here. John doesn’t say, “Because Jesus was humble, he went and washed their feet.” He says: Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands, knew that he had come from God and was going to God — and so he rose, took a towel, poured water, and washed their feet.

In other words, the Lord was able to stoop down precisely because he knew clearly where he had come from and where he was going.

Have you noticed that this is Romans 11:36 all over again? Coming from God is “of him”; going to God is “to him”; and the stretch in between, bending low to wash feet, is “through him”.

In those days, washing feet was the work of the lowest servant in the household. Some rabbinic rules even held that a Jewish slave need not wash his master’s feet — that was a job for a Gentile slave. Yet the Lord of the universe, at the very moment he knew he possessed all things, chose to pick up the towel.

Brothers and sisters, people who are insecure in their identity don’t dare to stoop. Only those who know their identity is secure in God dare to put themselves in the lowest place.

This is what 321 means: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

sections.heading: 2. The Most Important Key in Serving: To Whom the Glory Goes
sections.html:
Next comes the sharpest cut in this lesson.

The most important key in serving is not how much you’ve done, but to whom the glory goes.

“If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.” (1 Peter 4:11)

Here Peter sets down two “as” clauses. Speaking must be as the very words of God; serving must be as of the strength God supplies. Both of them remind us: the content isn’t yours, and the strength isn’t yours either.

And since the content isn’t mine and the strength isn’t mine, then the glory of the outcome is certainly not mine.

Paul puts it even more honestly: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Paul admits that he worked harder than the rest — that was a fact, and he wasn’t putting on false modesty. But he immediately adds: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.

Brothers and sisters, this is mature serving — being able to admit openly that you’ve done a great deal, while knowing clearly that none of it was really you.

sections.heading: 3. The Real Reason for Weariness: That Unnoticed Shift of Focus
sections.html:
So much serving is exhausting because, without our noticing, the focus has shifted onto ourselves.

Wanting to be seen.

Wanting to be affirmed.

Wanting to prove ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, most of us have probably admitted those three things to ourselves on some night or other. This is the self-centred life.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take the place of God. When I want to be seen in my serving, I quietly move God’s place over and give it to myself.

And self-centred serving has one fatal mark: it needs a return. It needs applause, it needs thanks, it needs to be remembered. Once the return stops, the serving stops; once someone criticises, bitterness sets in. 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Most of the tension in a church doesn’t come from monstrous sin; it comes from two self-centred lives colliding.

Here too psychology holds up a mirror for us.

In research published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect”: people significantly overestimate how much others are paying attention to them. In the experiment, participants walked into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt, and afterwards estimated that about half the people there would have noticed it — but the number who actually noticed was far lower.

Brothers and sisters, that’s a discovery that both stings and sets us free. It stings because we spend so much effort trying to be seen, and in fact not that many people are watching. It sets us free because, since not that many people are watching, we can stop performing.

There’s an even more positive line of research. Self-Determination Theory, developed from 1985 onwards by the American psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, shows that when a person’s behaviour springs from inner, autonomous motivation rather than from outward rewards or other people’s opinions, their engagement, creativity and well-being are all higher, and they are better able to keep going.

Science can only go as far as “inner motivation”. But the Bible tells us that deeper than inner motivation is the motivation of “Christ in me”.

sections.heading: 4. Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing; It Is Entering into the Infinite
sections.html:
So what is true serving?

It is selflessness — letting Jesus be King.

It is selflessness — letting the glory go to God.

But brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand. The “selflessness” 321 speaks of is not erasing yourself, not denying yourself until you’re nothing, and certainly not being without worth.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Paul says, “it is no longer I who live”, yet he didn’t disappear; on the contrary, he lived with more power than anyone. Because that limited “I” stepped aside, and the infinite Christ lived out his life within.

A cup filled with its own water can’t hold anything else. Only when it’s emptied can it be filled with living water. Emptying isn’t a loss; emptying is so that you can receive the infinite.

John the Baptist said it all in one line: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

Brothers and sisters, only serving like this will be light, will last, and will bear fruit.

The Lord himself has promised: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

A yoke is made for two oxen. When the yoke feels heavy, it’s often because you’re trying to pull it alone. Learning from him means coming alongside him and letting him share the yoke with you.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Not I, but Christ; All the Glory to God
sections.html:
The last two words on the Path of Serving, “Service” and “God”, are precisely the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Letting Jesus be King means asking in every decision: who has the final say here?

Letting Jesus receive all the glory means saying after every achievement: yet not I.

And these two core values together accomplish the one Goal — to establish God’s system. God’s system is not an organisation; it is a company of selfless people among whom Jesus truly reigns as King.

Brothers and sisters, there’s a deep comfort here. Since the glory goes to God, the outcome is handed over to God as well. You no longer need to be anxious about success or failure, because success and failure are not your responsibility — faithfulness is. The Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Matthew 25:21)

The Lord didn’t say “good and successful servant”. What he said was faithful.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal
1. Five Words, One Road
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, now that we’ve come this far, I want to lay today’s road out before you once more.

Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide. This is the first foundation; it is the source.

Understanding — the Bible is my standard. This is the second foundation; it is the direction.

Life — Jesus is my role model. This is the third foundation; it is the pattern.

Service — let Jesus be King. This is the first core value.

God — let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the second core value.

These five words together accomplish the one Goal: to establish God’s system.

You see, this isn’t forcing 321 onto the lesson; the five words of the lesson are themselves the skeleton of 321. The Path of Serving is the 321 road.

Now set it back alongside our theme verse: all things are “of him”, so serving begins with Spirit; all things are “through him”, so serving moves along through Understanding and Life; all things are “to him”, so serving ends in Service and God. Romans 11:36 is a verse, and it is also a map.

sections.heading: 2. From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
The mark of the old self is the self-centred life; the mark of the new self is selflessness.

Self-centred serving asks: How much have I done? Did anyone see? Has my effort been recognised?

Selfless serving asks: Lord, is this what you want? Have you received the glory?

The self-centred life is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; selflessness is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite attack isn’t to make you stop serving, but to make you, little by little, put yourself at the centre of your serving. He doesn’t need to make you fall; he only needs you to forget, while you’re shining, who gave you the oil.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change and the Priority of Relationships
sections.html:
321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with mindset. When your mindset about serving shifts from “doing things” to “the source”, your life begins to change; when your life changes, your daily living changes; when your daily living changes, your relationships change; and when your relationships change, ministry comes forth naturally.

That’s why we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Relationships have a priority too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. So much of the hurt in serving comes because we’ve turned that order upside down — we rush to get things done first, then deal with people, and only at the very end think of God. Once the order is upside down, serving becomes a burden.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
On the Path of Serving, 321 gives us two very concrete practices.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Before each “2”, as we practise living a selfless (0) life, we will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: the Bible says “fruit”, not “product”. A product is manufactured; fruit is grown. You can’t grit your teeth and manufacture patience; you can only stay joined to the Holy Spirit and let patience grow. That is exactly why “Spirit” has to come first.

235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, as spiritual companions to one another; build a “3”, having spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

One person can go fast; a company of selfless people can go far. The Path of Serving is not a road for lone rangers; it is a road with companions, with a legacy passed on, and with a team.

sections.heading: 5. A Fourfold Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
Finally, the Path of Serving brings a fourfold shift of perspective.

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: not asking “How do I feel about it?”, but “What does the Lord say?”

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective: not looking at the results in front of us, but at what heaven remembers.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective: not asking “Will this succeed this year?”, but “Will this count in eternity?”

From the worldly perspective to the godly perspective: not by might or by power, but by the Spirit of God.

Brothers and sisters, once the perspective turns, the whole road turns with it.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Five Practices, Plus the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
1. The Lesson’s Five Practices
sections.html:
First, establish the starting point: begin each day with “Spirit”.

Pray first every day, hand the day over to God, and deliberately rely on the Holy Spirit rather than on your own arrangements and plans.

Practice: pray aloud every day, “Lord, today I will not rely on myself, but only on your Spirit.”

Second, receive revelation: let God’s word into your heart.

Each day as you read the Bible, stop and reflect, and let the Holy Spirit speak to you.

Practice: write down one sentence God has spoken to you today, and turn it over again and again.

Third, live out the truth: turn knowing into doing.

Choose one truth you understand and deliberately put it into practice in daily living.

Practice: put at least one truth into practice today — forgiveness, patience or love, for example.

Fourth, serve proactively: let your life touch other lives.

Don’t wait to be moved before you act; go and show care to someone.

Practice: reach out to one person today — a message, a phone call, or a prayer on their behalf.

Fifth, give the glory to God: hand everything back to the Lord.

At the end of each day, hand all your serving and its results over to God.

Practice: pray, “Lord, you did it all; the glory is yours.”

sections.heading: 2. Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, a practice done only once is just a passing moment of being moved; a practice carried through all eight stages becomes a lifelong road.

Stage one: Information. Today you have received the information: the source of serving is the Holy Spirit, and the road of serving is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

Stage two: Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. You can ask right now: Lord, show me whom I have really been relying on in my serving these past days.

Stage three: Conviction. If revelation doesn’t reach the will, it remains mere knowledge. Conviction is saying: Lord, I acknowledge that you are right and I was wrong.

Stage four: Implementation. Start with that prayer tomorrow morning: “Lord, today I will not rely on myself, but only on your Spirit.” Fix the time and the place — what time, where, and towards whom.

Stage five: Evaluation. Set aside a time each week to be quiet and ask yourself: how many days this week did I really begin with the Spirit? Was there a time when, after finishing a task, I was secretly waiting for someone to praise me?

Stage six: Correction. Evaluation without correction is just regret. Correction is concrete: cross one item off that schedule where you overestimated yourself; make the phone call that mends the relationship you’ve long avoided.

Stage seven: Repetition. Doing it right once isn’t life; doing it until it comes naturally is life. Repeat it until relying on the Holy Spirit has become your instinct.

Stage eight: Multiplication. Once you’ve found your way through, take someone else along. Find a “2” and walk this road with them. The last mile of the Path of Serving is always handing the road on to the next person.

sections.heading: 3. A Gentle Reminder: When the Source Is Right, Serving Has Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson ends with a very important reminder for us:

The key to serving lies not in the tasks, but in the source.

When the source is right, serving has life; when the source is wrong, serving becomes a burden.

Don’t just ask, “What am I going to do?” First ask, “Whom am I relying on?”

The psalmist said it long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Labour in vain — those words are the gentlest and yet the most solemn reminder to every worn-out servant.

But God has also given a promise: “but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31)

Wait, and then be strengthened. The order cannot be reversed.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: It Isn’t You Working for God, but God Living in You
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, serving is not a short-lived enthusiasm; it is a lifelong road.

Enthusiasm fades, love grows cold, people change; but on this road, the Lord will walk with us to the very end.

As you walk this road, you will experience five “more and more”s:

You will be filled more and more with the Holy Spirit, because every day you begin with the Spirit.

You will understand the truth more and more, because the Holy Spirit guides you into God’s word.

You will live out life more and more, because you don’t only hear the word; you do it.

You will overflow with love more and more, because when life is full, it naturally spills over.

You will give the glory to God more and more, because you know it was not you.

And then, at the last, you’ll discover something wonderful:

You are not working for God; rather, God is in you, living out his own life.

Brothers and sisters, what a blessing this is. We used to think serving was what we gave to God; in the end we understand that serving is God living himself out through us.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

Even the good works we are to walk in, he prepared long ago. All we do is walk into them.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you.

The first invitation: plug back in. If you’ve been holding on by your own strength these past days, stop today and come back to the Holy Spirit, the source. Admitting you’re empty isn’t failure; it’s honesty.

The second invitation: bring the truth down to earth. Pick one thing God has said to you today, set a time, a place and a person, and go and do it today. Don’t leave it drifting in the air any longer.

The third invitation: hand over the glory. Tonight before you sleep, whatever you did or didn’t get done today, say one sentence to the Lord: Lord, you did it all; the glory is yours.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the end of the Path of Serving, and the starting point of every day.

May we all walk this road to the end, and on that day hear the Lord say: Well done, good and faithful servant.

keyVerses: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, let’s declare this aloud together:
Lord Jesus, I declare:
My serving begins from you, moves by you, and lives for you.
I do not rely on myself, but on the Holy Spirit.
I do not lift up myself, but lift up Jesus.
I will walk the road of Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God,
and let my life become your vessel.
All the glory belongs to you! Amen!
practices: Begin each day with “Spirit”: seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance and prompting first, then plan the day.
Each day, through “Understanding”, grasp and obey one truth from the Bible.
Before every “2”, practise selflessness and bear the fruit of the Spirit; walk with your spiritual companion.
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
You have shown us that all things are of you, through you and to you. Our life, our gifts, our time, our strength — not one of them did we earn ourselves; we received them all from you.

Lord, forgive us. So often we have done your work with our own cleverness and carried your burden with our own strength, until we grew tired, dry and discouraged — and then we thought it was you who had given us too much. Have mercy on us, we pray.
Holy Spirit, be our guide. Let us begin every day with you — not by might, not by power, but by your Spirit.
Open our hearts to understand your word; and even more, give us strength, so that we are not only hearers of the word but doers. Plant the truth within us, to take root and bear fruit.
Lord Jesus, reign as King in our serving. Take away the heart in us that wants to be seen, wants to be affirmed, wants to prove itself; make us selfless, so that you may receive all the glory.

May our serving no longer be a burden, but the rest of sharing your yoke with you. May we walk the road of Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God all our lives, and become vessels fit for your use.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Read Zechariah 4:6: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” Think back to a recent area of serving or responsibility that has left you feeling weary. Ask yourself honestly: in that matter, was I relying on the brain and on myself, or on the heart and the Holy Spirit? If you were to begin again with “Spirit”, what is the first thing you would need to lay down?

Read Matthew 7:24: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” Name one truth you have understood for a long time but have never put into practice. This week, at what time, in what place, and towards which person will you concretely put it into practice? Share it in your small group, and ask a spiritual companion to check in with you at the next meeting.
l161.title: The Path of Serving
l161.subtitle: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — A Lifelong Path Walked Before God
l161.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: The Starting Point of Serving Is Not Ability, but the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you a very simple question — but one that cuts deep.

When you hear the word “serving”, what is the first thought that rises in your heart?

My guess is that, for many people, the first sentence that rises up is: “What can I do?” Or else: “I can’t preach, I can’t play an instrument, I can’t lead a small group — what can I do?”

I once walked alongside a sister who had served in her church for seventeen years. Children’s Sunday school, welcoming, the kitchen, visiting, the finances — wherever there was a gap, she filled it. One year-end, at the church workers’ retreat, the pastor leading it asked everyone to share one sentence about how they’d been feeling lately. When her turn came, she was silent for a long time, and then she said something that hushed the whole room. She said, “I feel like a dishcloth that’s been wrung dry.”

She went on: “It isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. It’s just that … I don’t know when it started, but every time I go to church now, what’s on my mind is ‘how much is still left undone’, not ‘I’m going to meet my Lord’.”

Brothers and sisters, this is not an isolated case. It is the shared situation of many people today who love the Lord with real zeal. It isn’t that we don’t try hard enough; we try too hard. It isn’t that we do too little; we do too much, without setting out from the right source.

So today’s lesson takes us back to the most fundamental starting point of serving. The 321 Path of Serving has five stations: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. The first station isn’t “Service”, isn’t “doing” — the first station is “Spirit”: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Did you notice? In the 321 order, “Service” comes fourth, and “Spirit” comes first. That order isn’t arbitrary. That order decides whether your serving is an overflow of life or a draining of your strength.

The Bible gives us a starting point completely different from the world’s:

Serving does not begin with “I can”; serving begins with “the Holy Spirit”.

Look at the Lord Jesus. Before he began his ministry, something happened to him first. Luke records it like this: “Now when all the people were baptized, Jesus also had been baptized, and was praying. The sky was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form like a dove on him; and a voice came out of the sky, saying ‘You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased.’” (Luke 3:21–22)

Notice the order. The heavens opened, the Holy Spirit came down, the Father spoke, and then — only then — did he begin to serve. Thirty years of silence, and in return, a beginning anointed by the Holy Spirit.

This shows us a crucial truth: without the Holy Spirit there is no true serving; only with the Holy Spirit is there serving full of life and power.

Brothers and sisters, I want to say this very honestly: serving without the Holy Spirit isn’t serving with no results; it’s serving with a kind of “false result”. Numbers may grow, the atmosphere may be lively, the reports may look impressive, but lives are not touched, sin is not brought into the light, people are not brought before Jesus. The prophet Zechariah said it long ago: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

This verse was first spoken to Zerubbabel. At that time the people who had returned from exile were to rebuild the temple; they were short of hands, short of money, and surrounded by enemies who opposed them. God didn’t say, “I’ll give you more people and more money.” What God said was, “but by my Spirit”.

This morning, let’s find that starting point again together.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Settings, One Source
sections.html:
Today’s lesson has three theme scriptures, drawn from three different times and places, yet all pointing to the same source. Let’s first get the background clear, and they’ll be all the richer to read.

The first is Acts 1:8. The author of Acts is Luke, a physician and a co-worker on Paul’s missionary journeys. Luke’s Gospel and Acts are the two volumes of one work, by the same author, written to the same recipient, “Theophilus”, and they are generally thought to have been completed in the AD 60s. Luke’s Gospel records “all that Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), while Acts records what the ascended Lord went on doing in the church through the Holy Spirit. That’s why some say Acts could really be called “the Acts of the Holy Spirit”. Acts 1:8 is the last thing the Lord Jesus said before his ascension, and it is the key to the whole book — first power, and only then witness; first the coming of the Holy Spirit, and only then from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

The second is Galatians 5:25. Galatians is one of Paul’s earliest letters, generally thought to have been written around AD 49, to the churches in the region of Galatia. At that time a group of people had come into the churches teaching that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law to be saved. Paul was deeply troubled, and he asked a very heavy question: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3) Brothers and sisters, please hold on to that sentence.
