The Galatians’ mistake wasn’t that they didn’t believe in Jesus, but that they “began by the Spirit and then went on by themselves”. And that is exactly where most people who serve stumble today.

The third is Romans 8:6. Romans is the letter Paul wrote from Corinth to the church in Rome around AD 57, and it is the most complete exposition of salvation in the whole Bible. Chapter 7 describes a person’s struggle under the law — “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good” (Romans 7:18); chapter 8 changes key from its very first line: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:1–2) “Spirit” appears about twenty times in the chapter, making it the chapter with the greatest density of references to the Spirit in the whole Bible. Romans 8:6 sits right in this context: there are only two directions a life’s mind can take — one leads to death, the other to life and peace.

Let’s add one more piece of background: the word “spirit” itself. In Old Testament Hebrew the word is ruach; in New Testament Greek it is pneuma. Both words carry three meanings at once: wind, breath and spirit. So the Lord Jesus said to Nicodemus: “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8) In Greek, “wind” and “Spirit” are the same word, and the sentence is a beautiful play on words.

Brothers and sisters, the meaning of the word itself is teaching us. The wind is something you cannot make, but you can raise a sail to catch it. Breath is something you cannot store up, but you must take it in afresh every moment. The work of the Holy Spirit is the same: you cannot start him up, you can only yield to him; you cannot store up yesterday’s filling to live on today — you must come before him afresh every day.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Our Role Model — Beginning with the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
The first of the Three Foundations of 321 is “Jesus is my role model”. So when we talk about serving, the first thing to look at isn’t a successful church or a famous speaker, but the Lord Jesus himself.

The Lord Jesus’ ministry follows a very clear order: baptism, the coming of the Holy Spirit, being led by the Holy Spirit, and only then ministry full of power.

See how Luke records it: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil.” (Luke 4:1-2)

After the temptation was over, the text goes on: “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and news about him spread through all the surrounding area.” (Luke 4:14)

Read further and he goes into the synagogue in Nazareth, unrolls the scroll of Isaiah, and the first words he reads are: “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed.” (Luke 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, did you notice? In the Lord Jesus’ first sermon, the very first sentence is about the Holy Spirit. He didn’t say, “I have power.” He said, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me.”

Mark this well: it isn’t serving first and then the Holy Spirit; it’s the Holy Spirit first, and then serving begins.

Even more worth our attention is the stretch in the middle. After the Holy Spirit came, the first thing was not to bring Jesus into the synagogue, but to lead him “into the wilderness”. Forty days — no people, no applause, no results, only hunger and the devil’s temptations.

This tells us something extremely important: the Holy Spirit doesn’t only lead us into work; the Holy Spirit also shapes our life.

We often think that being filled with the Holy Spirit means plain sailing all the way, anointing overflowing, people healed wherever we go. But the first stop the Bible records is the wilderness. Because God first had to deal with those three temptations. “Turning stones into bread” is using your gifts to satisfy your own desires; “throwing yourself down from the pinnacle of the temple” is using miracles to prove your identity; “bowing down to worship me” is trading compromise for a bigger ministry territory. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? These three temptations are exactly the three places where servants of God in every generation most easily fall: gain, reputation and power. God had Jesus pass these three tests in the wilderness before he had any ministry at all.

A picture comes to mind. If you’re building a three-storey house, a foundation one metre deep is enough; if you’re building a thirty-storey tower, the foundation has to go down more than twenty metres. However high you build above ground, that’s how deep you must dig below. The wilderness is God digging the foundation beneath your life. Many people ask God to add more storeys but refuse to let him dig the foundation; and so the higher the building, the more dangerous it becomes.

Here we can also see an observation from psychology. In 1974 the American psychologist Herbert Freudenberger first used the word “burnout” to describe how the most passionate and committed people in the helping professions were in fact the most prone to exhaustion. Later, in 1981, Christina Maslach and Susan Jackson put forward a measurement scale identifying three dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (becoming cold towards the people one serves), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. In 2019 the World Health Organization included burnout in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, defining it as an occupational phenomenon resulting from “chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the people most prone to burnout aren’t the laziest, but the most zealous. Because zeal without a source is just burning yourself up. The lesson of the wilderness is God turning us from “burning ourselves up” to “burning with the Holy Spirit without being consumed” — like the bush Moses saw: “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2). The bush was not consumed because the fire did not come from the bush.

The 321 insight here is crystal clear: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

This is one of the most important orders in 321. Our natural order is often the reverse — ministry first, then relationships, and only at the very end do we think of life. As a result, the bigger the ministry grows, the more the relationships break down and the drier the life becomes. God’s order is: first let the Holy Spirit form life within me; when life is healthy, relationships come right; when relationships are right, ministry flows out naturally.

So: first be led by the Holy Spirit, and then you’ll have the Holy Spirit’s power.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Apostles’ Experience — Filled with the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
That’s how it was with the Lord Jesus; and what about his disciples? Exactly the same.

For forty days the risen Lord appeared to his disciples, and then he was about to ascend. He didn’t say, “Hurry up and go out and preach the gospel.” What he said was: “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.” (Acts 1:4)

Brothers and sisters, this is truly astonishing. What CEO in the world would say to a group of staff who had already had three and a half years of training, “Don’t do anything yet — go back and wait”? Yet that’s exactly what the Lord said. He knew that if the disciples went out without the Holy Spirit, they would only repeat Peter’s failure in the high priest’s courtyard.

The word “wait” in Greek is perimenō, which literally means “to wait around” — to stay where you are and not go away until the one you’re waiting for comes. And they obeyed. A hundred and twenty people, in the upper room, devoted themselves with one accord to prayer, and waited ten days.

Then the Lord’s words came true: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

The word “power” here is dynamis in Greek; the English words “dynamic” and “dynamite” both come from it. This is not a surge of emotion, but an explosive force that comes from heaven and is able to change lives.

The day of Pentecost arrived. “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.” (Acts 2:4) Peter, who had once denied the Lord three times, stood up and preached a message. And the result? “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

Brothers and sisters — three thousand. The same Peter, the same mouth, the same city of Jerusalem. Fifty days earlier he didn’t even dare acknowledge the Lord in front of a servant girl; fifty days later he preached boldly before thousands upon thousands. What made the difference? It wasn’t training in public speaking, it wasn’t a course in homiletics — what made the difference was the Holy Spirit.

So: the fruit of serving lies not in human ability, but in the work of the Holy Spirit.

Church history confirms this again and again. On the evening of 24 May 1738, an English clergyman — an Oxford graduate, already ordained, who had even crossed the ocean to serve as a missionary in America only to return defeated — went very reluctantly to a small meeting in Aldersgate Street, London. Someone was reading Martin Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. He later wrote in his journal the famous words: “I felt my heart strangely warmed.” That man’s name was John Wesley. Over the next fifty-odd years he rode some four hundred thousand kilometres on horseback, preached more than forty thousand sermons, and brought a great revival that shook England. Brothers and sisters, before that evening Wesley lacked nothing — theology, education, zeal, morality, he had them all; what he lacked was the fire the Holy Spirit lit in his heart.

The Welsh Revival of 1904 to 1905 was the same. Evan Roberts, a twenty-six-year-old coal miner, was deeply touched by the Holy Spirit in prayer, and the message he preached could not have been simpler: confess your sin, obey the Holy Spirit, confess Christ publicly, and do as the Spirit leads. Within a few short months, by common accounts some hundred thousand people came to the Lord, taverns closed their doors, and hymns rose up from the mine shafts. That wasn’t a strategy; that was the Holy Spirit.

But Paul reminds us of something even more crucial. Galatians 5:25 says: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.”

The word “walk” in Greek is stoicheō, which originally means “to advance in a line”, “to keep in step with”. Paul means: since our life was given by the Spirit, then every step must also line up with the Spirit and keep in step with the Spirit.

Begun by the Spirit, we must also go on by the Spirit. Not only “at the beginning”, but “every day”.

Ephesians 5:18 says: “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.” Here “be filled” in Greek is in the present tense, the passive voice and the imperative mood. The present tense means continuing without a break; the passive voice means it isn’t something I grab hold of, but something I come to be filled with; the imperative means this isn’t an optional extra — it’s the Lord’s command. So the most fitting sense of this sentence is: keep on being filled with the Holy Spirit, continually.

Let me use a picture from daily life. Your phone needs charging every day, doesn’t it? You don’t skip today’s charge just because you charged it yesterday. Yet with the Holy Spirit we often serve with the attitude, “I dedicated myself once, ten years ago.” No wonder the battery warning light has been red for so long.

Here’s another example from nature. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea are both fed by the Jordan — the same river. The Sea of Galilee has water flowing in and flowing out, so it teems with fish and is ringed with fishing villages; it was there that the Lord Jesus called his disciples. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; the water evaporates, salt keeps building up, its salinity is around 34 per cent — nearly ten times that of ordinary seawater — and any fish that enters it cannot survive. Brothers and sisters, the same living water becomes life where it has an outlet, and a dead sea where it has none; and in the same way, serving that has only an outlet and no inlet will sooner or later run dry to the bottom. What we need is “flowing in and flowing out” — being filled with the Holy Spirit every day, and pouring out our life to others every day.

This is exactly what 321 means by the 920 practice and 235 relationships. 920: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; we practise living a selfless (0) life, letting the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine (9) of its expressions in us — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice that this is “fruit”, not “product”. A product is manufactured; fruit is grown. You can’t squeeze out patience by willpower; you can only let the Holy Spirit grow patience within you.

235: become a “2” with selfless people, build a “3” of relationships between spiritual parents and spiritual children, and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Acts 2 is the finest model of this — the hundred and twenty filled with the Holy Spirit became spiritual parents to three thousand; one person’s filling brought the filling of a whole company.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: A Choice between Two Roads — Minding the Spirit or Minding the Flesh
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, having come this far, we must face a choice we have to make every single day.

In serving there are really only two roads: minding the Spirit, or minding the flesh.

“For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6)

The verse before puts it even more clearly: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit.” (Romans 8:5)

The word behind “mind” here is phroneō in Greek, meaning “to have something on your mind”, “the settled orientation of your thinking”. It doesn’t mean thinking about something now and then; it means the default direction of your whole mind — where the navigation system of your heart is set. So what this verse is really asking is: brothers and sisters, which way does your heart face by default?

So what is minding the flesh?

Don’t misunderstand: “the flesh” here doesn’t mean the body, nor only committing sin. What Paul calls “the flesh” is the nature of the old self that doesn’t rely on God and has itself at the centre. So minding the flesh is relying on yourself, satisfying yourself, and doing things your own way.

In serving, it often looks very “spiritual”: I have to make this succeed to prove I’m capable; I want everyone to see what I’ve put in; if others don’t do it well, it’s quicker if I do it myself; I can’t say no, or what will people think of me?

And the result? The more you serve, the more tired you get; the more you serve, the drier you become; and in the end you want to give up.

This is precisely what 321 calls the old self’s self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; when I want to take God’s place in my serving, I have to shoulder a weight only God can carry, and of course I’m crushed by it. What’s more, pride provokes pride, and both sides lose — between co-workers, one person’s “I know better” brings back the other’s “you don’t respect me”, and before the job gets done, the relationship has already broken.

And what is minding the Spirit?

It is yielding to God’s will and relying on the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

The result: life, peace and strength.

Brothers and sisters, I love the words in the second half of Romans 8:6 — “life and peace”. They make an excellent checklist. When you finish something, is there “life and peace” within you, or “emptiness and agitation”? This isn’t living by feelings; this is the scale the Bible gives us. Paul also says in Colossians: “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15). The word “rule”, brabeuō in Greek, originally meant the umpire at the games. Peace is the umpire God has placed in your heart; when he blows the whistle, you stop.

The Lord Jesus also warns us very solemnly. He said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’” (Matthew 7:21–23)

Brothers and sisters, look at that “ministry CV”: prophesying, casting out demons, doing mighty works — what an impressive triathlon! Yet the Lord’s answer is: “I never knew you.”

So the issue was never “how much was done”, but “whether it came from God” and “whether there was a real relationship with the Lord”. The first thing the Lord cares about is not your results, but whether you and he know each other.

Psychology offers some supporting evidence too. From the 1980s onwards, the American psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan developed Self-Determination Theory, distinguishing between “autonomous motivation” and “controlled motivation”: what we do out of inner endorsement and values brings greater persistence and well-being; what we do out of outward pressure, rewards and punishments, or concern for how others see us may work in the short term, but in the long run leads to exhaustion and withdrawal. Brothers and sisters, this confirms the Lord’s words from another angle: the very same act of service, done out of “fear of letting people down” or out of “a heart that loves the Lord”, will look completely different a year later.

Here’s another scientific fact. In the 1970s Dr Herbert Benson of Harvard Medical School described the “relaxation response”: he found that sustained, focused meditation and slow breathing can lower the heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen consumption, and activate the parasympathetic nervous system. That is also why a morning spent truly quiet in prayer before God doesn’t only strengthen the spirit; even the body is being restored. Isaiah said it long ago: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” (Isaiah 30:15)

The 321 insight puts it very precisely: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll be troubled.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is life and peace; rely on the brain and yourself, and there is toil and a heavy burden.

The Lord Jesus said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Take the yoke off.” He said, “Take my yoke upon you.” A yoke is borne by two oxen together. The Lord means: don’t pull alone; pull together with me. When he leads in front and you simply keep in step with him, the yoke is easy. Isn’t this exactly that “keeping in step with the Spirit” of Galatians 5:25?

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The First Station on the Path of Serving
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back into the whole picture of 321, and you’ll see it even more clearly.

The 321 Path of Serving has five stations: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”. Life is “Jesus is my role model”. Service is “let Jesus be King”. God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

Do you see the direction of this road? It runs from the inside outwards, flowing from the source to the outlet. Only with the Holy Spirit’s guidance can we understand the Bible; only when we understand the Bible can we live out the pattern of Jesus; only when we live out the pattern of Jesus can we truly let him be King in our serving; and once we let him be King, all the glory naturally goes to him and isn’t stolen by anyone halfway along.

Today we are standing at the first station — Spirit. If you get the first station wrong, the other four will all go astray. If you aren’t led by the Holy Spirit, your Bible reading will only turn into knowledge; if you have only knowledge, what you live out won’t be the life of Jesus but a religious performance; if there is no life in your serving, you’ll gradually, without noticing, make yourself king instead of letting Jesus be King; and in the end the glory falls on people, not on God.

That’s why 321 says: the Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal — establish God’s system.

Today’s lesson stands squarely on the foundation “the Holy Spirit is my guide”.

Now look at what 321 says about selflessness. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred serving is I do it, I hold it up, I carry it, I prove myself; selfless serving is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand dries up within half a day; a drop of water put into the ocean will never dry up. Giving yourself over isn’t losing yourself; it’s entering the source that never runs dry.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Minding the flesh is, in essence, the self-centred life; minding the Spirit is, in essence, selflessness. So the two roads of Romans 8:6, put into the language of 321, are: the road of the self-centred life leads to death; the road of selflessness leads to life and peace.

Then there is the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. This morning, the first domino God wants to tip is “mindset” — exchanging the mindset that “serving is me doing things for God” for “serving is God doing things through me”. Once that one mindset changes, the four dominoes behind it will fall, one after another.

Then there is the shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective asks, “Who’s going to do this?” God’s perspective asks, “Who is it that’s really doing this?” The earthly perspective looks at today’s results; the heavenly perspective looks at eternal fruit. The temporary perspective fears it won’t all get done; the eternal perspective knows that “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).

Finally, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The greatest weariness in serving often isn’t the work itself, but that our focus is wrong — one moment looking at ourselves (“How can I be so useless?”), the next at others (“Why does he never do anything?”), the next at our circumstances (“This church is hopeless”). Once the focus moves back onto Jesus, the strength comes back.

Brothers and sisters, this is why this lesson is called “The Path of Serving — Spirit”. Because if the first step on the road is right, the whole road will be right.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Five Practices You Can Do Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices, and they are very practical. Let’s take them one by one, and go deeper with each through the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Be Filled First Every Day — Let the Holy Spirit Be the Starting Point

Begin every day by praying, asking the Holy Spirit to fill you, rather than plunging straight into busyness. The concrete practice: every morning, say one sentence — “Lord, today I need your Spirit to fill me.”

The Lord Jesus promised with his own lips: “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13) Brothers and sisters, this is the Lord’s promise, not our guesswork. Ask, and it will be given.

How do we walk through the eight stages? Information: I know that being filled with the Holy Spirit is a command (Ephesians 5:18). Revelation: the Holy Spirit shows me that my weariness this past year comes from never truly asking him to fill me. Conviction: my heart is truly persuaded; I admit that I can’t. Implementation: from tomorrow morning, the first thing I do on opening my eyes won’t be to look at my phone, but to ask to be filled with the Holy Spirit. Evaluation: after a week, I look back — how many days did I manage it? What happened on the days I didn’t? Correction: put the phone outside the bedroom, and write the prayer at the head of the bed. Repetition: once a day, for a full forty days. Multiplication: find a brother or sister and say, “Let’s do this practice together.”

Practice 2: Learn to Pause — Seek Guidance in Everything

Before making a decision, pause and ask, “Lord, what is your will?” The concrete practice: before any major decision, pray for thirty seconds first.

Brothers and sisters, don’t underestimate those thirty seconds. On his second missionary journey, Paul originally intended to go to Asia, and Scripture says: “When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.” (Acts 16:6–7) Paul paused, and God gave him the vision of Macedonia, and so the gospel entered Europe. Brothers and sisters, that one “pause” changed the history of the whole Western world.

In his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman proposed that we have two systems of thinking: System 1 is fast, intuitive and automatic; System 2 is slow, effortful and has to be deliberately switched on. He pointed out that under pressure and in a hurry we run almost entirely on System 1, and System 1 is the most vulnerable to bias. It’s the same spiritually — hurry is the number-one enemy of hearing the Holy Spirit’s quiet voice. When God spoke to Elijah, it wasn’t in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire, but in “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

Going deeper with the eight stages: Information — I know God will guide me. Revelation — the Holy Spirit shines his light on me, and I see that several of my recent decisions were “do it first and think later”. Conviction — I admit that my hurry is unbelief. Implementation — from today, for any request I need to answer “yes” or “no” to, I’ll first pause for thirty seconds and pray. Evaluation — how many times did I pause this week? Correction — put “Pause thirty seconds first” on my phone’s wallpaper. Repetition — make it a habit. Multiplication — share in my small group the change this practice has brought.

Practice 3: Discern the Two Voices — Choose to Mind the Spirit

Learn to recognise whether an inner voice comes from the flesh or from the Holy Spirit. The concrete practice: when emotions rise, first ask one question — “Is this the peace of the Holy Spirit?”

How do we discern? The Bible gives us an objective standard, not one based on feelings. James says: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17) Lay the thought in your heart alongside this verse and compare: is it pure? Does it bring peace? Is it gentle? Is it full of mercy?

The voice of the flesh has a few familiar accents: urgency, comparison, self-pity, condemnation. It says, “I want it now”, “Look how good he is and how bad you are”, “No one understands what you put in”, “Someone like you isn’t fit to serve.” The voice of the Holy Spirit, by contrast, is like this: “When he rebukes you, it makes you want to come back to God; when the enemy accuses you, it only makes you want to hide from God.” Rebuke brings repentance; accusation brings despair — that’s a very practical way to discern.

Colossians 3:15 says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” Brothers and sisters, let peace be the umpire. If there’s no peace in your heart, don’t move yet.

The eight stages: Information — I know there are two voices. Revelation — the Holy Spirit shows me that my recent irritability actually comes from comparison. Conviction — I admit that it isn’t the Holy Spirit. Implementation — as soon as emotions rise, take a deep breath and ask, “Is this the peace of the Holy Spirit?” Evaluation — before bed, think back over how many times today I followed the voice of the flesh. Correction — copy out James 3:17 and stick it up in front of my desk. Repetition — every day, the same. Multiplication — teach your children and your co-workers to discern in the same way.

Practice 4: Don’t Rely on Yourself — Let Strength Come from God

When you’re weary, the answer isn’t to try harder but to turn to God. The concrete practice: when you’re tired, pray first rather than gritting your teeth and pushing on.

Brothers and sisters, we need to face this one very honestly. Our natural reaction is: if the work isn’t finished, do overtime; if the results aren’t enough, push harder; if we’re empty inside, find another ministry to fill the gap. This is exactly what Galatians 3:3 means: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”

The prophet Isaiah said: “but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31) Notice that the condition for “renewing strength” is “waiting”, not “trying twice as hard”.

The Lord Jesus himself said: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) If even the Son of God says he “can do nothing of himself”, what makes us think we can?

Hudson Taylor is generally credited with saying: “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” Brothers and sisters, the reverse holds true as well — if it’s done my way, I have to supply it myself, and very soon I won’t be able to.

The eight stages: Information — I know the source of strength is in God. Revelation — the Holy Spirit shows me that my “pushing on” is actually pride. Conviction — I admit that I need him. Implementation — next time I’m utterly exhausted, instead of pouring another cup of coffee, I’ll first be quiet and pray for ten minutes. Evaluation — after doing this, what’s different about how I am? Correction — move the quiet time earlier; don’t wait until I collapse before being still. Repetition — make it a fixed rhythm. Multiplication — encourage the co-worker near me who is about to be wrung dry to do the same.

Practice 5: Examine the Results — Measure by Life and Peace

Check your state every day: is it peace, or pressure? The concrete practice: before sleep, ask yourself one question — “Today, did I rely on the Holy Spirit, or on myself?”

Brothers and sisters, this question isn’t meant to condemn us; it’s meant to help us adjust our direction. Romans 8:6 is the measuring rod: life and peace mean minding the Spirit; deadness and dryness mean minding the flesh.

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine says: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” These words were written at the end of the fourth century, and more than sixteen hundred years later they still speak straight to our hearts.

The eight stages: Information — I know I can test myself by life and peace. Revelation — the examination before bed lets the Holy Spirit shine his light on my day. Conviction — I submit to his examination. Implementation — three minutes of self-examination every evening. Evaluation — a review once a week. Correction — when I see which kinds of things most easily make me slide into the flesh, I entrust those things to him in advance. Repetition — every day without a break. Multiplication — teach these three minutes before bed to your family.

Brothers and sisters, put simply, these five practices are five checkpoints in a day: be filled when you get up, pause when you make a decision, discern when emotions rise, turn to God when you’re weary, and examine yourself before you sleep. With these five checkpoints guarding your day, your serving will turn from draining into flowing.

A Gentle Reminder: The Problem Is Never the Tasks, but the Source

Brothers and sisters, I want to single out this “gentle reminder” from the lesson, because it is the key to the whole lesson.

The problem in serving has never been a problem of tasks; it is a problem of “source”.

When the source is the Holy Spirit, there is life; when the source is the flesh, there is only draining.

Don’t just ask, “What am I going to do?” First ask, “Whom am I relying on?”

I’m reminded of what the Lord Jesus said in the home of Martha and Mary. Martha was distracted with much serving, her heart in a flurry; the Lord said: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42)

Notice that the Lord didn’t rebuke Martha for “serving”; what he rebuked was her being “anxious and troubled”. Martha’s problem wasn’t doing the work; it was that the source of her work had run dry.

The Lord Jesus put this truth most clearly of all: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Brothers and sisters, the branch’s job isn’t “to bear fruit”; the branch’s job is “to stay joined to the vine”. Fruit is the natural result of the connection. A branch that strains with all its might to bear fruit while not joined to the vine — that’s called religion; a branch that quietly stays joined to the vine, and the fruit grows by itself — that’s called life.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: From “I Do It” to “God Does It”
sections.html:
The true starting point of serving is not ability, not enthusiasm, but the Holy Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, I’ll say it again, because these words are worth remembering all our lives: not ability, not enthusiasm, but the Holy Spirit.

Ability will one day be used up, enthusiasm will one day cool, but the Holy Spirit alone never runs dry.

When you come back to this starting point, you’ll discover something wonderful: it isn’t you striving to serve; it’s the Holy Spirit at work within you.

It isn’t you dragging yourself along; it’s God carrying you along.

This is the deepest mystery of serving: from “I do it” to “God does it”; from “forcing it” to “flowing”; from “weariness” to “life”.

So this morning I want to issue a call to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let Jesus be King. In your serving, ask the “self” that sits on the throne giving orders to step down, and let Jesus take the throne. No longer “what I think should be done”, but “Lord, what do you want me to do?”

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When the Holy Spirit accomplishes something beautiful through you, don’t keep even a little for yourself. Glory that sticks to our hands begins to rot; glory given wholly to the Lord bears eternal fruit.

Third, go back to the first station. Today, go back to the station of “Spirit”. Stop living today on yesterday’s anointing; stop propping up God’s work with your own talents.

Brothers and sisters, let’s respond to the Lord together with this declaration of faith from the lesson.

Lord Jesus, I declare: my life begins with the Holy Spirit, my daily living is led by the Holy Spirit, and my serving relies on the Holy Spirit’s power.

I will no longer rely on myself; I choose to mind the Spirit and live in life and peace.

Let your Spirit fill me, guide me and use me.

All glory be to you. Amen.

keyVerses: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)
“If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)
“For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6)
practices: Be filled first every day — let the Holy Spirit be the starting point
Learn to pause — seek guidance in everything
Discern the two voices — choose to mind the Spirit
Don’t rely on yourself — let strength come from God
Examine the results — measure by life and peace
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
Lord, we confess that so often we have set to work before we asked you, and poured out to others before we were filled by you. For all this self-confidence and haste, we confess our sin to you.
Lord, fill us with your Spirit. As you once filled your beloved Son, as you once filled the hundred and twenty disciples in the upper room, fill us too this morning.

Teach us to pause and listen for your voice before every decision; to discern who is speaking whenever emotions rise; and to turn to you whenever we are weary, rather than pushing on in our own strength.
Give us a mind set on the Spirit, so that all our lives we may walk in life and peace.
Lord, let our serving no longer be our doing, but yours; no longer forced, but flowing; no longer weariness, but life.
Reign as King within us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) Think back over the past three months: in your serving or your daily living, what is one thing you clearly did on your own, “apart from the Lord”? How did it turn out? If you could do it again, at which point would you stop first to pray?

Paul says: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6). Use this verse to examine how your week has been: at which moments was there “life and peace” within you? At which moments was there dryness and agitation? Of the lesson’s five practices, which one will you start with — and will you ask a spiritual companion to practise it with you for forty days?
l162.title: Serving Begins with the Holy Spirit
l162.subtitle: The First Station on the Path of Serving: Spirit
l162.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Saying We Rely on the Spirit While Still Gripping Our Own Methods
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a scene that many who serve have lived through, yet few will admit to.

A sister had served in her church for fifteen years. Sunday school, visitation, the choir, the kitchen — she was in all of it. One day she was sitting in the office with a stack of to-do lists spread across the desk, and suddenly the tears came. She said, “It isn’t that I’m too tired to carry on. It’s that I’ve suddenly realised — in the last three months, I haven’t done a single thing that I asked God about first. I did every one of them well. It’s just that every one of them was my own decision.”

It wasn’t that she never prayed. It was that her prayers all came at the very end: the plan drawn up, the volunteers rostered, the programme running smoothly — and only then did she bow her head and say, “Lord, please bless this.” She did not disbelieve God. She had put God at the end of the sentence.

Brothers and sisters, does that picture feel familiar?

In our last lesson we saw that the first step on the Path of Serving is “Spirit” — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, service is just religious activity; without the Holy Spirit, however zealous we are, we are only spinning on our own. But once we know that, a more pressing question rises to the surface:

“How” do we set our minds on the Spirit?

This question is sharper than we imagine. Because so often we say with our lips that we rely on the Holy Spirit, while in practice we still use our own methods, lean on our own experience and do what we ourselves want to do. We have turned “relying on the Holy Spirit” into a catchphrase, without turning it into a way of life.

Notice that Scripture uses a very particular word here. Paul says, “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit” (Romans 8:5). The Greek word behind “set their minds on” is φρονέω (phroneō). It means more than “thinking about something”; it means “fixing the mind there,” “being taken up with it,” “standing on that side.” The Lord Jesus used the very same word to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Think how reasonable Peter’s words sounded at the time: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you” (Matthew 16:22). He meant well. He spoke out of love. He spoke out of ordinary human feeling. Yet the Lord Jesus said it was the voice of Satan. Why? Because it was “the things of men,” not “the things of God.”

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s point: the problem is often not that we do bad things, but that we use good intentions to do our own thing.

So the key is not only “having the Holy Spirit” but “whether we set our minds on the Spirit.” Everyone who has truly been born again and saved has the Holy Spirit within — that is grace. But not everyone who has the Holy Spirit sets their mind on the Spirit — that is a choice.

Proverbs states this path very plainly: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). Notice that this verse has a positive side and a negative side. The positive is “trust with all your heart”; the negative is “don’t lean on your own understanding.” These two are like the two pans of a scale: when one grows heavier, the other must grow lighter. Trust God a little more, and you lean on yourself a little less; lean on yourself a little more, and you will inevitably trust God a little less.

Setting our minds on the Spirit is a path, and it is also a choice. It is not a once-for-all decision but a fresh choice made every day, in every matter, in every thought.

Today we will look together at three things: what the foundation of minding the Spirit is, where its key lies, and what fruit it brings.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A King’s Last Words, and a Lord’s Farewell
sections.html:
Before we come to the three key points, let us first get our footing in the background of two key passages, because the first step in letting Scripture interpret Scripture is to let each passage speak from within its own setting.

(1) The background of Proverbs 3:5-6

The principal author of Proverbs is Solomon. “The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel” (Proverbs 1:1) — so the book opens. Solomon reigned from roughly 970 to 930 BC, the wealthiest and wisest king in Israel’s history. Scripture says, “God gave Solomon abundant wisdom and understanding, and very great understanding, even as the sand that is on the seashore” (1 Kings 4:29).

Yet Proverbs is not a royal handbook on statecraft. Its form is “a father teaching his son.” Throughout chapters 1 to 9 the address “my son” appears again and again: “My son, don’t forget my teaching” (Proverbs 3:1); “My son, if you will receive my words” (Proverbs 2:1). This is the classic shape of wisdom literature in the ancient Near East — an elder who has walked the road of life and tasted its sweet and bitter sits down and says to the younger generation: child, listen to me; there are some walls you don’t need to run into yourself.

So Proverbs 3:5-6 is not a motivational slogan. It is what a man with the finest mind in the whole world said to the next generation: “Don’t lean on your own understanding.” Brothers and sisters, from the lips of a man without wisdom, those words would be an excuse; from the lips of Solomon, they are a testimony.

What is more, this saying sits in the middle of a whole passage. Proverbs 3:1-12 is a complete unit about “seven attitudes a young person who walks with God should have”: not forgetting the teaching, not forsaking kindness and truth, trusting with all the heart, acknowledging him, fearing Yahweh, honouring Yahweh with one’s wealth, and not despising discipline. Directly after 3:5-6 comes: “Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil” (Proverbs 3:7). You see — verse 5 says “don’t lean on your own understanding,” and verse 7 says “don’t be wise in your own eyes.” The same theme is stated twice. The Holy Spirit knows this is the thing people find hardest to let go of.

The phrase “with all your heart” is בְּכָל־לֵב (bechol-lev) in Hebrew, literally “with your whole heart.” Not giving God part of your heart, not holding something back — all of it. And the root of the verb “trust” (בָּטַח, batach) carries the sense of “leaning your whole weight on something,” like a person lying down on a bed and handing the whole weight of the body over to it. Trusting is not nodding in agreement; trusting is handing over your weight.

(2) The background of John 16:13

The second key passage comes from John 16. The apostle John wrote this Gospel around AD 80 to 90, for communities of believers who already followed the Lord but needed a deeper knowledge of the person of Christ. John 13 to 17 is known as the “Upper Room Discourse” or the “Farewell Discourse” — the last words the Lord Jesus spoke to the eleven disciples at the Last Supper, on the night he was betrayed.

Picture the scene: the candlelight flickering, the bread and the cup still on the Passover table, Judas already gone out into the night, the disciples’ hearts full of sorrow. The Lord Jesus is about to leave; they are to stay behind. Who will lead them? Across three whole chapters the Lord Jesus introduces “another Counselor” again and again: “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you” (John 14:26).

So the promise of John 16:13 was spoken at the moment when the disciples were at their most helpless and least sure of themselves. That reminds us of something important: the guidance of the Holy Spirit has never been a reward for the self-assured; it is grace for those who are unsure.

sections.heading: 3. First Teaching: The Foundation of Minding the Spirit — Humbly Laying Down Ourselves
sections.html:
The first key to setting our minds on the Spirit is “humility.”

Why humility? Because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, and he never works alongside human pride. James puts it with great directness: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The Greek word for “resists” is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: it is not that God merely dislikes the proud; God “draws up his ranks against” the proud. With a proud servant, it is not that the Holy Spirit won’t help him — it is that the Holy Spirit is standing on the opposite side.

(1) Humility is not weakness; humility is laying down ourselves

Humility is not weakness. Humility is laying down ourselves and letting God be Lord.

True humility has strength in it. The Lord Jesus said, “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29) — and the one who said it is the one who could calm the wind and the waves and raise the dead. Humility and power have never been at odds; on the contrary, humility is the very channel of power.

The American psychologist June Price Tangney, in a study published in 2000 in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, pointed out that the core of humility has never been self-deprecation, but a handful of observable traits: an accurate assessment of one’s own abilities and achievements, openness about one’s own mistakes and limitations, a readiness to receive new ideas, an appreciation of the value of all things, and “a relatively low focus on the self.” She put it vividly: humility is “a forgetting of the self.”

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly what 321 calls “selflessness”? Selflessness is not having no self; it is no longer having the self at the centre. It is not seeing ourselves as very low; it is no longer looking at ourselves all the time.

(2) The real question is not “Can I?” but “On whom am I relying?”

In Philippians Paul left us a line that many people can recite yet often misuse:

“I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13)

Notice the context. When Paul wrote Philippians, he was a prisoner in Rome. He did not say this at a victory banquet; he said it in a prison cell. And the two verses before it make things very clear: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need” (Philippians 4:11-12).

So “I can do all things” does not mean “whatever I want to do will succeed.” It means “whatever situation God places me in, I can stand firm.”

The weight of the verse rests on “through Christ, who strengthens me.” The Greek ἐνδυναμόω (endunamoō) means “to pour power into,” and it is a present participle, signalling continuous action — not charging up once to full, but staying plugged into the power source. Its root, δύναμις (dunamis), is where the English words dynamic and dynamite come from.

Brothers and sisters, the real question has never been “Can I?” but “On whom am I relying?”

Many people feel anxious and afraid in their service, and there are really only two reasons: they rely on themselves, so they have no confidence; or they rely on their circumstances, so they have no stability. Those who rely on themselves rise and fall with their own condition; those who rely on circumstances rise and fall with other people’s expressions. Both live exhausted lives, because their peace is built on things that shift.

But when you choose humility and depend on God, you discover that whatever your circumstances, you can rejoice; whatever your conditions, you can overcome. For your foundation no longer rests on yourself.

I often use a picture. A man crossing a river can choose to swim, or he can choose to take a boat. For the swimmer, his strength decides whether he reaches the far bank; for the one in the boat, the boat decides it. The swimmer grows more afraid the further he swims, because the river seems to grow wider and wider; the one in the boat grows steadier the further he goes, because the shore keeps drawing nearer. Service is just the same. Those who rely on themselves are swimming; those who set their minds on the Spirit are in the boat.

(3) The pursuit of self-esteem is a costly drain

Psychology gives us a piece of corroborating evidence well worth pondering. In 2004 the American psychologists Jennifer Crocker and Lora Park published a well-known paper in the Psychological Bulletin titled “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem.” Drawing together a large body of research, they showed that when people make “maintaining and raising their sense of self-worth” the centre of life, they gain emotional rewards in the short term but pay a heavy price in the long term — lower motivation to learn, relationships that turn sour, reduced autonomy, even harm to physical and mental health. For when someone treats everything as an exam on their own worth, they must constantly defend, constantly prove and constantly compare.

Brothers and sisters, what this research says is really what the Bible said long ago: the self-centred life is the most expensive way to live. The proud do not live more impressively; they live more wearily. They have to keep propping themselves up, because there is nothing underneath to hold them.

Augustine, in the history of the church, is commonly said to have answered someone who asked him “What is the way to the truth?” like this: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. He was not being coy. He was saying that this road has only one entrance, and the entrance is low — you have to stoop to get in.

(4) A 321 Insight: humility is returning to our originally intended position

The 321 insight makes this extremely clear: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Notice that humility is not pushing ourselves down into the ground; it is “returning to our originally intended position.” When God is in God’s place and man is in man’s place, heaven and earth are in good order. When man insists on sitting in God’s seat, chaos begins. That line in Eden, “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5), was humanity’s first step away from its originally intended position.

That is why 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite attack is to stir up our “self.” He doesn’t need to make you commit some great sin; he only needs you to think a little more about yourself while you serve, and that is enough.

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a serving team this proves true every day. When two people who each need to prove themselves serve together, the ministry gets done but the relationship gets damaged; when two people who are each willing to lay themselves down serve together, the ministry gets done and the relationship grows deeper.

When you lay yourself down, the Holy Spirit can lead you. This is a promise, and it is also an order: first lay down, then be led. If your hand won’t let go, God has no way of putting something better into it.

sections.heading: 4. Second Teaching: The Key to Minding the Spirit — Rely on the Heart, Not the Brain
sections.html:
“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)

Setting our minds on the Spirit does not depend on analysis; it depends on the “heart.”

(1) The biblical “heart” is the centre of the whole person

First we need to clear up something very important, so that we don’t slide into an anti-intellectual distortion. When 321 says “rely on the heart and not the brain,” it is not telling us not to think, not to study, not to prepare, not to work hard. Scripture never encourages laziness or ignorance. What “rely on the heart and not the brain” deals with is “leaning on our own understanding,” exactly as Proverbs 3:5 says.

The biblical “heart” — לֵב (lev) in Hebrew, καρδία (kardia) in Greek — refers to the command centre within a person: thought, will, emotion and conscience, the decision-making centre of the whole person. So “relying on the heart” does not mean relying on feelings alone; it means “the whole person turned towards God.” And “relying on the brain” here means that self which will only analyse and calculate, yet refuses to hand over its weight.

“Pure in heart” in the original Greek is καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ (katharoi tē kardia). When καθαρός is used of metal, it means “free of impurities,” “unalloyed.” From the same root comes the English word catharsis (cleansing). So the pure in heart are not people with blank minds, but people whose motives are single and unmixed.

(2) Relying on the heart and relying on the brain take two different roads

The road of the heart is simplicity, trust and obedience. The road of the brain is calculation, doubt and holding back.

Those who rely on the brain count the cost, weigh the gains and losses, and hold back their obedience. And the result? Faith is swallowed up and action gets stuck. It isn’t that they don’t believe — they are “still thinking about it.” It isn’t that they won’t obey — they want to “wait and see.” Yet spiritual promptings often have a shelf life. When the Holy Spirit moves you to care for someone, to make an apology, to give a gift of money, the moment you start calculating, that prompting slowly goes cold.

A classic psychology experiment can help us understand this. In a study published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a jam-tasting stall in a supermarket. One version displayed 24 flavours; the other displayed only 6. The result: the 24 flavours drew more people to stop, but in the end only about 3% actually bought; the stall with 6 flavours had fewer people stop, yet about 30% went on to buy. The more choices, the longer the analysis, and the harder the action. Psychologists call this “choice overload.”

Brothers and sisters, that was only jam in a supermarket. What about spiritual obedience? When we set out twenty-four considerations in front of God’s prompting — do I have enough time, what will people think, will I be misunderstood, am I being a busybody, what if it bears no fruit — the result is very often that 3%: we think for a long time and do nothing.

The French mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal (1623-1662) left a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He himself had one of the finest scientific minds of his day and invented one of the earliest mechanical calculators, yet after his famous “Night of Fire” experience he wrote that knowing God is a matter of the heart, not of pure reason.

(3) Why do so many hear so much preaching, yet not understand?

After telling the parable of the sower, the Lord Jesus said: “He said to them, ‘To you is given the mystery of God’s Kingdom, but to those who are outside, all things are done in parables, that “seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest perhaps they should turn again, and their sins should be forgiven them.”’” (Mark 4:11-12)

At first hearing this sounds harsh, as if God were deliberately keeping people from understanding. In fact the Lord Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9-10 and pointing to a spiritual fact: the door to truth opens from the inside. God’s mysteries are not a question of intellectual difficulty but of the heart’s attitude. In the New Testament “mystery” (μυστήριον, mustērion) does not mean “a riddle hard to solve,” but “something once hidden and now made known to those who love God.”

Paul says it even more clearly: “Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” (1 Corinthians 2:14)

So why do so many hear so much preaching, yet not understand? Because they grasp it with the brain but do not receive it with the heart. They sit in the meeting and comment as they listen: this speaker’s logic is good, that sentence wasn’t quite rigorous, I knew this part already. They take a whole service’s worth of notes, yet make not one act of surrender.

The Lord Jesus himself said the same thing: “I thank you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little children.” (Luke 10:21) It isn’t that God plays favourites. It’s that little children are willing to reach out their hands, while the wise and understanding are busy evaluating.

Here is a picture. These days many people drive with satnav. The key to using satnav is not whether you know the way, but whether you are willing to turn where it tells you. Anyone who listens to the satnav while changing route on the strength of his own experience will sooner or later hear the words, “Recalculating route.” Brothers and sisters, how many times in our lives has the route been “recalculated” because the Holy Spirit clearly spoke, yet we felt our own road was shorter?

(4) A 321 Insight: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled

321 has a very vivid saying: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The heart is joined to the Holy Spirit; the brain easily relies on itself.

This is not wordplay; it is spiritual reality. For the “heart” is the place God made for communion with himself: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The wellspring of life does not flow from the brain; it flows from the heart.

321 also reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The moment our focus leaves Jesus, the brain immediately takes over and starts calculating, comparing and worrying. The moment Peter walked on the water is the best illustration: looking at Jesus, he walked on the water; looking at the wind and waves, he began to sink (see Matthew 14:29-30).

sections.heading: 5. Third Teaching: The Fruit of Minding the Spirit — Revelation and Power
sections.html:
When someone truly sets their mind on the Spirit, they experience two things: first revelation, and second power.

(1) First: revelation — understanding God’s word

“However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.” (John 16:13)

Notice two details. First, the Holy Spirit is called “the Spirit of truth” — his work always agrees with the truth and will never lead you somewhere that contradicts Scripture. This is our first measuring rod for discerning a prompting: the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, and the two never conflict.

Second, the verb “guide” is ὁδηγέω (hodēgeō) in Greek, made up of “way” (ὁδός) and “lead” (ἡγέομαι); literally it means “to lead someone along the way.” The Chinese Union Version reads “guide you to understand,” with a small-print note that the original reads “into” — which is just what the English gives: “guide you into all truth.” So the Holy Spirit does not stand far off pointing the way; he takes you by the hand and brings you, step by step, into the truth.

Brothers and sisters, this is the difference between revelation and information. Information is knowing the road; revelation is walking on it. This is why many people have a whole cupboard full of Bible knowledge but not one step of spiritual experience.

When the Holy Spirit opens us up, God’s word is no longer mere knowledge; it becomes power:

“For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

“Living” in Greek is ζῶν (zōn), simply “alive”; “active” is ἐνεργής (energēs), from which the English word energy comes. So this verse, rendered literally, says: the word of God is alive and charged with energy.

It can pierce the heart, change lives and bring about real renewal. It can even do something no human can do —

“for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:4-5)

(2) A two-thousand-year-old seed

“The word of God is living” — this has a startling witness from the natural world.

In the 1960s, archaeologists excavating the site of Masada beside the Dead Sea in Israel uncovered a cache of Judean date palm seeds. Carbon-14 dating placed them between about 155 BC and AD 64 — in other words, they had been sealed in the ground at roughly the time of the Lord Jesus. They lay there for nearly two thousand years.

In 2005 the Israeli scientists Elaine Solowey and Sarah Sallon tried to grow one of the seeds. No one held out much hope. Yet a few weeks later, that seed, asleep for two thousand years, sprouted. The tree was named “Methuselah,” and the research was published in the journal Science in 2008. Today it has grown into a mature, flowering tree.

Brothers and sisters, two thousand years of drought, darkness and burial did not kill the life inside that seed. It was only waiting for one thing — for water, for soil, for someone to plant it.

God’s word is like that. “The word of God is living” — it has never been dead. Do you think the verse you heard in Sunday school years ago has long since stopped being useful? Do you think the verse you memorised and then forgot is just old data? No. When the Holy Spirit pours the water, that seed will sprout. This is also why we do our morning reading every day — not to pile up information, but to let living seed fall into soft soil of the heart.

(3) Second: power — signs following

“They went out, and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.” (Mark 16:20)

Look carefully at who does what in this verse. The one acting is “the Lord,” not the disciples. What the disciples did was “preach”; what the Lord did was “work with them” and “confirm.”

So it is not people who prove God; it is God who proves his word.

That is a tremendous release. Brothers and sisters, you don’t need your eloquence to prove that God exists, you don’t need your success to prove that God is faithful, and you don’t need your perfection to prove that the gospel is true. You need only faithfully pass the word on, and God will bear witness himself.

When you rely on the Holy Spirit, you will experience God’s presence, see God’s work and enter into God’s power. This is exactly the promise the Lord gave before he ascended: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

The Old Testament had set the tone long before: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6) This word was spoken to Zerubbabel. At the time, the rebuilding of the temple had stalled for years; conditions were harsh, workers were few and enemies surrounded them. God did not give him more resources. God gave him a word: not by might, nor by power.

(4) A 321 Insight: first revelation, then power

The 321 insight says: the work of the Holy Spirit = revelation + power; first revelation, then power.

This order cannot be reversed. Many people chase power but will not receive revelation, and what they end up with is an emotional high, not a changed life. God’s order is always this: first he opens your eyes, then he opens your hands. First he lets you see, then he sends you to act.

This is precisely the fivefold change 321 speaks of: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Revelation changes the mindset; power shows itself in ministry. Skipping the mindset to grab hold of ministry is like skipping the foundation to put on the roof.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Path of Serving Begins with the Spirit
sections.html:
Let us set today’s message back into the larger picture of 321.

(1) The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — when he served on earth, he said in everything, “the Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19). The Bible is my standard — every prompting must be brought back to God’s word to be tested. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it isn’t that I take God along with me; it is God who takes me along with him.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the biggest question in service is always “who is reigning as King”; let Jesus receive all the glory — this is the Holy Spirit’s own desire: “He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you” (John 16:14). Brothers and sisters, if the Holy Spirit himself does not exalt himself, what right do we have to exalt ourselves in our service?

The Goal: establish God’s system. Minding the Spirit is not for the sake of feeling good spiritually as individuals; it is so that God’s kingdom may come and God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven (see Matthew 6:10).

(2) The five rungs of the Path of Serving

321 divides the Path of Serving into five rungs: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; this is where today’s lesson stands. Understanding — the Bible is my standard; only when the Holy Spirit opens us do we truly understand God’s word. Life — Jesus is my role model; once we understand, we must live it out, and it becomes life. Service — let Jesus be King; only when life is lived out is there true service. God — let Jesus receive all the glory; this is the destination.

Notice that these five rungs cannot be skipped. Skip “Spirit” and go straight to “Service,” and you are serving in the flesh; skip “Life” and go straight to “Service,” and you have gifts without life. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

(3) Selflessness: “I” no longer live, but Christ

The heart of today’s whole lesson is really just one word: “self.”

Humbly laying ourselves down deals with the exalting of “self”; relying on the heart and not the brain deals with the cleverness of “self”; depending on the power of the Holy Spirit deals with the abilities of “self.”

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. This is exactly Paul’s testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, selflessness is the best bargain there is. What you lay down is a limited self; what you gain is a limitless Christ.

(4) A change of perspective and the 920 practice

321 says we must shift our perspective from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Those who rely on the brain look at what is earthly, temporary and calculable; those who rely on the heart look at what is heavenly, eternal and drawn on by faith.

In everyday life this has to take shape as the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — so that the Holy Spirit may bear the “9”, the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Five Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five very practical exercises. We will use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deeper.

Practice 1: Learn humility; lay yourself down every day

In everything, deliberately choose not to rely on yourself but to depend on God. The concrete practice: pray every day — “Lord, I will not rely on myself; I choose to depend on you.”

Information: today you have heard Proverbs 3:5-6. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you the specific matter in which you are leaning on your own understanding. Conviction: admit that without God you really cannot move forward in it. Implementation: tomorrow morning, make this prayer the first thing you say when you open your eyes. Evaluation: in the evening, look back and notice the moment today when you took over again. Correction: don’t blame yourself; simply entrust it to him afresh. Repetition: do this for twenty-one days in a row. Multiplication: tell a spiritual companion about this practice, and do it together.

Practice 2: Live from the heart; stop over-analysing

When God prompts you, don’t keep thinking it over; learn to obey. The concrete practice: today, obey at least one spiritual prompting in your heart.

Remember the jam experiment: the more options, the less action. Spiritual promptings have a shelf life too. “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) When a person’s name comes to mind, make that phone call; when a wrong you’ve done comes to mind, say that sorry. Act first, then think.

When you evaluate, ask yourself one question: today, what did I turn a prompting into by thinking about it? Into an action, or into an excuse?

Practice 3: Cultivate simplicity; keep a clean heart

Don’t let your motives get complicated; learn simply to love God and love people. The concrete practice: examine today’s motives — was it for myself, or for the Lord?

This is the hardest one, because motives hide deep down. “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) So examine yourself with David’s prayer: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)

Practice 4: Declare the truth; fight with God’s word

When your thoughts come under attack, answer with Scripture. The concrete practice: choose one verse and declare it again and again today.

When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, three times he began with the same words: “It is written” (see Matthew 4:4). He did not debate with Satan; he simply set God’s word before him.

Today, choose one verse — Proverbs 3:5-6, for example, or Philippians 4:13. Say it once in the morning, once at midday and once before you sleep. Repetition is the most underrated of the eight stages. Truth is not mastered once it is understood; it is repeated until it becomes instinct.

Practice 5: Follow the Holy Spirit; expect God to work

In your service, don’t just do tasks; expect God to act. The concrete practice: today, pray about one matter and expect God to step in.

Write down specifically what that matter is and the date, and leave a column to fill in with what God does. When you tell others what God has done, the next person begins to believe — and that is “Multiplication.”

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder: Minding the Spirit Is a State of Life
sections.html:
Finally, the lesson gives us a very important reminder: setting our minds on the Spirit is not a technique but a state of life.

Be proud, and you won’t hear God; be humble, and God will lead you. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

Rely on the brain, and you limit God; rely on the heart, and you experience God.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call: Not Only Doing the Right Thing, but Doing It the Right Way
sections.html:
The Path of Serving is not only about “doing the right thing” but about “doing it the right way.”

Not by relying on ourselves, but by relying on the Holy Spirit.

When you learn to set your mind on the Spirit, you will find three things beginning to change: God’s word carries power, your life begins to change, and your service begins to bear fruit.

And in the end you will enter a deeper place —

Selfless, so that Jesus lives; selfless, so that the Spirit leads; selfless, so that God is glorified.

This is the deepest secret of service.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you a very simple call. Not a call to do more, but a call to loosen one hand.

That plan you are holding, that method, that “I know how this should be done” — today, lay it at the Lord’s feet and say: Lord, you be King.

For letting Jesus be King is not a slogan; it is a handover. There may be no applause at the moment of handover; there may even be a little sense of loss, because our name has stepped back from the centre of the stage. But that is the very moment the glory begins to go to Jesus.

“not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5)

May we no longer be the ones who tack “Lord, please bless this” onto the end of the sentence, but the ones who begin the sentence with “Lord, what do you say?”

keyVerses: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6)

“For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:5-6)
practices: Learn humility; lay yourself down every day
Live from the heart; stop over-analysing
Cultivate simplicity; keep a clean heart
Declare the truth; fight with God’s word
Follow the Holy Spirit; expect God to work
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare:
I choose humility. I lay myself down; I will not lean on my own understanding, but trust in you alone.
I will not rely on the brain and myself; I will rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit.
May your Spirit guide me, so that I understand your truth and experience your mighty power.

Lord, forgive me for the many times I have said with my lips that I depend on you, while my hands still gripped my own methods. Forgive me for putting you at the end of the sentence instead of the beginning. Today I lay my plans, my experience and my cleverness at your feet.
Make my life your vessel, and let your word carry power to change lives.
It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
All glory to you! In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
