In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6) Please share: recently, in what specific matter did you find that you had actually made the decision first and only added the prayer afterwards? If you could do it again, how would you put God back at the beginning of the sentence?

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8) Please share: have you ever had an experience of “obeying from the heart”? What were you calculating in your heart at the time? What did God do afterwards? How does that experience help you choose today to rely on the heart and not the brain in your service?
l163.title: Minding the Holy Spirit
l163.subtitle: The Path of Serving — Spirit (Part 2)
l163.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Without Insight, Truth Is Only Information
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin by asking you a question that may sting a little.

How many years have you believed in the Lord? How many times have you read the Bible through? How many hundreds of sermons have you heard? How many conferences have you attended? How many notebooks have you filled? Add all that up, and each of us probably carries more Bible knowledge than many believers did a hundred years ago. Information has never been so easy to come by. One swipe of the phone and the whole Bible is in the palm of your hand; one tap on a video platform and well-known pastors from all over the world are preaching whenever you like.

But I have to ask, honestly, one more question: after all these years, has our life really changed?

I once met a brother who had been in the church for over twenty years and almost never lost a Bible quiz. He could recite the names of the twelve tribes, trace the routes of Paul’s three missionary journeys and explain the difference between premillennialism and postmillennialism. Yet his wife said privately, with tears in her eyes, “He understands everything — except how to say one gentle word to me.” Brothers and sisters, couldn’t the same thing happen to us? Our heads full to the brim, but our hearts untouched; the Bible well known to us, but our temper not changed one bit.

Where does the problem lie? The lesson puts its finger right on it: one key thing is missing — there is no “understanding.”

Paul says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). This is not belittling the words of Scripture; it is reminding us that the very same Bible can stay in our heads as cold “information,” or it can enter our hearts as burning “revelation.” Information is what someone else tells you; revelation is what God himself says to you. Information means you know one more thing; revelation makes you a new creation.

This is what Kingdom 321 means when it says: information cannot change a life; only revelation can change a life.

We often say the Path of Serving has five stages: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. In the last lesson we talked about “Spirit,” learning how to set our minds on the Spirit and be led by the Spirit. Today we take a step forward into the second stage: “Understanding.”

Why must there be “Understanding”? The lesson uses a vivid picture: if the Path of Serving has only “Spirit,” it drifts; add “Understanding,” and it becomes steady. I often think of it as a sailing boat. The Holy Spirit is the wind that fills the sails; without wind the boat can’t move an inch. But wind alone is not enough — the boat also needs a rudder. A boat without a rudder only drifts further the stronger the wind blows, until no one knows where it will end up. God’s word is that rudder. The wind gives you power; the rudder gives you direction. The Spirit lets you experience God; Understanding lets you know God.

So this morning I want to invite every brother and sister, with a humble and hungry heart, to walk three stretches of road with me: first, the balance of Spirit and Understanding; second, from the letter to revelation; third, how to gain understanding. May God, in these fifteen minutes, give us not just some new information but a real revelation.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Why Paul Speaks of “the Letter” and “the Spirit”
sections.html:
To receive this theme verse rightly, we first need to go back to its setting.

The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally thought to have been written around AD 56, when Paul had finished his ministry in Ephesus and was on his way to Macedonia. It was addressed to the church in Corinth, which he had planted himself. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, an international trading port set on an isthmus; its two harbours, east and west, made it a crossroads of trade and ideas in the Mediterranean world of the day. Its wealth was astonishing, its currents of thought turbulent and its morals loose — which is why the church there had so many problems.

The immediate reason Paul wrote 2 Corinthians was that a group of self-styled apostles had come into the church and were questioning his credentials. They carried “letters of commendation” — the letters of recommendation fashionable at the time — and built their authority on qualifications, titles, eloquence and appearance. Then they turned and accused Paul: no letters of commendation, unimpressive in person, crude in speech.

How did Paul answer? At the very start of chapter 3 he says: “Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as do some, letters of commendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men, being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.” (2 Corinthians 3:1-3)

Brothers and sisters, notice the contrast: ink and Spirit, tablets of stone and tablets of the heart. Paul is saying: my letter of commendation is not a piece of paper; it is a group of changed lives. From there he moves naturally into the contrast between the old covenant and the new. The law Moses received on Mount Sinai was carved by God’s finger on tablets of stone; it was holy and glorious, yet tablets of stone could not change the human heart. The new covenant, however, is written by God’s Spirit on the tablets of the human heart, and only this can give life.

So verse 6 says: “who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” “Letter” here is gramma in the original, meaning written characters, a written code; “Spirit” is pneuma — and the Chinese Union Version, which renders it “the spirit of the law,” notes in small print that it may also be read “the Holy Spirit.” Paul is not saying the words of Scripture don’t matter — he quotes Scripture all through this very letter. He is saying that if there is only the code written on the outside, with no work of the Holy Spirit on the inside, that code can only condemn us and bring us death. Only when the Spirit of God writes God’s word on the tablet of the heart can a person live.

Read on, and Paul speaks of how Moses’ face shone when he came down the mountain, yet he covered it with a veil; and he says that to this day, when the Jews read the Old Testament, that veil still lies over their hearts. “But their minds were hardened, for until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains, because in Christ it passes away.” (2 Corinthians 3:14) Then comes that glorious declaration: “Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.” (2 Corinthians 3:17) “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Brothers and sisters, that is the whole picture of “Understanding”: the veil removed, the face unveiled, the glory of the Lord seen, and then being transformed into his image, from glory to glory. “Understanding” has never been about making us better at debating; it is about making us more like Jesus.

With the background in place, let us walk into the lesson’s three teachings.

sections.heading: 3. First Teaching: The Balance of Spirit and Understanding — the Holy Spirit Plus the Truth
sections.html:
The lesson says: “Spirit” without “Understanding” loses its foundation; “Understanding” without “Spirit” turns into mere knowledge. Truly healthy service is the power of the Holy Spirit together with the word of God.

This balance is enormously important. In church history we have seen far too many distortions. Some groups stress experience, promptings and gifts but make light of the Bible’s teaching; they burn hot for a season and a few years later have drifted from the true way. Other groups stress doctrine, system and rigour but refuse the work of the Holy Spirit; they end up correct but cold, like a very neatly built tomb.

What, then, is the right pattern? The answer is Jesus.

“For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.” (John 3:34) Brothers and sisters, see how perfect the structure of this verse is: he “speaks the words of God” — that is truth; “God gives the Spirit without measure” — that is power. In the Lord Jesus, truth and power are perfectly one, without the slightest tension.

So look at his ministry: “Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.” (Matthew 9:35) Teaching and preaching the good news — that is the word; healing every disease — that is power. He never preached without working miracles, nor worked miracles without preaching. In one hand he held the truth, in the other he carried power, and both hands worked together.

The apostles did the same. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down, the disciples were filled with the Spirit and spoke in other languages — that was a display of power. But what happened next? “But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and spoke out to them, ‘You men of Judea, and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.’” (Acts 2:14) Peter stood up and preached, and nearly his whole sermon was quotation from the Old Testament — from Joel, from Psalm 16, from Psalm 110. And the result? “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

Brothers and sisters, notice: the three thousand were not baptised because they saw tongues of fire; it was “those who gladly received his word” who were baptised. Not power alone, and not preaching alone, but the Holy Spirit and the word of God at work together.

I often use a picture: the Holy Spirit is like electricity, and the Bible is like the wiring. Electricity without wiring is a lightning strike — a flash and it’s gone, and it may even hurt someone. Wiring without electricity is just a heap of useless copper. But when the current runs through the wires, the lights come on, the fridge keeps cold, and the whole house has light and life. God gives us his Spirit so that he may flow into our lives through his word.

The Reformer John Calvin, in his Institutes of the Christian Religion, used a beautiful picture: our eyes are dim, and everything we look at is a blur; Scripture is like a pair of spectacles — put them on, and the works of God come clearly into view. And what makes those spectacles truly work is the inner witness of the Holy Spirit in our hearts. Spectacles and eyes, word and Spirit — neither can do without the other.

Science offers an interesting angle too. For the human eye to see, two things are needed: light, and focus. However strong the light, if the lens cannot focus, all you see is a dazzling white blur; however precise the lens, without light you see nothing at all. The Holy Spirit is the light; the Bible is the focus. Many brothers and sisters are moved to tears in a meeting — that is the light. But they go home not knowing what the next step is — that is losing focus.

The 321 insight puts it this way: the Spirit lets people experience God, Understanding lets people know God, and neither can do without the other.

This is also the beauty of the order in the Three Foundations of 321: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The role model gives me direction, the standard gives me boundaries, the guide gives me power. If there is guidance without a standard, we will mistake our own ideas for the voice of the Holy Spirit; if there is a standard without guidance, we will treat the Bible as a textbook. Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit will never lead us to do anything contrary to Scripture, because the Holy Spirit is the very Spirit who inspired Scripture. Any “prompting” that departs from Scripture must be carefully discerned.

Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) The treasure is God’s word and God’s Spirit; the clay vessels are us. May the Lord make these clay vessels of ours carry both the truth and the power.

sections.heading: 4. Second Teaching: From the Letter to Revelation — Truth Entering Life
sections.html:
The lesson says: many people read the Bible and stop at the “letter.”

That sentence is worth each of us quietly pondering. What does it mean to stop at the letter? It means the eyes have run over the page, we recognise every word, we have finished the passage, we have ticked off the reading plan — yet not one sentence has stayed in our hearts.

When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he said: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” (Matthew 4:4) Notice the words “that proceeds out of God’s mouth.” The original here uses rhema, meaning a word that is spoken. God’s word is not a fossil lying on paper; it is a word spoken from God’s mouth right now, carrying breath and carrying life.

So the key is whether this word is “alive” in you.

The writer of Hebrews says: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12) “Living” in the original is zōn, simply “alive”; “active” is energēs, from which the English word energy comes, meaning something at work, giving off energy right now. God’s word itself is alive and at work. The question has never been whether the word has power, but whether it has entered into us.

When the Holy Spirit opens you up, you will experience three things, and the lesson describes them precisely: the same passage of Scripture suddenly “makes sense”; the same sentence suddenly “pierces the heart”; the same truth suddenly becomes “the power of life.”

That is “Understanding.”

One of the most beautiful scenes in Scripture is the road to Emmaus. Two disciples are trudging along, downcast, and Jesus walks with them. “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” (Luke 24:27) Afterwards they said to each other, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) They had read the same Old Testament since childhood — so why did their hearts suddenly burn that day? Because “Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.” (Luke 24:45) The word “opened” is dianoigō in the original, meaning to open up something tightly shut. Brothers and sisters, true understanding is the Lord himself opening up our hearts and minds.

Another scene is the Ethiopian eunuch. He was sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah. “Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, ‘Do you understand what you are reading?’ He said, ‘How can I, unless someone explains it to me?’” (Acts 8:30-31) He was reading, but he did not understand. Reading is the letter; understanding is revelation.

The lesson uses a very down-to-earth picture: the letter is like raw rice; revelation is like cooked rice that can be eaten. In scientific terms the picture is remarkably accurate. The starch in raw rice is packed in a tight crystalline structure that the body’s amylase can barely touch; only when water is added and it is heated to around 60 to 80 degrees Celsius does the starch “gelatinise,” its structure loosening so that digestive enzymes can get in and break it down. The same grain of rice means something utterly different to the body cooked or uncooked. God’s word is the same. The same verse, without the fire of the Holy Spirit and the water of life, is just hard information; through prayer, meditation and the work of the Holy Spirit, it becomes the bread of life that we can absorb.

Go a step further: even eating is not yet the same as taking in. In 2014 the Swedish researchers Helander and Fändriks published a study in the Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology showing that, because the lining of the small intestine is multiplied layer upon layer by folds, villi and microvilli, its actual absorptive surface is about thirty square metres — roughly the floor of a small studio flat. God has prepared such a large absorptive surface in our bodies so that food can truly become part of us. Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, do we give God’s word that kind of “absorptive surface”? Or do we shut the book as soon as we finish, with nothing left behind?

The 321 insight says it plainly: without Understanding, hard to digest; with Understanding, able to grow.

And when truth really becomes revelation, change begins. The lesson says: the mindset changes, the life changes, daily living changes. This is exactly the fivefold change 321 speaks of: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice where the starting point is — the mindset. It is not changing behaviour first; it is changing the mindset first. People will not do what they do not believe; whatever a person truly believes, that is what they live out. So when God changes a person, he always begins by changing their mindset.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Transformed by the renewing of your mind” is the turning over of our mindset; “proving the will of God” is the daily living and ministry that follow.

321 also reminds us of a great shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. “Understanding” is the moment when that shift takes place. When you read a verse and suddenly realise, “So this is how God sees it,” your whole world has been rearranged once again.

This is exactly what Paul prayed for the church in Ephesus: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” (Ephesians 1:17-18) Brothers and sisters, shall we pray this for one another too? Ask God to enlighten the eyes of our hearts.

sections.heading: 5. Third Teaching: How to Gain Understanding — Humility and Repeated Meditation
sections.html:
The lesson says: understanding does not come by cleverness but by “humility.”

That is a sentence worth carving on the tablet of our hearts. For our easiest mistake is to think that “understanding” is the preserve of clever people — that those who have read a lot understand more, those with higher degrees understand more, those with good memories understand more. But what did the Lord Jesus say?

“At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.’” (Matthew 11:25)

The word “revealed” is apokalyptō in the original, the verb form of the word “revelation” — to pull back what was covered. “Infants” is nēpios in the original, meaning little children not yet able to speak. The ones to whom God gives revelation are not those who think they understand, but those who admit they don’t.

Why, then, did the Pharisees, who had read so much Scripture, fail to understand? The Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah: “seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand.” (Mark 4:12) Their eyes were fine, their ears were fine, their minds were fine; what was broken was the heart — because of pride, because they assumed they already understood.

The 321 insight says: the humble receive revelation; the proud receive knowledge.

This is the very core of 321: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. If, when I open the Bible, there sits in my heart a judge ready to rule on whether this passage suits me, then I am sitting in God’s seat — I may be reading the Bible, but in fact I am putting the Bible on trial. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When I open the Bible, I kneel down and say, “Lord, I need you to teach me.” At that moment, the veil is taken away.

Psychology gives us an interesting piece of corroboration too. In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that the least competent people tend to overestimate their performance the most, because they lack the very competence needed to recognise their own shortcomings. This is the famous “Dunning-Kruger effect.” On the other side, a series of studies published in 2017 by Mark Leary and colleagues in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin showed that people with “intellectual humility” — that is, people willing to admit they might be wrong — are better at telling strong evidence from weak and more willing to revise their views.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research tells us: the more we think we already know, the less we learn; the more we admit we don’t know, the more we can take in. How much more is that true of the things of God? Paul puts it even more absolutely: “Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” (1 Corinthians 2:14)

So before every time we read the Bible, let us first learn this prayer: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.” (Psalm 119:18) The man who wrote this psalm treasured God’s word above all else, and even he asked God to open his eyes — how much more do we need to?

The lesson then raises a second key: repeated meditation.

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

This was the command God gave Joshua in person, before he took up the baton and led Israel across the Jordan. Notice that God did not say, “Win more battles,” nor did he say, “Hold more meetings.” God said: meditate on my word day and night. The Hebrew word for “meditate” is hagah, and it is fascinating. Its basic meaning is to recite in a low voice, to murmur to oneself; it is even used of the low growl in a lion’s throat as it stands over its prey (Isaiah 31:4). So “meditating day and night” is not sitting and staring into space; it is keeping God’s word in our mouths, chewing it over and over, murmuring it again and again, like a lion standing over its food and refusing to let go.

Psalm 1 uses the same word: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” (Psalm 1:2-3) The one who meditates is like a tree planted by streams of water. A tree doesn’t run off to look for water; a tree sends its roots down into the water. Repeated meditation is sending the roots of our life, inch by inch, down into God’s word.

The lesson gives us a very clear process for gaining understanding: See (reading Scripture), Listen (receiving), Think (repeated meditation), Speak (sharing), Do (living it out).

Let’s look at them one by one.

First, See. This is the most basic: our eyes must actually rest on the text. “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.” (Acts 17:11) The Bereans didn’t just listen casually; they examined the Scriptures every day.

Second, Listen. Seeing is my reading; listening is God speaking. After Ezra led the people back, “They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.” (Nehemiah 8:8) Reading is seeing; giving the sense so that the people understood is listening. We need to be still and ask: Lord, what do you want to say to me today?

Third, Think. This is the crucial step, and the one most people skip. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus ran memory experiments using nonsense syllables and found that without review, after one day only about a third of the material was still remembered. Later research went further: in 2006 Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues published a large meta-analysis in the Psychological Bulletin showing that spreading learning out and repeating it over time is far more effective than doing it all in one go — this is the “spacing effect.” In neuroscience, the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed as early as 1949 that neurons that fire together wire together. Repetition lays down a real road in our brains.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly how God made us. When God told Joshua to “meditate day and night,” it wasn’t that God was nagging; it was that God understands the people he made.

Fourth, Speak. The lesson says: open your mouth and share, and the revelation deepens. This is not just spiritual intuition; there is evidence for it. In 2013 Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer published a study in Contemporary Educational Psychology showing that people who, after learning, prepared to teach others and actually explained it aloud understood and retained the material markedly better than those who studied only for themselves. When we tell others the truth we have received, we ourselves see it more clearly. Paul wrote to Philemon: “that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.” (Philemon 6) Faith that is shared is faith that becomes effective.

Fifth, Do. “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) In the parable of the sower the Lord Jesus said: “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.” (Matthew 13:23) Notice the order: hearing the word, understanding it, and then bearing fruit. Without understanding, there is no fruit.

When you meditate repeatedly, share and put it into practice, the lesson says three things will happen: revelation will deepen, faith will grow and life will change.

And in the end you will discover something wonderful: it is not people pushing you to serve; it is God’s word within you that drives you.

Jeremiah is the best example. He was beaten, imprisoned and mocked, and at one point he wanted to give up. He said: “If I say, I will not make mention of him, or speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones. I am weary with holding it in. I can’t.” (Jeremiah 20:9) Brothers and sisters, this is the ultimate fruit of “Understanding.” It wasn’t a rota telling him to go and speak; it was God’s word burning in his bones.

Paul says too: “for which I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily.” (Colossians 1:29) Notice: it is his working, which works in me mightily. Only service like that will last.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Understanding Is Letting the Bible Truly Become My Standard
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is really the second of the Three Foundations of 321: the Bible is my standard.

What is a “standard”? A standard is not a reference book, not a collection of maxims, not chicken soup for the soul. A standard is a measuring rule, the line that cannot be moved. When my feelings conflict with the Bible, I adjust my feelings; when my experience conflicts with the Bible, I adjust my experience; when my tradition conflicts with the Bible, I adjust my tradition. That is letting God be God.

Let us connect several main threads of 321 with today’s message.

First, the order of the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Spirit is the guidance of the Holy Spirit; Understanding is the standard of the Bible; Life is following the role model of Jesus; Service is letting Jesus be King; God is letting Jesus receive all the glory. Today we are at the second station. Skip “Understanding,” and our service will be like a boat without a rudder; stop at “Understanding” and go no further, and we become students who are only good at exams. Understanding is not the destination; it is the force that pushes us on towards life and service.

Second, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The lesson’s “the mindset changes, the life changes, daily living changes” is exactly this road. And for the mindset to change, what it takes is revelation. Information can only move the furniture around in our heads; revelation can knock down the walls inside us.

Third, humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Today we have seen that the proud receive knowledge and the humble receive revelation. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. Satan has never been afraid of us reading a few more chapters of the Bible; what he fears is that we will truly kneel before God’s word. Because the moment the humble kneel, God’s word opens, the veil falls away and life is changed.

Fourth, selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) When I lay down “I understand,” I gain “his wisdom”; when I admit I can’t, I experience that he can.

Fifth, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Nothing fits this lesson better. The letter stays in the brain; the Spirit enters the heart. Read the Bible with the brain, and you finish tired; read it with the heart, and you finish refreshed. “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6)

Sixth, the shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Every true moment of “Understanding” is a house move for our perspective.

Seventh, the 920 practice. What is 920? Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; we are to practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — so that the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in front of them. Brothers and sisters, the word you receive this morning must be lived out tonight before your spouse, before your children, before your colleagues. Truth is not for memorising; it is for living. If the revelation you receive does not bear love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control before your “2,” it has most likely stopped at the letter.

Eighth, the 235 relationships. The lesson’s “open your mouth and share, and the revelation deepens” is exactly the training ground of 235. The “2” is becoming spiritual companions with a selfless person, sharing with each other the word you receive from God each day; the “3” is building spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing on what you have received to the next person; the “5” is joining a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together. The last stage of changing our mindset is called “Multiplication” — if the revelation you have received is not passed on to the next person, the cycle is not yet complete.

Ninth, Jesus is the focal point. On the road to Emmaus, when Jesus explained the Scriptures, “he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” (Luke 24:27) Brothers and sisters, the deepest “Understanding” in Bible reading is seeing Jesus on every page. Not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances — our focus on Jesus alone.

All of this has only one purpose: to establish God’s system, to let Jesus be King and to let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 7. Practice for Daily Living: Walking It Through with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
321 tells us that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let us use these eight stages to take the lesson’s five practices deeper.

Practice 1: Don’t just read the Bible; seek revelation every day. When you read, don’t rush to finish; instead ask, “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?” Each day, write down one sentence God has spoken to you.

This practice corresponds to the leap “from Information to Revelation.” Information is: I read three chapters. Revelation is: one sentence stood up and spoke to me. Brothers and sisters, change the goal of your Bible reading from “finishing” to “hearing.” Writing it down matters, because writing it down is an admission: this sentence is what God has said to me today.

Practice 2: Meditate repeatedly; let the truth enter your heart. Turn over and over the word you have received, and carry that sentence with you all day. Today, choose one verse and meditate on it again and again.

This practice corresponds to “Conviction” and “Repetition.” Of the eight stages, the most neglected is “Repetition.” We always want to get it all at once and change all at once, but the way God made us is through repetition. Recite it once on the drive to work, think it over once at the red light, and meditate on it once more before you sleep. This is hagah; this is meditating day and night.

Practice 3: Open your mouth and share; let the revelation deepen. Share the truth you have received with someone else. Today, share what you have received with one person.

This practice corresponds to “Multiplication,” and it also deepens “Conviction” in turn. Sharing has a wonderful effect: when I have to explain something to someone, I must first think it through clearly; and when I say it, it moves from my brain to my mouth, and then from my mouth back down into my heart. This is the first step of 235, and the beginning of spiritual parenting.

Practice 4: Take real action; let the truth become life. Live out the word you have received, instead of leaving it in your thoughts. Today, deliberately live out one truth.

This practice corresponds to “Implementation,” “Evaluation” and “Correction.” Notice that these three stages go together: after doing it, evaluate — did I live it out today? Where did I get stuck? Then correct, and go again tomorrow. Spiritual growth does not happen in one go; it is correction day by day. “Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.” (1 Timothy 4:15)

Practice 5: Stay humble; be ready to receive revelation. Lay down the attitude that you already understand, and say often, “Lord, I need you to teach me.” Before every Bible reading, first pray for the Holy Spirit to open you up.

This practice is the foundation of the other four; it corresponds to the door between the first and second of the eight stages. Information is available to everyone, but revelation is given only to the humble. So please build a habit: before you open the Bible, bow your head for thirty seconds and say, “Lord, please open my eyes and open my heart and mind; I need you to teach me.”

Brothers and sisters, these five practices are not hard; what is hard is keeping them up. But remember: you are not doing this alone. The Spirit of God is at work within you.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder: Understanding Makes All the Difference in Service
sections.html:
At the end the lesson gives us a very practical contrast, one every co-worker should keep close to the heart.

Service without understanding: it wears you out, it is unstable, it easily gives up.

Why does it wear you out? Because it is propped up by your own strength. Why is it unstable? Because it is built on feelings, and when the feelings go, the person collapses. Why does it easily give up? Because it can’t find meaning; the moment it meets misunderstanding, criticism or being unnoticed, it can’t keep going.

Service with understanding: it has a foundation, it has direction, it has drive.

It has a foundation, because it is built on God’s word — “He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock.” (Luke 6:48) It has direction, because “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105) It has drive, because God’s word is like fire in the bones that cannot be held in.

Brothers and sisters, remember this sentence from the lesson: revelation is the key to service that lasts.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words are beautiful: if the Path of Serving has only “Spirit,” it drifts; add “Understanding,” and it becomes steady.

Come back to the sailing boat we began with. However fierce the wind, without a rudder the boat only spins in circles; but when the helmsman grips the tiller, that same wind becomes the force that drives you forward. Brothers and sisters, the wind of the Holy Spirit is blowing; the question is whether our hands are holding the rudder of God’s word.

When you truly enter into “Understanding,” two things will happen.

First, God’s word is no longer a book; it is the power of your life. Jeremiah says: “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.” (Jeremiah 15:16) He didn’t just read these words; he ate them.

Second, you are no longer just “doing service” but “living out the truth.” Doing service is a job; living out the truth is a life. Doing service keeps count of who notices and who affirms; living out the truth cares only whether the Lord is pleased.

In the end you will discover a truth that brings rest: it is not you holding up your service; it is God’s word within you holding you up.

Paul said to the believers in Thessalonica: “For this cause we also thank God without ceasing, that when you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which also works in you who believe.” (1 Thessalonians 2:13) “Works” — God’s word is at work in you right now.

So, brothers and sisters, this morning I want to issue three calls, to you and to me.

The first call: let us change the goal of our Bible reading from “finishing” to “hearing.” From today on, ask each day for one sentence that God speaks to you.

The second call: let us truly kneel before God’s word. Lay down the attitude that we already understand, and admit, Lord, I need you to teach me. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The third call: let us live out what we have received and pass it on. Live selflessly before every “2” of yours, and multiply the revelation through the relationships of 235.

For the end of it all is not that we know more, but that Jesus reigns as King in our lives and receives all the glory. May all of us, with unveiled face, see the glory of the Lord and be transformed into his image, from glory to glory.

keyVerses: “who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6)
practices: Don’t just read the Bible; seek revelation every day
Meditate repeatedly; let the truth enter your heart
Open your mouth and share; let the revelation deepen
Take real action; let the truth become life
Stay humble; be ready to receive revelation
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I will not only read your word; I will understand your word and live out your word.
May your Holy Spirit open me up, so that I move from the letter into revelation, from knowledge into life.

Lord, forgive me for reading your word with my head in the past, while refusing to listen with my heart to what you say. Forgive me for so often assuming I already understood, and so losing the place of receiving. Today I bring my pride before you; please take away the veil over my heart.
Give me a humble heart, so that I meditate on your word day and night and live it out. Make your word like a burning fire within me, driving me to serve and holding me up so that I do not fall.
Renew my life, and give my service a foundation and power. May what I receive become a blessing to others; may I spend my whole life as nothing but a servant of your word.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray; all glory be to you. Amen.
discussion: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6) Think back over the last three months: which verse truly “pierced” your heart and changed your mindset? How did what you received then go on to affect your daily living?

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” (Joshua 1:8) Of the five steps — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — which one do you most easily get stuck on? What specific way do you plan to take the next step this week?

l164.subtitle: The Path of Serving: Understanding · The Bible Is My Standard
l164.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: Without Life, Service Has No Influence
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to picture two scenes in your heart.

The first: the night sky on Lunar New Year’s Eve. A firework shoots upward — bang! — and the whole sky bursts into golden flowers, while tens of thousands of people below look up at once and gasp, “Wow!” But three seconds later? The light has scattered, the smoke has thinned, and the sky is pitch black again, as though nothing had ever happened.

The second: the mouth of the stove in an old family home out in the countryside. A lump of charcoal, glowing quietly red. It doesn’t dazzle anyone, it draws no gasps, and it will never make it into a single photograph. Yet slowly the pot of water comes to the boil, slowly the whole room full of people grows warm, a whole night passes, the dawn comes — and when you brush aside the ash, it is still glowing red.

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask you a question, and I ask it of myself too: is our service a firework, or a charcoal fire?

I have seen far too much firework service in the church. A special conference: tears flow, decision cards are filled in, the prayer is so fervent it seems about to lift the roof off, and everyone says, “This time it’s different!” Yet three months later the people have disappeared; six months later, no one can even remember what moved them in the first place.

I have also seen charcoal-fire service. There was a sister who, for twenty years without a break, came to church an hour early every Lord’s Day. She boiled the water, straightened the chairs and wiped the floor of the children’s Sunday school room. She couldn’t preach; her testimony was over in three minutes. Yet half the people in that church, in the very hardest stretch of their lives, were held up by a bowl of noodles she had cooked, a pair of hands she had held, an afternoon she had sat with them in silence.

Why is some service like fireworks, and some like a charcoal fire?

This lesson puts its finger on the key right at the start: many people have been moved, have received revelation, and love the Lord dearly — so why doesn’t the influence of their service last? Because one word is missing: “Life.”

In the 321 vision, the Path of Serving has five stations: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”; Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

In the last two lessons we walked together through “Spirit” and “Understanding”. We saw that if service does not begin with the Holy Spirit, it is all just human zeal, human talent and human effort; and we saw that if truth stops at the letter, stops in the head, it can never change a person’s life.

This morning we come to the third station: “Life”.

Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest station on the whole road. Why? Because the journey from “Spirit” to “Understanding” runs from the outside in; but the journey from “Understanding” to “Life” runs from the inside back out. Receiving costs nothing; living it out always costs something. To hear a sermon takes you an hour; to live out a single sentence of it may take you a lifetime.

James puts it very bluntly: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17)

Notice the word James uses: “dead”. The Greek is nekros (νεκρός) — the “dead” of a corpse. Brothers and sisters, a corpse is not without form. A corpse has hands and feet and a face, every feature in place, everything there — except one thing: there is no breath. At the end of the same chapter James says it even more plainly: “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.” (James 2:26)

A faith that has the stirring of the Spirit and the knowledge of Understanding, yet never comes to be lived out, looks just like that in God’s eyes: everything complete, except that it doesn’t move.

Spirit and Understanding, but no action; being moved and receiving revelation, but never living it out — a faith like that is still stuck in the head and the feelings. It has not yet entered life.

True service must walk all three steps: from Spirit, to Understanding, and on to Life. Only when truth becomes life does real influence follow.

This morning, let’s reflect together on three things: first, from revelation to life — living the truth out; second, the change of life — renewal from the inside out; third, the witness of life — passing on life by life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Books, Two Settings, One Question
sections.html:
This lesson has two theme passages, one from the letter of James and one from the Gospel of John. They were written nearly half a century apart and addressed different people, yet both point to the same thing: a faith that has not entered life does not count.

Let’s look at James first.

The author of this letter, James, is generally held to be the Lord Jesus’ own younger brother in the flesh. Matthew 13:55 records the people of Nazareth talking about Jesus and saying, aren’t his brothers James, Joses, Simon and Judas? John 7:5 tells us with great honesty: “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” In other words, James did not believe at first. It was only after the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7) that this younger brother became a disciple. Later he became a leader of the church in Jerusalem; in Galatians 2:9 Paul names him, together with Cephas and John, as a pillar of the church; and at the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15, it was he who gave the closing word.

James is generally dated to around AD 45–50, which may well make it one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written. Its recipients, according to James 1:1, were “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” — Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as guests under other people’s roofs, suffered endless discrimination, and spent their days in the tension of a yawning gap between rich and poor, under the hand of oppressors. In a setting like that, what does faith most easily turn into? Words. Because words cost nothing.

So the whole of James really says just one thing: true faith is always visible. In 2:15–16 he gives a very pointed example: if a brother or sister has no clothes to wear and nothing to eat, and you say to them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled,” yet don’t give them what the body needs — what good is it?

Brothers and sisters, please note: James is not saying that works save us. Paul puts it as clearly as it can be put in Ephesians 2:8–9: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” What James is saying is that saving faith will always bear the fruit of works. An apple cannot turn a tree into an apple tree — but an apple tree will always bear apples. Works are not the ticket that gets you in the door; works are the evidence that someone lives in the house.

Next, let’s look at John 6.

The author of John’s Gospel is the apostle John, and it is generally dated to around AD 85–95, very probably written in Ephesus. The setting of chapter 6 is especially important, because it is practically a living textbook for the third key point of this lesson.

That day Jesus fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–13). The crowd took one look and thought: isn’t this the one we’ve waited a thousand years for? They wanted to take him by force and make him king (6:15). The next day the crowd crossed the lake by boat and searched for him high and low. Jesus saw right through them and said, “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” (John 6:26)

From there Jesus began to speak more and more deeply. He said, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.” (John 6:35) He even spoke of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, “This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?” (John 6:60)

It was at that very moment that Jesus spoke our theme verse for today: “It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)

Brothers and sisters, the verse that follows close on its heels is chilling to read: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” (John 6:66)

The very people who had cheered over the bread yesterday and wanted to crown him king turned their backs and left today, because of one saying that was hard to understand and hard to live. Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” (John 6:67) Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” (John 6:68)

The same miracle, the same preaching, the same Jesus. Some left, some stayed. Where was the difference? The difference lay in that one word: Life. Those who left had come to get something; those who stayed were ready to hand over their whole lives.

Brothers and sisters, put these two passages side by side and you have what God wants to say to us this morning: faith that stops at the lips is dead; truth that stops in the head cannot give life. Only when it enters life does service have roots, have strength, and last.

Key Point 1: From Revelation to Life — Living the Truth Out

“It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)

Brothers and sisters, notice one word in what the Lord Jesus says here: “life”.

New Testament Greek has more than one word for “life”. Bios (βίος) is the biological, visible kind of life that gets used up — our physical strength, our span of years, our family fortune. But the word the Lord Jesus uses here is zōē (ζωή): the life that comes from God, eternal, with the very nature of God in it.

The Lord Jesus’ meaning is clear: the words I speak are not meant to add data to your head; they are meant to put the life of God inside you.

But where do so many people stop? This lesson nails it: they stop at “hear the sermon, be moved, the end.”

The morning message is wonderful. As you listen your heart grows warm, and your eyes may even mist over. But you walk out the door, take a phone call, sit through a whole day of meetings, get home — and that stirring has evaporated without a trace. The next day you hear another sermon, are moved again, and it evaporates again. Fifty-two Lord’s Days a year, moved fifty-two times — and your life hasn’t budged.

But that is not God’s intention. God’s intention is this: hear the word, understand it, do the word, and so it becomes life.

The Lord Jesus’ own conclusion was: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24)

The Greek word for “wise” here is phronimos (φρόνιμος). It doesn’t mean someone with a high IQ or a quick mind; it means someone with foresight, who knows how to plan for the future. And notice: the Lord Jesus didn’t say “everyone who hears these words of mine and understands them”, nor “everyone who hears these words of mine and is moved by them”. He said, “and does them”.

Two verses later the Lord Jesus says, “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” (Matthew 7:26)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully: the wise man and the foolish man heard the same sermon. The difference wasn’t in the hearing; the difference was in the doing.

Luke records an even more direct question from the Lord Jesus: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46) And James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice James’s phrase: “deluding your own selves”. The greatest danger for someone who only hears and never does is not that other people are fooled, but that they are fooled by themselves — thinking they already have what they don’t.

Two professors at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business, Jeffrey Pfeffer and Robert Sutton, published a book in 1999 called The Knowing-Doing Gap. They studied a great many companies and reached this conclusion: the problem in the vast majority of organisations is not that they don’t know what to do, but that they know and still don’t do it. They found that the more meetings a company holds, the more polished its presentations and the more persuasive its reasoning, the more easily an illusion sets in — that “we’ve talked about it” is the same as “we’ve done it”.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this even worse in the church?

Psychology offers a deeper explanation. In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of cognitive dissonance: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t match, an uncomfortable tension arises inside. There are two ways to resolve that tension. The first is to change your behaviour to fit your beliefs; the second is to change your beliefs to accommodate your behaviour. In an experiment with a colleague in 1959, Festinger found that people very often choose the second — quietly lowering the standard and persuading themselves that “it isn’t really that serious”.

What a frightening thing that is. When someone hears the word for years and never does it, the end is not a conscience that hurts more and more, but a conscience that hurts less and less. The truth didn’t lift his life up; instead his life dragged the truth down.

That is why this lesson’s insight is so well put: it isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out.

Let me use a very ordinary picture. You have a cookbook at home, beautifully printed, with mouth-watering photos. You read it cover to cover — three times, even — and you can recite the steps of every dish. Tell me: are you full? No. To be fed, you have to walk into the kitchen, wash the rice, light the stove, heat the oil, put up with the smoke and wash that pile of pots and pans. Reading the cookbook is comfortable; cooking is a bother. But only cooking can feed anyone.

Brothers and sisters, far too many of us spend our whole lives reading the cookbook.

Let me change the picture. You sit your driving test and score a hundred per cent on the written exam. Traffic rules, road signs and markings, who’s liable in an accident — you know them backwards. But that sheet of paper won’t drive the car for you. The real test is the moment you’re in the driver’s seat, the traffic is jammed at the crossroads and the car behind you keeps blasting its horn. Faith is like that too. Being able to recite “love is patient” is the written exam; still holding your patience the third time a family member talks back to you — that’s the road test.

In 321 language, this is the first checkpoint of the five-fold change. The five-fold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. But brothers and sisters, for a mindset to become life, there is a door to pass through, and that door is “Implementation”.

Among the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — “Information” comes before “Understanding”, “Revelation” is the stage of “Understanding”, and “Implementation” is exactly where “Life” begins. Many people spend their whole lives going round and round the first three stages — gathering information, waiting for revelation, being convinced in their hearts — and simply refuse to take the fourth step.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to say this with all sincerity: God doesn’t owe us a new revelation; God is waiting for us to give him an old obedience.

When you begin to live it out, the truth moves from “outside” to “inside”, from “mindset” to “life”.

Key Point 2: The Change of Life — Renewal from the Inside Out

Brothers and sisters, we might say: but I’ve tried. I really did try to live it out, and I failed.

Yes — and that is exactly the second thing we need to talk about. Because living it out has never depended on us gritting our teeth. The word of God itself has power to change a person’s life.

“Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s covenant is sure, making wise the simple.” (Psalm 19:7)

David’s words here are beautiful in Hebrew. “Restoring the soul” is literally “bringing back the soul” (meshivat nephesh), and the root of “restoring” is shuv, meaning to turn back, to return. Brothers and sisters, here is a picture: a person’s soul has wandered far off, has scattered, has got lost — and when the word of God comes, it leads that soul back to its originally intended position.

This is exactly what 321 means by humility — returning to our originally intended position. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The word of God is not a burden pressed down on us; the word of God is the road that leads the runaway heart back to the Father’s house.

Paul describes this process even more clearly: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

There are two key Greek words in this verse, and the contrast between them is striking.

“Conformed” is syschēmatizō (συσχηματίζω), from the root schēma, which refers to an outward pattern, an external shape — like the cut of a garment, changing with every passing fashion.

“Transformed” is metamorphoō (μεταμορφόω), from the root morphē, which refers to the inner essence, the true form. It is the very word Matthew 17:2 uses to describe the Lord Jesus being “changed” — transfigured — on the mountain.

Paul’s meaning is this: don’t let the world, like a mould, press you from the outside into its shape; let God change your very essence from the inside.

And notice that in the original, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is a present passive imperative. Passive — it isn’t you transforming yourself; it is letting God transform you. Present — it isn’t done once and for all; it is happening continually, on and on.

Paul uses the same idea in Colossians: “and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator” (Colossians 3:10).

“Being renewed” is anakainoumenon in the original, a present passive participle meaning “continually being renewed” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “gradually renewed”. Brothers and sisters, keep that word “gradually” in your heart. A change of life doesn’t happen in an instant; it is a process of gradual renewal.

One of the greatest temptations of our age is to demand everything “right now”. Web pages must load in a second, parcels must arrive the next day, diets must show results within a week. And so we make the same demand of our lives: one special conference and we should be completely made over; one prayer and we should overcome for ever. When it doesn’t happen, we lose heart, we give up, and we say, “I suppose I’m just not cut out for this.”

That isn’t how God works.

Let me use an old picture. In the old days, when a bolt of white cloth was to be dyed blue, you didn’t just toss it in the dye vat for a soak. It went into the vat, up onto the rack, out to dry and oxidise — then back into the vat, up onto the rack, out to dry again. Dipped again and again, exposed to the light again and again. Each time it looked only a shade darker, but after thirty times that cloth was blue through and through, and no washing could get it out.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what the word of God does in us.

Science also offers us a remarkable piece of supporting evidence. People used to think that the adult brain was fixed and could no longer change. But research by Professor Eleanor Maguire of University College London and her colleagues, published in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), found that London taxi drivers, because they have to memorise the city’s whole tangled web of streets, have noticeably more grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than most people — and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference.

In other words, when someone walks the same road over and over for years, that road really does get engraved into his brain.

Another study is worth remembering too. Research by Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit — ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days depending on the person and the behaviour.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: sixty-six days. Not six days, and not six hours.

These two studies can’t prove the Bible, and the Bible doesn’t need science to prove it. But they let us see that this is simply how God made human beings — we can be changed, and change takes repetition. That is precisely the meaning of the “Repetition” stage among the eight.

So this lesson reminds us of two things: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; from relying on ourselves, we turn to relying on Christ.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very core of 321. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. The essence of the old self is “self” — my opinions, my rights, my face, my credit. The essence of the new self is selflessness — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Please note: selflessness doesn’t mean turning yourself into zero, into nothing. Selflessness is entering into the fullness without limit and living it out. Because when that limited “I” steps aside, the limitless Christ lives himself out within me.

We often say it too: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Everything we do flows from the heart. Many people can’t change, not because they don’t try hard enough, but precisely because they try too hard — relying on the brain, relying on themselves, gritting their teeth and forcing it until, in the end, they are the first to collapse.

Real change happens like this: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the three movements in this verse. First, “with unveiled face” — the veil taken away, no more covering up, no more pretending. Second, “seeing the glory of the Lord” — fixing our focus on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Third, “are transformed into the same image” — and that “transformed” is, in the original, once again that word metamorphoō.

So here is the order: not first striving to change and only then daring to look at the Lord, but first looking at the Lord with unveiled face — and then being changed.

This is the insight of this lesson: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Brothers and sisters, when your life changes, your service will naturally have power. Not power you squeeze out of yourself, but power that flows out from within you.

Key Point 3: The Witness of Life — Passing On Life by Life

Jesus’ service was not just preaching; it was something he lived out with his life.

He lived it before our eyes. He died it before our eyes.

Of a life of thirty-three and a half years, only three and a half were spent in public ministry. And during those three and a half years he didn’t stand on a platform directing his disciples by remote control. He ate with them, lived with them, walked the roads with them, slept in the boat with them, and got caught in the same rain. The disciples saw how he prayed, and they saw how he grew weary; they saw how he worked miracles, and they saw how he wept.

On the last night he took off his outer garment, tied a towel round his waist, and stooped down to wash the disciples’ feet — including the feet of the man who would betray him. Then he said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)

Brothers and sisters, the Greek word for “example” here is hypodeigma (ὑπόδειγμα), meaning “a sample set down below for people to see”. The Lord Jesus didn’t hang the standard up high for us to gaze up at; he got down on the floor and did it once in front of us.

Peter later wrote: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). The word for “example” here is hypogrammos — the copybook children used in ancient times to learn to write. The teacher would write out a line first, and the child would trace over it, stroke by stroke.

But this lesson reminds us of something unusual and sobering: many people followed him because of the miracles, and then left him when hard times came.

We’ve already read it. In John 6, the crowds who wanted to crown him king yesterday scattered today over one saying that was hard to live: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” (John 6:66)

What does this tell us? It tells us that with only Spirit and Understanding, the influence is short-lived; add Life, and there is a foundation.

The Lord Jesus’ own conclusion comes at the very end of the Sermon on the Mount: “The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:25)

Notice: the wise man’s house wasn’t spared the storm. The rain still fell, the floods still came, the winds still blew. The difference wasn’t the weather; the difference was the foundation.

Speaking of foundations, there is a real-life observation well worth pondering. In Arizona there is a famous enclosed ecological research facility called Biosphere 2. The researchers found that the trees inside grew fast and tall, yet toppled over one after another before they reached maturity. Scientists later pointed to one important reason: inside that glasshouse there was no wind. Trees in the natural world stand firm because they are buffeted by wind year after year, and so grow a strengthened tissue commonly called “stress wood”, which makes the trunk tougher and drives the roots deeper.

Brothers and sisters, a tree that has never faced the wind grows fast but cannot stand.

It isn’t that God doesn’t love us when he lets the wind blow. The wind is God’s tool for driving our roots downward. Spirit and Understanding are growing upward; Life is putting down roots. The part that grows upward everyone can see; the part that goes down only God can see — yet what decides whether a tree will stand is the part no one sees.

So what truly influences people’s lives is not doctrine but life. This is what 321 means by passing on life by life — life influencing life.

Psychology gives us a very clear confirmation of this. The American psychologist Albert Bandura, in a series of studies at Stanford University — including the famous “Bobo doll experiment” of 1961, and the “social learning theory” he set out systematically in 1977 — pointed to one and the same conclusion: people, and children above all, mainly do not do what adults “say”; they do what adults “do”. The power of watching and imitating is far greater than that of spoken instruction.

Brothers and sisters, in the family and in the church alike, this is brutally accurate. Our children won’t grow up into what we say; they will grow up into how we live.

Albert Schweitzer is generally believed to have said something like this: example is not the main thing in influencing others — it is the only thing.

So why were the apostles able to change the world?

Not because they were eloquent. Paul himself tells us that some criticised him, saying, “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). They changed the world because they didn’t merely preach; they lived out Jesus, even to the point of being willing to lay down their lives.

Paul’s words to the church in Thessalonica are the finest commentary on passing on life by life: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:8)

Brothers and sisters, listen to that: not the Good News only, but our own souls as well — our very lives. The Good News is a message; our souls are our life. To give only the message is to pass on the word; to give your life along with it — that is to pass on life.

Church history bears witness to this again and again. Around AD 155, Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was brought to the stake. The proconsul urged him to deny Christ and save his life. The old man replied: eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never done me wrong — how can I blaspheme my King who saved me? That day Polycarp left behind no sermon; what he left behind was a life lived out. And a life like that multiplies into more lives. That is why Tertullian, in his Apology, could write the line usually rendered “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church”.

Closer to us is the Canadian missionary George Leslie Mackay. He arrived in Tamsui in March 1872, and in Taiwan he practised medicine, pulled teeth, preached and founded schools; in 1901 he died of illness in Taiwan and was buried there. He is generally believed to have left us this saying: “Rather burn out than rust out.” Brothers and sisters, to burn out is to give your life away; to rust out is to keep your life for yourself.

The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

So this lesson’s insight says: what has the most influence is not eloquence but life.

In the 321 vision, this is the 920 practice and the 235 relationships.

What is 920? Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2” — your spouse, your children, your colleagues, your neighbours, the elderly person you pass at the end of the lane in the early morning. Before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life, letting the self-centred “self” step aside so that Christ may live himself out in me; and so we bear the “9” — the fruit the Holy Spirit produces, in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

What is 235? When you pass on life by life, God places people around you: first a “2”, one or two selfless spiritual companions who hold each other up; then a “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children, one generation passing it on to the next; and at last a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together to establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Not first finding people to get things done, but first living out life. When the life is right, the relationships will be right; when the relationships are right, the ministry will follow naturally. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Life Means Letting Jesus Live Himself Out in Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we have seen today back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

The five stages of the Path of Serving — Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — correspond exactly to these Three Foundations and Two Core Values. Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”; Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

Today we stand at the third station. “Life” is the place where the words “Jesus is my role model” actually come true.

A role model isn’t a portrait hanging on the wall; a role model is the line in the copybook that I trace over, day after day. God’s intention has never been for us to admire Jesus, but for us to become like Jesus: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (Romans 8:29)

So what stops us from becoming like Jesus?

The self-centred life.

The mark of the old self is being self-centred; the mark of the new self is selflessness. When we are self-centred, we keep score — who spoke better, who got noticed, who got the applause, who got the short end of the stick. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Brothers and sisters, the biggest breach in our service has never been a lack of ability; it is an “I” that is too big.

So to enter “Life”, we must first pass through the cross. Paul says: “always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:10). First death, then life; first selflessness, then Christ. And that is precisely the lesson we will go deeper into next time — the denying of self that holds nothing back.

To enter “Life” also takes a great reversal of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective, from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective, from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Brothers and sisters, why do so many people refuse to live the truth out? Because from a human, earthly, temporary point of view, living it out is a very bad deal. If I forgive him, don’t I lose out? If I tell the truth, won’t it cost me? If I spend my time keeping that person company, won’t I fall behind schedule?

But from God’s, heaven’s, eternity’s point of view, everything is turned the other way round. Loss on earth is a deposit in heaven; losing out today is gain for eternity. That is why Paul could say, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21)

Finally, don’t forget that the direction of “Life” is multiplication. God gives us life not so that we can store it away for ourselves, but so that we will pass it on. This is the last of the eight stages — Multiplication — and it is what 920 and 235 look like in practice: living out selflessness before every “2” and bearing the fruit of the Spirit; letting spiritual parents bring forth spiritual children, letting one overcomer walk alongside others until there are many more overcomers — until God’s system is established, the Lord’s Prayer is fulfilled, and we press on into the end time revival.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Eight Stages into Daily Living
sections.html: This lesson gives us five practices. We’ll take them one by one in their original order, and deepen each using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

sections.heading: 1. Choose to Act: Live Out One Truth
