sections.html:
Each day, don’t just receive; choose one truth and put it into practice. Practice: today, deliberately live out one word of God — for example, loving others, forgiving, being patient.

This practice corresponds to the fourth of the eight stages — Implementation. Brothers and sisters, notice that the practice says “choose one”, not “all of them”. Biting off more than we can chew is an old habit of ours: today we resolve to love others, to forgive, to be patient, to be humble, to get up early — and in the end we manage none of them.

This morning, just choose one sentence. Write it on a piece of paper and stick it somewhere you’ll see it. Then, before today is over, find one concrete thing to do that puts it into action. Not being moved by it, not agreeing with it — doing it.

sections.heading: 2. Examine Your Life: See Whether Inside and Outside Match
sections.html:
Reflect on whether what you believe is already alive in your daily living. Practice: ask yourself, “Did I live out what I believe today?”

This practice corresponds to the fifth stage — Evaluation.

Evaluation isn’t self-accusation. Satan’s accusation drives people to despair; the Holy Spirit’s rebuke turns people back. Evaluation means placing yourself in the light and looking honestly: is the person who speaks the same person who lives?

Brothers and sisters, I suggest you set aside three minutes before bed at night and ask just three questions: In what did I live out Christ today? In what did I slip back into the old self today? If I could do it over again, what would I do?

sections.heading: 3. Keep Being Renewed: Let Your Life Change Day by Day
sections.html:
Let the word of God adjust your thinking and your behaviour. Practice: each day, write down one mindset that needs to change.

This practice corresponds to the sixth and seventh stages — Correction and Repetition.

We said earlier that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become a habit. Brothers and sisters, don’t give up because you fall on the third day. Falling isn’t the end; giving up is.

“The new man, who is being renewed in knowledge” (Colossians 3:10) — that “gradually”, as the Chinese Union Version renders it, is God’s grace to us, and God’s patience with us too. Get yourself a little notebook and each day write down one mindset that needs to change. Look back a year from now, and you’ll see what a work God has done in you.

sections.heading: 4. Live Out an Example: Influence Others with Your Life
sections.html:
Don’t just preach; let people see Jesus in you. Practice: today, live out the likeness of Christ in one matter.

This practice corresponds to the eighth stage — Multiplication — and it is the 920 practice itself.

The Lord Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Notice the last phrase: the glory doesn’t go to us; it goes to the Father. This is the second of 321’s Two Core Values — let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, start today with the “2” closest to you. Family is often the hardest, yet also the most honest exam room there is.

sections.heading: 5. Be Willing to Pay the Price: Let Your Life Be Shaped by the Lord
sections.html:
Following Jesus always has a cost, but it also brings real life. Practice: today, in one thing that isn’t easy, choose to obey God.

This practice corresponds to the third stage — Conviction.

Conviction is saying “yes” before you have seen the outcome. In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said, “Not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) That night his sweat was like drops of blood. That wasn’t an easy obedience; it was an obedience that bled.

Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to look for some earth-shaking deed today. Just choose to obey in one small thing that isn’t easy — the phone call you’ve never wanted to make, the apology you’ve never been able to get out, the right you’ve never been willing to lay down.

A Gentle Reminder

Service without life has three marks: quick, hot, but it doesn’t last.

Service with life also has three marks: steady, rooted, and influential.

Brothers and sisters, the key isn’t how much you do, but how much you live out.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Living Out Jesus with Our Lives
sections.html:
If the Path of Serving stops at “Spirit” and “Understanding”, it is still incomplete. It must enter “Life”.

When you enter life, truth is no longer just something you hear but something you live out; faith is no longer just a mindset but a life.

And in the end you’ll discover something wonderful: it isn’t you who influences people; it is the life of Christ influencing people through you.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The branch doesn’t have to strain to manufacture fruit; the branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Fruit is the natural overflow of life, not the product of a forced will.

So this morning, the call isn’t for you to push harder, but to draw closer. It isn’t for you to do a little more, but to let Jesus live a little more.

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King — and a king is not a consultant; a king is the one whose word is final. Let Jesus receive all the glory — all of it, keeping none back for ourselves.

This is the deepest power of service: living out Jesus with our lives.

keyVerses: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17)
“It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)
practices: Choose to act: today, deliberately live out one word of God — for example, loving others, forgiving, being patient.
Examine your life: before bed, ask yourself, “Did I live out what I believe today?”
Keep being renewed: each day, write down one mindset that needs to change.
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I don’t only want to understand your word; I want to live out your word.

Lord, forgive me. So often I have stopped at being moved, stopped at knowing, and never stepped into doing. I have heard so much and lived out so little. This morning I no longer ask for a new revelation; I want to offer you an old obedience.
Let your life grow within me, carrying me from knowledge into life, from receiving into living it out.
I am willing to be changed by you — to put off the old self and put on the new self, day by day, being gradually renewed, living out the likeness of Christ.
Lord, I place my “self” in your hands. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Make my life a witness, so that life influences life; may everyone around me be able to see you in me.
Reign as King in my home, reign as King in my service, reign as King over my whole life.
All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24) Share: is there a word of God you have “heard” for a long time but have never gone and “done”? What is holding you back — is it inconvenient, is it a bad deal, or are you simply unwilling?

“Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:8) Share: in your own life, is there someone who has “influenced you with their life”? What did they do? This week, whose “someone” is God calling you to be?
l165.title: From Knowing into Living It Out
l165.subtitle: The Path of Serving — Life (Part 1): Letting Truth Become Life
l165.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: A Choice That Holds Nothing Back
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this early morning, let’s begin with a diary.

On 28 October 1949, a twenty-two-year-old American wrote one sentence in his journal: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” The man who wrote it was Jim Elliot. Seven years later, on 8 January 1956, he and four companions — Nate Saint, Ed McCully, Pete Fleming and Roger Youderian — were speared to death on a river beach while trying to bring the gospel to the Waodani people in the jungles of Ecuador. Five young families lost their husbands and fathers overnight.

In the eyes of the world, it was a total waste. Five young lives, five bright futures, and what they bought was five bodies lying on a riverbank. Yet the story that followed went far beyond anything anyone could have imagined. Their wives and sisters went back to the same tribe, settled there and learned their language. Years later, the very men who had speared their husbands were baptising others, with their own hands, in that same river.

Brothers and sisters, this is the lesson we are going to reflect on today. On the road of service, what matters most has never been ability; it has always been life.

Many people think service means doing lots of things, giving lots of time and completing lots of tasks. What we value is a calendar packed with ministry, how fast we reply in the group chat, how we perform up front. But what the Lord Jesus values has never been the outward ministry; it is the life within us.

Our series of lessons on “the Path of Serving” follows this road: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First comes the guidance of the Holy Spirit, then the understanding of truth; once there is understanding, life grows; once there is life, we can speak of service; and in the end, all service returns to God, letting Jesus receive all the glory. Today we come to the third station: “Life”.

What is “Life”? “Life” is the life of Jesus. At the heart of this life is not the self-centred life but selflessness; not living for ourselves, but living for Jesus and living for others.

The Lord Jesus has given us the most perfect example. Paul says, “He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). John says, “For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son” (John 3:16). God’s love towards us holds nothing back; Jesus’ giving of himself for us holds nothing back.

So what we are to learn today is not how to do more, but how to live out a life like this — a life that “holds nothing back”.

Let me ask you a question right at the start, and please don’t answer it too quickly: on this road of following the Lord, is there anything that, to this very day, you have still not truly handed over?

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Two Scenes Behind Two Verses
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of the words “holding nothing back”, we first need to go back to the scenes behind our two theme verses.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul, around AD 56–57, very probably from Corinth in Greece, as his third missionary journey was drawing to a close. At the time Paul was preparing to take the collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26), and afterwards to head west to Spain, passing through Rome on the way. This letter has one unusual feature: Paul was writing to a church he had never visited himself. The church in Rome was made up of both Jewish and Gentile believers, and between the two groups there was tension and misunderstanding. So Paul spent eleven chapters moving from humanity’s total depravity to justification by faith, from justification to sanctification, and from sanctification to God’s whole plan for Israel and the Gentiles.

And Romans 8 is the summit of that great mountain. Starting from verse 1 — “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” — it climbs higher and higher, until from verse 31 onwards Paul’s pen suddenly breaks into song: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31)

Then comes our theme verse. Here Paul uses a form of argument the Jewish rabbis often used, known as the argument “from the greater to the lesser”: if the greater has already been given, what lesser thing would be begrudged? God has already handed over his own one and only Son — what is there left that he would hold back from giving us?

There is a word here that deserves special attention. “Didn’t spare” is the Greek φείδομαι (pheidomai), meaning to begrudge, to hold back, to be unable to let go. Paul did not pick this word at random. In the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, Genesis 22:12 uses this very word when the angel speaks to Abraham: “you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” (Genesis 22:12)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? On Mount Moriah, at the moment Abraham raised the knife, the angel stopped him. But on the hill of Golgotha, God the Father raised the knife, and no one stopped him. Abraham’s Isaac was in the end replaced by a ram, but the Son of God had no substitute, because he himself was the Lamb. “Didn’t spare” means held nothing back. The first one in the whole Bible to “hold nothing back” was not us; it was God.

John 3:16 has a different setting again. This verse comes in the middle of a conversation by night. A Pharisee named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, came to Jesus at night (John 3:1–2). Jesus spoke to him of being born again, of being born of water and the Spirit, of heavenly things. When he reached verse 14, Jesus drew on the story in Numbers 21: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). In the wilderness, the people bitten by snakes had only to look at the bronze serpent on the pole, and they lived. Only then comes verse 16 — the best-known sentence in the world.

John’s Gospel is generally held to have been written by the apostle John in his old age in Ephesus, around AD 85–90. By the time he looked back and wrote it all down, he had seen with his own eyes the Lord who was lifted up, and he had seen the gospel spread from little Galilee across the whole Roman Empire.

Two verses, two scenes, pointing to one thing: God’s love is not an emotion but an action; not a declaration but a handing over. He gave away what was most precious to him, and kept nothing back in his hand.

The denying of self we are speaking of today doesn’t begin with us; it begins with God. Our giving is only ever a response to his one great giving that held nothing back.

sections.heading: 3. First Teaching: Denying of Self Is the Only Road into the Selfless Life
sections.html:
Selflessness is not a slogan; it is a life built up from one choice after another to deny ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, in our 321 teaching we often speak of “selflessness”. But I must be honest: nobody wakes up one morning and finds they’ve become selfless. Selflessness isn’t a fruit that drops from the sky; selflessness is a road, and every step on that road is called “denying of self”.

So what is denying of self? The answer is actually very simple — so simple it takes only three phrases: for Jesus, for others, not for myself.

This is the way of the cross.

1. The Weight of “Deny Himself”

The Lord Jesus said, “He who doesn’t take his cross and follow after me, isn’t worthy of me.” (Matthew 10:38)

The essence of the cross is denying of self. In Matthew 16 the Lord says it more fully: “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.’” (Matthew 16:24–25)

“Deny himself” is the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning to disown utterly, to break off all connection flatly, to declare, “I do not know this man.”

The Bible uses this word in another place too. Again in Matthew, the Lord says to Peter, “Tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Matthew 26:34) And later, in the courtyard, Peter really did say, “I don’t know the man.” (Matthew 26:72) The New Testament uses the very same root.

Brothers and sisters, the contrast is staggering. When Peter said of Jesus, “I don’t know the man,” that was failure; yet the Lord calls us to say of ourselves, “I don’t know the man” — and that is victory. Denying of self isn’t trimming yourself into a slightly nicer shape or turning your temper down a notch. Denying of self means that at every critical moment you point at the old self that wants to be king and say: I don’t know him, I won’t listen to him, he is not my master.

When we choose ourselves, we live in the self-centred life; when we choose Jesus, we enter into selflessness.

2. Two Groups of People, Two Endings

There are two groups of people in the Bible who make this crystal clear.

The first group is on the shore of Galilee. “Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. He said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.’ They immediately left their nets and followed him.” (Matthew 4:18–20) Close behind come James and John: “They immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him.” (Matthew 4:22)

The nets were their skill; the boat was their livelihood; their father was their family ties and their fallback. Those three things stood for a fisherman’s whole life. And twice the Bible uses the word “immediately”.

Where did the key lie for them? Not in being more spiritual, not in being more gifted, but in “holding nothing back”.

The second group is just one man: the rich young ruler. He had good conduct — he had kept the commandments since his youth. He had moral standing — no one could fault him. He had a hunger — he came running and knelt before Jesus to ask about eternal life (Mark 10:17). By the standards of today’s church, a young man like that would have been drafted onto the ministry team long ago. But the Lord said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)

And the result? “But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.” (Matthew 19:22)

Notice: the Lord didn’t rebuke him, and the Lord didn’t run after him either. All the Bible leaves us is a retreating back, and one word to describe him: sad.

Brothers and sisters, this man’s biggest problem wasn’t that he was rich; it was that he “held something back”. The fishermen left their nets; he couldn’t bear to part with his possessions. The fishermen went “immediately”; he went away “sad”.

So it isn’t how much you do that decides your life; it is how much you “hold back” that decides whether you can follow the Lord.

3. The Science of a Grain of Wheat

The Lord Jesus himself gave us the most beautiful picture: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Modern botany gives us a vivid footnote to this. For a seed to germinate, it must go through three stages: it takes in water and swells, the seed coat splits open, and the nutrients stored in its endosperm are completely broken down and used up. The seed coat is the seed’s protective layer, its sense of security — but as long as the seed coat doesn’t split, the root can never come out. And more crucially still, the starch and protein stored in the endosperm must be broken down completely by enzymes before the new shoot has the energy to push up through the soil. In other words, the seed doesn’t give “a little” to the new life; it gives itself away “entirely”.

A grain of wheat left in the barn is still just a grain of wheat — and it grows drier by the day. A grain of wheat that falls into the ground is no longer a single grain; it becomes thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual condition of many of us is that of a “well-preserved seed”. We very carefully protect our time, our face, our rights, our wounds — and in the end we have preserved ourselves but borne no fruit.

4. What Psychology Has Seen Too

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl (1905–1997) was himself a survivor of the Auschwitz concentration camp. In his book Man’s Search for Meaning (first published in 1946), he put forward an idea he called “self-transcendence”. Human beings, he said, are by nature directed towards something beyond themselves: the more a person forgets himself and gives himself to a mission or to someone he loves, the more human he becomes and the more he fulfils himself. Conversely, the more he pursues self-fulfilment as a goal, the more it eludes him.

This scholar, who was no theologian, drew on what he observed in the camps to bear witness alongside the Bible: the way to gain life is to lose it.

And the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), in The Cost of Discipleship (published in 1937), wrote these famous words: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Eight years later he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, signing those words with his own life.

5. A 321 Insight

Brothers and sisters, here is the message of this section in the language of 321:

First, the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. In the Garden of Eden, “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5) was the first time humanity tried to put itself in God’s place.

Second, pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The rich young ruler’s problem wasn’t that he had too much money; it was that his money sat on the throne. The fishermen’s victory wasn’t that their boats were too shabby to matter; it was that they were willing to let Jesus sit on the throne.

Third, then, the point isn’t striving more but letting go more; it isn’t a question of ability but a question of “whether I will deny myself”.

Brothers and sisters, if this morning you feel your service has become a heavy slog, don’t rush off to look for a new method. First ask one question: what am I still clutching in my hands?

sections.heading: 4. Second Teaching: Holding Nothing Back Is a Resolve That Does Not Fear Death
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus spelled out the conditions of discipleship very clearly — so clearly that it is a little frightening.

1. Three times “can’t be my disciple”

In Luke 14 the Lord says three times over, “can’t be my disciple”:

“If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.” (Luke 14:26)

“Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross, and come after me, can’t be my disciple.” (Luke 14:27)

“So therefore whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.” (Luke 14:33)

First we need to clear up a difficulty that is often misunderstood. The Chinese Union Version renders the first verse “love me more than”, with a small footnote under it: the original reads “hate”. The Greek is indeed μισέω (miseō) — “hate”. Does the Lord Jesus really want us to hate our parents? Of course not. For the same Lord commands us to honour our parents (Matthew 15:4), and commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves (Matthew 22:39).

This is a Semitic way of expressing comparison. Hebrew has no dedicated grammar for the comparative; to say “love A more than B”, it says “love A, hate B”. Genesis 29:30–31 is the best example: Jacob “loved also Rachel more than Leah”, and the very next verse says that “Leah was hated” — literally, “hated”. So “hate” here is a contrast, not hostility.

That is why Matthew puts the same teaching in comparative terms: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me isn’t worthy of me.” (Matthew 10:37)

The Lord’s meaning is clear: only one can sit on the throne of your heart. He isn’t asking you not to love your family; he is asking you to love him so much that your love for your family is itself lifted up, purified and enlarged.

Then the Lord states the most basic law of the spiritual world: “He who seeks his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it.” (Matthew 10:39)

Brothers and sisters, keep this law in your heart: what you clutch, you will lose; what you let go of, you will gain.

This isn’t a motivational slogan; it is the physics of the kingdom of heaven, as real as gravity. Grab a fistful of sand, and the tighter you grip, the faster it runs out; open your palm, and the sand stays.

2. The four “no fears” of holding nothing back

So what does “holding nothing back” actually look like? It looks like four “no fears”: no fear of loss, no fear of being hurt, no fear of paying the price, no fear of death.

Let’s be honest: much of what we hold back isn’t because we’re greedy; it’s because we’re afraid. Afraid of losing our security, afraid that giving won’t be repaid, afraid of being misunderstood, afraid that once we’re hurt no one will come and help us up. So in our service we keep something up our sleeve; in our relationships we keep a wall; in our giving we keep a separate account; in our obedience we keep a “provided that”.

But the Bible says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” (1 John 4:18) What really drives out fear is not our becoming braver; it is our being loved deeply enough.

3. Daniel: An Old Man Who Did Not Fear Death

Daniel is the finest example.

Let’s get the dates straight first. Daniel was carried off to Babylon by King Nebuchadnezzar in the third year of King Jehoiakim of Judah, around 605 BC (Daniel 1:1–6). He was only a youth then. The lions’ den, however, took place in the reign of Darius the Mede (Daniel 5:31) — that is, after Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians around 539 BC. In other words, the Daniel who walked into the lions’ den was an old man in his eighties.

A man in his eighties, at the very top of the government, only a few years from a peaceful retirement, had a hundred reasons to compromise. Besides, the decree only lasted thirty days — he could have just waited it out. Besides, he only had to close his window, and nobody would have known.

But the Bible records it like this: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.” (Daniel 6:10)

Brothers and sisters, notice those last few words: “as he did before.”

He didn’t double his praying to show how brave he was, nor cut back on it to lower the risk. He simply carried on as usual. Because someone who holds nothing back doesn’t need to change for a crisis — he handed everything over long ago, and the crisis merely takes a photograph of what he is like every day.

He was thrown into the lions’ den. Early the next morning the king, sick with worry, ran to the den and called out to him, and Daniel answered, “My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me.” (Daniel 6:22)

In the end a pagan king issued this decree: “for he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end.” (Daniel 6:26)

Think about the weight of that: an old captive from a fallen nation, with no army, no pulpit and no media, moved the king of the greatest empire of his day to issue a nationwide decree on behalf of the God of Israel.

Daniel didn’t influence the world by ability, but by “a life that did not fear death”.

The three young men before the furnace spoke with the same resolve: “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.” (Daniel 3:18) Those three words, “But if not”, are the signature of a life that holds nothing back.

4. What Draws People Is Life

It is the same today. People aren’t drawn by your eloquence; they’re drawn by your life.

The Lord Jesus said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32) The very next verse explains it: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.” (John 12:33)

Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: Jesus’ most compelling moment was not when he worked miracles, nor when he preached the Sermon on the Mount, but when he hung on the cross, looking utterly powerless. The life of the cross carries its own power to draw people.

Revelation describes the overcoming saints of the last days by the same logic: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)

Notice those words, “didn’t love their life”. Remember the “didn’t spare” of Romans 8:32? In the Chinese Union Version the two verses use the same phrase: God did not spare his own Son; the overcomers did not spare their own lives. As the Father gave holding nothing back, so the overcomers give back holding nothing back.

Paul’s own confession was: “But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.” (Acts 20:24)

5. Supporting Evidence from Science

Interestingly, science is nodding in the same direction.

Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues, in a study published in 2003 in the journal Psychological Science, followed more than four hundred older married couples for five years. They found that, after controlling for health, finances and other variables, those who regularly gave practical help to others had a markedly lower risk of dying within the five years than those who did not; while simply “receiving help from others” brought no such benefit.

The researchers’ own title is telling: “Providing social support may be more beneficial than receiving it.”

Brothers and sisters, this of course doesn’t mean we deny ourselves in order to live longer. It means the Creator has written the logic of his life into our very bodies — human beings were made to “give themselves away”. When we cling tightly to ourselves, it isn’t only that we dry up spiritually; even our bodies protest.

6. A 321 Insight

In the language of 321:

First, selflessness is not the absence of life; selflessness is the most powerful life there is. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness without limit and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul says it best: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Second, true influence is not control but denying of self. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Third, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not a Christian who is very good at getting things done, but a Christian who “doesn’t love their life” — because the last card in his hand is death, and against someone who doesn’t fear death he has no card left to play.

sections.heading: 5. Third Teaching: Living Out the Selfless Life through See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do
sections.html:
Many people imagine that denying ourselves is very hard and very far away, as if it had to mean martyrdom. In fact, denying of self is hidden in the choices of everyday life.

Every day we make five choices: what to look at, what to listen to, what to think, what to say and what to do.

These five are the steering wheel of your life.

1. This Is How Jesus Himself Lived

To see how important these five choices are, the best way is to look at how the Lord Jesus himself lived.

About “seeing”, the Lord said: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19)

About “listening” and “doing”, the Lord said: “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

About “speaking”, the Lord said: “As my Father taught me, I say these things.” (John 8:28)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The Lord who became flesh, in his thirty-three years on earth — not one bit of his seeing, listening, thinking, speaking or doing started from himself. The selfless life isn’t a slogan we invented; it is the pattern Jesus lived out in person. “Jesus is my role model” — here those words become very concrete.

2. Two Roads, Chosen Every Day

When you choose to “see” through your own eyes, to “listen” by your own standards and to “think” by your own ideas, you are living in the self-centred life.

When you choose to see through God’s eyes, listen to God’s voice and think with God’s truth, you begin to enter into selflessness.

The Bible gives clear instructions for each of these five links:

On seeing: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” (Psalm 101:3)

On listening: “When you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” (Isaiah 30:21)

On thinking: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

On speaking: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

On doing: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father, through him.” (Colossians 3:17)

And the master switch for all of this, the Bible says, is the “heart”: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

3. The starting point is not outside but in the “Spirit”

The starting point of these five choices is not outside but inside; not in method, but in the “Spirit”.

The 321 Path of Serving runs in this order: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

The Holy Spirit is my guide, so first comes “Spirit”. As the Holy Spirit guides me, I can “see” and “listen” rightly, and this brings me into “Understanding” — the Bible is my standard. When I see rightly, listen rightly and think rightly, my life is shaped, and this is “Life” — Jesus is my role model. Once there is life, there can be “Service” — let Jesus be King. And finally everything returns to “God” — let Jesus receive all the glory.

That is why Paul says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t depend on effort; it depends on connection. The Lord says, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

A branch doesn’t have to strain to bear grapes; a branch only needs to stay joined to the vine. Have you ever seen a branch gritting its teeth, dripping with sweat, trying to bear fruit? Never. It simply stays connected, and the fruit grows.

4. What the Brain Tells Us

Here is a scientific fact that can help us understand why “everyday choices” matter so much.

The Canadian psychologist Donald O. Hebb, in his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior, put forward a principle that later generations have often summed up as: neurons that fire together wire together. That is, if two nerve cells are repeatedly activated at the same time, the connection between them grows stronger. This is the foundation of what we now call “neuroplasticity”.

In other words, what you choose each day to look at, to listen to and to think about is not a one-off act; you are paving a road in your brain. Walk it once and you’ve crossed a lawn; walk it a hundred times and it becomes a path; walk it ten thousand times and it becomes a highway. No wonder the Bible says “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — that “transformed” is the Greek μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō), the word we use for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. It means a complete change of form, and it is in the present continuous and the passive voice: let God keep on changing you.

You can’t decide your whole life in one go, but you can decide one thing this morning. And ten thousand of these mornings make a lifetime.

5. Joy Is a Dashboard

As you keep choosing to deny yourself in your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, you will experience one very real sign: joy.

The Lord Jesus said, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11)

Paul lists joy second among the fruit of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Nehemiah said to the weeping people: “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10)

Notice: joy is a fruit, not a fruit juice. Juice is squeezed out; fruit grows. We cannot squeeze out joy by willpower; we can only grow joy through connection.

So joy is the dashboard of the spiritual life. If you find that the more you serve the more tired you get, the more you do the more bitter it feels, and that your joy is draining away — please don’t immediately blame yourself, and don’t immediately switch to a different ministry. First go and look at what the dashboard is telling you.

Usually it isn’t because there’s too much to do, but because there’s been “no denying of self”. A lot of work doesn’t dry a person up; a lot of work plus “doing it for myself” is what dries a person up. When, in my service, I secretly want to be noticed, want to be affirmed, want to prove myself, I am carrying two burdens at once: the Lord’s yoke, and my own “self”. The Lord’s yoke is easy and his burden is light (Matthew 11:30), but the “self” is heavy.

The American psychologist Martin Seligman, in Authentic Happiness (2002), proposed three paths to happiness: the pleasant life, the engaged life and the meaningful life. His research indicated that the happiness brought by sensory pleasure alone is the most fleeting, while the “meaningful life” — using your strengths in the service of something bigger than yourself — brings the deepest and most lasting satisfaction.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms the Bible from the other side: those who live for themselves have the shortest-lived happiness; those who live for the One who is greater than themselves have the deepest joy.

True joy isn’t things going smoothly; it is a life brought into alignment.

6. A 321 Insight

In the language of 321:

First, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23).

Second, follow the Holy Spirit and there is life; follow yourself and there is pressure. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Third, the five-fold change happens like this: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. And the doorway into all of this is precisely our everyday seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Life Map for Denying of Self
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s message into the whole map of 321 and take a look.

1. The Three Foundations: We Don’t Deny Ourselves Empty-Handed

Jesus is my role model. Our denying of self is not some religious self-torment; it is following a Lord who has already walked this road ahead of us. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8) “Emptied himself” is the Greek κενόω (kenoō) — to pour oneself out. From heaven to the manger, from the manger to the cross, the Lord Jesus poured himself out all the way down, until not a drop was left.

The Bible is my standard. Denying of self cannot go by feelings, nor by other people’s expectations. What should be given up and what should be kept must follow the Bible. Without the Bible as our standard, denying of self easily turns into people-pleasing, into having no boundaries, into being used by others and growing bitter inside.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Denying of self without the Holy Spirit is nothing but gritted teeth. It is the Holy Spirit who pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5), and the Holy Spirit who enables us to put to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13). That is why we say: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — everything begins with the Spirit.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive the Glory

At its heart, denying of self is really a change of king.

There is only one throne in the heart. When I sit on it, I have to keep up my own face, fight for my own interests, take my own revenge and hold everything up by myself — what a crushing weight that is. When Jesus takes the throne, I can let go, because a Lord who is greater, more loving and more powerful than I am is reigning.

Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15) This verse lays out “for Jesus, for others, not for myself” as plainly as can be.

And when Jesus is King, the result will always be that Jesus receives the glory. We don’t deny ourselves so that people will see “how much I’ve sacrificed”; if that were so, it would only be using self-denial to serve the “self” — a more refined kind of pride. True denying of self means people can’t see me; they see only him. John the Baptist put it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

The end point of our denying of self is not that we become a bit more spiritual, but that we “establish God’s system”.

What is God’s system? It is that line in the Lord’s Prayer: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) The system of heaven is centred on God; the system of earth is centred on self. Every choice to deny ourselves sets one piece of “heaven’s order” down on earth.

If one person in a family is willing to deny themselves, that home begins to have the flavour of the kingdom of heaven; if two or three people in a small group are willing to deny themselves, that group becomes a living stone in God’s system.

4. A Shift in Perspective

Denying of self becomes possible because our perspective has changed. 321 speaks of four shifts: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Paul says, “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.” (Philippians 3:7) He didn’t become aloof; he changed account books. What used to be entered in the “assets” column is now entered in the “liabilities” column; what he once held precious he now counts as refuse, “that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:8).

Brothers and sisters, people who deny themselves aren’t losing; they’re converting. Exchanging the temporary for the eternal isn’t sacrifice; it’s wisdom. Jim Elliot was right: he is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.

5. The 920 Practice

The 321 practice of 920 is exactly how today’s message is put into practice in our relationships.

Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2” — spouse, children, parents, colleagues, neighbours, the brother in your small group who is hardest to get along with. When I face this “2”, I practise living out the selfless life, which is the “0”: not for myself, not contending, not grabbing, not judging, not demanding anything in return. And when the “0” is truly lived out, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control — grow naturally in that relationship.

Notice the order: not first striving to bear fruit, but first going back to zero. Zero isn’t nothing at all; zero is giving up the throne. Once it is given up, the nine graces have room to grow.

6. The 235 Relationships

A life of denying of self will always move towards the 235 relationships.

The “2” is a spiritual companion: walking with another person who is willing to be selfless, holding each other up and reminding each other. Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9)

The “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children: passing life on. Paul says to Timothy, “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:1–2)

The “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Brothers and sisters, see the direction of the flow: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson drives in the very first stake — life. When the life is right, the relationships will be right; when the relationships are right, the ministry will be alive.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Living Out a Life of Denying of Self in Everyday Choices
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing it is. This week, please practise three things. And for each of them I’ll use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to help you go deeper.

Practice 1: One “choice to deny myself” each day

Deliberately make one decision in the course of the day that is “not for myself”. For example: where you wanted to react from your emotions, choose gentleness; where you wanted to fight for yourself, choose to let go; where you wanted to run away, choose to obey.

Start with small things, and you’ll find your life beginning to change.

Information: today you have already received the information — denying of self is the only road into selflessness; the Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24).

Revelation: information doesn’t change people; revelation does. Be still and ask the Holy Spirit to point out “that one thing” — not self-denial in general, but your one specific thing, the thing you have never been willing to let go of. Ask the Lord to let you see that while you think you’re holding on to it, it is actually holding on to you.

Conviction: say to the Lord in your heart, “Yes, Lord, you are right.” Conviction isn’t intellectual agreement; it is the surrender of the will. The rich young ruler agreed with Jesus completely in his mind, but he was never convinced.

Implementation: do it today; don’t wait until you’re in the mood. Denying of self has never been something you do only once you feel like it.

Evaluation: at night, spend three minutes looking back — did I deny myself today? When I did, was there joy inside me? Or a sense of being hard done by? That sense of grievance often shows that I gave up a behaviour but did not give up the “self” that demands to be repaid.

Correction: if you failed today, don’t beat yourself up; just adjust. Failure isn’t the end; self-blame is.

Repetition: once a day, seven days in a row. Neural pathways are made by walking them, and so are the habits of life.

Multiplication: find someone, tell them about your week, and invite them to practise with you. Change that doesn’t multiply is only personal growth; change that multiplies is God’s system.

Practice 2: Bring your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing into line with God

Each evening, take five minutes to check item by item:

What I looked at today — was it of God or of the world?

What I listened to today — was it the voice of the Holy Spirit or my own emotions?

What I thought today — was it faith or fear?

What I said today — did it build people up or hurt them?

What I did today — was it for the Lord or for myself?

Bring each link back before God to be adjusted.

Information: these five choices are the steering wheel of life. Revelation: ask the Lord to show you which link you most easily give way on — most people have one regular breach; for some it’s “seeing”, for others it’s “speaking”. Conviction: admit that this breach is no small thing; it is the stronghold the “self” holds in you. Implementation: do your first check tonight and write it down. Evaluation and Correction: look back after a week — which area has improved, and which is still where it was? Repetition: make it a fixed habit before bed, like brushing your teeth. Multiplication: share your checklist in your small group and get the members practising together.

Practice 3: Use “joy” to test the direction of your life

When you have no joy, don’t blame yourself; instead ask one question: have I chosen myself again?

Then choose afresh: for Jesus, for others, not for myself.

You’ll find that joy comes back again.

Information: joy is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) — not a thermometer of your emotions, but the dashboard of your life. Revelation: ask the Lord to help you discern — is this lack of joy because my circumstances are hard, or because I’ve climbed back onto the throne? Conviction: accept that the loss of joy is a reminder from grace, not a mark of shame. Implementation: right there and then, pray a prayer of choosing afresh. Evaluation and Correction: note down the three situations that most often rob you of joy. Repetition: every time joy is missing, run the same test. Multiplication: when your family ask you, “Why are you so different lately?”, you’ll have a story to tell.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, here are three sentences — please keep them in your heart:

Denying of self isn’t suppressing yourself; it is letting Jesus live in you. Suppression locks the old self away, but he is still in there; denying of self hands over the throne, and the Lord is in there.

Selflessness isn’t loss; it is entering a fuller life. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A drop of water in a cup will dry up; a drop of water in the ocean becomes part of the ocean. That is why we say: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness without limit and living it out.

Don’t strain to be a Christian; let Christ live himself out. The Lord says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:29–30)

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s come back to the question we started with.

The key to service isn’t how much you have done, but whom you have lived out.

As you choose to deny yourself again and again, step by step you enter into selflessness; as you live out the selfless life, people will see Jesus in you.

The focus is not on ourselves, not on ministry, not on people, but on Jesus alone.

When Jesus becomes everything, you become the most powerful vessel in God’s hands.

So this early morning I want to issue a call to you — not a call to go and do more, but a call to hand over the throne.

You may have been serving for many years; you may have led a great many people. But please ask yourself quietly: in my heart, who is sitting on that chair?

If it is me, then all my service is my kingdom, my authority, my glory; if it is Jesus, then even the smallest service is his kingdom, his authority, his glory.

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Father who did not spare his own Son is still waiting for your response today; the Lord who gave himself for you, holding nothing back, is still saying to you today, “Come, follow me.”

Brothers and sisters, don’t go away sad. Today, put down the nets, leave the boat, and follow him.

keyVerses: Romans 8:32
“He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?”
John 3:16
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
practices: Bring your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing into line with God
Use “joy” to test the direction of your life
prayer: Lord Jesus, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to follow you.
I will no longer live for myself; I will live for you, and live for others.
Lord, I confess that there are still things I am holding back, things I have kept clutching and would not let go. Today I place them in your hands.
I declare: as I choose to deny myself, I live out the selfless life; as I choose humility, I let Jesus reign as King within me.
Holy Spirit, guide my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing today, so that in every small choice I can say: for Jesus, for others, not for myself.
Let my life be a life that draws people, so that they see the glory of Jesus.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 19:22: “But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.” This young ruler had everything, yet walked away because he “held something back”. In your life right now, is there anything the Lord has already spoken to you about that you have still not truly handed over? Say specifically what it is, and why you can’t bear to let it go.

Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Think back to the last time you “lost your joy”. Examine it in the light of today’s lesson: in which link — seeing, listening, thinking, speaking or doing — did you choose yourself again? How will you practise this week so that joy comes back again?
l166.title: Denying of Self Without Holding Back
l166.subtitle: The Path of Serving · Life (Part 2): Living Out the Life of Jesus
l166.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Problem Is Not Serving, but “Who Is Doing It”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion I want to begin with a very practical question: have you ever had this experience — you are clearly serving God, and yet your heart grows heavier and heavier?

I know a sister who served in her church for twelve years. Sunday school, the choir, welcoming, visitation, the kitchen — wherever there was a need, she was there. One day she sat in my office and said to me, “Pastor, I don’t want to do it any more.” I asked her why. She was silent for a long time, and then she said something I have never forgotten: “It’s not that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just so tired. I feel like I’m holding it all up on my own.”

She said, “I’m holding it all up on my own.” Those few words are the truest confession in the hearts of many who serve — and the one they least dare to say out loud.

Brothers and sisters, if you have ever felt this way, please hear one thing clearly: the problem usually is not serving itself. Serving is one of the greatest graces God gives us. The problem lies somewhere deeper — in “who is doing it”.

If I am the one doing it, what is the result? Pressure, burden, comparison, frustration. Because my strength is limited, my wisdom is limited, my patience is limited. When I do well, I become proud; when I do badly, I blame myself; when someone else does better than me, I become jealous; when others don’t appreciate me, I get hurt. Everything revolves around that “I” — and that “I” cannot hold it all up.

If Jesus is the one doing it, what is the result then? Lightness, joy, power, fruitfulness. Because his strength is limitless, his wisdom is limitless, his love is limitless. He works, I cooperate; he reigns, I obey; he receives the glory, I receive rest.

So the heart of “Service” has never been a question of ability. It is a question of sovereignty.

This is the one sentence to grasp in this lesson: the key to serving is not how much ability I have, but how much sovereignty Jesus has in my service.

When Jesus truly reigns as King, serving changes from “people doing things” to “God doing his work”. The difference between the two is not a difference of degree; it is a difference of nature. When people do things, they do them until their strength runs out; when God works, he works until glory comes. When people do things, what they see is results; when God works, what we see is life. When people do things, people get the applause; when God works, God gets the glory.

Peter puts it very clearly: “If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). Notice the two keys in this verse. First, the source of the strength is “which God supplies”. Second, the aim of serving is “that God may be glorified”. The source is not me, and the aim is not me. If neither the beginning nor the end is me, then surely the part in the middle shouldn’t be me either.

Today we are going to take up two key questions: first, what is true service? Second, how do we let Jesus reign as King in our service?

On the 321 Path of Serving we have been climbing five steps: “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God”. Spirit is the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding is the Bible is my standard; Life is Jesus is my role model; Service is let Jesus be King; God is let Jesus receive all the glory. The first three steps are the “inflow” — receiving. The fourth step, “Service”, is the “outflow” — pouring out. Today we stand on the fourth step.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Letter Written to Those Who Suffer
sections.html:
To truly understand 1 Peter 4:11, we first need to get to know this letter.

The Author and the Date

The author of this letter calls himself “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1). He is Simon, the fisherman from Galilee; the disciple who denied the Lord three times in the high priest’s courtyard; the man whom the Lord asked three times by the Sea of Tiberias, “Do you love me?” and who was given his commission afresh. The Lord said to him, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

By the time he wrote this letter, Peter was no longer young. He calls himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). Most evangelical scholars hold that the letter was written between AD 62 and 64, from “Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), generally taken to be a code name for Rome. In other words, not long after this letter was written, Nero’s persecution fell, and Peter himself was martyred in Rome.

This matters a great deal: the man who wrote this letter was not a scholar sitting in his study discussing theory, but an old servant about to lay down his life for the Lord. Every word he wrote was made ready with his blood.

The Readers and Their Situation

Peter writes “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). All five regions were in Asia Minor — the north-central part of what is Turkey today.

The word for “living as foreigners” is the Greek παρεπίδημος (parepidēmos), meaning “a temporary resident from elsewhere” — people with no citizenship, no property and no social standing. In Roman society they were already on the margins; after they believed, they were slandered by their neighbours, shut out by their relatives and watched by the authorities. They were a company of “suffering believers”.

In this letter Peter mentions “suffering” sixteen times and “glory” ten times. He binds suffering and glory together, because that is exactly the road Jesus walked.

Brothers and sisters, keep this background in mind: when Peter speaks about serving, he is not speaking to people with plenty of resources and strength to spare; he is speaking to people who can barely keep themselves going, people who have been crushed. That means the serving Peter describes can never be something piled up by human strength. How can people with no resources serve? There is only one answer — “as of the strength which God supplies”.

The Context

1 Peter 4:7–11 is one complete unit.

Verse 7: “But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.” This is the overarching principle: an end-times awareness.

Verse 8: “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” This is the motive: love.

Verse 9: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” This is the attitude: willingness.

Verse 10: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” This is the identity: stewards.

Verse 11: “If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” This is the standard and the purpose.

Do you see the order? First an end-times perspective, then the motive of love, then a willing attitude, then the identity of a steward — and only last of all the method and the purpose. This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Peter doesn’t open his mouth by talking about ministry. He starts from life, goes through relationships, and only at the end comes down to serving.

Two Key Words in the Original

The word for “managers” in verse 10 is the Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonomos), a servant who manages a household’s estate — a steward. The most important quality in a steward is not capability but faithfulness, because nothing a steward manages belongs to him. The gifts are the master’s, the time is the master’s, the fruit is the master’s too. A steward who treats his master’s estate as his own is an unfaithful steward.

The word “supplies” in verse 11 is the Greek χορηγέω (chorēgeō). In the ancient Greek city-states this word had a special use. When a city held a drama festival, it needed a large chorus, and the chorus’s training, costumes, instruments and meals were all paid for by one wealthy citizen. What this sponsor did was called chorēgeō. In other words, Peter is saying: God is the great sponsor who covers every expense — all you have to do is go on stage and sing.

Brothers and sisters, what a beautiful picture this is. Many who serve run dry because they are trying to be both the one who sings and the one who pays. God says: I am the one who pays. You just sing.

sections.heading: 3. The First Teaching: A Life without “Service” Is a Stagnant, Even a Dying, Life
sections.html:
1. All “inflow” and no “outflow” — life is bound to stagnate

The purpose of “Spirit, Understanding, Life” is not to stop at the growth of our own life; it is to move on into “Service”.

Brothers and sisters, picture this scene. Israel has two famous bodies of water, and they drink from the same river — the Jordan.

The one in the north is the Sea of Galilee. The Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again at the southern end. Its water is alive: there are fish in the lake and grass along the shore. Two thousand years ago Peter fished there, and today it is still a fishing ground.

The one in the south is the Dead Sea. The Jordan flows in and never flows out again. It is the lowest point on the earth’s land surface, its surface about 430 metres below sea level. Water can only evaporate, so salt keeps building up, until the salt content reaches around thirty per cent — nearly ten times that of ordinary sea water. And the result? No fish, no water plants; even bacteria struggle to survive. That is why people call it the “Dead Sea”.

The same source of water, the same sky, the same sunshine. There is only one difference: one has an outlet, and the other has none.

That is a picture of spiritual life. A pond that only takes water in and never moves will go foul; a life that only absorbs and never gives will dry up.

Some brothers and sisters have believed for many years. They keep listening to sermons, keep receiving, keep learning. They have filled several notebooks and sat through dozens of talks — and yet they notice something very strange: they are moved less and less, their passion is lower and lower, their life is more and more stagnant.

Why? Not because the word is poor, but because there is no outlet.

Because life was designed from the start to be this: receive, pour out, receive again, pour out again. That is the cycle of “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service”.

2. Letting Scripture interpret Scripture: the Lord himself says so

The Lord Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38).

Notice the word the Lord uses: not “pools” but “rivers”. A pool stores; a river flows. The Lord never promised to turn us into reservoirs. He promised to turn us into rivers.

The vision the prophet Ezekiel saw is even clearer. The water flowing out from under the threshold of the temple grew deeper and deeper: “It will happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes” (Ezekiel 47:9).

Brothers and sisters, notice the phrase “wherever the river comes”. Where the water doesn’t reach, nothing lives. The fruit of life always appears where the water flows to — never where the water sits still.

When the Lord Jesus sent out his disciples, he said, “Freely you received, so freely give” (Matthew 10:8). “Receiving” and “giving” belong together. If you only receive and never give, what you have received will spoil — like the manna in the wilderness, which bred worms and stank when it was kept until morning.

The Lord also said, “Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38). We pour out so that we can receive more.

3. Evidence from science and psychology

This spiritual principle can be seen in our own bodies too.

An adult heart, at an average of seventy beats a minute, beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day. Why must the heart keep beating without a break? Because once the blood stops flowing, we die. And the heart has one striking feature: it never keeps blood for itself. Blood comes in and is immediately pumped out; it comes in again and is pumped out again. The heart is not an organ for storing blood; it is an organ for sending it. God has written the principle “only what flows has life” into every beat in our chests.

Psychology bears this out as well. In 2005 Professor Stephen Post of Case Western Reserve University in the United States published a review in the International Journal of Behavioral Medicine showing that altruistic, helping behaviour is significantly associated with better physical and mental health and greater life satisfaction. Put simply: people who give live better.

But an important caution needs adding here. Professor Adam Grant of the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, in his book Give and Take (2013), points to a paradoxical finding: in the workplace, the worst performers are “givers” — and so are the best performers. The same giving, so why such opposite outcomes? The key is that the givers who burn out are giving from their own reserves, while the givers who are blessed over the long haul know how to attend to their own replenishment and boundaries at the same time.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms Peter’s words from the other side. If you serve with “your strength”, sooner or later you will become that burnt-out giver; if you serve “as of the strength which God supplies”, you will always have something to give. Because the one paying is the great sponsor, not you.

4. A 321 Insight

Life is not meant to be hoarded; life is meant to flow.

It is not how much you know, but how much flows out of you.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the fivefold change 321 speaks of: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Many people get stuck at the second step and go no further — they want their life to grow, but they won’t move on into relationships and ministry. Yet the order God designed is this: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you move into ministry. Ministry is not an extra burden. Ministry is the natural outlet of a maturing life.

When you begin to serve, you will discover three things: you need God more, you rely on God more, you experience God more.

Why? Because “Service” will draw you into a deeper life. If you don’t serve, you will never know how limited you are; the moment you serve, you immediately hit the end of yourself. And the end of man is exactly where God begins.

This is also the true meaning of “the 920 practice”. Every person you are in relationship with is your “2”; before each “2”, you practise living a life of selflessness (0), and you bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions (9). Serving doesn’t wait until you have become perfect before it begins; serving is itself the training ground for selflessness. Your co-workers, the members of your group, that family member who is hardest to get along with — they are all the “2” God has measured out to you.

5. An illustration from daily life

I once urged a brother who had been spiritually low for years to go and visit an elderly man in hospital. He said, “Pastor, I can’t even look after myself — how am I supposed to look after someone else?” I said, “You’re not going because you have something. You’re going because he does.”

He went. He sat by the hospital bed, didn’t know what to say, so he read a psalm aloud — and when he finished, he wept. Three months later he told me, “Pastor, that day I thought I was going to give. It turned out I was going to receive. In that hospital room I met God again.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the river of living water. You think you are giving, but in fact God is pouring more water into you so that you have something to let flow. If you don’t let it flow, he has no need to keep pouring.

sections.heading: 4. The Second Teaching: Service without “Spirit, Understanding, Life” Is Incomplete Service
sections.html:
1. True service contains three elements

If the first teaching was about “whether anything flows out”, the second is about “what it is that flows out”.

Because not all busyness is service, and not all service is complete service. True service always contains three elements together: Spirit — the guidance of the Holy Spirit; Understanding — the truth of God’s word; Life — the life of Jesus.

None of the three can be missing. Lose any one of them and service is bent out of shape. Let’s look at them one at a time.

2. Understanding without Spirit

This kind of service looks like this: a gifted preacher, someone who knows the Bible well, someone with a great deal of knowledge. They can get a Bible study group going, they can speak the theological terms, they know the references by heart.

But there is no presence of the Holy Spirit.

And the result? It cannot touch hearts, it cannot bring life. There is only doctrine, without power.

The listeners nod and say, “That was a great talk,” and then go home exactly as before. The message got into their heads but couldn’t get into their hearts.

Brothers and sisters, Scripture itself warns of this danger. Paul says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). The Lord Jesus said to those who were best at searching the Scriptures, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:39–40).

So it turns out that Bible knowledge can exist apart from the Holy Spirit — but life cannot.

Paul himself was one of the most learned men of his day, an outstanding student under Gamaliel. Yet what did he say when he came to Corinth? “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

Notice Paul’s reason: not that eloquence is unimportant, but “that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men”. If people are persuaded by your eloquence, their faith rests on you; and one day when you can no longer preach, their faith collapses too. The work of the Holy Spirit is to rest people’s faith on God.

An illustration from daily life: there is such a thing as wax fruit. Set on the dining table, its colours are bright and its shape is perfect — it looks better than the real thing. But bite into it and you know the difference at once: no juice, no flavour, no nourishment. Service that has Understanding without Spirit is spiritual wax fruit. Lovely to look at, impossible to eat.

A saying worth remembering: the nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with saying something like this — don’t speak God’s word with your mouth; let God’s word speak out of your life. Whatever its true source, the point is right: truth that has not passed through the fire of the Holy Spirit is only cold ash.

3. Spirit without Understanding

The second distortion is exactly the opposite. This kind of service looks like this: deeply moved, full of passion, rich in experiences.

Tears in the meetings, fire in prayer, always ready to tell you a string of signs and wonders.

But there is no foundation of truth.

And the result? Instability, a tendency to drift off course, easily swayed by circumstances.

If they feel moved today, they do it; if they don’t feel moved tomorrow, they don’t. If one meeting has a strong feeling, they keep going; if another church has no feeling, they never come back. More dangerous still, they take their own emotions for the leading of the Holy Spirit and their own desires for the will of God.

Scripture is not vague about this at all. John says, “Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1).

And what do we test them with? With God’s word. The Bereans are our example: “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so” (Acts 17:11).

Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit and the Bible never fight each other, because the Bible is inspired by the Holy Spirit. “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). If your “prompting” clashes with the clear teaching of Scripture, that is not the Holy Spirit — it is something else.

An illustration from daily life: a ship has a sail, and it also has a rudder. The sail receives the push of the wind; the rudder sets the direction. A ship with a sail but no rudder is in more danger the stronger the wind blows, because it will only be blown where it should never go. “Spirit” is the sail; “Understanding” is the rudder. God never wants us hoisting the sail on a ship with no rudder.

Evidence from psychology: since the 1970s psychologists have done a great deal of research on “emotion regulation”. The process model of emotion regulation put forward by Professor James Gross of Stanford University shows that our emotional responses are deeply shaped by “cognitive appraisal” — how you interpret something determines how you feel about it. In other words, feelings don’t come from nowhere; they follow the mindset you hold. This corresponds exactly to the first of the changes 321 speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life. If the mindset (Understanding) is not right, the feelings (whether or not you sense the Spirit moving) will be misled.

4. Spirit and Understanding, but no Life

The third distortion is the most hidden and the most regrettable. These people have gifts, knowledge and experiences — they lack nothing.

But their life has not been dealt with.

And the result? They easily become proud, they offer no example to follow, and they cannot pass on life.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most dangerous kind of all. Because others can spot the first two distortions, but nobody can spot this one — only God can see it.

Gifts are a present God gives; life is a project God builds. A present can be handed to you in a day; a project takes a lifetime to build. And Scripture says plainly that the gifts are not taken back: “For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). So a person can go on having gifts while their life has already gone wrong.

The Lord Jesus spoke some of his most solemn words about this: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:21–23).

Notice that these people were not lying — they really did preach, cast out demons and do mighty works. The problem was not in the ministry but in the relationship: “I never knew you.”

Paul also says, “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). What is special about brass and cymbals? They are very loud, and empty inside.

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.
