Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. For someone who serves with gifts but whose life has not been dealt with, the greatest temptation is to grab God’s rights into their own hands: the pulpit is mine, the ministry is mine, the people are mine. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

An illustration from daily life: a fine instrument can play moving music; but if its strings are out of tune, the louder it plays, the more obvious the wrong notes. The gift is the instrument; life is the tuning. God will allow circumstances to tune us. The process is often uncomfortable, but it is so that we play true.

An analogy from science: a redwood can grow to nearly a hundred metres tall, yet its roots are not deep. What keeps it standing in the wind is that its roots intertwine with one another as the trees grow together in groves. Without those connected roots, height becomes a danger. If the depth of a life cannot keep pace with the height of its gifts, the higher it grows, the more dangerous it becomes.

5. True service: life touching life

So true service is three in one: the guidance of the Holy Spirit (Spirit), a foundation of truth (Understanding), and the witness of a life (Life).

Service like this is not merely teaching; it is “life touching life”.

What does Paul say? “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). And again: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul gave two things: the gospel, and his own life. Giving the gospel without giving your life is a lecture; giving the gospel together with your life — that is service.

As Scripture says, “But we have Christ’s mind” (1 Corinthians 2:16).

The first half of that verse is: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” Paul is quoting Isaiah 40:13, whose original meaning is that no one can instruct God. But Paul immediately follows it with an astonishing declaration — “But we have Christ’s mind.” The word “mind” here is the Greek νοῦς (nous), meaning one’s thinking, way of thinking, the angle from which one sees things.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very heart of 321: turning from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. To have the mind of Christ is to see people, things and ourselves through Christ’s eyes.

6. A 321 Insight

It is not I who serve; it is Christ who serves in me.

It is not passing on knowledge; it is passing on life.

This is the reality of Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. Only when I am no longer “I” do I begin to become the person God wants me to be. A single drop of water on its own will evaporate; but once a drop enters the ocean, it will never dry up again. Selfless service is placing this drop that is me into God’s ocean.

This is also the foundation of “the 235 relationships”: becoming a “2” with a selfless person, as spiritual companions to each other; establishing the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally becoming the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades — a fivefold-ministry team working together. Life touching life is not a slogan; it is a road you can actually walk.

sections.heading: 5. The Third Teaching: Service That Begins with the “Spirit” Brings Authority and Power
sections.html:
1. Ask the Holy Spirit first; don’t start with methods

True service always begins with the “Spirit”.

Don’t start by thinking about how to do it; start by asking: what does the Holy Spirit want me to do?

Brothers and sisters, this order matters enormously. Our natural reaction is this: first we see a need, then we think up a plan, then we find the people, then we fix the schedule, and only at the very end do we pray and ask God to bless the plan we have already decided on. That is not seeking guidance — that is asking God to sign off on it.

How did the Lord Jesus himself serve? “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19).

Notice: Jesus is the Son of God and has all power, yet he chose not to act on his own. He first “sees” what the Father is doing, and only then does it. The order is: first see, then act.

Moses understood this too. When God said he could send an angel to lead the Israelites up into Canaan, Moses answered, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). Moses would rather not move at all than have success without God going with him.

2. Four things “right” when the Holy Spirit is in charge

Scripture says, “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13:11).

The full context of this verse is: “When they lead you away and deliver you up, don’t be anxious beforehand, or premeditate what you will say, but say whatever will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13:11).

The setting in which the Lord said this was the time when the disciples would face trial and persecution. At the moment when people are least sure of themselves, the Lord’s assurance is not “make sure you are well prepared” but “it is not you who speak”.

When the Holy Spirit is in charge, you will experience four things being “right”: at the right time, to the right person, you say the right words and do the right thing.

Philip is the best example. The Holy Spirit said to him, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot” (Acts 8:29). And he obeyed. The result? On a road in the wilderness he met the Ethiopian eunuch, who was reading Isaiah 53 without understanding it. The right time, the right person, the right passage, the right words. Philip did only one thing: he listened, and then he went.

Brothers and sisters, this is not technique; this is guidance. Technique can be learned; guidance can only be asked for. Technique helps you get things done; guidance lets you accomplish the things of God.

3. Service like this carries power

“For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

The word “strongholds” is the Greek ὀχύρωμα (ochyrōma), meaning a fortress or citadel. Behind the city of Corinth towered a great citadel rock about 575 metres high — a natural stronghold almost impossible to take in the ancient world. When Paul used the word “strongholds” in writing to the Corinthians, all they had to do was look up and they could see that mountain.

So what are today’s strongholds? Paul explains it himself: “imaginations”, “every high thing”, “every thought”. It turns out that the real fortresses are not outside; they are in people’s thinking.

So true service is not surface change; it is throwing down patterns of thought, renewing mindsets and setting lives free. This is spiritual warfare.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly why 321 stresses “changing the mindset” from the very start. Behind a person’s behaviour are their habits; behind their habits are their values; behind their values is their mindset. If you only change the behaviour, in a couple of days it springs back; change the mindset and the life is turned around from the root. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

And what is the key to all this? Praying in the Holy Spirit and using God’s word: “And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints” (Ephesians 6:17–18).

See how Paul puts two things side by side: the word of God, and prayer in the Spirit. Isn’t that exactly “Understanding” and “Spirit”? However sharp the sword, without a hand to hold it, it cuts nothing; however strong the hand, without a sword it is only swinging empty fists.

4. Three times “not you, but God”

When you let Jesus reign as King, you will discover three things.

It is not you who are striving; it is God who is at work. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

It is not you who change people; it is God who changes them. “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

It is not you who serve; it is Jesus who serves. “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Brothers and sisters, the story of Gideon shows this most clearly. Thirty-two thousand men were ready to fight the Midianites, and God said there were too many; ten thousand were left, and God still said there were too many. “Yahweh said to Gideon, ‘The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, “My own hand has saved me”’” (Judges 7:2). In the end only three hundred were left, and what they carried were jars, torches and trumpets.

God was not afraid of too few people; he was afraid of too many — so many that they could take the credit for themselves.

When David faced Goliath, he too said, “For the battle is Yahweh’s” (1 Samuel 17:47).

And the prophet Zechariah left us these words that never go out of date: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6).

5. Evidence from psychology: where burnout comes from

Modern psychology has done quite solid research on the fact that “serving for a long time wears you out”.

From 1981 onward, Professor Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley, developed the well-known Maslach Burnout Inventory, which identifies three core dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (treating people as tasks to be processed), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. In 2019 the World Health Organization, in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, formally defined burnout as “a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”.

Brothers and sisters, notice Maslach’s second dimension — depersonalisation. The most obvious sign of a burnt-out servant is this: they begin to treat people as items on a to-do list. The list has to be got through, the visits have to be got through, the meetings have to be got through. People have become tasks.

And how clearly 321 puts it: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When someone starts putting “ministry” ahead of “relationships”, burnout has already begun.

In addition, the “self-determination theory” developed by the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan from the 1980s shows that when people act from intrinsic motivation, and their three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — are met, both their engagement and their persistence rise significantly; whereas if their actions are driven mainly by external pressure, they tire easily. In spiritual terms: what you do out of love you can do for a lifetime; what you do under pressure won’t last long.

6. A 321 Insight

To serve relying on the brain is to rely on yourself, and the result is pressure; to serve relying on the heart is to rely on the Holy Spirit, and the result is power.

Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. Because “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Let Jesus be King, and serving becomes light.

The Lord himself said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord didn’t say “take the yoke off”; he said “take my yoke upon you”. A yoke is made for two oxen — one lighter, one heavier, one older, one younger. The old ox leads in front; the young ox learns alongside. The Lord’s meaning is not that you don’t have to work, but this: you don’t have to pull alone.

“I’m holding it all up on my own” — those words have never been the Lord’s heart for you.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: 321 on the Path of Serving
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we have seen today back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. He said, “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). He took up a basin and a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). Our role model for serving is not a set of methods; it is a person.

The Bible is my standard. If service has no foundation of truth, zeal turns into distortion. Only by examining the Scriptures daily do we know what God wants, and what I merely think God wants.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Don’t start by thinking how to do it; start by asking what the Holy Spirit wants me to do. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6).

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. This is the very theme of this lesson. What does it mean to be King? It means to have the right to decide. In your service, who has the final say? The calendar? Your gifts? People’s expectations? Or Jesus?

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Peter states this with absolute firmness: “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever” (1 Peter 4:11). Glory is something that cannot be divided. Take a share of it, and God has that much less. John the Baptist’s attitude is the healthiest one: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The Goal

Establish God’s system. Service is not running one event after another; it is establishing on earth a system in which Jesus reigns as King — a family in which people are loved, built up and sent out. The building materials of this system are lives, not programmes; relationships, not organisational charts.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

Brothers and sisters, the most piercing line in this lesson is this one from the text: if serving makes you more and more tired, it is not that you are doing too much — it is that “self” is doing too much.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In service, pride wears many disguises: I won’t let go, because others won’t do it well; I’m so busy, because I’m the only one who can do it; I’m hurt, because nobody sees what I put in. The subject of every one of those sentences is “I”.

Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Letting God be God means no longer carrying for God what he himself means to carry; letting man be man means accepting our own limits, and accepting the limits of others too.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When a team of co-workers splits apart, it is usually not because they disagree; it is because two “I”s both want to be King at the same time.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When I step back to zero, God’s fullness has a channel to flow out through.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

What mindset is this lesson meant to change? The mindset that “serving is me doing things for God” must change into “serving is God doing things through me”.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes: you no longer need results to prove yourself. Once the life changes, daily living changes: you have rest, you have rhythm. Once daily living changes, relationships change: you begin to see people, not just tasks. Once relationships change, ministry changes: your service begins to give birth to life, not merely to activities.

A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s: not asking “Does this work?” but “Does this please God?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: not asking “What do others think of me?” but “How does the Lord see me?”

From the temporary to the eternal: not asking “How much did I get done this year?” but “Will this person still be standing twenty years from now?”

From the worldly to the godly: not relying on methods, connections and resources, but on the Holy Spirit.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: every person you are in relationship with is your “2”. Before each “2”, practise selflessness (0), and you will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). In the end, the fruit of your service is not measured by how many meetings you ran, but by how many of these fruit you lived out before those people.

The 235 relationships: first find a selfless companion, and become a “2”; then have spiritual parents above you and spiritual children below you, and become a “3”; and finally work together within the fivefold ministry, and become a team of “5”. Brothers and sisters, if today you feel “I’m holding it all up on my own”, that is not just a matter of physical strength; it is a matter of relationships. God never designed anyone to serve alone. When the Lord sent out his disciples, he sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7).

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Letting Jesus Truly Reign as King in Our Service
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work each of them out one by one.

Practice 1: Before every time you serve, return first to the “Spirit”

Don’t rush to act; first be still before God.

Pray: Lord, today it’s not about what I want to do — what do you want to do?

Learn to wait first, then act.

Information: first know this truth — Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19). Even the Son of God, when he served, first looked at what the Father was doing.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see how much of your past service has been “decide first, pray afterwards”. That moment of seeing is revelation.

Conviction: say to God in your heart: I agree, this is right, I need to change.

Implementation: starting this week, before every time you serve, give God five minutes. Just be still, and just ask one question: Lord, what do you want to do?

Evaluation: after a week, look back — have those five minutes changed the spirit in which you serve?

Correction: if you can’t manage five minutes, start with two; if you often forget, set a reminder.

Repetition: four weeks in a row, without a break. A new habit needs time; a new mindset needs repetition.

Multiplication: bring a co-worker along. Be still together before you serve, and ask this one question together.

Practice 2: Practise “not I, but Christ”

As you serve, keep reminding yourself: it is not I who speak, it is the Holy Spirit who speaks; it is not I who do it, it is Jesus who does it.

Turn your focus from “me” to “Jesus”.

Information: memorise Galatians 2:20 — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Revelation: as you serve, when you notice you are tense, or notice you are enjoying the applause, stop and ask God to show you who the subject of the sentence is at that moment.

Conviction: admit that the “I” is really there; don’t pretend you are already selfless.

Implementation: every time before you go on stage, every time before you open your mouth, say silently in your heart: not I, but Christ.

Evaluation: has this sentence changed the way you react to applause and to criticism?

Correction: if you find you still care a great deal about what others think of you, change your prayer to this: Lord, please take away my fear of people.

Repetition: let this sentence become your catchphrase — become your very breathing.

Multiplication: share this practice in your small group, and invite everyone to use this sentence to remind one another.

Practice 3: Use “the fruit” to test whether you are letting the Lord be King

Examine your service: is it pressure or joy? Does it rely on methods or on the Holy Spirit? Is it surface change or change of life?

If serving makes you more and more tired, it is not that you are doing too much — it is that “self” is doing too much. Hand the sovereignty back to Jesus again.

Information: know the Lord’s promise — “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). The Lord never intended to crush you.

Revelation: face your answers to these three questions honestly. Don’t dress them up, don’t spiritualise them.

Conviction: admit that exhaustion is not glory; exhaustion is often a warning sign.

Implementation: take a sheet of paper and list everything you are serving in right now. Next to each item write: did God give me this, or did I take it on myself?

Evaluation: go over this sheet with your pastor or your spiritual companion.

Correction: lay down what should be laid down; hand over what should be handed over. Laying something down is not unfaithfulness; letting go is trusting God.

Repetition: review it again every quarter.

Multiplication: once you have learned a healthy rhythm of serving, go and hold up a co-worker who is about to fall.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please keep these few sentences in your heart.

Serving is not proving yourself; it is displaying Jesus.

Don’t hold up your service with your own ability; let the Holy Spirit lead.

You are not the source; Jesus is.

Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with this saying: God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply. That is exactly Peter’s chorēgeō — the one who pays for everything is God.

The psalmist said it long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain” (Psalm 127:1). In vain — not because people didn’t work hard, but because they worked hard for the wrong object.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have seen three things together.

First, a life without “Service” is a stagnant, even a dying, life. Life is not meant to be hoarded; life is meant to flow.

Second, service without “Spirit, Understanding, Life” is incomplete service. True service is life touching life.

Third, service that begins with the “Spirit” brings authority and power. It is not you who are striving; it is God who is at work.

So true service is not about how impressive you are, but about how much room you give Jesus.

This is a very simple yet very deep measuring rod. It does not measure how great your gifts are; it measures how much room you have yielded. Yield a little, and he reigns a little; yield everything, and he reigns completely.

When you let Jesus be King, your service has power, your service bears fruit, your service has joy.

The focus is not on yourself, not on methods, not on results. Only on Jesus.

Letting Jesus be King is the most powerful service there is.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to invite you to make a decision.

If you are already exhausted, please stop holding it all up. Put that burden of “I’m holding it all up on my own” into the Lord’s hands. He says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

If you have been receiving all along but have not yet let anything flow out, ask the Lord to give you an outlet. Even if it is just one phone call, one visit, one time of keeping someone company. From today, let the living water flow out.

If you are serving, but have realised that all these years you have been sitting in the Lord’s seat, please give up that seat today. Let Jesus be King: give the pulpit back to him, give the ministry back to him, give the people back to him, give the glory back to him.

Because “to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen” (1 Peter 4:11).

keyVerses: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms. If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.” (1 Peter 4:10–11)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord Jesus, I am willing to hand the sovereignty of my service over to you.
I will no longer rely on myself; I will rely on the guidance and power of the Holy Spirit.
I declare: it is not I who serve, but Christ who serves in me; it is not I who receive the glory, but Jesus who receives all the glory.
My service will bring power, life and change.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Use “the fruit” to test whether you are letting the Lord be King
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you — you are the King who serves. Though you were in the form of God, you took up a basin and a towel and washed your disciples’ feet. You are my role model in serving.
Lord, I confess that in my service there has been far too much “me”. I have held it up with my own strength, done it my own way, measured myself by my own results. I am tired, and I have run dry.
Lord, today I hand the sovereignty of my service back to you.
Forgive my pride; forgive me for taking your seat. Put that “I” in me that wants to be King on the cross, and bring me into selflessness, so that your fullness can flow out from within me.

Holy Spirit, please guide me. Teach me not to rush to act, but first to be still and wait; teach me not to start with methods, but first to ask for your will. Plant your word deep within me, to be my standard.

Lord, let my service be not merely the completing of tasks but the passing on of life; not merely surface change, but the throwing down of strongholds, the renewing of people’s mindsets and the setting free of their lives.
Give me, too, people to walk alongside me — a spiritual companion, spiritual parents, spiritual children — so that I am no longer holding it all up on my own.
May my service bring power, life and change. May you, in all things, receive all the glory through Jesus Christ.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “Every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes.” (Ezekiel 47:9) Please share: is your spiritual life right now more like the Sea of Galilee or more like the Dead Sea? Where is your “outlet”? If you don’t have one yet, with which person could you begin this week?

“If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” (1 Peter 4:11) Please examine your current service honestly: is it pressure or joy? Does it rely on methods or on the Holy Spirit? Is there something you have never yet handed to the Lord to be King over? Pray for one another in your group.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Ultimate Goal of Serving Is Not to Get Things Done Well, but to Pass On Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are going to reflect together on the second talk on the Path of Serving — a deeper layer of “Service”: the passing on of life and the multiplication of disciples.

First, please be still for three seconds and answer one question honestly in your heart: if the Lord took you home tomorrow morning, what would the area of service you are responsible for in your church leave behind?

I imagine that what comes to most people’s minds is a to-do list: the bulletin hasn’t been laid out, the songs haven’t been chosen, the venue hasn’t been booked, the list hasn’t been handed in. These things all matter. But please think one layer further down — apart from these “tasks”, is there a “person” who, because you have walked alongside them these past few years, can now stand up and take the baton from your hand, and carry it even more freely and joyfully than you?

If there is, your service has a legacy; if there isn’t, everything you have done may very well come to an end on the day you leave.

This is exactly the point today’s lesson makes right at the start: the ultimate goal of serving is not to get things done well, but to pass on life.

We often measure the success of service by three indicators: growing numbers, expanding ministry and power on display. When the numbers go up, we assume God is blessing; when the ministry grows, we assume God is with us; when power shows itself, we assume God is using us greatly. None of these three things is bad in itself, and God really does often bless in these ways. But brothers and sisters, please notice: before the Lord Jesus ascended, he stated the last command he left his church very clearly. He did not say, “Go and make the meetings bigger,” nor did he say, “Go and perform miracles among all the nations.” What he said was — “Go and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19).

Not “make the meetings bigger”, but “make disciples”.

Not “get the job done”, but “pass on life”.

These two sentences deserve to be written on the heart of every one of us who serves.

I know a sister who was responsible for the children’s Sunday school in her church for more than twenty years. She was very gifted: when she told a story, the whole room of children went quiet, and even the parents in the corridor would poke their heads in to listen. One year she had to step away from serving for three months to care for her sick mother. Within those three months the children’s Sunday school all but collapsed — nobody knew how to lead it, nobody dared to lead it, and in the end the children had to be moved into the main hall to sit drawing in the back rows. When she came back, she said to the pastor, with tears in her eyes, something I have always remembered: “So for these twenty years I’ve been doing the work, not raising up people.”

Brothers and sisters, those words are not a rebuke at all; they are an extremely precious insight. Because the greatest danger in serving is not doing it badly — it is doing it too well: so well that nobody else can get a hand in, so well that you become the irreplaceable one, so well that the whole team runs on your gifts rather than on the life of Jesus.

True service does not make people depend on you; it helps people follow Jesus, just as you do.

This is the deeper meaning of “Service”. On the Path of Serving we have gone from “Spirit” (the Holy Spirit is my guide), to “Understanding” (the Bible is my standard), to “Life” (Jesus is my role model), and on into “Service” (let Jesus be King). In the last talk we looked at the attitude of serving — serving is not doing great things, but letting Jesus reign as King in me. In this talk we take one step further: when Jesus truly reigns as King in me, he will surely make the life within me flow, through me, into others.

A lamp is lit not so that people will look at that lamp, but so that other lamps can be lit too. This morning, may God show us the baton in our own hands that has not yet been passed on.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The One Main Verb of the Great Commission
sections.html:
To ground today’s message firmly, we first need to go back to the scene of our theme passage.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve disciples, also called Levi, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum. He is generally thought to have written between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish believers scattered in many places. That is why Matthew’s Gospel quotes the Old Testament at every turn, and at every turn proves that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — the Son of David, the new Moses.

Matthew 28:16–20 is the summit of the whole Gospel, and the most famous “Great Commission” in the whole Bible. The scene is a mountain in Galilee. This detail is very important: Jesus’ public ministry began in Galilee, and now, after the resurrection, he brings the disciples back to Galilee — back to the starting point, to send them out afresh. And Scripture records honestly: “When they saw him, they bowed down to him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17). Those the Lord sends have never been a flawless group of people, but a group who still carry their doubts and yet are willing to obey. What a comfort that is for brothers and sisters today who feel they aren’t qualified to lead anyone.

Then Jesus says, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18). Notice that the Great Commission is built on the Lord’s authority, not on our ability. Only on that basis — the “therefore” that follows in many translations — comes “Go”.

In the original Greek, Matthew 28:19–20 has four verb forms, but only one of them is a main verb in the imperative: “make disciples” (μαθητεύσατε, mathēteusate). The other three — “go” (πορευθέντες), “baptizing” (βαπτίζοντες) and “teaching” (διδάσκοντες) — are participles, actions that take place around this one main command.

This point of grammar brings out a point of life: going is the means; baptising is the starting point; teaching is the process; making disciples is the goal.

The word “disciple” is the Greek μαθητής (mathētēs), whose root means “a learner”. In first-century Jewish society, to be a rabbi’s disciple was not to attend his classes and listen to his lectures, but to live with him — to watch how he ate, how he prayed, how he treated people, how he faced hostility and humiliation. A saying handed down among the Jews describes being a disciple as “covering yourself in the dust of your rabbi’s feet”. In other words, discipleship has never been a course; it is a road walked together.

So when the Lord Jesus said “make disciples of all nations”, he did not mean “let all nations hear my name”, but “let all nations live out my life”.

The three other passages quoted in today’s lesson each have their own setting too:

1 Corinthians 11:1, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” — when Paul wrote this letter, the Corinthian church was mired in factions, quarrels, sexual immorality and pride in knowledge. Paul didn’t just drop a pile of rules on them; he set his whole self before them and said: watch how I walk, and walk the same way.

The foot-washing in John 13 took place on the eve of the Passover. John 13:1 says, “Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” This was the Lord’s last night on earth. He did not settle his property or arrange an organisation; the first thing he did was to kneel down and wash feet.

Matthew 20:28, “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” — the context of this verse is that the mother of Zebedee’s sons had asked for the seats on his right and left for James and John, and the other ten disciples were indignant with them. In the middle of a group arguing over who was greatest, the Lord spoke these world-changing words.

The grain of wheat in John 12:24 was spoken after Jesus’ triumphal entry into Jerusalem, when some Greeks came asking to see him. Just as the nations began to stream towards him, he said that to bear much fruit, a seed must first fall into the earth and die.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Behind every passage that speaks of passing life on lies one common movement — going down. Only by going down does life flow out.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Purpose of Serving Is Not a Display of Power, but the Passing On of Life
sections.html:
In serving we often see some exciting things: miracles, being deeply moved, power. Someone is healed in prayer, someone weeps in repentance in a meeting, someone opens their mouth and speaks with great power. These are all real, and they are all God’s grace. But brothers and sisters, please hear one thing clearly: none of these is the final goal.

We can imagine a person like this: he has experienced many miracles, he is often deeply moved in meetings, and when he shares his testimony the whole room is shaken. Yet three years go by, five years go by, and his temper hasn’t changed, his family hasn’t been influenced by him, and there isn’t a single person around him who loves Jesus more because of him. Where, then, is such service still stuck? Still at the level of “Spirit” — feelings without life; experiences without legacy.

The Lord Jesus himself warned about this: “Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

Notice that the Lord doesn’t deny their preaching, their casting out of demons or their mighty works. What the Lord weighs is not how many powerful things they did, but “I never knew you” — relationship and life are the standard by which he examines us.

Paul says it just as directly: “If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

What, then, is true service? The lesson gives us three levels: helping people’s lives to change; helping people to follow Jesus; helping people to go and influence others.

These three statements are really one complete conveyor belt of life. The first is “people are changed”; the second is “people are placed in the Lord’s hands”; the third is “people are sent out to change others”. Leave out the third, and life stops at my station.

Paul put this in one extraordinarily bold sentence: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).

“Imitators” in Greek is μιμηταί (mimētai); the word later came into English as “mimic”. It doesn’t mean “agree with my ideas”, but “live the way I live”. Paul dared to say this not because he thought himself perfect — he had only just said in Philippians 3:12, “Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect” — but because he knew clearly that making disciples has never depended on passing on ideas, but on passing on life.

The key to this sentence is a three-link chain: I imitate Christ; you imitate me; you in turn lead others to imitate Christ.

In 2 Timothy, Paul spells this chain out even more fully: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). Count them: there are four generations in this one verse — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. Four generations — that is multiplication.

Church history has left a moving witness to this chain. The second-century church father Irenaeus recalls in one of his letters that as a young man he heard with his own ears the preaching of Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna; and Polycarp himself said that he had walked with the apostle John and heard from John’s own lips what he taught about the Lord Jesus. Look — from John, to Polycarp, to Irenaeus. The gospel did not reach the second century by way of one huge evangelistic rally; it was handed down generation by generation, one old man leading one young man.

Psychology bears out this spiritual principle too. The social learning theory (Social Learning Theory, 1977) put forward at Stanford University by the American psychologist Albert Bandura, together with his famous “Bobo doll experiment” (1961), established one thing: human behaviour is changed mainly not by lecturing, but by “observing a model” (modelling). Children don’t do what adults “say”; they do what adults “do”.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly how the Lord Jesus led his disciples. He did not first set up a three-year theology course; he appointed them “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14). Life is something seen, not something heard.

The nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with saying something like this: “It is better to train ten men to work than to do the work of ten men.” That sentence goes straight to the point: one person’s ability has a ceiling, but a company of lives that have been built up has none.

So the first insight of this lesson is this:

Receiving life is not the finish line; passing life on is the goal.

It is not that I am blessed, but that I become a blessing.

Truly receiving means being able to give it away.

This is exactly the pattern God set when he called Abraham: “I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). The blessing God gives has never been a terminus; it is a relay station.

Looked at through our 321 vision, the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The reason many people’s service gets stuck is that they skip the first four and rush straight to the fifth. The result: the ministry is very busy, and the life is very empty. And among the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — the very last one is precisely “Multiplication”.

Brothers and sisters, please remember: if a mindset stops with you, it has not yet run its full course. Only when it goes all the way to “Multiplication” is that change truly complete.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Heart of Serving Is Not Doing Tasks, but Building Relationships
sections.html:
On his last night on earth, at the table of the Last Supper, the Lord Jesus did something that has shaken every generation since: he washed his disciples’ feet.

John’s Gospel records it like this: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him” (John 13:3–5).

Notice where the word “knowing” appears. He knew that all things were in his hands; he knew where he had come from and where he was going — and precisely because he knew his identity completely, he was able to kneel down. Brothers and sisters, humility has never been low self-esteem; humility is something only a person secure in their identity can do. Someone who is still trying to prove themselves cannot kneel down.

When he had finished washing, the Lord said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

In first-century Palestine people wore sandals and walked on dirt roads. Washing feet at the door was a slave’s job; and according to the rules of the Jewish rabbis, even Hebrew slaves could be excused from it — only Gentile slaves did it. What the Lord Jesus did was the lowest task in that society.

But behind this “task” lay two purposes.

First, to restore our relationship with God. The Lord said, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean” (John 13:10).

In Greek this verse uses two different verbs: “bathed” is λούω (louō), meaning to wash the whole body; “have his feet washed” is νίπτω (niptō), meaning to wash part of the body. This distinction is a very important point of interpretation. The whole-body bath is accomplished once and is valid for ever — that is the salvation the Lord accomplished for us on the cross: new birth, justification. Foot-washing is a daily matter — as we walk in this world our feet pick up dust, and we need to come before the Lord every day to be cleansed, so as to keep our close fellowship with him. The apostle John later put this very clearly in his letter: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Second, to build our relationships with one another. The Lord said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15).

Then, in the same chapter, he went on: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35).

Brothers and sisters, do you see the Lord’s order? First he washes clean our relationship with God, then he builds up our relationships with one another. And the tools he used to accomplish both were a basin of water and a towel — a “task”.

So we must distinguish clearly: tasks are the tool; relationships are the goal.

Many problems in serving are not that the task wasn’t done well, but that a relationship has broken. The choir’s problem is seldom singing out of tune; mostly it is that someone feels overlooked. The welcome team’s problem is seldom standing in the wrong place; mostly it is that someone spoke too harshly. The leaders’ meeting’s problem is seldom a poor proposal; mostly it is that after one particular meeting, two people never spoke to each other again.

I once heard an old pastor say something very profound: “Most of the hurt in the church isn’t from the enemy breaking in; it’s from our own people bumping into each other while moving the tables.” We often press the people around us until they can hardly breathe, all to get one task done perfectly; and when the task is beautifully finished, the people are gone. What a loss that is.

Harvard University has a study that began in 1938 and has run for more than eighty years — the Harvard Study of Adult Development — one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, having worked through decades of data, points out that what best predicts whether a person will be healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, not fame, not achievement, but “good relationships”.

The people God made were always meant to live in relationship. No wonder the first “not good” God speaks in Genesis is “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18).

So the second insight of this lesson is this:

People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than results.

Don’t hurt people to get things done; build people through getting things done.

This is one of the most central orders in the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry. And relationships themselves have an order — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Most of the chaos in serving comes from putting the last of these first.

So true service draws people closer to God and helps people love one another. That is the heart of Jesus.

What we need to practise is 321’s “920”: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. In this “2” relationship we practise living a life of selflessness (0), so that the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grow in that relationship.

Brothers and sisters, the next time you are serving and feel you are about to lose your temper, ask yourself in your heart: right now, am I trying to get this task finished, or to raise this person up?

sections.heading: Key Point 3: With a Parent’s Heart, Bring About the Passing On of Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, service that truly produces a legacy always comes from “a parent’s heart”.

What is the difference between a co-worker’s heart and a parent’s heart? A co-worker looks at “who is going to do this job”; a parent looks at “how this person is going to grow up”. A co-worker cares about progress; a parent cares about maturity. A co-worker hopes the other person will finish the task; a parent hopes the other person will one day no longer need them.

Paul captures this difference vividly: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

The word “tutors” is the Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgos). In Roman times this was a household servant whose job was to take the master’s child to and from school each day and to supervise his conduct. He had duties but no bond of flesh and blood; he could correct the child, but he could not father the child. Paul says there are ten thousand people like that, but very few fathers.

A parent’s heart has one very clear mark: a willingness to build others up, even gladly letting others surpass you.

To the Thessalonian church Paul uses, in one breath, the images of both a mother and a father. The mother’s side: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8). The father’s side: “As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:11).

He even uses the pain of a woman in labour to describe it: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

Brothers and sisters, notice that a heart like this always involves “denying of self”. No mother can raise a child without paying a price; and no spiritual parent can bring up a disciple without tears, without sleepless nights, without being misunderstood.

The Lord Jesus himself is the source of this road: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

This is the highest level of service: I die, so that you may live.

The Lord used a picture every farmer understands to drive this home to the bone: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

Botanically, this picture is astonishingly precise. When a grain of wheat is buried in the soil, the first thing that happens is that it takes in water, and its seed coat swells and splits. Next, the endosperm stored in the seed begins to be broken down by enzymes — that is all the nourishment it has stored up in its whole life, now taken apart and used up, just to supply the tiny shoot that has only just appeared. By the time the new seedling breaks through the soil, the original grain of wheat can no longer be found. It doesn’t disappear “incidentally”; it “has to” disappear.

Without dying, there is no multiplying; without denying of self, there is no legacy.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in The Cost of Discipleship words that have shaken generations: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” It sounds severe, but it is full of hope — because in Christ, death is never the end; death is where multiplication begins.

So how, in practice, do we walk this road of passing life on? The lesson gives us three stages, very practical and very easy to remember — “lead, accompany, release”.

Stage one: Lead. You do it while they watch; they do it alongside you.

The key to this stage is “being together”. Mark records that the first purpose for which the Lord chose the twelve was “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14). Don’t start by tossing them an instruction manual; let them stand beside you and watch how you pray, how you phone someone to check on them, how you face a meeting that flopped, how you keep your mouth shut when you are misunderstood. The most important thing at this stage is not teaching them technique, but letting them see the real you.

Stage two: Accompany. Let them start doing it, while you stand alongside to support, encourage and correct.

This stage is the hardest, because you have to put up with “them doing it worse than you”. The Bible study they lead isn’t as lively as yours, the invitation card they write isn’t as beautiful as yours, they have been talking for thirty minutes and still haven’t reached the point. At this moment you will feel a very strong urge — “I’d better just do it myself.” Brothers and sisters, please hold that hand back. Because every time you take over, they take one step back.

Educational psychology has a widely used concept called “scaffolding”, put forward in 1976 by three scholars — Wood, Bruner and Ross — and rooted in the Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky’s “zone of proximal development”. Building a house needs scaffolding, but the value of scaffolding lies not in how firmly it is put up but in this — in the end it must come down. If the scaffolding never comes down, the house is forever boxed in by it. In the same way, a training motto has long circulated in medical education: “See one, do one, teach one.” It is generally traced to the residency system established in the late nineteenth century by William Halsted, a surgeon at Johns Hopkins Hospital in the United States. Even doctors know that if you only watch and never do, you will never operate.

Stage three: Release. They can stand on their own; you let go, and let them go and lead others.

“Release” is the step among the three that takes the most faith. Because “release” means I am no longer needed, my name is no longer mentioned, and the applause turns towards someone else.

One of the most beautiful examples in Scripture is Barnabas. When Saul had just come to faith, the disciples were all afraid of him and wouldn’t accept him; it was Barnabas who “took him and brought him to the apostles” (see Acts 9:27). Later Barnabas went all the way to Tarsus to look for Saul and brought him to Antioch, where they served together for a whole year (see Acts 11:25–26). When they set out on the first mission, Luke’s record reads “Barnabas and Saul” (Acts 13:2) — the name in front is Barnabas. But before long the record has become “Paul and his company” (Acts 13:13). Barnabas’s name quietly stepped back behind.

More beautiful still, later on, because of Mark, Barnabas and Paul parted ways, and Barnabas took this young man who had once given up halfway and started again with him (see Acts 15:37–39). Many years later Paul wrote from prison to Timothy: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). And this Mark went on to write the Gospel of Mark.

Brothers and sisters, if Barnabas had not “released” back then, the church would have had one Paul fewer, and one Gospel of Mark fewer.

John the Baptist put the resolve to “release” into words that have echoed down the ages: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The Lord Jesus also said, “A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (Luke 6:40). Meaning: however far you bring someone, that is as far as they will go. So our own lives must keep moving forward, so that our disciples have room to move forward too.

This is the cycle of life: I am led, I am accompanied, I am released, and I go and lead others.

So the third insight of this lesson is this:

Not holding on to people, but building them up.

Not controlling people, but setting them free.

True love is letting people go out on their own.

Seen through 321, “lead, accompany, release” is precisely the practical path of “the 235 relationships”. First I become a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions, holding each other up; then I move into the “3” — establishing relationships of spiritual parents and spiritual children, with someone leading me and me leading others; and finally I become part of the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together.

Brothers and sisters, hold on to someone’s hand and you can hold only one person; open your hand, and you can gain a generation.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Service to a Selfless Legacy
sections.html:
If we sum up today’s message in the language of 321, it is actually very clear.

Our Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

What the Lord Jesus said after washing the feet — “For I have given you an example” (John 13:15) — is the most direct basis for “Jesus is my role model”. Passing on life is possible because we have a living pattern in our hands. The Bible is my standard, so the ruler by which we measure the effectiveness of service is not an attendance report but that one line of the Great Commission: “make disciples of all nations”. The Holy Spirit is my guide, so we are able to let go — because the one who truly keeps a disciple has never been us, but the Holy Spirit who lives within them.

Our Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, the greatest temptation in serving is to make ourselves king. When the team can’t function without me, when other people’s growth has to pass my approval first, when deep down I secretly enjoy the feeling that “they can’t do without me” — at that moment it is I, not Jesus, who sits on the throne. And the deepest obstacle to passing life on is also a question of glory: I am afraid of others surpassing me, I am afraid of the applause turning to someone else. If the glory goes to Jesus, then who is on the stage and who is off it is no longer an issue.

Our Goal is: establish God’s system.

A system is not held up by one capable person; it is joined together by generation after generation of lives that have been built up. That is why Paul says, “commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). That is a system.

Looking further in, the real watershed of this lesson is “the self-centred life” versus “selflessness”.

The old self is “self-centred”, so when it serves, the ministry becomes an extension of me, my co-workers become my resources, and the results become my proof. Self-centred people seize rights and leave their originally intended position, wanting to take God’s place in other people’s lives — this is pride, and pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

The new self is “selfless”, so I can be like that grain of wheat that falls into the earth. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (see Galatians 2:20). Selfless people lay down their rights and return to their originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. This is humility, and humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

We also need to experience the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the first thing that must change is the mindset — changing “serving = doing tasks” into “serving = passing on life”. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry naturally changes. The order must never be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Finally, there is the shift in perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s — no longer asking “Does this month’s report look good?” but “Is anyone more like Jesus because of me?” From the earthly to the heavenly. From the temporary to the eternal — buildings grow old, programmes pass, only lives last for ever. From the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, this is how the Path of Serving is walked: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Today we are walking at the “Service” station, and the fruit of “Service” is the multiplication of disciples.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Living a Life of Service That Leaves a Legacy
sections.html:
If we understand the teaching but it never lands in our daily living, tomorrow morning everything will carry on as before. So we are going to take the three practices the lesson gives us and do them one by one.

Practice 1: Ask yourself one question every day

In the past we have been used to taking stock before bed: how much did I get done today? From today, please replace that question and ask instead: today, whose life did I influence?

That small change of wording is a shift of focus — from “doing tasks” to “raising up people”.

The practical way to do it is very simple: every evening, write down one name and one sentence in a notebook or in the notes app on your phone. For example: “Phoned Sister Su-zhen today; she mentioned her husband’s illness, and I prayed with her for five minutes.” When you look back at those seven names after a week, you will see clearly which people God has placed among your “2”.

Don’t underestimate that one line. Where a person’s attention goes, their life grows.

Practice 2: Practise building “life relationships”

As you serve, deliberately do three things: care about the other person’s life; walk alongside their growth; help them draw closer to God.

First, care about the other person’s life. After the meeting, stay ten minutes longer. Don’t just ask, “Can you come next week?” Ask, “How have you been lately?” Ministry topics are covered in three minutes; life topics take time to dig out.

Second, walk alongside their growth. The heart of walking alongside someone is “consistency”. One deep conversation can’t match ten brief check-ins, because trust is built up over time.

Third, help them draw closer to God. This is the most crucial of the three. When we lead people, the aim in the end is not to bring them to ourselves but to bring them to the Lord. So every conversation can end with one sentence: “Shall we pray about this together?” — handing the person to the Lord rather than keeping them in our own hands.

Don’t just complete the task; put your heart into building the relationship.

Practice 3: Begin to practise “lead, accompany, release”

This week, please find one specific person. Not “a group of people” — “one person”. The Lord Jesus did the same: he preached to the crowds, but led only twelve; and among the twelve, he led three in a special way.

Once you have found this person, begin to take three steps: lead them — do it while they watch; accompany them — let them learn; release them — let them go and lead others.

Give yourself a timetable, for example: three months of “leading”, six months of “accompanying”, and “release” after a year. The lengths can be adjusted, but there must be a date for “release”; otherwise “accompanying” will turn into dependence without end.

Please hold firmly to this last sentence: don’t be afraid that they won’t do it well, because growth always goes through a process. Didn’t you yourself start out by not doing it well?

Taking the Practices All the Way with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

For a mindset truly to become life, it has to go through all eight stages. Let’s place today’s practices into these eight steps:

Step one, Information. Today you have received the information: the purpose of serving is passing on life, not a display of power. Please write the lesson’s three key points as three sentences in your own words.

Step two, Revelation. For information to become revelation, it has to pass through the Holy Spirit. Please be still and ask the Lord to shine his light: Lord, in my service, what is the thing I have been holding on to and won’t let go?

Step three, Conviction. Revelation without conviction becomes a burden of knowledge. Conviction is saying “yes” to the Lord in your heart — I admit that my serving has been doing tasks, not raising up people.

Step four, Implementation. Starting tonight, write down the first name. Implementation always begins with the smallest step.

Step five, Evaluation. After a week, look back honestly: whom did I really walk alongside these seven days? Did I once again give in and take the task back into my own hands?

Step six, Correction. The problems your evaluation turns up need specific correction. If you find you are too hurried, slow the pace; if you find you have no time, cut out one area of ministry that you can hand over.

Step seven, Repetition. One week isn’t enough; one month isn’t enough either. Life lessons are learned through repeated practice, just as Hebrews says: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14).

Step eight, Multiplication. This is the last step, and the heart of today’s whole lesson. When the person you are leading begins to lead someone else, only then has your mindset truly run its full course.

Brothers and sisters, multiplication is the destination of changing our mindset, and the destination of serving too.

A Gentle Reminder

Serving is not making people rely on you; it is helping people follow Jesus.

Don’t just be a good co-worker; become a spiritual parent.

Don’t just complete tasks; build up lives.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let the Life of Jesus Flow Out from You
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end.

Truly successful service is not how much you did, but how much life you leave behind.

One day we will all stand before the Lord. On that day the Lord will not ask how many special conferences you ran, how many people took part in your ministry, or on how many posters your name was printed. What the Lord will look at is this: those people I put into your hands — where are they today? Are they more like me?

When you are willing to deny yourself, life will grow, disciples will be raised up and a legacy will be born.

So the focus is not on tasks, not on people, not on results — only on Jesus.

Not on tasks — because tasks pass away; not on people — because people change; not on results — because results are in God’s hands. If our focus is on Jesus, we can stay faithful when we are overlooked, stay joyful when we are surpassed, and stay at peace when we let go.

This is letting Jesus be King, and it is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

This morning I want to invite you to make a decision.

First, open your hand. That area of service you have gripped for so long that nobody else may touch it — ask the Lord for courage, and begin to hand it over.

Second, write the name down. Within these seven days, find that one person God wants you to lead.

Third, turn your focus back. Don’t look at yourself, don’t look at others, don’t look at circumstances — look only at Jesus.

May God make every one of us that grain of wheat that is willing to fall into the earth. Because if it dies, it bears much fruit.

Let the life of Jesus flow out from you, and be passed on from generation to generation.

keyVerses: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to become someone who passes on life.
I don’t only want to follow you; I want to bring others to follow you too.
I declare:
I am not someone who only does tasks; I am someone who passes on life;
I am not building a ministry; I am building disciples;
I am willing to deny myself, so that many more may live out the life of Christ.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: Ask yourself one question every day
Practise building “life relationships”
Begin to practise “lead, accompany, release”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You are the first grain of wheat that fell into the earth; you gave up your own life so that we might receive eternal life. This morning you have once again shone the light of your word on us and let us see that our service has often stopped at doing tasks, stopped at displays of power, without passing life on.
Lord, forgive our clinging, forgive our fear, forgive that bit of pride in our hearts that doesn’t want to be surpassed.
Give us a parent’s heart: willing to build people up, willing to set people free, willing to let people go out and go further than we have.
Holy Spirit, please place one name in our hearts today, so that from this week we may lead them, accompany them, and, on the right day, release them.
Make us no longer people who only know how to do tasks, but people who pass on life; no longer only building ministries, but building disciples.
May you reign as King in our service, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) Paul dared to say this — do you? In your life and service right now, which part would you be willing to let others learn from by following you? And which part do you first need to let the Lord renew?

“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Of the three stages — “lead, accompany, release” — which one are you most stuck in right now? If you had to “release” someone now, what would be the biggest obstacle in your heart?
l168.title: Passing On Life and Multiplying Disciples
l168.subtitle: The Path of Serving · Service (Part 2): Leaving Behind Not a Ministry, but a Life
l168.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: Introduction: At the End of the Road of Service, There Is Only One Question
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for half a minute and call one picture to mind.

Think of a time of service you took part in that went extremely well. Perhaps it was a meeting packed to the doors, perhaps a time of worship in song that moved the whole room, perhaps a sharing that many people praised. Hold that picture in your heart, and then honestly ask yourself one question —

After the meeting ended that day, what was the very first thought that rose up in your heart?

Was it, “Thank you, Lord, you did all of this,” or was it, “Good thing I prepared,” or “Lucky I was here today”?

Brothers and sisters, that thought looks small — so small that no one else will ever know about it. Yet in God’s eyes, that one small thought is the last and most decisive checkpoint on the whole road of service.

The Path of Serving in Kingdom 321 has five stations.

The first station is “Spirit” — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit’s guidance, everything we do is merely religious activity.

The second station is “Understanding” — the Bible is my standard. Without the foundation of truth, zeal will carry us off in the wrong direction.

The third station is “Life” — Jesus is my role model. Without a changed life, service is just a performance.

The fourth station is “Service” — let Jesus be King. When a life has been changed, practical giving and service will inevitably flow out of it.

The fifth station is “God” — let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the destination, and the purpose of the whole road.

Right at its opening the lesson sums up the entire road: the starting point of service is Jesus; the process of service is Jesus; the end point of service is still Jesus.

But brothers and sisters, we cannot avoid facing a heartbreaking reality.

In church history, far too many people have walked the first four stations beautifully. They had the Holy Spirit’s leading, the foundation of truth, a changed life and practical service; their preaching had power, their prayers were answered, and revival broke out wherever they went. And yet at the very end, they fell. They did not fall for lack of gifts, nor for lack of fruit. They fell because — the glory went to themselves.

Why? Because the last and most decisive station was missing: “God” — giving all the glory to God.

If, at the end of the road of service, the focus has turned to ourselves, then even the greatest ministry becomes the beginning of ruin.

So this morning, let us go together into the deepest core of all.

The end point of service is not success; the end point of service is glorifying God.

The final question on this road is just one question, and it has only one right answer: to whom does the glory go?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Men, Two Endings
sections.html:
Today’s theme passages set two men before our eyes: Herod, seated on a throne, and John the Baptist, standing in the wilderness. One wanted glory and lost his life; the other laid glory down and was called by the Lord the greatest of all born of women. And between them stands Paul, whose whole life of toil gives us the best commentary on both.

The first passage is John 3:30.

The Gospel of John was written by the disciple whom the Lord loved, the apostle John; it is generally thought to have been completed between AD 80 and 90, and its place of writing is most often held to be Ephesus in Asia Minor. John himself states his purpose for writing: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

“He must increase, but I must decrease” — these words were not spoken in quiet meditation. They were spoken in a deeply awkward situation. John 3:23 records: “John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized.” At that point John’s ministry was at its height. But his disciples came running to him with news they could not accept: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” (John 3:26)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the point of what the disciples said — “everyone is coming to him.” Put into today’s words, it means: Teacher, we’re losing our people, and the meeting across the way keeps getting bigger.

This is a temptation every servant of God will face sooner or later: when someone else flourishes, what do I do?

John’s answer comes in three layers. The first concerns the source of everything: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) The second concerns his own position: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) The third is the declaration that has shaken the ages: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The second passage is Acts 12:23.

The Acts of the Apostles was written by Luke, Paul’s co-worker and the beloved physician, and the book is addressed to Theophilus (Acts 1:1). The Herod of chapter 12 is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled over all Judea from about AD 41 to 44. To please the Jews, he killed James, John’s brother, with the sword (Acts 12:2), and then moved to arrest Peter.

The event took place in Caesarea. Scripture records: “On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them. The people shouted, ‘The voice of a god, and not of a man!’” (Acts 12:21–22) Then come these fearful words: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

The Jewish historian Josephus records the same event in Book 19 of his Antiquities of the Jews: Herod wore a garment woven of silver that glittered in the early-morning sun; the crowd flattered him as a god; he was at once seized by violent pain in his belly and died a few days later. The year was AD 44. Scripture and the historical record confirm one another.

The third passage is 1 Corinthians 15:10.

1 Corinthians is the letter Paul wrote from Ephesus to the church in Corinth around AD 55. Corinth was a prosperous and chaotic port city, and the church there had factions and quarrels — some exalted Paul, others exalted Apollos. Chapter 15 is the greatest chapter on the resurrection in the whole Bible. Paul first lists the witnesses of the resurrection, and then speaks of himself: “and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.” (1 Corinthians 15:8) Immediately after comes his moving account of himself.

Two men, two endings. One kept the glory for himself and died on the spot; the other yielded the glory to Christ and was exalted in the Kingdom of Heaven. Brothers and sisters, today’s message begins right here.

sections.heading: 1. Not Giving the Glory to God Is the Beginning of Spiritual Ruin
sections.html:
1. One Verse, One Solemn Law

Scripture gives us a very solemn warning:

“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

Notice that Scripture does not say Herod spoke badly. It does not say he governed incompetently, or that he did anything wrong that day. That day he wore his royal robes, sat on his throne, and the people cheered — from a human point of view it was the most glorious day of his life.

What he did wrong was not a lack of ability; it was keeping the glory for himself.

Here is a spiritual law: the greater our ability and the wider our influence, the easier it is to give the glory to ourselves.

Someone nobody knows finds it hard to take the glory for himself, because no one is giving him any. But when the applause comes, when the fruit appears, when people start saying, “This is the voice of a god” — that is the moment of the real exam.

2. The Original Meaning of Glory Is “Weight”

The word “glory” is well worth pausing over. In Greek it is doxa, which corresponds to the Old Testament Hebrew kabod, and the root meaning of kabod is “heavy,” “weighty.”
