So the glory of God originally means God’s weight, God’s substance, God’s true being made visible.

Brothers and sisters, this explains something: why is it that as soon as a person gives the glory to himself, things go wrong?

Because glory has weight. When someone hoists onto his shoulders a weight that doesn’t belong to him, there is only one outcome — he is crushed.

What Herod took on that day was not a weight he was meant to bear. His shoulders could not carry the title “god,” and so he fell.

God said long ago: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” (Isaiah 42:8)

God does not withhold his glory from false gods because he is stingy; he does it out of mercy. He knows that what has been created cannot bear the weight of the Creator.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: From Nebuchadnezzar to the King of Tyre

This law appears again and again in the Bible.

Nebuchadnezzar was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon when he said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) Scripture goes on: “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, ‘O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: “The kingdom has departed from you.”’” (Daniel 4:31) Before he had even finished speaking, his kingdom was gone. Thank the Lord, Nebuchadnezzar later repented, and he said: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)

And the king of Tyre? God said through Ezekiel: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” (Ezekiel 28:17a) Notice “corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” Splendour itself was not the fault; the fault was that his eyes were dazzled by his own splendour.

Isaiah 14 records the five “I will”s in the heart of the shining morning star: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Those five “I will”s are the whole story of every fall in miniature.

So Scripture’s conclusion is perfectly clear:

“Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5b)

4. An Illustration from Life: The Moon Never Shines

Let me take an illustration from the sky.

The moon is the brightest body in the night sky, yet the moon itself gives off no light at all. Its albedo is only about 12 per cent: of the sunlight that falls on the lunar surface, only about one-eighth is reflected back. Of all the clear moonlight we admire, not one particle belongs to the moon.

The moon is at its loveliest when it keeps to its place and faithfully reflects the light of the sun.

And when is the moon at its worst? When it moves between the sun and the earth and blocks the sun — that is called an eclipse. At that moment the moon stands in the most “central” position, and plunges the whole earth into darkness.

Brothers and sisters, it is the same for those who serve. If we keep to our place as reflectors, people see the beauty of God; if we step in between God and people and block his light, that isn’t called shining — it’s called eclipsing.

5. Confirmation from Psychology: Taking the Credit Is Instinct

Psychology has a classic finding called the “self-serving attribution bias.” In 1975 two scholars, Miller and Ross, published a widely cited review article in the Psychological Bulletin, bringing together a large body of research and showing that people generally tend to attribute their successes to their own ability and effort, and their failures to outside circumstances and bad luck.

Another related finding is the study Kruger and Dunning published in 1999 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: those with weaker abilities are often the most likely to overestimate themselves, because they lack the very ability needed to recognise their own shortcomings.

Brothers and sisters, together these two studies point to one thing: taking the credit for ourselves doesn’t need to be learned. It’s instinct.

In other words, “giving the glory to ourselves” is not an occasional slip; it is the old self’s automatic reflex. We don’t have to work at being proud. If we simply do nothing, pride will grow all by itself.

The British writer C. S. Lewis, in the chapter on “The Great Sin” in Book Three of Mere Christianity, calls pride the most fundamental evil, the state of mind that is completely opposed to God. He is right. Pride is not one sin among many; pride is the root of every sin.

6. Applying 321: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position

This is exactly the core truth that 321 teaches.

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life; the mark of the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

What is pride? 321 gives a very precise definition: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take the place of God.

That is exactly what Herod did that day. The people said, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” He did not deny it. He left his originally intended position as a man and sat down in the seat of God.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a serving team, as soon as one person starts grabbing glory, others start defending themselves, comparing, competing, until everyone is worn down. On the other hand, as soon as one person sincerely gives the glory to God and yields the credit to a brother, the whole atmosphere of the team relaxes.

So the 321 insight the lesson gives us is this —

It isn’t failure that destroys people; it is pride in the midst of success.

It isn’t a question of ability; it’s a question of where the glory goes.

When we begin to feel “I did it,” “it was my effort,” “I’m brilliant,” we have already drifted off course.

The real danger has never been outside us; it lies in “the focus of the heart.”

sections.heading: 2. Only When Everything Is Grace Can We Live in True Humility
sections.html:
1. How Paul Saw Himself

Paul was a man God used mightily in the New Testament. Thirteen letters, three missionary journeys, countless churches — all came through his hands. But how did he see himself?

“For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10)

Brothers and sisters, listen closely to the structure of what Paul says here. It is the most beautiful specimen of spiritual maturity.

First, he acknowledges the facts: “I worked more than all of them.” Paul isn’t being falsely modest. He really did labour harder than anyone. The Greek for “worked” is kopiaō, the kind of toil that leaves you utterly exhausted. He doesn’t deny what he gave.

Second, he immediately disowns the credit: “yet not I.”

Third, he returns everything to its source: “but the grace of God which was with me.”

Do you see it? True humility doesn’t say, “I did nothing” — that would be a lie. True humility says, “I did it, but it wasn’t I who did it.”

The Greek for “grace” is charis, meaning a free gift that is utterly undeserved. Paul’s whole life of theology could be condensed into that one word.

2. Humility Is Not Belittling Ourselves; It Is Seeing the Truth

Many people misunderstand humility. They think humility means talking yourself down, hiding your gifts, and hurrying to deny it whenever someone praises you. That isn’t humility; sometimes it’s just another form of self-preoccupation — still thinking about ourselves.

The lesson puts it very precisely: humility isn’t belittling ourselves; it is seeing the truth clearly.

What truth?

All my abilities were given by God.

All my opportunities were given by God.

All my fruit was produced by God.

What does Scripture say? “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

Three questions, each one cutting deeper than the last. First: who makes you different? Second: what do you have that you didn’t receive? Third: since you received it, what right do you have to boast?

James says too: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

And John the Baptist puts it all in a single sentence: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27)

Brothers and sisters, even the very fact that we are able to serve is grace. If God had not chosen you, you wouldn’t even have the opportunity to stand here and serve.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Clay Jars, Unworthy Servants, the God Who Works in Me

Scripture says the same thing from every angle.

From the angle of the vessel: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Clay jars were the cheapest, plainest containers of the day. God deliberately put the treasure in clay jars so that people would see the treasure, not the vessel.

From the angle of the servant: “Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’” (Luke 17:10) Only doing everything commanded counts as doing our duty. So there is never any room for us to claim credit.

From the angle of motivation: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) Even the very desire to serve was put there by God first.

From the angle of weakness: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9a)

From the angle of conclusion: “that, as it is written, ‘He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.’” (1 Corinthians 1:31)

4. Illustrations from Life: The Postman and the Light Bulb

Let me use two very everyday illustrations.

The first: the postman.

Suppose a postman delivers a registered letter, and inside the envelope is a cheque for ten million. The recipient is so delighted that he throws his arms round the postman and won’t let go, thanking him again and again. Now, would that postman say, “You’re welcome — that ten million is my gift to you”?

Of course not. He knows perfectly well: I’m the one delivering it, not the one paying it.

Brothers and sisters, every bit of grace, every word of comfort, every passage of truth we hand out in our service — not one of them is our own. We are the postman, not the benefactor.

The second: the light bulb.

A light bulb gives light, but a light bulb doesn’t generate electricity. Pull the plug, and the most expensive bulb in the world is just a piece of glass.

Jesus said it even more thoroughly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Apart from me you will do a little less,” but “you can do nothing.” Zero.

5. Confirmation from Psychology: Gratitude Is the Ability to See the Truth

Since everything is grace, the most natural response of a life lived in grace is gratitude.

In 2003 the psychologists Emmons and McCullough published a well-known study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, “Counting Blessings Versus Burdens.” They divided participants into groups: one group wrote down each week things they were grateful for, another wrote down hassles, and another neutral events. The group that kept recording gratitude scored markedly higher in overall well-being and optimism about the future, and also reported fewer physical complaints.

Brothers and sisters, this study tells us something: gratitude isn’t just good manners. Gratitude is an ability — the ability to see the truth.

Ungrateful people aren’t worse; they’re blinder. They can’t see the grace that holds them up every day, so they assume they earned everything themselves.

6. Applying 321: Change the Mindset and the Life Changes

321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

“Everything is grace” is a mindset. But once that mindset truly enters the heart, the whole life turns over.

The mindset changes: everything I have, I have received.

The life changes: I no longer need to prove myself by performance.

Daily living changes: I no longer compare myself with others, or fear that someone is better than me.

Relationships change: when others flourish, I can sincerely rejoice.

Ministry changes: I serve not to be seen but so that God will be seen.

This is precisely the shift of perspective that 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from the Worldly perspective to God’s perspective.

The lesson’s 321 insight says it so well —

It’s not that I deserve it; it’s that I’ve received mercy.

It’s not that I can; it’s that God can.

It’s not what I have done; it’s what God has done in me.

When you truly see “grace,” you won’t be proud; instead you’ll become more grateful and more humble.

sections.heading: 3. Letting Jesus Increase Is the Highest Expression of a Selfless Life
sections.html:
1. The Most Stunning Words

John the Baptist spoke one of the most stunning sentences ever spoken:

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Greek of this sentence is worth a close look. “Increase” is auxanō, which basically means to grow, to multiply — the word used for a plant growing or a child growing up. “Decrease” is elattoō, which means to lessen, to become smaller.

And the word “must” in the sentence is the Greek dei, meaning “it is necessary, it ought to be, this is how it should be.”

Notice that John is not sighing, “Oh dear, what a pity I have to get smaller.” He is declaring: “This is right, this is fitting, this is how things were always meant to be.”

Brothers and sisters, this sentence is selflessness at its very height.

It isn’t that I am seen; it is that Jesus is seen.

It isn’t that I am exalted; it is that Jesus is exalted.

It isn’t that people remember me; it is that people come to know Jesus.

2. The Friend of the Bridegroom: Knowing Who We Are

How could John say such a thing? Because he knew who he was.

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29)

In Jewish wedding custom, “the friend of the bridegroom” was a role with real duties, much like today’s best man. He ran errands for the bridegroom, prepared the wedding feast, escorted the bride, and was busy right up to the last moment. But when the bridegroom’s voice rang out and the feast began, the best man had only one thing left to do: step aside and stand there rejoicing.

The best man’s greatest joy is hearing the bridegroom’s voice.

Brothers and sisters, there’s an extremely serious warning hidden here: if the best man falls in love with the bride, the whole wedding is ruined.

The church is the bride of Christ, not ours. We are the best man, not the bridegroom. We may give everything for this wedding feast, but we must never take possession of the bride’s heart.

Scripture says: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18) Preeminence in all things — that is Jesus’ right, not ours.

The Lord himself also said: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.” (John 7:18)

3. A Thorough Check of Our Motives for Serving

The lesson honestly points out that many people serve in order to be affirmed, to be needed and to be seen.

Brothers and sisters, we have to admit that these three things have an enormous pull. Being affirmed makes us feel valuable; being needed makes us feel irreplaceable; being seen makes us feel we exist.

But the Lord Jesus spoke very sternly about that kind of service:

“Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1)

“Therefore when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” (Matthew 6:2)

“They have received their reward” — this is the most chilling final reckoning in the whole Bible. The moment the applause rings out, the account is settled, and there is nothing left on deposit in heaven.

So what is true service? The lesson puts it beautifully: true service is helping people forget you and remember only Jesus.

The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

The Lord didn’t tell us to hide our light. He wants us to shine — but the purpose of shining is that people give glory to the Father, not to us.

4. Illustrations from Life: The Lighting Technician and the Windowpane

I want to use two illustrations to say the same thing.

First, the stage lighting technician. When a performance ends, all the applause goes to the people on stage. The best lighting technician is the one nobody in the whole audience noticed. If the audience keeps looking at the lighting, it means the lights were done badly.

Second, the windowpane. The value of a window lies in its transparency. The cleaner the window, the less you see the window and the more you see the sunlight outside. A window that keeps drawing your attention to itself is usually dirty.

Brothers and sisters, you and I are people who pass on the fire, not people who light it.

5. The Arithmetic of the Kingdom: The Smaller, the Greater

There is something wonderful here.

John said, “I must decrease.” Did he really decrease? From an earthly point of view, yes. He was thrown into prison and finally beheaded. His disciples scattered, and his name left behind no school, no building.

But what did the Lord Jesus say of him?

“Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer; yet he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he.” (Matthew 11:11)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? The man who willingly decreased was called by the Lord the greatest of all born of women.

This is the arithmetic of the Kingdom: the more you decrease, the greater you become. The further you step back, the higher you are lifted.

“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6)

Notice the words “in due time.” Lifting up is not our work but God’s; it runs not on our timetable but on God’s. We have only one responsibility: to humble ourselves.

6. Applying 321: Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing — It Is Entering into the Infinite

321 has a saying that gets right to the heart of this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

Many people are frightened as soon as they hear the word “selflessness.” They think it means erasing themselves and becoming someone with no value, no personality, no presence. Not at all.

Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“It is no longer I who live” moves the limited “I” out of the way; “but Christ lives in me” lets the infinite Lord come in.

If a cup is full of its own water, it can’t hold anything else; only when it is emptied of its own water can it hold rivers of living water.

So the lesson’s 321 insight says —

The focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is being filled with Jesus.

True success is letting Jesus be glorified.

Brothers and sisters, the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances. This must become the habit of a lifetime.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Last Station on the Path of Serving
sections.html:
Today’s lesson is precisely the fifth station on 321’s Path of Serving — the last one.

Let’s walk the whole road once more.

Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Service begins with the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Understanding — the Bible is my standard. Service is corrected by the truth.

Life — Jesus is my role model. Service flows from a changed life.

Service — let Jesus be King. Service means letting the King reign, not letting me be master.

God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The end point of service is that God is glorified.

Brothers and sisters, notice that 321’s Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. These two core values are two sides of one coin. If Jesus truly reigns as King, the glory will naturally go to him; if the glory goes to me, that proves it is still I who sit on the throne.

And the Goal is: establish God’s system. The biggest difference between God’s system and the Worldly system lies right here — the Worldly system runs on glorifying self; God’s system runs on glorifying God.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Once the glory goes to ourselves, this order is turned completely upside down — ministry comes first, people become tools, and God becomes a resource. That isn’t God’s system; that is the Babylonian system.

For our practice, 321 gives us two keys.

The first is the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” In every “2” relationship, we practise living out selflessness — the life of “0” — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (see Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that fruit is grown, not manufactured; it is the fruit of the Spirit, not my achievement. So not even the fruit can be used for boasting.

The second is the 235 relationships. Becoming a “2” with a selfless person means having a spiritual companion; establishing the “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming the “5” means a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Only when I no longer need to be exalted can I sincerely lift others up.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart, rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down. Where the glory goes is precisely a matter of the “heart.” The brain calculates how much I’ve given and how much I’m owed; the heart only says, Lord, you did all of this.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living a Life That Gives All the Glory to God
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s look at them one by one, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: After Every Time of Service, Deliberately Give the Glory to God

Whether the outcome is good or bad, after you serve, pray to God: “Lord, you did all of this; the glory is yours.”

Notice the words “whether the outcome is good or bad.” When things go well, give him the glory; when they don’t, give him the glory all the more. Because if we only think of God when we succeed, it shows that the real leading character in our hearts is still results.

Don’t let your heart linger on “how well did I do?”; turn it to “has God received the glory?”

That one turn is the turn from being centred on self to being centred on God, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one.

Practice 2: Practise Tearing Down Self-Centredness in Your Heart

When thoughts like these come up in your heart —

“I did really well.”

“They can’t manage without me.”

“I’m the one who brought the change.”

Don’t argue with yourself, and don’t try to suppress them by willpower. Replace them with the truth at once. The Lord himself said: “apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) So we declare, in line with the Lord’s word: without the Lord, I can do nothing.

Brothers and sisters, you can’t stop thoughts from coming, but you can replace them. An empty heart can’t stay empty; if you don’t fill it with truth, lies will take it over.

Returning the glory to God is a movement we must practise all our lives.

Practice 3: Deliberately Exalt Jesus, Not Yourself

When you share, testify or serve, consciously adjust the proportions: speak more about what God has done and less about what you have done.

A testimony isn’t an autobiography. After a good testimony, people say, “God is so good,” not “You’re amazing.”

What people should see is God’s works, God’s grace, God’s glory.

The Eight Stages: Driving the Truth Deep into Life

Stage one, Information: today you have heard the truth — the glory belongs to God alone. First write it down: copy today’s three passages into your notebook.

Stage two, Revelation: information isn’t yet revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you and show you one specific scene in your life where you are clinging to glory. Ask the Lord to let you “see” within that scene.

Stage three, Conviction: not just agreeing in your head, but surrendering in your heart. Tell the Lord: Lord, I admit there really is a longing in me to be seen; I need you.

Stage four, Implementation: starting today, do the three things the lesson describes. Especially the first — however your service went today, before you sleep be sure to tell the Lord: you did all of this.

Stage five, Evaluation: each night spend three minutes asking yourself: did I grab any glory in my heart today? Over what?

Stage six, Correction: the moment you notice it, give it back. There’s no need for long self-reproach — dwelling on self-reproach is another form of self-centredness. Simply say: Lord, I’m sorry; this is yours, and I give it back to you.

Stage seven, Repetition: once isn’t enough. Our instinct is self-serving attribution, so this practice must be repeated, every single day. As 321 so rightly says, only repetition turns it into a habit of life.

Stage eight, Multiplication: find a brother or sister, share this lesson with them, remind each other, and ask each other, “Where did the glory go today?” That is the “2” relationship; that is the 920 practice. When the truth bears fruit in you, it should bear fruit in others too.

A Gentle Reminder

Glory isn’t something you can take; glory belongs to God alone.

You can take part, but you cannot take possession.

You are the vessel, not the source.

Brothers and sisters, please keep these three sentences in your heart. The value of a vessel doesn’t lie in how precious it is in itself, but in whom it holds.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the end of the road of service, what counts is not how much you did, nor how successful you were, but one thing only:

To whom does the glory go?

When all the glory goes to God, three things happen.

First, you can go on being used by the Lord. Because God “will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8), with a vessel that grabs glory, God — precisely to protect that person — dares not use them greatly.

Second, you can go the distance. Those who grab glory run fast but not far, because they keep needing applause to refuel; those who give the glory away may be a little slower, but they can keep going for a lifetime, because their strength comes from grace, and grace never runs dry.

Third, you can live in true victory. 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan fell long ago through pride, and pride is the only weapon he can use against us. A truly selfless person gives the enemy nothing to work with, because there is no handle for him to grab.

So the focus is not on ourselves, not on people, not on tasks — only on Jesus.

Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory — this is the most glorious ending service can have.

The worship of heaven has long been singing this ending: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed, and were created!” (Revelation 4:11)

“Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12b)

Brothers and sisters, what we do on earth today is simply rehearsing ahead of time what we will do on that day.

Paul says it best: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

Of him — he is the beginning. Through him — he is the way. To him — he is the end.

So: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Today, let us settle this: I will be someone who gives the glory back.

keyVerses: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)
“But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to give all the glory to you.
I acknowledge that everything I have is your grace.
I declare: not I, but Christ; not my glory, but Jesus’ glory; he must increase, but I must decrease!
May my life exalt you alone!
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: After every time of service, deliberately give the glory to God
Practise tearing down self-centredness in your heart
Deliberately exalt Jesus, not yourself
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
This morning you have shone on us through your word. We have seen Herod’s end and John’s beauty; we have seen how terrible pride is and how vast grace is.

Lord, please forgive us. Forgive us that in our service we so often, without even noticing, keep the glory for ourselves; forgive us for loving to be affirmed, needed and seen more than we love to see you exalted.

Holy Spirit, shine on our hearts every day, so that the moment we find we have grabbed the glory, we give it straight back. Help us, after every time of service, to make our first words: Lord, you did all of this.
Make us clean, transparent vessels, so that people see you through us, forget us, and remember only you.
Lord, you must increase, and I must decrease. May our families, our fellowship and our church see you increase because we decrease.
Be King, and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Acts 12:23 says: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” Share a time when, after your service or work went well, the thought “I did it” rose up in your heart. How did you handle it then? What does today’s passage remind you of?

John 3:30 says: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” In your current relationships or service, what is the hardest area in which to let “him increase and me decrease”? Name one specific action you’re willing to practise this week, and ask the group to pray for you.
l169.title: Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
l169.subtitle: The End of the Path of Serving Is God
l169.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Final Move Is to “Step Aside”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today I’d like to start with a picture.

A symphony performance has just ended, and the whole audience is on its feet applauding. The conductor walks back onto the stage. He doesn’t bow to the audience first; instead he turns round and holds out his hand towards the orchestra. Then he steps to one side and points to the first violins, to the French horns, to the timpanist in the back row who struck only a few times all evening, but struck at the most decisive moments. Wave after wave of applause surges towards the front of the stage, and time after time he sends it off to the side. At the very end he withdraws to the edge of the stage and leaves the centre empty. In that moment, what the audience sees is not him but the whole orchestra.

A true master’s final move is very often to “step aside.”

Brothers and sisters, service is like that too. At its deepest, service is not about our being seen more, but about our seeing less and less of ourselves. Truly mature service is not standing at the front being exalted; it is turning everyone’s eyes towards Jesus.

We often assume that spiritual growth is a “rising” curve: our gifts become more evident, our stage gets bigger, more and more people know who we are. But what Scripture shows us is a “descending” curve. John the Baptist said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Paul said: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) The Lord Jesus himself said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

What rises is Jesus; what descends is me. That isn’t failure; that is maturity.

Today’s theme passage points out this road very clearly. The Lord Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain and was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Moses and Elijah also appeared, talking with Jesus. It was the summit of two thousand years of Old Testament history — the Law and the Prophets standing together before Grace.

Peter’s reaction was sincere, and very human. He said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4) He wanted to put up three tents — one for Jesus, one for Moses, one for Elijah. He wanted to hold on to this moment, to settle the glory into a structure he could manage, and to place the Lord Jesus side by side with two spiritual giants.

But God himself interrupted him. Before he had finished speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” (Matthew 17:5)

Then the final scene appeared: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

Brothers and sisters, Moses was gone, Elijah was gone, and there was no need to build any tents. Only one remained on the mountain — Jesus.

This is the highest place service can reach: seeing no one but Jesus.

Seeing no one does not mean looking down on people; it means no longer putting people in Jesus’ place. Seeing only Jesus does not mean we don’t need co-workers; it means all our co-workers point together towards that One. Today we will reflect together on three things: first, why “not pushing ourselves forward” is the key to keeping the glory for God; second, how, through passing on the life and through teamwork, we let Jesus be the only Head; and third, how to enter into Kingdom service and live out a deeper hiddenness.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Cloud on the Mount of Transfiguration
sections.html:
To understand “seeing no one but Jesus,” we first have to step into the scene in Matthew’s Gospel.

1. Author, Date and Audience

The author of the Gospel of Matthew is Matthew, also called Levi, once a tax collector in Capernaum, who was later called by the Lord to be one of the twelve apostles (Matthew 9:9; Mark 2:14). His book is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish believers scattered around the region of Palestine.

Matthew’s central concern in writing is to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the true King. So the whole book quotes the Old Testament again and again, saying, “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet.” And the passage on the Mount of Transfiguration is precisely the hinge on which the book turns from “knowing the King” to “following the King to the cross.”

2. The Context: From Confession to the Cross

The Mount of Transfiguration doesn’t come out of nowhere. In the chapter just before, at Caesarea Philippi, the Lord Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16) That was the high point of the disciples’ faith.

But straight afterwards, the Lord Jesus said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem to suffer, be killed and rise on the third day. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” The Lord Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. Peter had just been commended, and the next moment he was rebuked. He had just made the most heavenly confession, and the next moment he made the most earthly suggestion. These aren’t two Peters; this is one and the same Peter — a self-centred life that God was using but had not yet dealt with.

Then the Lord Jesus spoke the words that run through all the Gospels: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

“After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves.” (Matthew 17:1) The Transfiguration follows immediately after the call to deny oneself. This order matters enormously: first the call to deny oneself, then the revealing of glory; first the cross is spoken of, then the glory shines out.

3. Place, People and Symbolism

This “high mountain” was identified in early tradition mostly as Mount Tabor, about 575 metres high; but following the geography, going up from Caesarea Philippi, Mount Hermon is more likely — about 2,800 metres high, with snow on its summit all year round. Whichever it was, the point is not the mountain but what happened on it.

Moses represents the Law, and Elijah the Prophets. These two have something in common: both once saw the glory of God at Horeb — Moses in the cleft of the rock, Elijah at the mouth of the cave (Exodus 33:18–23; 1 Kings 19:9–13). Back then, on the mountain, they caught only a glimpse of God’s glory; now they stood before the very substance of God’s glory. The One to whom the Law and the Prophets had pointed all their lives was standing right there among them.

Peter proposed making “tents.” The Greek is σκηνή (skēnē), meaning a tent or tabernacle. The word would immediately make a Jew think of the Feast of Tabernacles: “You shall dwell in temporary shelters for seven days … that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in temporary shelters when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” (Leviticus 23:42–43) Peter’s heart was in the right place. He thought the Messiah’s kingdom had come and it was time to keep the Feast of Tabernacles. But he was wrong on two counts: first, the time had not yet come — the cross had not yet been passed through; second, he set three tents side by side, demoting Jesus to one of three great men.

John’s Gospel uses exactly the same root: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us.” (John 1:14) The word “lived” literally means “pitched his tent.” Brothers and sisters, the true tent didn’t need Peter to put it up, because God’s own tent had already become flesh and was standing right in front of him.

4. The Cloud, the Voice and That Word “Alone”

“Behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.” (Matthew 17:5) In the Old Testament the cloud is the sign of God’s presence. When Israel came out of Egypt, the pillar of cloud led them by day; when the tabernacle was completed, “the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Peter was still talking about how to put up buildings, and God covered the whole mountain with his own cloud. Before human construction had even begun, God’s glory had already covered everything.

The voice that came out of the cloud said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” These words echo three Old Testament passages at once: “You are my son” in Psalm 2:7; “my chosen, in whom my soul delights” in Isaiah 42:1; and Moses’ prophecy in Deuteronomy 18:15 that God would raise up a prophet like Moses — “You shall listen to him.”

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the Father’s words. He didn’t say, “These are my three servants”; he said, “This is my beloved Son.” He didn’t say, “Listen to them”; he said, “Listen to him.” Singular. The first thing the highest voice in heaven did was to “narrow the focus.”

At this the disciples fell on their faces and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” (Matthew 17:7) Notice the detail: at the most glorious moment, what the Lord did was bend down, reach out his hand and touch people. The result of glory revealed was not to leave people collapsed on the ground but to raise them to their feet.

“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) In the original this verse contains a strong word: μόνον (monon), meaning “only, alone.” Literally: apart from Jesus himself alone, they saw no one. Mark records it even more vividly: “Suddenly looking around, they saw no one with them any more, except Jesus only.” (Mark 9:8) They looked all around for Moses, for Elijah — nothing. Only Jesus, and the Jesus who was “with them.”

Many years later, when Peter was old and facing martyrdom, he wrote: “For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.” (2 Peter 1:16) The tent that was never put up became the deepest lesson of his life.

Brothers and sisters, this is our starting point today. It isn’t that God didn’t love Moses, or Elijah, still less Peter. God simply wanted to make sure of one thing: the focus must not be blurred. For “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images” (Isaiah 42:8).

sections.heading: 3. Not Pushing Ourselves Forward Is the Key to Keeping the Glory for God
sections.html:
1. The Heart’s Most Natural Longing, and the Greatest Spiritual Temptation

It is entirely natural for people to want to be affirmed, to be seen and to be given important work. These three things are not sins in themselves. They are needs God placed in us when he made us — we were created to be loved, to be known and to be used. The problem is this: when these three become the motive and the payment for our service, the focus quietly shifts.

The Lord Jesus spoke about this very directly: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) He also said: “But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:6)

Someone may ask: didn’t the Lord also say, “let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works”? Yes — but read the verse to the end: “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) The difference isn’t whether or not we are seen, but where people’s eyes come to rest once they have seen. There’s nothing wrong with the light being seen, as long as people follow the light and see its source.

Brothers and sisters, that is the whole key. We’re not meant to live furtively; we’re meant to live transparently — so transparently that people look straight through us and see Jesus.

2. The Brightest Fish in the Tank

The lesson uses a very vivid picture: in a fish tank, the brightly coloured fish easily catch the eye.

Put a tank of fish in the living room, and when the children crowd round, the first thing they’ll say is, “Look at that red one!” No one starts by saying, “Look how well designed the water filtration system is.” The bright one is the natural centre of attention.

It’s the same in service. The eloquent, the highly gifted, the quick-witted are naturally noticed. That isn’t their fault, but it is a dangerous position. Because when a person is seen, the focus shifts from Jesus to that person; and once the glory is divided, it has in effect been stolen. God’s glory is not something that can be cut in half: either it goes to God whole, or it has already been stolen.

So the spiritual principle is this: the more you push yourself forward, the more danger you’re in; the more hidden you are, the safer you are.

Push yourself forward and you become a target; a conspicuous target is easily attacked and easily brought down. The brightest fish in the tank is also the one the angler and the predator lock onto first. How many gifted servants in history fell not for lack of ability but from overexposure! Satan doesn’t trouble himself much to attack someone with no position; he aims precisely at those who stand on high places.

3. A Reminder from Psychology: The Spotlight Effect

Here is a fascinating piece of research. In a study published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the Cornell University psychologist Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect.” They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room full of people, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed the picture on their shirt. On average participants estimated that about half had noticed; in reality, only about a quarter actually had.

In other words, we often overestimate how much attention others pay us. We imagine a spotlight overhead following us everywhere, when in fact that light mostly shines only inside our own heads.

Brothers and sisters, this study offers us two comforts. First, you aren’t noticed nearly as much as you imagine, so there’s no need to guard your image so anxiously. Second, you aren’t overlooked nearly as much as you think, so there’s no need to strive so hard for exposure. There is only one true spotlight. It shines down from heaven and falls on one Person — “This is my beloved Son.”

Another classic study is also worth mentioning. In 1973 Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett of Stanford University found that children who already enjoyed drawing, once they were promised “a certificate if you draw well,” spent far less time drawing of their own accord after the reward was withdrawn. Psychology calls this the “overjustification effect”: external rewards erode internal motivation.

Being seen is the sweetest certificate there is in service. Once we get used to relying on applause to get our service going, the day the applause stops, we can’t move. The Lord Jesus said of those who do good deliberately to be seen, “they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). Reward received — case closed.

4. Hiddenness Is Not Disappearing — It Is Changing Position

When we choose to be hidden — not fighting for position, not stealing the focus, not seeking a name — people won’t be drawn to us; they’ll be drawn to Jesus.

But be careful: hiddenness doesn’t mean laziness, or retreat, still less low self-worth. True hiddenness is “changing position”: moving from centre stage to the side of the stage, from the one being looked at to the one pointing the way.

There is a painting in history that captures this to perfection. In the early sixteenth century the German painter Matthias Grünewald painted the famous Isenheim Altarpiece. At its centre is Christ crucified; to the right stands John the Baptist, his index finger deliberately painted long and prominent, pointing straight at the Lord on the cross. Beside him is a line of Latin, the very words of John 3:30: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The twentieth-century theologian Karl Barth kept a reproduction of this painting by his desk all his life, and said that finger was the picture of all his theological work.

Brothers and sisters, our whole life is that finger. A finger’s value doesn’t lie in whether it is beautiful but in whether it points accurately. A signpost never exists so that people can admire the signpost; it exists so that people can find their destination. A finger that people praise is useless if it points the wrong way; a finger no one remembers, if it has pointed people to Christ, heaven will remember for ever.

Nature paints the same picture. The moon never shines by its own light. Its surface albedo is only about 12 per cent, so the proportion of sunlight it reflects is actually very low; yet in the dark of night it is enough to light the whole road home. The moon’s glory lies precisely in the fact that it is not the source of light. Brothers and sisters, let us be the moon, not the sun. There is only one Sun.

5. A 321 Insight: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

The 321 message is very clear here. The old self is the self-centred life; the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Peter’s wish to put up three tents was, at bottom, “leaving his originally intended position”: he put himself in the director’s chair and arranged the distribution of glory on God’s behalf. And the Father’s answer was to bring everything back to its proper place: “This is my beloved Son … Listen to him.”

So we say: it isn’t that I am seen, but that Jesus is seen; it isn’t that I am exalted, but that Jesus is exalted; hiding myself is protecting God’s glory.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a team, as soon as someone starts competing for the halo, others instinctively get defensive, compare and grab, until everyone is hurt and the work is ruined. But as soon as one person is willing to go low first, something wonderful happens: others begin to relax, to give way, to appreciate one another. Humility is contagious.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is not being erased. Selflessness is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, what you lay down is a limited self; what you gain is an infinite Christ. That’s no loss — it’s the best exchange in the whole world.

sections.heading: 4. Through Passing On the Life and Through Teamwork, Let Jesus Be the Only Head
sections.html:
To live out “seeing no one but Jesus,” good intentions alone aren’t enough; we need a practical strategy. The lesson gives us two paths: first, a life that passes itself on; second, service as a body.

1. A Life That Passes Itself On: Lead, Accompany, Release

Brothers and sisters, “seeing no one” isn’t achieved by hiding; it’s achieved by “raising people up.” When you’re the only one on the stage, it’s hard not to be seen; when the stage is full of people you have equipped, the focus naturally spreads out, until in the end only the one true Leading Character remains.

So the first step in passing on the life is to “lead.” Paul said to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) The Greek for “commit” is παρατίθημι (paratithēmi), whose basic meaning is “to set beside, to deposit” — like entrusting a valuable to a trustworthy person for safekeeping. Paul didn’t lock the truth away in his own hands; he handed it on. There are four generations in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. When Paul wrote this letter he was already in prison and about to be martyred, and what was on his mind was not “How many more meetings can I still preach?” but “How many generations will there be after me?”

The second step is to “accompany.” Leading isn’t a one-off lecture; it is walking together over time. When the Lord Jesus chose the twelve disciples, Scripture says it plainly: “that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” (Mark 3:14) Notice the order — first being with him, then being sent; first relationships, then ministry. Over those three and a half years, most of the Lord’s teaching happened not in the synagogue but on the road, in the boat, at the dinner table. The essence of accompanying someone is letting them see how you live, not just hear what you say.

The third step is to “release.” This is the hardest step. Barnabas is a fine role model here. When Saul had only just come to faith, no one dared to accept him; it was Barnabas who took him and brought him to the apostles (Acts 9:27). Later Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul and brought him to Antioch, where they served together for a whole year (Acts 11:25–26). At first Scripture always says “Barnabas and Saul,” with Barnabas first; but from Acts 13 onwards, the record gradually becomes “Paul and Barnabas” (Acts 13:43; 13:50). The order of the names was swapped, and Barnabas did not protest. He willingly stepped back and let the man he had raised up go on ahead.

Brothers and sisters, are you willing to let others be better than you? That question decides how far your service can go.

Space technology gives us a beautiful picture. The first stage of the Saturn V rocket that took humans to the moon burned for only about 168 seconds, pushing the whole rocket to an altitude of about 67 kilometres; then it separated, fell away and sank into the sea. It never reached orbit, yet without it nothing would have gone up at all. Passing on the life means willingly being the first stage: pushing the next generation up, then letting go and leaving the scene.

Educational psychology offers us a matching model. In 1976 David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross put forward the well-known theory of “scaffolding,” echoing Lev Vygotsky’s concept of the “zone of proximal development”: the more mature person first builds a support around the learner and helps them do what they can’t yet do alone; then, as the learner’s ability grows, the scaffolding is taken away piece by piece until they can do it independently. The success of scaffolding lies precisely in its eventually being dismantled.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly “lead, accompany, release”? No finished building still has its scaffolding on it. You and I are scaffolding, not the building. There is only one true Architect — “For every house is built by someone; but he who built all things is God.” (Hebrews 3:4)

So what we are building is not “I’m brilliant” but “many people have been equipped.” When you are willing to let others be better than you, the focus is no longer on you, and the glory goes to God. When each generation flourishes more than the last, no “star figures” will emerge in the church; only God’s work and God’s glory will be seen.

Paul puts it with complete simplicity: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7) Planting and watering are real work, but before the fruit of life, the workers are nothing. These words don’t belittle us; they set us free — we can do our very best and then hand the results over to God with peace of mind.

2. Service as a Body: Only Jesus Is the Head

“Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)

Brothers and sisters, read this verse once more. Paul doesn’t say, “You are like the body of Christ”; he says, “you are.” The church is not a stage; the church is a body. The logic of a stage is “who stands in the middle”; the logic of a body is “who is in their originally intended position.”

In a body, no one is the whole; everyone is a part. The eye can’t say, “I have no need for you,” nor can the head say to the feet, “I have no need for you” (1 Corinthians 12:21). Paul even says: “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22) What we think unimportant, God calls necessary.

Science gives us a staggering number. In 2013 Eva Bianconi and fellow researchers at the University of Bologna in Italy published an estimate in the Annals of Human Biology: an adult human body is made up of roughly 37 trillion cells. Thirty-seven trillion cells — not one of them can survive on its own, and not one of them needs to be famous. A heart muscle cell beats billions of times in a lifetime and is never once commended; yet if it stops for a minute, the whole person is gone.

That is the glory of a member of the body: unseen, yet indispensable.

When everyone lives in their place as a member, no one stands out, and no one takes Jesus’ place. Because a body has only one head. “He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” (Ephesians 1:22–23) “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18) The Greek for “head” is κεφαλή (kephalē), which means both the head of a body and a source, a chief. If a body grows a second head, that isn’t double health; it’s a serious disease.

Ephesians spells out the purpose of the fivefold ministry very clearly: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12) Notice that the fivefold ministry is not five ranks but five functions; they exist not to be served but “for the perfecting of the saints.” The measure of a leader’s success is not how much they have done themselves, but how many saints have been equipped, each doing their part.

Modern research on teams confirms this principle too. Google’s “Project Aristotle,” begun in 2012, analysed more than 180 teams to find the common factors behind highly effective ones. It found that the most important factor was not how clever the members were, nor their seniority, but “psychological safety” — a concept put forward in 1999 by Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, meaning that team members dare to admit mistakes and voice different opinions without fear of being humiliated.

Brothers and sisters, what does a team with high psychological safety look like? It’s a place where no one needs to prove their worth by performance. The church ought to be the place with the highest psychological safety in the world, because our worth has already been settled once for all by the cross; we don’t need to earn extra points by fighting for position.

California’s coast redwoods can grow to over 115 metres, the tallest trees on earth. The remarkable thing is that their roots aren’t deep — usually only two or three metres. So why don’t they fall? Because a redwood’s roots spread sideways for dozens of metres, intertwining with the roots of neighbouring trees and linking into a network. A redwood stays standing not because its own roots go deep, but because it has taken hold of the hands beside it. A redwood never grows into a forest on its own.

Brothers and sisters, that is the body. True unity isn’t everyone holding the same opinion; it’s everyone together letting Jesus reign as King.

3. A 321 Insight: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

321 gives us an order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Many teams squabble endlessly because they have turned the order upside down — chasing ministry first, then talking about relationships, and only thinking of life last of all. Once ministry runs ahead of life, people become tools for getting ministry done; and between tools there is only comparison of efficiency, never real love.

Relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. When your relationship with God is right, you know who you are; when you know who you are, you don’t have to scavenge your identity from other people’s opinions; when you don’t have to get your identity from others, you can truly love people; and when you can love people, the work naturally gets done well.

321’s 235 relationships take root right here: become a “2” with a selfless person, so that two people first become genuine spiritual companions; then establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, which is passing on the life through lead, accompany, release; and finally gather into the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together. Brothers and sisters, the “2” can’t be skipped, the “3” can’t be outsourced, and the “5” can’t be rushed. The things of life can’t be hurried.

sections.heading: 5. Entering Kingdom Service and Living Out a Deeper Hiddenness
sections.html:
1. From the Fish Tank to the Ocean

The lesson gives a beautiful contrast. Serve in a small setting and it’s easy to be seen — like a fish tank, where every fish stands out. But when you enter “Kingdom” service, the scope grows, the focus widens, and you are naturally hidden. Just as in the ocean, you are no longer the focus; God is the focus.

Behind this picture lies a real sense of scale. The oceans cover about 71 per cent of the earth’s surface, with an average depth of about 3,700 metres; according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, only about a quarter of the global seabed has so far been mapped precisely at high resolution.

Brothers and sisters, a fish in a tank will think it is very big; put the same fish in the Pacific and it will learn afresh how small it is — and how deep the water is. The wonderful thing is that it won’t live any worse for it; it will live more freely. Fish in a tank have to fight over a tiny patch of water; fish in the ocean don’t need to fight, because the sea is big enough.

A great deal of spiritual rivalry is, frankly, a “fish tank problem”: too few positions, too small a vision, too short a sight, so co-workers turn into competitors. But once your eyes are opened to see how vast God’s Kingdom is — to see the unreached peoples, the next generation, the nations — you’ll find you simply have no time to fight over a tiny patch of ground.

David said: “When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him?” (Psalm 8:3–4) Astronomy tells us that our own galaxy, the Milky Way, alone contains more than a hundred billion stars. Yet the same God who made all this cares for you, and even gave up his only Son for you. Brothers and sisters, when you truly see how great this God is, the question “Was I thanked today?” suddenly becomes very small.

2. Let Go of Owning; Care Only About Giving

One thing is key to Kingdom service: let go of owning, and care only about giving.

It is not building our own territory but building God’s Kingdom; not getting people to remember me but helping people know Jesus.

The “owning” mindset asks: whose disciple is this? Who pioneered this outpost? Whose name is this resource registered under? The “giving” mindset asks only one thing: has God’s Kingdom moved forward?

Paul says: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” (2 Corinthians 4:5) He also says: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Clay jars were the cheapest containers of the day; when they broke, they were thrown away. Paul’s meaning is this: the plainer the container, the more easily people see the treasure inside.

There is a famous example in the Old Testament. Gideon mustered thirty-two thousand men to fight the Midianites, but Yahweh said to him: “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) So God cut the army down to three hundred. God wasn’t afraid of too few people; God was afraid of people boasting. Sometimes when God shrinks our team, it isn’t punishment; it’s protection.

History has communities like this too. On 13 August 1727 the Moravian Brethren at Herrnhut in Germany experienced a profound revival, after which they began a relay of prayer, day and night without a break, that lasted more than a hundred years, and sent hundreds of missionaries to the hardest places, such as the West Indies and Greenland. They often entered the field as labourers and left no name behind. Their motto is generally held to have been: “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.” Their leader, Count Zinzendorf (1700–1760), left a much-loved saying, generally rendered: “I have one passion: it is he, he alone.”

The world of music bears the same witness. Bach (1685–1750) wrote three letters at the end of many of his scores: S.D.G., short for the Latin Soli Deo Gloria, meaning “glory to God alone.” What the world remembers is the great music; what the composer himself remembered was those three letters.

Brothers and sisters, when your service is over, whose name do you sign?

3. The More Hidden, the More God Uses Us

A life like this is a selfless life, a servant’s life, a Kingdom life.

The Lord Jesus said: “But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:11–12) Peter also says: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:5–6)

Notice the words “in due time.” It isn’t that being lifted up will never come; it’s that we don’t get to set the time. Our responsibility is to humble ourselves; God’s responsibility is to lift us up. The moment we rush to lift ourselves up, we take over God’s work — and that is exactly the definition of pride: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God.

In Colossians Paul writes a profoundly deep sentence: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Colossians 3:3) The Greek for “is hidden,” κέκρυπται, is in the perfect tense, describing a state that has been completed and continues in force. Your life hasn’t been hidden away temporarily; it has already been securely stored up in God. That’s why the next verse says: “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory.” (Colossians 3:4)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Now is the season of hiddenness; there is a day coming when we will be revealed with him. Not being seen now isn’t a loss; it’s safe storage. On that day, it won’t be glory we have grabbed, but glory he shares with us.

Business research has noticed a similar pattern. In Good to Great, published in 2001, Jim Collins analysed eleven companies that leapt from mediocrity to excellence and went on beating the market for at least fifteen years. He found that the leaders of these companies had one thing in common, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: a combination of extreme personal humility and intense professional will. When things went well, they looked out of the window and gave the credit to colleagues and good fortune; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took the responsibility on themselves.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research has found that the most lasting fruit comes from the people who least need to be seen. How much more in the Kingdom of God!

4. A 321 Insight: From My Ministry to God’s Kingdom

321 says: we are not building my ministry but building God’s Kingdom; not extending my influence but extending the glory of Jesus; the more hidden we are, the more God uses us.

This is exactly the fourfold shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from the Worldly perspective to God’s perspective.

From man’s perspective, hiddenness is a loss; from God’s perspective, hiddenness is being kept safe.

From an earthly perspective, not being remembered is failure; from a heavenly perspective, the books of heaven never miss a single name.

From a temporary perspective, applause is the reward; from an eternal perspective, applause fades in three minutes.

From the Worldly perspective, influence is an asset; from God’s perspective, influence that doesn’t point to Christ is a liability.

The Hebrew for “glory” is כָּבוֹד (kavod), whose root meaning is “weight, heaviness.” True glory is something with weight — not atmosphere, not volume, not view counts. Human praise is light; a gust of wind blows it away. God’s glory is heavy — so heavy that Moses could not enter the Tent of Meeting, so heavy that when the cloud came, the whole mountain fell silent.

Brothers and sisters, don’t trade the heavy for the light.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson is the second talk on “the Path of Serving — God.” The Path of Serving has five steps: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

“Spirit” is: the Holy Spirit is my guide; “Understanding” is: the Bible is my standard; “Life” is: Jesus is my role model; “Service” is: let Jesus be King; “God” is: let Jesus receive all the glory. At the last step, everything is gathered up into one sentence — seeing no one but Jesus.

The Three Foundations all appear together on the Mount of Transfiguration: Jesus is my role model, because he emptied himself and was obedient to death; the Bible is my standard, because the Father said, “Listen to him,” not to our own plans; the Holy Spirit is my guide, because that bright cloud is the very sign of God’s presence — human arrangements must stop for God’s guidance to become clear.

The Two Core Values are revealed here too: let Jesus be King — only One is left on the stage; let Jesus receive all the glory — the glory need not be split three ways, and cannot be.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Here lies the difference between God’s system and a human system: a human system needs stars to hold it up, and when the star leaves, the system collapses; God’s system runs on life being passed on, generation after generation taking up the baton — no one is irreplaceable, and yet no one is superfluous.

Look again at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. So the starting point of this lesson isn’t “I’ll start keeping a lower profile,” but “my mindset about glory must be turned upside down.” When you truly believe that glory can go to only One, your life will loosen; when your life loosens, your daily living will grow quiet; when your daily living grows quiet, your relationships will be restored; and when your relationships are restored, your ministry will truly carry God’s presence.

321’s 920 practice is put into practice here too: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” In every “2” relationship, we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that not one fruit of the Spirit is “being seen.” Fruit by its nature is for others to eat; no tree eats its own fruit.

Finally, focus. 321 says: the focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances. Focus on ourselves and we become proud or insecure; focus on others and we compare or envy; focus on circumstances and we worry or complain. Focus on Jesus and we have peace. The moment the disciples lifted their eyes, God himself brought their focus into alignment — “they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”

And one more thing to keep in your heart: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart, rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down. Peter’s proposal to put up tents was a classic case of “relying on the brain and ourselves” — he was trying hard, and he was full of zeal, but his plan interrupted God’s work. Brothers and sisters, what wears us out most in service isn’t having too much to do; it’s using our own brains to write God’s script for him.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Living a Life That Sees “No One but Jesus”
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Deliberately Turn the Focus from Yourself to Jesus

In any service, sharing or testimony, mention yourself less and Jesus more. Let what people remember be what God has done and how God works.

Information: first memorise this verse — “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.” (Psalm 115:1)

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you and show you which of your words, when you share, are really scoring points for yourself.

Conviction: admit before God that the glory was never mine in the first place. “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

Implementation: this week, before you give any testimony, first ask yourself one question: “Do I want people to remember me, or God?” Afterwards, check the subjects of your sentences — how many have “I” as the subject, and how many have “God”?

Evaluation: in the evening, be still for three minutes and recall whether there was a moment today when you quietly wanted to be praised.

Correction: not self-reproach, but adjustment. Say that sentence again in your heart, this time with God as the subject.

Repetition: practise it for twenty-one days in a row. Doing it once isn’t practice; only repetition is practice.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion, share this practice with them, and remind each other.

Practice 2: Practise “Not Grabbing Position”

In a team, don’t fight for credit, don’t talk over others, don’t force yourself to the front; learn to let others be equipped and let others be seen. The more you let go, the more God lifts you up.

Information: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

Revelation: ask God to show you the setting in which you most easily “can’t help putting in a word.” Is it in meetings? In the group chat? Or when someone else is being praised?

Conviction: believe that God’s record is more accurate than man’s. Nothing hidden goes unseen by God.

Implementation: this week, at every gathering or meeting, deliberately do three things — let others finish speaking first; actively give a piece of credit to someone else out loud; and take one area of service you’d really like to have and, after prayer, give it to another brother or sister.

Evaluation: did you feel uncomfortable inside at that moment? The place where you feel uncomfortable is the place where God wants to work.

Correction: take the discomfort into prayer, not out on people.

Repetition: let “giving way” become your reflex rather than your moral effort.

Multiplication: when you see someone on the team willing to step back, affirm them publicly. Humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Practice 3: Step Actively into Passing On the Life — Lead, Accompany, Release

Don’t just do tasks; start bringing people along. Lead people, accompany people, release people. Let life multiply continually, so that the focus is no longer concentrated on you but spreads out to many more people, and finally goes to Jesus.

Information: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Revelation: ask God to show you a name — the person God wants you to lead.

Conviction: believe that you have something to give. You don’t have to wait until you’re perfect to start passing it on.

Implementation: this month, arrange to meet that person once. In the first quarter, “lead” — lead them in reading the Bible, lead them in prayer; in the second quarter, “accompany” — let them start doing it, with you beside them; in the third quarter, “release” — let them lead on their own, while you simply pray behind the scenes.

Evaluation: when you “release,” do you breathe a sigh of relief, or feel a sense of loss? See your own heart honestly.

Correction: if you feel loss, go back to the cross and hand over your sense of “ownership” once again.

Repetition: when you’ve led one, lead the next. Passing on the life isn’t an event; it’s a way of life.

Multiplication: teach the one you lead to go and lead someone too. On that day you’ll find the focus has spread out, and only Jesus is lifted high.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please keep these few sentences in your heart:

Don’t be afraid of being overlooked; that is God protecting you.

Don’t be in a hurry to be seen; that may become a temptation.

True safety is being hidden in the glory of God.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
