sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the highest place service can reach is not how much influence you have, but how much influence you let Jesus have.

When people can’t see you but see Jesus, that is the most glorious service of all.

Let’s go back to that mountain once more. When the disciples went up, they saw three people; when they came down, they recognised only One. They hadn’t lost anything; they had been brought into focus. Moses and Elijah were not rejected; all their life’s work was fulfilled in that One — just as our service won’t disappear, but will be gathered up into Christ.

The Lord Jesus said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32) Brothers and sisters, he is the one lifted up; all people are the ones drawn. Our responsibility is very simple: don’t stand in the way.

So let us walk the road of “Spirit — Understanding — Life — Service — God”: let the Holy Spirit guide us, let the Bible be our standard, let Jesus be our role model, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Without stopping, without straying.

Until one day the tents come down, the cloud lifts, and all the applause has passed; we lift our eyes and see no one but Jesus — and then we will see the Lord’s face with our own eyes.

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:2)

Brothers and sisters, lift your eyes today. Take your eyes off yourself, off others, off your circumstances, and fix them on him alone. Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory!

keyVerses: While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone. (Matthew 17:5–8)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to hide myself and exalt you.
I no longer pursue being seen; I long only for you to be exalted.
I declare: no one but Jesus; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; all glory goes to you!
May my life be a sign pointing to you! In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Deliberately turn the focus from yourself to Jesus
Practise “not grabbing position”
Step actively into passing on the life — lead, accompany, release
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Though you existed in the form of God, you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant; you came down from the highest place in order to bring us to the highest place. Yet Lord, we so often do the opposite — trying to climb from low places to high ones, wanting to be seen, affirmed and remembered.

Lord, forgive our self-centred life; forgive us for quietly taking your glory for ourselves in our service. Today we take down the three tents; we will no longer set you side by side with anyone else; we give the centre of the stage back to you.

Give us hearts that are willing to be hidden: not fighting for credit in our teams, not talking over others in our relationships, and in passing on the life, gladly letting others be better than us. Help us to lead people, accompany people and release people, so that life keeps on multiplying.

Holy Spirit, guide us, so that we rely on the heart and not the brain, on you and not on ourselves. Make our lives a finger that points accurately to you; make us a moon that quietly reflects your light.
May our families, our fellowship and our church all become God’s system; and may those who come among us see no one but Jesus.
All glory, praise and power be yours, for ever and ever.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Matthew 17:4–5: “Peter answered, and said to Jesus, ‘Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’ While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” Please share: Peter wanted to make three tents, putting Jesus alongside Moses and Elijah; yet the Father said, “Listen to him.” In your serving, have there been times when you, too, quietly wanted to “make a tent” for yourself and be seen? How can people come to see “no one but Jesus”?

2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” Please share: who is the one person God wants you to lead? Of the three steps — lead, accompany, release — which one can you take first this month? What is the biggest obstacle in your heart?

l170.subtitle: The Path of Serving — God (Part 2)
l170.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Secret of a Life That Never Drifts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today is the final lesson of our 321 Morning Devotion series. Having come this far, I have a question in my heart, and perhaps it is the very question in yours: how can a person walk in God’s way for a whole lifetime — without drifting, without drying up, without falling?

This isn’t a theoretical question. It is an intensely practical one. We have all seen people like this: when they first came to faith they were on fire, never missed a meeting, and their faces shone as they gave their testimony. But three years, five years, ten years go by, and they are gone; or they are still here, but their hearts have gone cold. There is another kind of person: they know the Bible better than anyone, they explain doctrine more clearly than anyone, yet their life is parched, their family can’t stand them, and neither can their co-workers. And there is yet another kind: run off their feet in ministry, carrying everything on their own shoulders, until in the end they collapse in the middle of their serving, complaining even as they work.

In aviation there is a piece of simple geometry: if an aircraft’s heading is off by a single degree, then after flying a hundred kilometres it will land about 1.7 kilometres off course; after a thousand kilometres, more than seventeen kilometres off. At the moment of take-off, one degree is almost invisible; but the further you fly, the more deadly that one degree becomes. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is just the same. We rarely leave God overnight. We all drift away one degree at a time.

So is there a way that lets us correct our heading every day, and come back to the centre line every day? There is. The answer lies in five words:

Spirit — Understanding — Life — Service — God.

Please notice: these are not five stages, as though once you have passed through the first you can leave it behind. This is a road of life that goes round and round, without end. It isn’t enough to have walked it once; we walk it every single day. From the first day we believe until the day we see the Lord face to face, we are to keep living on this road.

And at the heart of this road there is one key, and only one: selflessness.

Please remember this sentence: live the self-centred life, and there is no road; live selflessly, and there is a road.

Why? Because the Lord Jesus himself said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me” (John 14:6). The road isn’t something I carve out; the road is the person of Jesus. So when “self” stands tall in the middle, Jesus is pushed to the side, and I have no road; when “self” steps back and Jesus steps up, I am walking on the road. Selflessness isn’t erasing yourself into nothingness; selflessness is coming out of your limited self and entering into the limitless Christ. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

This morning we are going to walk this road together, from start to finish: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. And when we have walked it, I want to invite you to walk it every day, starting tomorrow morning.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Romans — Its Author, Its Readers and Its Setting
sections.html:
Our theme passage today comes from Romans. Romans was written by the apostle Paul, generally dated to around AD 56–57, in Corinth, just as Paul’s third missionary journey was drawing to a close and he was preparing to take the collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26). He was writing to the church in Rome, a group of believers he had never yet met (Romans 1:10–13).

The setting of this letter is remarkable. Rome was the capital of the world at that time, the centre of power, wealth, law and idols. The Roman church had believers from a Jewish background and believers from a Gentile background. The Jewish believers carried the tradition of the law and were prone to boast in works and in tradition; the Gentile believers carried the thinking of Greco-Roman culture and were easily bound by the passions of the flesh and the values of the world. In AD 49 the Emperor Claudius ordered the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2); a few years later they began to return, and you can imagine the tension between old and new in the church. Paul wrote this letter to set the foundation of the gospel, the grace of justification and the way of sanctification firmly and clearly in their midst.

The structure of Romans is very clear. Chapters 1 to 3 deal with human sin and God’s judgement — Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin. Chapters 4 to 5 deal with the grace of justification by faith — how Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and how we too have peace with God through the Lord Jesus. Chapters 6 to 8 deal with the sanctified life — dying and rising with Christ, being freed from the power of sin, living under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Chapters 9 to 11 deal with God’s plan for Israel. From chapter 12 onward come practical daily living and service.

Our theme passage falls right in chapter 8. Romans 7 ends with a cry of despair: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24). Paul describes a real struggle: the will to do good is there, but the power to carry it out is not. Then, as chapter 8 opens, the day breaks: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Paul goes on to explain: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death” (Romans 8:2).

In other words, the failure of chapter 7 is the failure of “keeping the law by my own effort”; the victory of chapter 8 is the victory of “living out life by the Holy Spirit”. That is exactly where the word “Spirit” stands — it is the starting point of the whole road. Straight after this, in Romans 8:5–6, Paul sets two roads before us: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:5–6).

And Romans 12:2 is where chapter 8 lands in practice. With the word “therefore”, Paul ties doctrine to daily living: since God’s mercies are so great, we should present our bodies as a living sacrifice; we should not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of our mind. “The renewing of your mind” is precisely “Understanding”; “presenting your bodies” is precisely “Life”; “having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith; or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching; or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Romans 12:6–8) is precisely “Service”. And at the very end of Romans, Paul lifts his voice: “to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen” (Romans 16:27) — and that is precisely “God”.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God is not a slogan we invented. It is the direction Romans itself travels, and the direction of the whole Bible.

sections.heading: 3. The First Station, “Spirit”: The Holy Spirit is my guide
sections.html:
“For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).

The starting point of life is not in what we do, but in “choosing whom to follow”.

The word Paul uses here for “mind” is the Greek noun phronēma, from the verb phroneō used in verse 5, meaning “to think on, to set one’s purpose, the orientation of one’s thoughts”. It isn’t an occasional passing thought; it is the habitual direction of a person’s mind, like the needle of a compass that always points the same way. So what this verse is really asking is this: where does your heart habitually face? Towards the flesh, or towards the Spirit?

Notice Paul’s choice of words. He does not say the mind of the flesh “will lead to death”; he says it “is death”. That is not a future punishment; it is a present condition. Someone whose mind habitually faces towards themselves is already living, right now, with the smell of death about them: strained relationships, an unquiet heart, nothing seeming worthwhile. Conversely, “the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” — and that too is not a future reward, but something we can taste right now: living water welling up within, and harmony between people.

“Spirit” means this: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

This is the third of the Three Foundations of 321. What does it mean to be guided by the Holy Spirit? Not relying on our own cleverness, not relying on past experience, but at every moment asking one question: what does the Holy Spirit want me to do?

Scripture says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” (Romans 8:14). And again: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). The Lord Jesus promised: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). The word “guide” in Greek is hodēgeō, which literally means “to lead the way, to lead someone along a road”; within it is the root hodos, “road”. Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit is not a consultant sitting in the passenger seat offering suggestions; he is the guide who goes ahead and leads the way.

Here is a mistake we often make: we treat the Holy Spirit’s guidance as something needed only at the big moments. We pray about changing jobs, we pray about getting married, we pray about buying a house; but how to say the first words to our spouse this morning, how to reply to that infuriating email at the office, whether to spend those two hours scrolling on our phone tonight — those we decide for ourselves. And the result? We seek God on the big things, yet drift one degree on countless small ones. Aircraft don’t crash in the big turns; they fly into the mountain through one small degree of drift after another.

Let me use an everyday picture. These days almost everyone drives with satnav. The value of satnav isn’t that it knows the destination — you know the destination yourself. Its value is that it recalculates your position every second, and the moment you go off course it says at once, “Please make a U-turn ahead.” The Holy Spirit is like that. He doesn’t just hand you a map at the start; he speaks up at every junction. The trouble is that much of the time we mute the satnav, because we think we know the way. Scripture warns us very seriously: “Don’t quench the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19); “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). Turn off the sound, and the road is still there — but we can no longer hear.

Psychology has a related observation. In a study published in 1994 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologists Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec found that when people look back over their lives, their deepest regrets are mostly not about “what I did wrong” but about “what I never did”. Brothers and sisters, the deepest regret of the spiritual life is often not some great fall either, but the many times when “the Holy Spirit prompted me and I didn’t respond”. That phone call never made, that apology never spoken, that person never visited. How precious the Holy Spirit’s guidance is — yet the chance to obey does not wait for us for ever.

Look at another passage: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6). Notice “in all your ways” — not the important ones, all of them. This is what 321 means when it says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll fret, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Where does the 321 vision apply here? In a change of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one. Not living by feelings, but living by the Holy Spirit. Brothers and sisters, this morning, as you leave this devotion, please take the first question with you: at this very moment, what does the Holy Spirit want me to do?

sections.heading: 4. The Second Station, “Understanding”: The Bible is my standard
sections.html:
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

The Holy Spirit leads us into truth, and truth renews our mindset. “Understanding” means this: the Bible is my standard. This is the second of the Three Foundations of 321.

In this verse Paul uses two sharply contrasting verbs. “Conformed” is the Greek syschēmatizō, from the root schēma, meaning an outward shape or pattern; it means “to be pressed into the same mould as what is outside”. “Transformed” is the Greek metamorphoō, from the root morphē, meaning essential form; this is the very word used in the Gospels when the Lord Jesus was “transfigured” on the mountain (Matthew 17:2), and the word used in 2 Corinthians 3:18 for being “transformed into the same image”. Put the two words together and Paul’s meaning is perfectly clear: don’t let the world press you from the outside into its shape; let the word of God change you from the inside into a different life.

Even more crucial is “the renewing of your mind”. “Mind” in Greek is nous: a person’s thinking, their mindset, the way their mind works. Paul does not say “be transformed by the renewing of your behaviour”; he says “by the renewing of your mind”. This is precisely the starting point of the fivefold change that 321 emphasises: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Change doesn’t begin with gritting your teeth; change begins with a new way of thinking.

Why does mindset matter so much? Because mindset is the pair of glasses through which we see the world. If the lenses are skewed, everything we see is skewed. Take an example. Someone who is convinced deep down that “I only have worth if people notice me” walks into church, sees someone else being praised, and feels a pang of envy. Someone who is convinced deep down that “my worth has already been settled in Christ” sees someone else being praised and is glad. The same event, two reactions; the difference lies not in the event but in the mindset.

On this point, modern psychology is actually writing footnotes to the Bible. In the 1960s the American psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy, whose central finding is that what causes people pain is often not the event itself but their automatic thoughts and core beliefs about the event; when the core beliefs are corrected, emotions and behaviour change with them. Decades of research by the Stanford psychology professor Carol Dweck likewise show that whether a person holds a “fixed mindset” or a “growth mindset” significantly affects how they respond to failure and how they perform afterwards. Brothers and sisters, if even the world’s learning admits that mindset shapes a life, how much more the word of God! “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12).

But please hear this clearly: the Bible is to be our standard, not our decoration. A standard means this — when my thinking differs from the Bible, I am the one who is wrong. Many people read the Bible looking for verses that back them up. That is not taking the Bible as the standard; that is taking ourselves as the standard and treating the Bible as supplementary material. The attitude of letting Scripture interpret Scripture is the opposite: I place myself under the text and let the text judge my mindset. “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). “Reproof” and “correction” both mean being set right by the Bible. Someone who has never been set right by the word of God will never have a truly renewed mindset.

“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). Brothers and sisters, a lamp lights only the step in front of your feet. God seldom lights the whole road for us at once; he gives us light for today’s step. So “Understanding” has to be daily, not once and done.

One thing deserves special mention here: Spirit and Understanding must be bound together. With the Holy Spirit’s promptings but without the Bible as our standard, we can easily mistake our own emotions for the voice of God; with knowledge of the Bible but without the Holy Spirit’s illumination, we can easily turn truth into a club to beat people with. The Lord Jesus said, “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). Spirit and truth have never been an either-or.

Applying the 321 vision: not living by feelings, but by the Holy Spirit; not following my own ideas, but God’s truth. From an earthly perspective into a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective into an eternal one. This morning, please take the second question with you: what does the Bible say about this thought of mine?

sections.heading: 5. The Third Station, “Life”: Jesus is my role model
sections.html:
Once we have “Spirit” and “Understanding”, the next step is not to stop at “knowing”, but to go on into “living it out”. This is “Life” — Jesus is my role model. This is the first of the Three Foundations of 321.

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23) — and the Chinese Union Version, with many other translations, reads “take up his cross daily”. Notice the three things the Lord says: deny yourself, daily, take up the cross. “Deny” in Greek is aparneomai, meaning “to disown, to refuse to acknowledge, to draw a clear line between oneself and something”; when Peter three times “denied” the Lord, this is exactly the word used. So denying of self is not self-torment. Denying of self is saying to the old self that wants to be king: I don’t know you; you are not my master.

Even more crucial is “daily”. The Lord did not say “take it up once”; he said “take it up daily”. That is exactly what the lesson text says: these are not five stages, but a road of life that goes round and round, without end.

So where does denying of self happen? In five small things every day: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.

What do we see? Wherever the eyes land, the heart follows. Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1). What do we listen to? Whatever the ears feed on, the heart grows into. What do we think about? “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). What do we speak? “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). What do we do? “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Brothers and sisters, seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing — these five actions we perform hundreds, even thousands, of times a day. Every single time is a choice: for myself, or for Jesus? As you choose, time after time, to deny yourself, time after time you live out a selfless life.

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, the University College London psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed ninety-six participants and found that the median time for a new habit to become automatic was about sixty-six days, with wide individual variation, ranging from eighteen days to two hundred and fifty-four. These figures give us two reminders. First, don’t assume that because a few days of practice brought no change you have failed; changing a life simply takes repetition. Second, what truly changes people has never been one great decision, but small choices, day after day.

But there is a vitally important distinction here: “Life” is not imitation; it is letting Jesus live himself out.

Imitation is me copying his ways from the outside, and that will wear you out. Letting Jesus live himself out is him living out his own life from within. Paul could not have said it more clearly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). The Lord Jesus also said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch doesn’t need to imitate a grape; a branch only needs to stay joined to the vine.

This is what 321 means when it says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living that fullness out. When a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, that is not the end; “if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). This morning, please take the third question with you: in this act of seeing, listening, thinking, speaking or doing, am I doing it for myself, or for Jesus?

sections.heading: 6. The Fourth Station, “Service”: Let Jesus be King
sections.html:
Having come this far, we enter “Service” — let Jesus be King. This is the first of the Two Core Values of 321.

Serving is not me doing the work; it is Jesus doing the work in me. To put it in one sentence: I step back, and Jesus steps up.

John the Baptist is the finest role model here. When his disciples came running to report that everyone was going to Jesus, John was not anxious. He said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The Greek of this sentence is vividly pictorial: one is to rise, the other is to go down. Brothers and sisters, the hardest lesson in serving is often not whether we can do it, but whether we are willing to go down.

Paul also said, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). Notice the order here: we preach Jesus as “Lord”, and ourselves as everyone’s “servants”. Who is master and who is servant — once that gets reversed, serving immediately becomes a heavy burden.

Serving in which Jesus is King carries three marks. First, there is power in the serving — “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6). Second, there is fruit in the serving — “He who remains in me … bears much fruit” (John 15:5). Third, there is life in the serving — because it isn’t something I squeeze out of myself; it is something he supplies.

Conversely, when “I” am king, serving can end in only three ways: exhaustion, resentment, collapse. In the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, adopted in 2019, the World Health Organization listed “burn-out” as an occupational phenomenon and described its three features: energy depletion; mental distance from one’s job, with negative feelings towards it; and reduced professional efficacy. Brothers and sisters, these three features are no strangers to us in the serving of the church. Why do we burn out? Often it isn’t because we do too much, but because while we are doing it, the sovereignty is in our own hands. If the sovereignty is mine, all the responsibility is mine; if all the responsibility is mine, the burden crushes me.

What does the Lord Jesus say? “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). Notice, the Lord didn’t say “take the yoke off”; he said “take my yoke upon you”. A yoke is carried by two oxen together. What the Lord means is: don’t pull the cart on your own; come and share one yoke with me — I go in front, and you follow me.

This is what 321 means when it says: it is not I who live, but Christ who lives in me; it is not I who serve, but Jesus who serves. It is also the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. How many church conflicts have come from turning this order upside down — crushing “people” in order to get the “task” done well!

This morning, please take the fourth question with you: in this piece of service, am I asking, “How am I going to do it?” or am I asking, “Lord, how do you want to do it?”

sections.heading: 7. The Fifth Station, “God”: Let Jesus receive all the glory
sections.html:
The final key is “God” — let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the second of the Two Core Values of 321.

Brothers and sisters, many people reach “Service” and stop there, overlooking the last and most important step. Why is this step the most important? Because without “God”, the four stations before it will turn round and harm us: we will grow proud, we will snatch the glory, and we will fall.

This is no scaremongering; Scripture records it in blood. Herod Agrippa I put on his royal robes, sat on his throne and made a speech to the people, and the people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” The result: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died” (Acts 12:23). Notice the wording of the text: it was not because he spoke blasphemy, but “because he didn’t give God the glory”. The moment a person takes the glory for himself, he is finished.

So it was with Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Walking on the roof of his palace, he said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” While the word was still in his mouth, a voice came from heaven (Daniel 4:30–31). He was driven away from people, until the day he lifted his eyes to heaven and blessed the Most High, and his reason returned to him. And the source of all pride was written long before, in Isaiah: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Five times “I will” — that is the complete portrait of the self-centred life.

Why does God set such store by glory? Not because he is short of applause, but because glory belongs to him in the first place. “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images” (Isaiah 42:8). When a creature snatches the Creator’s glory, it is not merely bad manners; it is leaving our originally intended position. 321 puts it exactly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

But when a person truly sees that everything is grace, that everything is God’s doing, he will naturally live in humility. The key word here is “naturally”. True humility is not forced down; it is not hurriedly saying “Oh, it was nothing” when someone praises you. True humility is how we respond once we have seen the truth. Paul says, “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). If someone truly thinks it through — their mind, their health, their family, their opportunities, their gifts: which of these did they not receive? — how could they possibly be proud?

A series of studies by the University of California, Berkeley psychologist Dacher Keltner and his colleagues found that when people experience “awe” — facing something vast that far exceeds themselves — what is called the “small-self effect” appears: their sense of self shrinks relatively, and at the same time they become more willing to help others and value the group more. An experiment by Paul Piff, Keltner and others, published in 2015 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, observed that awe increases prosocial behaviour. Brothers and sisters, this confirms one thing from the other side: people become arrogant so often because what they see is too small. When we truly see the greatness of God, the “I” naturally shrinks back to its proper size. So worship is not an emotional activity; worship is a recalibration — putting God back at the centre, and putting me back in my originally intended position.

The Lord Jesus’ whole life is our role model: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:6–9). He humbled himself to the uttermost, and in the end received all the glory. And the end of this passage states the purpose: “that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

This is our road too: humility, and then being lifted up by God. “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). And “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan; pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

This morning, please take the fifth question with you: when this thing succeeds, is my first thought “I did it” — or “Thank you, Lord”?

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder: Don’t Stop at Any Station
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us a very precise reminder. Each of the five stations on this road is indispensable:

Only Spirit, and you will drift. There are promptings, feelings and tears, but no anchor of truth; today you are moved by this message, tomorrow you are carried off by that trend, like a ship that has never dropped anchor.

Only Understanding, and you will dry up. You know the Bible well, your theology is clear, you have doctrine down to a system, but without the Holy Spirit’s refreshing, knowledge puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1), and you become hard and cold.

Only Life, and you will stall. You practise denying yourself every day, and your life really is changing, yet you won’t come out and serve; your gifts stay buried in the ground, and all your life you care only for your own spirituality.

Only Service, and you will burn out. One task after another, one meeting after another, but with no supply of life, until in the end you have worn yourself dry and made life bitter for those around you too.

Without God, you will certainly fall. Everything before it is in place, the fruit has appeared, people’s praise has followed; but if you don’t give the glory back, that very fruit becomes the stone you stumble over.

So keep walking the whole road of “Spirit — Understanding — Life — Service — God”. Brothers and sisters, these five stations are not five legs of a journey; they are one circle to be completed every day. Walk it today, and walk it again tomorrow; walk it tomorrow, and walk it again the day after — until the day we see the Lord face to face.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let us set this lesson back into the whole picture of 321. You will find that “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God” is simply another way of saying 321.

Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide” among the Three Foundations; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”. Service is “let Jesus be King” among the Two Core Values; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”. And what walking this road accomplishes is the Goal: establish God’s system.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal — they turn out to be one road. 321 doesn’t want us to memorise five terms; 321 wants us to walk one road.

The driving force of this road is selflessness. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Live the self-centred life, and there is no road; live selflessly, and there is a road. For the road is Jesus himself. When I put myself in the middle, I block the road; when I step aside, the road opens up beneath my feet.

The order of this road is life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fivefold change is a chain, each link joined to the next: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. You see, “Understanding” is changing our mindset; “Life” is changing our life and daily living; “Service” is changing our relationships and ministry; and “God” keeps all of it from going bad. To skip what comes first and go straight to ministry is to build a house on sand.

The practice of this road is 920. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When we practise living out the selfless “0” before them, the “9” — the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — grow: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, please notice: the fruit isn’t something we squeeze out; the fruit is borne by the Holy Spirit. All we have to do is move the “self” out of the way and give the Holy Spirit room.

The companionship of this road is 235. Become a “2” with someone who is selfless, each a spiritual companion to the other; build the “3”, having spiritual parents and spiritual children too; and finally become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades (Ephesians 4:11–12). This road is long; no one can walk it alone. “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor” (Ecclesiastes 4:9).

The perspective of this road is four shifts: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the Worldly system to God’s system.

And the destination of this road is not our success, but the fulfilment of the Lord’s Prayer: “May your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:9–10).

sections.heading: 10. Putting It into Practice: Walking the Road of Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service and God Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us five “every days”. Let us use the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to practise them thoroughly and solidly.

First, begin every day with “Spirit”. Ask yourself each day: today, am I following the Holy Spirit, or following myself? Learn to heed the Holy Spirit’s promptings in every decision. How, in concrete terms? When you open your eyes in the morning, don’t let your first words be “What am I going to do today?” but “Lord, what do you want me to do today?”

Second, use “Understanding” every day to adjust your mindset. Through the word of God, correct your thinking, renew your mindset and align yourself with the truth; don’t let old mindsets run your life. How, in concrete terms? When you read the Bible, ask one more question: which of my thoughts does this passage want to change?

Third, practise denying of self every day in your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Choose deliberately: not for myself, but for Jesus and for others. How, in concrete terms? Each day, pick the area where you most easily give way — perhaps your tongue, perhaps your eyes — and ask the Lord for victory in that very area.

Fourth, let Jesus be King in your serving every day. Don’t ask, “How am I going to do it?” Ask, “Lord, how do you want to do it?” Hand the sovereignty over to Jesus. How, in concrete terms? Before every meeting, every visit, every small group you lead, be still for thirty seconds and lay your crown at the Lord’s feet first.

Fifth, give all the glory to God every day. Whether you succeed or fail, declare: it is all grace; all the glory goes to God. Let your heart stay humble. How, in concrete terms? Before you sleep, count three graces from that day, and name them one by one in thanksgiving.

Now let us lay the eight stages over this. Information: today you have heard these five words, “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God” — that is Information. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to drive one of these words into your heart, so that it becomes something you truly see today — that is Revelation. Conviction: not merely thinking it makes sense, but being willing to say, “Lord, I yield” — that is Conviction. Implementation: begin those five “every days” tomorrow morning — that is Implementation. Evaluation: spend three minutes in the evening looking back — which station did I walk steadily today, which did I miss? — that is Evaluation. Correction: give special attention tomorrow to the station you missed — that is Correction. Repetition: don’t do it for just three days; do it for sixty-six days, for six hundred days, until it becomes as natural as breathing — that is Repetition. Multiplication: bring this road to your “2”, to your spiritual children, so that they step onto it too — that is Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, the first seven stages are about us receiving; the eighth is about others receiving. A road walked by you alone is a footpath; when thousands upon thousands walk it, it becomes a highway.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this road is not a sprint; it is a marathon.

A full marathon is 42.195 kilometres. Anyone who has run one knows that the hardest part is not the start, but “hitting the wall” at around thirty kilometres — the glycogen in the body is almost exhausted, the legs feel as if they have been filled with lead, and at that moment what keeps a runner going is no longer stamina, but will and goal. The spiritual road is the same. It isn’t a moment of fervour; it is a lifetime of following.

Scripture uses exactly the picture of a race to describe this road: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2). Notice two things. First, we are to lay aside every weight — that is selflessness. Second, we are to look to Jesus — that is “Jesus is the focal point, not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances”.

As you keep walking the road of “Spirit — Understanding — Life — Service — God”, what will happen? “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). You will become more and more like Jesus: more and more full of life, more and more full of power, more and more full of joy, more and more full of glory.

At the end of his life Paul said, “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). Brothers and sisters, may each one of us, one day, be able to say the same.

And the promise at the final station is this: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). Overcoming together with the Lord, reigning together with the Lord.

This is the final lesson of the 321 Morning Devotion series — but it is not the end; it is the starting line. This morning I want to invite you to make a decision: from today on, walk Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God once through every day. Don’t aim to walk fast; aim never to stop. For “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord Jesus, I am willing to walk in your way all my life.
I choose to set my mind on the Spirit and live out life;
I choose to align with the truth and renew my mindset;
I choose to follow Jesus’ example and live out selflessness;
I choose to let the Lord be King and bring forth service;
I choose to give all the glory to God.
I will walk the road of “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God” all my life, until the day I see your face. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: Begin every day with “Spirit”.
Use “Understanding” every day to adjust your mindset.
Practise denying of self every day in seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.
Let Jesus be King in your serving every day.
Give all the glory to God every day.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You said that you are the way, so we no longer have to find the way ourselves.

Lord, forgive us for these many days we have so often walked by our own cleverness, by our past experience, by what others think of us. Please take away the “self” within us, for in the self-centred life there is no road, but in selflessness there is a road.

Holy Spirit, be our guide today, so that in every matter, great or small, we ask you first; may your word be our standard, renewing our mindset day by day; Lord Jesus, be our role model, so that in our seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing we choose, time after time, to deny ourselves; reign as King in our serving, so that we step back and you step up; and guard our hearts, so that whether we succeed or fail, we give all the glory to you.
Lord, this road is a marathon; we do not ask to run fast, but to run to the end. Walk with us until the day we see your face.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!

May the Lord’s blessing come upon every brother and sister: “Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26).
discussion: Of the five stations, “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God”, which one do you feel you are walking most steadily at the moment? Which is the one you most easily miss? Please share something specific that happened recently. Scripture: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).

In your present service or work, what is the one thing you have kept holding in your own hands and have not yet truly handed over for the Lord to be King over? How do you plan to hand it over this week? Scripture: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).
